# INTRODUCTION

**IN** introducing the first volume of S'ārngadeva's <term>Ocean of Music <note>original: "Saṅgītaratnākara"</note></term>, containing the first <term>chapter <note>original: "adhyāya"</note></term>, along with the two commentaries, namely, Kallinātha's <term>Treasure of Art <note>original: "Kalānidhi"</note></term> and Siṃhabhūpāla's <term>Moon-light <note>original: "Sudhākara"</note></term>, my first duty is to record the gratitude of the Adyar Library to that great scholar, the late Pandit S. Subrahmanya Sastri, who undertook the edition of this important work. He had corrected the entire material for all the seven chapters of the work for the press and the first chapter was completely printed before his death. In the normal course, this Introduction would have come from his pen. Having regard to his solid erudition, his profound knowledge of music both on the practical and the theoretical side, his wide reading, his deep insight into subjects allied to music like dancing, I must confess that the present Introduction is only a poor substitute for what could have been expected from him.

The *Ocean of Music* of S'ārngadeva is one of the most important works on music now available. It is besides, one of the longest works on music in Sanskrit. It is a very comprehensive exposition of the subject, dealing with all aspects. Ever since it was written it has remained the standard work on music; it has been

<summary>This introductory page acknowledges the late Pandit S. Subrahmanya Sastri for his editorial work on S'ārngadeva's Saṅgītaratnākara and establishes the text's significance as a comprehensive Sanskrit authority on music.</summary>
<keywords>S'ārngadeva, Saṅgītaratnākara, music theory, Sanskrit literature, Adyar Library, S. Subrahmanya Sastri, Kallinātha, Siṃhabhūpāla</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion regarding the publication history and manuscript sources of the Saṅgītaratnākara, specifically focusing on previous attempts at complete editions and the commentaries used by earlier scholars.</meta>

<page-num>VI</page-num>

drawn upon profusely, as authority, by all subsequent writers on the subject. Perhaps it has superseded many earlier works and obscured them, and they have disappeared from the field. But it has never been superseded till now.

A complete edition of the work was undertaken by Kalīvara Vedāntavāgiśa and Śārada Prasāda Ghosha from Calcutta with the commentary of Siṃhabhūpāla <note>Siṃhabhūpāla was a 14th-century king and scholar who wrote the 'Sudhākara' commentary on this musical treatise.</note> some time back, and the first volume containing the <term>Svarādhyāya</term> <note>The first chapter of the text, focusing on notes and sound.</note> was published in 1879 from the New Arya Press, Calcutta.¹ In the Preface to that edition,² it had been promised that the remaining portions too would be published, but it does not seem that any further progress had been made in that direction. At that time they had access only to a very defective copy of the commentary of Kallinātha <note>A 15th-century commentator known for his exhaustive explanations of musical theory.</note>, which, as they say, was “very unintelligible, owing to numerous clerical mistakes.”³ As for Siṃhabhūpāla’s commentary appearing in this edition, there is no indication of the source of the manuscripts. The Preface does not mention the point at all. Evidently they must have had access to a complete copy, since they had projected a complete edition. The manuscripts known to us and utilised for this edition will be noticed in the course of this introduction.

The text of <term>Saṅgītaratnākara</term> <note>Literally "The Ocean of Music," a foundational 13th-century Sanskrit text on Indian music and dance.</note> with the commentary of Kallinātha has been edited in the Anandasrama <note>A famous research institute and publishing house in Pune known for its collection of Sanskrit manuscripts.</note>

<page-num>VII</page-num>

Sanskrit Series as Number 35 in 1896 <note>original: "In two volumes"</note> In preparing this present edition, <term>Pandit</term> <note>A title for a learned scholar or teacher in India</note> Subrahmanya Sastri has made use of both the previous editions. The text has been compared with manuscripts available in the various libraries in and near Madras <note>now known as Chennai</note> and the commentary of Kallinātha has been compared with the manuscript in the Tanjore Palace Library <note>original: "Descriptive Catalogue, Vol XVI, No 10749"</note>. The printed editions have been carefully compared with these manuscripts and the readings have been improved.

The plan was to add an English translation of the text at the end of each volume for the portion contained in it. It is very unfortunate that the late Pandit Subrahmanya Sastri was not able to prepare the translation. That work has devolved on me, along with the responsibility to see through the press the matter for the later portions which he had got ready. The English translation for the first <term>chapter</term> <note>original: "adhyāya"</note> is ready. The delay in issuing this first volume, which had been printed more than a year ago, is due to the time taken for getting the English translation ready. At this stage, the problem of printing-paper became a very acute one and it is not found possible at present to print the English translation. Therefore the first volume containing the first chapter is being issued, along with the commentaries and also appendices. The second and the third chapters have been printed and the printing of the fourth chapter has begun and the second volume containing these three chapters.

<page-num>viii</page-num>
<header>viii</header>

will appear very soon. Unfortunately, we have to hold up printing any further matter on account of difficulty in securing the needed paper. It is proposed to publish the remaining portion in a few convenient volumes, and the English translation will appear in a separate volume for the entire text.

The appendices added in this volume from page 293 illustrate certain details given in the text. Of these, the <term>Svaraprastāras</term> <note>Permutations and combinations of musical notes</note> from page 297 and the next one on p. 394 are given at the end of the whole work in the Anandasrama edition; since the matter relates to the first <term>adhyāya</term> <note>chapter</note>, it is given at the end of this volume containing the <term>adhyāya</term>. It is hoped that these and the other appendices which were prepared by Pandit Subrahmanya Sastri, and the index of half-verses will be of help to the readers in making use of the book.

As is well known, the <term>Saṅgītaratnākara</term> <note>literally "The Ocean of Music," a definitive 13th-century Sanskrit text on Indian music and dance</note> is divided into seven <term>adhyāyas</term> <note>chapters</note> dealing with:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| 1. <term>Svara</term> <note>Notes/Sound</note> | 4. <term>Prabandha</term> <note>Composition</note> | 7. <term>Nrtya</term> <note>Dance</note> |
| 2. <term>Rāga</term> <note>Melodic modes</note> | 5. <term>Tāla</term> <note>Rhythm/Meter</note> | |
| 3. <term>Prakīrnaka</term> <note>Miscellaneous topics</note> | 6. <term>Vādya</term> <note>Instruments</note> | |

The first <term>adhyāya</term> containing the <term>Svara</term> is divided into eight sections, called <term>prakaranas</term>, and they deal with:

1. <term>Padārthasaṅgraha</term> <note>Summary of topics</note>
2. <term>Piṇḍotpatti</term> <note>The origin of the human body/embodiment</note>
3. <term>Nāda</term> (Sound), <term>sthāna</term> (Resonance locations), <term>śruti</term> (Micro-tones), <term>svara</term> (Notes), <term>jātī</term> (Lineage), <term>kula</term> (Family), <term>daivata</term> (Deities), <term>ṛṣı</term> (Sages), <term>chando</term> (Metre), and <term>rasa</term> (Emotional essence).
4. <term>Grāma</term> (Scales), <term>murchanā</term> (Modes), <term>krama</term> (Sequences), and <term>tāna</term> (Melodic variations).

<page-num>IX</page-num>

5 <term>Sādhāraṇa</term> <note>Overlapping or common features of notes and melodies</note>
6 <term>Varṇālaṅkāra</term> <note>Melodic patterns and embellishments</note>
7. <term>Jāti</term> <note>The melodic prototypes or "parent" modes that preceded the modern Raga system</note>
8 <term>Gīti</term> <note>Styles of song or rhythmic lyrics</note>

In the Calcutta edition,¹ the first of these <term>prakaranas</term> <note>chapters or subdivisions</note> is called the Introductory section and the rest of the <term>adhyāya</term> <note>major book or chapter</note> is divided into seven sections. In the Preface² there, the fifth section is called <term>Sādhāraṇa</term> and the <term>Varṇālaṅkāra</term> is spoken of as the fourth, but in the text itself the order of these sections is as given in the present edition. I am adding a detailed list of contents, which, it is hoped, will be of use to the readers to understand the whole subject matter at a glance.

Śārṅgadeva, the author of the <term>Saṅgītaratnākara</term> <note>literally "The Ocean of Music," the most definitive 13th-century Sanskrit treatise on Indian music</note>, gives some information about himself in the beginning of the work,³ before he begins the summary of the work, in the first <term>prakaraṇa</term> of the first <term>adhyāya</term>. The first verse is a <term>mangala</term> <note>an auspicious invocation or prayer at the start of a literary work</note>. Then he speaks of his family,⁴ which traces its origin to Kashmere.⁵ The family goes back to the sage Vṛṣagaṇa.⁶ In that family there was one Bhāskara,⁷ who migrated to the south.⁸ His son

Of the two important commentaries, those by Kallinātha and Simhabhūpāla, the commentary of Simhabhūpāla is earlier. Simhabhūpāla belongs to the Recherla dynasty. His father was Anapota, who had a younger brother called Mada. They built up a strong kingdom and they divided the kingdom between themselves, the northern part going to Anapota with the capital at Rajukonda and the southern part to Mada with the capital at Devarakonda ⁴ Anapota had two sons; Devagirīs'vara was the elder, who must have died young since it is Simhabhūpāla who succeeded Anapota ⁵ About Simhabhūpāla there is enough material available in his own works. In the commentary on the <term>Sangītaratnākara</term> <note>The "Ocean of Music," a definitive 13th-century Sanskrit text on Indian classical music and dance</note> itself, there is not much information available. He simply says that he has discussed the matter with scholars well-versed in—

Singa Prabhu, Vennama Nayaka, and Reca¹ Singa became the king² after the death of Dacana. His brother Reca had a son named Nāgaya Nāyaka³ who held the title of *Kuthārirāya*⁴ <note>original: "Kuthārirāya-biruda"; likely meaning "Lord of the Axe," a title of military prowess</note> and who was also called *Rāhuttarāya*⁵ <note>original: "Rāhuttarāya"; a title signifying a "Lord among troopers" or a cavalry commander</note>. Singa Prabhu had two sons named Ananta and Mādhava⁶. This Mādhava had many sons⁷ of whom Vedagirīndra was the eldest⁸. The elder brother of Madhava, namely, Ananta, became known as Anapota also⁹. His wife was Annamāmbā¹⁰. They had two sons,¹¹ the elder was Devagirīs'vara¹² and the second was Singabhūpati¹³. He lived in his ancestral city of Rājācala¹⁴ <note>Modern-day Rachakonda</note>. His kingdom lay between the Vindhya mountains and the S'rīs'aila¹⁵.

Another work of Simhabhūpāla is *Kuvalayāvalī* or *Ratnapāñcālikā* <note>The Emerald Doll</note>, published in the Trivandrum Sanskrit Series by Dr. L. A. Ravi Varma as No. 146 in 1941. This is a small drama in four Acts. In the Prologue, the author is mentioned as Śrī Siṅgabhūpāla,¹ otherwise known as Khadganārāyaṇa <note>The Sword-Narayana; a title of prowess</note>² who lived at the capital city named Rājaśaila <note>Royal Hill</note>.³ His mother was Annamātā.⁴ It is also stated there that one Viśveśvara had spoken very highly of his poetry.⁵ The Viśveśvara mentioned in the Prologue must be the author of *Camatkāracandrikā* <note>The Moonlight of Literary Surprise</note>; in the colophon of this work there is the mention of Simhabhūpāla.⁶

There is a Telugu work called *Velugotivārivaṃśāvalī* <note>The Genealogy of the Velugoti Family</note>.⁷ In the Introduction to that work, Dr. Venkata Ramanayya deals with Simhabhūpāla on pages 13 ff.

<meta>This page continues the biographical and bibliographical analysis of the scholar-king Simhabhūpāla, focusing on his known works and the clarification of manuscript attributions.</meta>

<page-num>XVI</page-num>

Simhabhūpāla is a versatile scholar and a profuse writer. Apart from his *The Row of Water Lilies* <note>original: "Kuvalayāvalī"</note> and *The Ocean of the Essence of Aesthetic Emotion* <note>original: "Rasārnavasudhākara"</note>, both published in the Trivandrum Sanskrit Series, he must have written many other works. In *The Ocean of the Essence of Aesthetic Emotion*, he mentions a work called *The Birth of the God of Love* <note>original: "Kandarpasambhava"</note> as his own composition.¹ In the whole of this *Ocean of the Essence of Aesthetic Emotion*, he quotes from his own works about twenty-five verses in illustration of various statements he makes, with the remark, *as in my own work* <note>original: "yathā mamaiva"</note>. A few of them are traceable to his *The Row of Water Lilies* as is mentioned in the Preface to that Drama in the Trivandrum Sanskrit Series. We have as yet no information about the other verses quoted from his works.

In Aufrecht’s *Complete Catalog of Catalogs* <note>original: "Catalogus Catalogorum"</note>, there is an entry of *Definitions of Dramaturgy* <note>original: "Nāṭakaparibhāṣā"</note> as a work of Siṅgadharanīsena. The entry is made on page 284 as found in Buhler’s Report and on page 791 as found in the India Office. The manuscripts in the India Office are described by Eggeling under Nos. 1201 and 1202. Evidently the author is Siṅgadharanīs'a and Siṅgadharanīsena must be the Instrumental Singular form with 'sa' for 's'a'.² It is not a separate work; it is only a part of Simhabhūpāla’s *Ocean of the Essence of Aesthetic Emotion* beginning from verse 290 on page 298.

There is no reason to believe that the *Ocean of the Essence of Aesthetic Emotion* was written by Vis'ves'vara on the ground that—

> wishing to unite the hearts of both, 
> melted them with the very heat of love 
> through their warm, wandering sighs.

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion regarding the authorship of the Rasārṇava-sudhākara and the cultural role of Indian kingship.</meta>

<page-num>XVII</page-num>
<sig>c</sig>

In the *Moonlight of Artistic Surprise* <note>original: "Camatkāracandrikā"</note>, the author Viśveśvara refers to the *Moon-nectar of the Ocean of Sentiment* <note>original: "Rasārṇava-sudhākara"</note> for further details. $^1$ It is becoming a fashion nowadays to refer all works bearing the name of a king to some court poet or court scholar <term>Pandit: a learned scholar or teacher in Hindu law, philosophy, or music</term>. Unless there is definite evidence—as in the case of the *Nectar of Music* <note>original: "Saṅgītasudhā"</note> assigned to King Raghunātha but mentioned as being by Govinda Dīkṣita by his son Veṅkaṭamakhin $^2$—we have to accept that the king himself wrote these works. 

The kings in ancient and even in medieval India were not mere figure-heads in administration, nor were they mere administrators. They were the true representatives of the civilization of the country. In intellectual equipment, in cultural accomplishments, and in every aspect of their lives, they represented the civilization in its ideal form. They maintained <term>Dharma: the eternal and inherent nature of reality, often translated as duty, righteousness, or cosmic order</term>, which is another word for civilization; they lived according to Dharma also. Besides being warriors, conquerors, and rulers, they were learned scholars, poets, philosophers, and authors, as well as patrons of learning and arts. They recognized only an Indian Dharma or civilization without any racial prejudices. Siṃhabhūpāla himself says that he belonged to the lowest caste $^3$, yet at the same time he honored the Brahmins <note>The priestly and scholarly class</note> and protected religion. Neither caste distinction nor sectarian differences interfered with the unity of culture under the rule of those great Indian kings.

---

$^1$ Compare Dr. M. Krishnamacharyar's *Classical Sanskrit Literature*, paragraph 879, page 771.
$^2$ See note 1 on page XI above.
$^3$ See note 4 on page XIII above.

<summary>The author argues for the genuine authorship of King Siṃhabhūpāla, asserting that Indian monarchs were historically scholars and embodiments of Dharma rather than just administrative figureheads. He highlights that cultural unity and patronage of the arts transcended caste distinctions during this period.</summary>
<keywords>authorship, kingship, Dharma, Siṃhabhūpāla, Viśveśvara, Rasārṇava-sudhākara, Sanskrit literature, cultural unity, patronage</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the scholarly debate regarding the authorship of the Rasārṇavasudhākara and the commentary on the Saṅgītaratnākara, specifically addressing the claims made by Dr. M. Krishnamacharyar.</meta>

<page-num>xviii</page-num>

Dr. M. Krishnamacharyar says that Siṃhabhūpāla, who wrote the commentary on the *Ocean of Music* <note>original: "Saṅgītaratnākara," a foundational 13th-century Sanskrit text on Indian music and dance</note>, is different from the author of the *Moonlight of the Ocean of Rasa* <note>original: "Rasārṇavasudhākara," a major work on aesthetics and dramaturgy</note>.¹ He does not give any explanation. It is true that while he gives an elaborate description of his ancestry in the introductory portion of the *Moonlight of the Ocean of Rasa*, he gives little information about himself in his commentary. This must be due to the fact that he wrote the commentary after he wrote the *Moonlight of the Ocean of Rasa*. It is not possible at this stage to investigate the point on the basis of any internal evidence. I must wait for that till the whole of the commentary is published. But the colophon <note>a concluding statement in a manuscript giving facts about its production</note> in the two works proves the identity of the authors beyond any doubt.² The question of a work called *Definitions of Drama* <note>original: "Nāṭakaparibhāsa"</note>, the question of the *Moonlight of the Ocean of Rasa* having been written by another person who was a favorite in the court, and the question of the authors of the two works being different—such questions should not have been raised, and if the points had been properly investigated such doubts would not have been raised. But since they are found in works well known and relied on by many, it has become necessary for me to investigate the points and make certain remarks on them.

¹ See *Classical Sanskrit Literature*, footnote 1, p. 853.
² The colophon in the *Moonlight of the Ocean of Rasa* reads as follows:
> Thus ends the work named *The Moonlight of the Ocean of Rasa*, composed by the illustrious Siṃhabhūpāla, who is the son of the glorious King Anapota, the formidable Bhima in strength of arm, and the "Ganda-Bhairava" <note>a title meaning "formidable hero"</note> lord of the prosperous Andhra region, etc. <note>original: "इति श्रीमदन्ध्रमण्डलाधीश्वरप्रतिगण्डभैरवश्रीयनपोतनरेन्द्रनन्दनभुजबलभीमश्री-शिङ्गभूपालविरचिते रसार्णवसुधाकरनाम्नि etc"</note>

This may be compared with the colophon at the end of the first chapter of the commentary. Further, the identity of the names <term>Sudhākara</term> <note>meaning "Moon" or "Source of Nectar"</note> in both works too point out to the identity of the authors.

<summary>The author argues against Dr. M. Krishnamacharyar's claim that the two works were written by different people, citing matching colophons and titles as proof of Siṃhabhūpāla's authorship.</summary>

On the banks of the Tungabhadrā river, there is the city called Vidyānagarī (also known as Vijayanagar)¹ where there ruled the king Devarāya, son of Vijaya of the Yadava dynasty.² Devarāya's son was Immadi Devarāya.³ Kallinātha lived there at that time.⁴ His grandfather was Vallabhadeva,⁵ his mother was Nārāyaṇī,⁶ and his father was Laksmīdhara.⁷ He belonged to the Śāṇḍilya Gotra <note>A lineage or clan tracing descent from the sage Śāṇḍilya</note>.⁸ Under the orders of the king, he wrote a commentary on the *Saṅgītaratnākara* <note>The "Ocean of Music," a definitive 13th-century Sanskrit treatise on Indian music and dance</note>.⁹

Vijaya I, mentioned by Kallinātha, reigned from 1418 to 1423; his son Devarāya II reigned from 1423 to 1446.¹⁰ Immadi Devarāya reigned from 1446 to 1465. Thus, Kallinātha must have lived in the second half of the fifteenth century.

² <note>original: "एता शास्ति प्रौढ श्रीदेवरायो विजयनृपसुतो यादवाना वरेण्य"</note> "The great King Devarāya, son of King Vijaya and eminent among the Yadavas, rules this [city]." — verse 7

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the Sangītaratnākara, focusing on the author's credentials and the publication history of musicological texts by the Adyar Library.</meta>

<page-num>XXI</page-num>
<header>XXI</header>

S'ārngadeva, the author of the <term>Sangītaratnākara</term> <note>Ocean of Music, a definitive 13th-century treatise</note>, mentions many previous writers on the subject in verses 15 to 19 in the first <term>prakarana</term> <note>section</note> of the first <term>adhyaya</term> <note>chapter</note>. Of these authorities, some are very well known. A detailed notice of them will be more appropriate when the whole book is out. He must have eclipsed most of them. He styles himself as <term>Nis's'anka</term>, "free from doubts." He also refers to himself as <term>Karanāgranīh</term>, which shows that he was the accountant-general of his king. Thus the author of the original was a high official in the service of the king; the commentator <term>Kallinātha</term> was a prominent figure in the royal court, held in high esteem by the king; the other commentator is a king. This shows what a close relation there existed between the government and the culture of the country.

The <term>Adyar Library</term> has already published two works on Music, the <term>Melarāgamālikā</term> of <term>Mahāvaidyanātha S'ivan</term> and the <term>Sangrahacūdāmani</term>, which were both edited by the late <term>Pandit S. Subrahmanya Sastrī</term> and which appeared as Nos. 16 and 17 in the <term>Adyar Library Series</term>. The <term>Rāgavibodha</term> of <term>Somanātha</term> is already available in more than one edition and there is also an English translation. But the book is known to be out of print. The <term>Adyar Library</term> has already started printing a fresh edition of the work prepared by the late <term>Pandit S. Subrahmanya Sastrī</term>, where he has been able to improve the readings in many places. This edition will be out very soon.

The plan of the <term>Adyar Library</term> is to publish works in all aspects of ancient Indian Culture, of which we

<meta>This page continues the introductory remarks regarding the cultural and religious significance of Indian music and the editorial acknowledgments for the current publication.</meta>

<page-num>XXII</page-num>

consider music and other fine arts as very important ones. In India, music did not develop as a secular entertainment; music in India is a fundamental phase of religion, rather music has become a religion itself, with a philosophy attached to it. The musical notes are the physical manifestations of the Highest Reality termed <term>Nāda-Brahman</term> <note>The concept of the "Sound-God" or the cosmos as primordial sound</note>. Music is not a mere accompaniment in religious worship, it is religious worship itself, like <term>Yāgas</term> <note>Vedic sacrificial rituals or offerings</note> and Temple worship. In India there has never been an antithesis between aesthetics and morality; there has never been developed an aesthetic doctrine which was not acceptable to the most orthodox follower of religion. Thus the <term>Saṅgītaratnākara</term> <note>literally "The Ocean of Music," a foundational 13th-century Sanskrit text on Indian music and dance</note> and other works on music undertaken for publication by the Adyar Library are presentations of orthodox phases of Hindu religion and of Indian civilization as much as the commentaries on the <term>Vedas</term> <note>The oldest and most sacred scriptures of Hinduism</note> and the works on religion and philosophy like the <term>Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā</term> <note>A sacred text of the Pañcarātra tradition dealing with philosophy and occultism</note> and the <term>Vedāntaparibhāṣā</term> <note>A 17th-century manual on the epistemology of the Vedanta school of philosophy</note>. Through our publications we desire to exhibit the unity of Indian culture and the harmony that exists among the various phases of the Culture.

Now what remains for me is to acknowledge the help that has been received in the preparation of this edition. Our gratitude to Pandit S. Subrahmanya Sastri, who prepared the edition, is far beyond words to be adequately expressed. His whole life was spent in scholarly pursuits; it is a great privilege for me to be able to associate myself with this great work even in this very humble capacity. Dr. G. Srinivasa Murti,

The air born there, moving through the navel, heart, nose, and mouth, is the breath called *Prana*, which is the cause of speech production and other functions. By the mind acting as the instrument following that breath, following the path of the *Shrutis*—the place of origin of the words of the Vedas...

<page-num>4</page-num>
# The Ocean of Music [The Nature of Categories]

The location, meaning the *Pranava* <note>The sacred syllable 'Om'</note>, follows after that. Here, the word "after" (*anu*) functions as a preposition indicating a relationship, which governs the grammatical case of the word "Shruti" <note>The smallest audible unit of sound or sacred revelation</note> in the objective case. The term "delighting" (*ranjaka*) refers to that which incorporates everything other than itself into its own essence, much like a great king. Alternatively, the term "Shruti" refers to the intermediate sentences of the Vedas; their "place" or "footing" (*padam*) is established through the Great Sayings (*Mahavakyas*), such as the progression from "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" to "That Thou Art" <note>original: "Tat Tvam Asi"</note>. Following this (*anu*), after hearing these truths, the distinction between the individual self and the supreme reality is removed through the practice of their unity. When it is said, "This which is," the word "which" indicates that it is known through sacred tradition, while the word "this" indicates that it becomes mentally perceptible after reflection. It "shines by itself," meaning it is self-luminous; once direct realization occurs and the limitations of the mind are dissolved, it shines eternally in its true form. As stated in the *Yoga Yajnavalkya*:

> "Holding the breath with the mind while chanting the syllable *Om*,
> One sits in a secret place with senses conquered and mind focused on no other.
> When the breath reaches the *Sushumna* <note>The central energy channel of the subtle body</note>, O fair-faced one,
> The wise one, chanting the mantra mentally, should hold it within the heart.
> When the space within the body and its limbs is filled with breath,
> Then the Soul shines there like the sun in the sky.
> Whatever one sees, one should see all that within the Self, as the Self."

<margin>¹ are defined</margin>
The divisions of the *Grama* <note>musical scales or 'villages' of notes</note>, the arrangement of *Varnas* <note>melodic movements or social orders</note>, the *Alankaras* <note>musical ornaments</note>, and the *Jatis* <note>melodic types or parent scales</note> follow in order. By the word *Grama*, the worlds <margin>¹</margin> are meant; their "division" refers to their classification. The *Varnas* refer to the social orders like Brahmins and others; their "arrangement" refers to the castes produced by the regular and reverse order of these classes. Because these embellish the *Varnas*, they are called the classes of *Alankaras* <note>The author is drawing a parallel between musical ornamentation and social structure</note>.

# Chapter One: On Notes (Swaras)

<page-num>5</page-num>
<header>—Compendium 1] First Chapter: On Notes</header>

The sequence of the divisions of the *Gramas* <note>The fundamental scales or "villages" of notes in ancient Indian music</note> and so forth arises from Him—this is the implied meaning. This follows the linguistic rule: "Where no other action is specified, the verb 'to be' is understood." By this, the author shows that the Lord is the efficient cause of the world, just as it is explained in the *Aphorisms on Brahman* regarding the verse "From whom indeed [these beings are born]," and in the Vedas where it says, "The Priest (*Brahmin*) was His mouth." 

He is "embodied in sound" (*nadatanu*), meaning His form is sound itself, according to the Vedic scripture: "Having created that, He entered into it." I bow to that Lord Shankara <note>A name for Shiva</note> for the attainment of unsurpassed happiness—He who is "praised by the world" (*uddharajagadgitam*), meaning He is extolled by the universe in a sublime manner.

Now, regarding the interpretation concerning the musical notes (*swaras*) which are implied here: In the "heart-lotus" of the wise (the experts), which is the lower register (*mandra*). The term "Knot of Brahma" (*brahmagranthi*) <note>A psychic center or chakra located near the heart</note> refers to this same meaning. By the "mind" (*cittena*), meaning the mind impelled by the desire to speak. 

The word "Step" (*shrutipadam*): The *Shrutis* <note>Micro-tones or intervals</note> are the manifestors of the notes like *Shadja* <note>The tonic or first note</note>, such as *Chandovati* and others. Their "step" (*padam*)—here the word "step" is used in the singular to denote a class, meaning "positions." Sound is characterized by the word "step" because it is produced by the strike of the air, drawn by the mind, against the transverse channels attached to the upward-moving channel (*nadi*). 

Following that, without interruption, it is "pleasing" (*ranjaka*). Because it produces its own form and generates delight in the listener, it is that which is experienced as famous in the scientific treatises. "It shines by itself" (*svayam rajate*), meaning it manifests in performance without needing any other supporting cause. By this similarity of syllables, the etymology of the word *Swara* <note>Note; derived from 'svayam' (self) and 'raj' (shine)</note> is shown. 

Regarding "the *Gramas* and so forth": The *Gramas* are the *Shadja-grama* and others; their "division" is the arrangement of the *Varnas* <note>Melodic movements like staying, rising, or falling</note> such as the "steady" (*sthayi*) and others; the "Ornaments" (*alankaras*) are the "bright" (*prasanna*) and others; the "Modes" (*jatis*) are the *Shadjis* and others. The sequence of these *Gramas*, divisions, and so forth—whose characteristics will be described later—arises from the Note (*Swara*) as the causal source. 

"Embodied in sound" means consisting of sound. "The song of the world is raised": Song is a specific composition of notes; it is so called because the song of the world is raised or extracted from Him. I praise that Shankara, the "Giver of Happiness," for the manifestation of bliss. || 1 ||

## First Chapter on Notes (Svaras)

> Those who know only the theory <note>original: "lakshana"</note> do not possess confidence without practical performance <note>original: "lakshya"</note>. Conversely, those who know only performance but are devoid of scriptural knowledge are put to shame in the assemblies of the learned. Therefore, this new work by King Singhana—who possesses clear knowledge of both theory and practice—should not be disregarded by wise men of profound intellect. || 12 ||

> He who does not offer praise for the pure essence of this work does not concern us; he is like a deaf man attempting to praise a singer. However, the leader among the wise, speaking after certain deliberation in his own mind, brings joy. Indeed, applying lime to the lips <note>A reference to the preparation of betel leaf, signifying refinement or the removal of bitterness</note> calms the irritation of men. || 13 ||

> Who, even if superior in all qualities, would dare out of pride to explain the *Sangita Ratnakara* <note>The "Ocean of Music," the foundational 13th-century text by Sharngadeva</note>? Nevertheless, this is an effort to please those who are discerning. || 14 ||

Considering that the musical scriptures composed by Bharata, Dattila, Kohala, and others <note>Legendary sages and musicologists of ancient India</note> contain secrets difficult to grasp for those on earth with limited intellect, the most compassionate Sharngadeva—whose mind is devoted to the lotus feet of the Moon-adorned God <note>Shiva</note>—desired to create the "Ocean of Music" (*Sangita Ratnakara*) for the benefit of the world. To ensure its completion without obstacles and its propagation through lineages of students, he performs the auspicious invocation <note>term: Mangalacarana; a traditional prayer at the start of a Sanskrit work to ensure success</note> prescribed by the Vedas and Smritis. In a single verse, he also explains the subject matter, the purpose, and the relationship of the work, beginning with the words: *Born from the knot of Brahma...*

By placing the word "Brahma" first, he intends an auspicious beginning, as it reminds the heart of the Supreme Soul who destroys all obstacles. He uses the word "Brahma" first because the nature of Sound <note>term: Nada; the primordial vibration</note> is the cause of liberation.

"I bow" <note>original: "vande"</note>: I salute and I praise. According to the lexicons, the root *vad* implies both salutation and praise. If he had used other terms for bowing or stilled-praise, only one meaning would be gained; thus, he uses *vande* to encompass both. Here, the three types of salutation—mental, vocal, and physical—are understood even without specific mention. Alternatively, it should be connected with the word "with the mind" found in the first line, because a mental salutation performed with faith is primary, as the scripture says: "Whatever one does with knowledge and faith..." Since the vocal salutation is established by the very act of writing the book, and for the faithful, vocal salutation is inseparable from physical salutation, all three types of bowing are established.

To whom do I bow? To Shankara <note>A name for Shiva</note>, meaning the Lord. Alternatively, "Shankara" means "He who creates (kara) happiness (sham)." Only God grants happiness independently. By this definition, kings and others who grant happiness only dependently are excluded.

# Sangita Ratnakara: [The Nature of Matter]

One might ask: if the Supreme Being is supremely compassionate and has no needs of His own, why does He strive to bring joy to others? To address this, the author says:

**"Exalted..."** The world sings to—that is, praises—Him with exalted voices. Although the root *gai* (to sing) refers to sound, because it is directed toward the Lord, it takes on the meaning of "praise." What are the characteristics of this Lord? He is **"the Body of Sound"** (*nadatanu*); He whose very form is sound (*nada*), as it is said that He is the **"Word-Brahman"** <note>original: *shabdabrahma*; the concept that the ultimate reality is composed of sacred sound</note>. Alternatively, one may perceive the cause (Space) through its effect (Sound); thus, He is of the nature of Space. Space is also one of the eight forms of the Supreme Lord. This description is used because the Supreme Lord is the cause of sound, and His grace is the means to successfully complete this extensive written work composed of words. The word "Him" is used to connect with the relative pronoun "Whom," following the rule that "who" and "he" share an eternal relationship.

Who is He? **"From whom the Villages..."** By the word "Village" (*grama*), we should understand the various worlds (earth, etc.), or perhaps cities, suburbs, villages, and hamlets. **"Division"** (*vibhaga*) refers to the distribution of wealth, grain, and so on. Or, it refers to the distinct arrangement of the worlds, as the Scripture says: "He is the bridge, the boundary that keeps these worlds from blending together." **"Colors"** (*varna*) <note>original: *varna*; here referring to the social orders like Brahmins</note> refers to the social classes; **"Structure"** (*rachana*) refers to the creation of two-legged, four-legged, and six-legged beings; **"Ornaments"** (*alamkara*) refers to bracelets, crowns, and the like; **"Genera"** (*jati*) refers to the essential nature of things, such as "cowness" or "horseness"; and **"Order"** (*krama*) refers to stages like childhood, or the cycle of creation and destruction, or the sequence of the seasons. All these have arisen from Him. Because the rule states "the source of birth takes the fifth case," the grammar itself indicates He is the source. Here, a compound is formed: "Villages and Divisions and Colors and Structures and Ornaments and Genera," and this is then joined with the word "Order." Alternatively, it means the "Order" or systematic arrangement of everything from the Villages to the Genera originates from Him.

He is further described: **"He who shines by Himself"**—meaning He is **Self-luminous** (*svaprakasha*). Now, what is this "Self-luminosity"? It is the capacity to be immediately present in experience without being an object of ordinary sensory knowledge. As stated in the *Tattvadipika* <note>A philosophical treatise on "The Illumination of Truth"</note>:

> "For that which is worthy of immediate experience, yet beyond the reach of the mind... how can there be a lack of definition for the Self-luminous?"

Where does He shine? In the **lotus-heart of the wise**, as it is said: "The Person, the size of a thumb, resides in the center of the self." One might ask: how can the all-pervading Supreme Self possess the physical attribute of residing in a heart? To this, he says: **"The Delighter."** Even though the Supreme Lord is all-pervading, He manifests within the heart-lotus of living beings. As Vyasa stated: "Because of manifestation, as Ashmarathya holds." By what is He manifested in the heart? By the **Mind** (*citta*). Of what kind? **"That which follows the breath born from the Knot of Brahma."** The **"Knot of Brahma"** (*brahmagranthi*) is the place where the *Ida* and *Pingala* channels meet the *Sushumna* <note>The central energy channel in the subtle body</note>. The "breath" is that which is born from there, and the mind "follows" or moves along with it. The prefix "after" (*anu*) here implies "together with." Or, it means that which is "followed" or "contained" within it...

<summary>This page provides a philosophical and grammatical commentary on the opening of the Sangita Ratnakara, equating the Supreme Lord with "Sound-Brahman" and explaining how the entire order of the universe—from social classes to physical structures—emanates from Him.</summary>
<keywords>Shabdabrahma, Nadatanu, Self-luminosity, Brahmagranthi, Sushumna, Metaphysics of Sound, Creation, Heart-lotus</keywords>

# Chapter 1: On Swara (Musical Notes)
## Section 1: Introduction

The suffix *-in* is applied here. The compound "one who follows the wind" <note>Sanskrit: *mārutānugatinā*</note> is analyzed as such because <gloss>1</gloss> it is a well-known tenet among Yogis that the mind and the breath always move together. Sri Harsha also expressed this in the *Naishadha Charita* <note>A famous 12th-century Sanskrit epic poem</note>:

> "O daughter of Bhima, though you are outside, you dwell in my heart; you have become my very breath through the movement of my nostrils and mouth. It is no wonder that you occupy my mind, for the mind and the breath function as one."

The connection in the text is: "I bow to that specific Supreme Lord for the sake of joy." Alternatively, in the second interpretation, "I bow to Song" <note>Sanskrit: *Gītam*</note>. Song is defined as a "collection of notes that colors the mind," as the author will later state: "A melodic composition that pleases the ear is called Song." By using the word "Song" as the primary term, it is implied that Instrumental Music and Dance are also included, thus indicating that the subject of this book is *Sangita* <term>Sangita: the threefold arts of vocal music, instrumental music, and dance</term>. If these were not the subject, mentioning them in the prayer at the beginning of the book would be inappropriate <gloss>2</gloss>.

Or, "I bow to the one whose body is Sound" <note>Sanskrit: *Nādatanu*</note>. I bow to that melodic arrangement whose very essence is Sound. What kind of sound? One from which the "songs of the exalted world" <note>Sanskrit: *uddhurajagadgītam*</note>—such as the *Jati* and *Ela* compositions—originate. For what purpose? For joy or bliss. Furthermore, what is its nature? It is "Shankara," meaning it creates (*kara*) happiness (*sham*). By this, the author shows that the purpose of music is happiness, and there is a cause-and-effect relationship between the subject matter and that happiness.

To what else do I bow? To that from which the *Gramas* and other elements arise. The *Gramas* <term>Grama: basic scales or "villages" of notes</term> are groups of notes, divided into three: the *Shadja-grama*, the *Madhyama-grama*, and the *Gandhara-grama*. Their "division" refers to their distinctness. *Varna* <term>Varna: melodic movement</term> is the act of singing, which is fourfold: staying on a note, ascending, descending, or wandering; as will be said later: "The act of singing is called Varna." Its "arrangement" refers to its execution or its beauty. *Alankaras* <term>Alankara: musical ornaments</term> are specific melodic patterns like *Mandra*, etc. The *Jatis* <term>Jati: the melodic prototypes or parent modes of ancient music</term> are eighteen in number—seven pure types like *Shadjya*, and eleven modified types like *Shadja-kaishiki*. Their "sequence" refers to the order in which they arise.

This Sound "shines by itself" <note>Sanskrit: *svayam rājate*</note> because it gives bliss without needing anything else. This also explains the etymology of the word *Swara* <term>Swara: a musical note; literally "that which shines by itself"</term>. What is its nature? It is "pleasing to the wise" <note>Sanskrit: *sūrīṇām*</note>, meaning it creates passion and delight in those who know the essence of music. Where does it shine? In the "heart-lotus." The mention of the heart-lotus is an illustration; one should understand it to include all the places where sound is produced: the heart, the throat, and the head. By what is it perceived? By the mind, for the mind is a cause in the production of sound, as will be stated: "The Soul, desiring to speak, impels the mind." The description "born from the knot of Brahma" <note>Sanskrit: *brahmagranthija*</note> is as explained previously. ॥ 1 ॥

<gloss>2</gloss> Because it would lead to the fallacy of irrelevance.

(Kallinatha) <note>Kallinatha is a 15th-century commentator whose notes are marked with (Ka).</note> Now the author, **Sharngadeva**, after praising his homeland and lineage, specifies the purpose and subject of the book—starting from the phrase "There is a home of well-being" and ending with "the noble-minded reveals the Ocean of Music." || 2—14 ||

(Simhabhupala) <note>Simhabhupala is a 14th-century commentator whose notes are marked with (Su).</note> Thus, after performing the auspicious opening and stating the subject matter and purpose, the author describes his own lineage to establish the excellence of the work—starting with "There is." By using the present tense "There is," he suggests the permanence of his lineage until the end of time. The word "Well-being" <note>svasti</note> is an indeclinable word meaning welfare; his lineage is the "home" or refuge of that welfare. He was born in the illustrious land of Kashmir. He was born from the Sage named Vrishagana, meaning he was born into the Vrishagana clan. He now describes the religious nature of the lineage:

->**Lord Shiva, Goddess Parvati, Brahma, Bharata, and the Sage Kashyapa;**<-
->**Matanga, Yashtika, Durga, Shakti, Shardula, and Kohala;**<-
->**Vishakhila, Dattila, Kambala, and Ashvatara;**<-

<note>Verses 15–16: This is a "lineage of masters" (parampara). The author lists divine, semi-divine, and historical figures credited with founding the science of music and drama.</note>

Regarding the phrase *by the sacrificers*: It means adorned by those who perform Vedic sacrifices. The meaning is that such distinguished people were born in this lineage. In that lineage, he describes the eminent founding ancestor: *Therein*. There was a man named Bhaskara <note>original: "Bhaskara" means Sun</note> who was like the sun, a treasury of splendor and a locus of spiritual luster. In another sense, he was a locus of physical beauty. He made a journey from the land of Kashmir toward the southern direction <note>original: "dakshinayana"</note>; or rather, he became a worthy recipient for the distribution of sacrificial gifts <note>original: "dakshina"</note> to satisfy the desires of the skillful. In the case of the sun, the term "southern solstice" is well known.

The author of the book now speaks of his father: *His*. He served King Bhillama in the city of Jaitra. He then describes his sovereign, King Singhana: *The One*. The fire of his majesty, though pervading the entire universe, burns only the hearts of his enemies. Since the effect (burning) is restricted despite the cause (all-pervading fire) being present, this employs the poetic figure of speech called *Visheshokti* <note>peculiar allegation</note>.

He describes the influence of King Singhana’s favor: *Having pleased him*. Having made Singhana pleased through a multitude of virtues. Because the king is described as "a lover of virtues," this employs the figure of speech called *Parikara* <note>the device of significant epithets</note>. Through his favors—meaning through the provision of wealth, clothing, food, and so on—what did the king not give? The meaning is that he gave everything. This logic applies to the phrase "what did he not know?" and so on.

From such a man named Sodhala, who was like an ocean of milk, Sharngadeva was born like the moon. Regarding the phrase *Above all*: Because the word "above" is repeated, it governs the objective case, meaning he stands above everyone. To demonstrate the excellence of the work, he describes himself: *Having performed...* He reveals his own scholarship: *Various...* He mentions his "dwelling together" with the Goddess of Learning (Saraswati) because she resides in Kashmir, and Sharngadeva’s family originated from Kashmir.

*He*: That Sharngadeva manifests—meaning composes—the *Ocean of Music* (Sangita Ratnakara). This is for the *attainment of the highest good*, meaning the achievement of liberation. This is because it will be stated later that songs like the *Madraka* and other formal compositions used in the praise of Shiva were ordained by the Creator for the purpose of liberation. // 2–14 //

(Kallinatha's Commentary): In this scripture, to encourage the engagement of discerning readers, the author shows that this work is accepted by many authorities starting with Lord Shiva. By doing so, he highlights the excellence of his own book as a compendium of the essence of their views.

<summary>Sharngadeva traces his lineage from Kashmir to the court of King Singhana and lists the legendary sages and deities who founded the musical tradition. He asserts that the study of music, as presented in this compendium, leads to spiritual liberation (moksha).</summary>

**Sadashiva** <note>The commentator refers to the opening invocation to Lord Shiva</note> and so on, up to **"produced this extraction of the essence."** "Extraction of the essence" is a metaphor for butter; or it can be understood as an adverbial phrase describing the action by which the essence is drawn out. || 15—20 ||

(Su.) <note>Commentary by Simhabhupala</note> Now, one might ask: since there already exist musical treatises composed by Sadashiva, Bharata, and others, why undergo the trouble of this new, seemingly fruitless composition? To this, he replies: **"Sadashiva..."** etc. By churning the ocean of their doctrines, he has produced this extraction of the essence. Because those earlier texts are vast, difficult to grasp, and numerous, they cannot be fully explored by humans of short lifespans. Therefore, since the secret of all music can be realized here with little effort, this labor is not in vain. Furthermore, by stating that this work was created after studying those classical sciences, he indicates that it is well-founded and should be accepted as authoritative by discerning scholars. || 15—20 ||

# Ocean of Music [Subject Matter]

## It is of two kinds: *Marga* (The Path) and *Deshi* (The Regional). *Marga* is said to be that
## which was sought out by Brahma <note>original: "Virinchi"; the creator god in Hindu cosmology</note> and others, and performed by Bharata <note>The legendary sage and author of the Natyashastra, the foundational text of Indian performance</note> and his followers. || 22 ||
## It bestows certain spiritual liberation when performed before the Lord Shambhu <note>Shiva, the patron deity of dance and music</note>.
## That which pleases the hearts of people according to their local tastes in various regions [is called *Deshi*]. || 23 ||

<margin>Commentary by Kallinatha</margin>
Wishing to avoid the doubt that the term might only apply to vocal music, and not to instrumental music and dance, the author explains the meaning of the word *Sangita* <term>Sangita: the tripartite arts of vocal music, instrumental music, and dance</term> by saying "Song, Instrument..." If only song were to be discussed, he would have used the word "Song" (*Gita*) alone, rather than the word with the prefix *Sam-* (*Sam-gita*). Now, if one argues that the prefix *Sam-* is merely to indicate the excellence of the song, that is not so; for the definition "a composition of pleasing tones is called Song" already establishes the excellence of the song without a prefix. The prefix *Sam-*, when used with the word "Song," does not add a new quality to the song itself, but rather indicates its association with others—namely, with instrumental music (due to their shared nature as sound) and with dance (which is manifested by both). Therefore, wherever the word *Sangita* is used, one should understand that the "Triple Symphony" <note>original: "Tauryatrika"; the union of song, instrument, and dance</note> is intended. Occasionally, the word *Sangita* is used for song alone, but this is a figurative use of the whole for the part, much like calling a piece of cloth "a garment." || -21 ||

<margin>Commentary by Simhabhupala (Sudhakara)</margin>
It has been stated that this "Treatise on Music" is being composed. To the question "What is this *Sangita*?", he says: "Song..." etc. Now, if *Sangita* only refers to the three combined, would it mean that each one individually is not *Sangita*? Not so; for the definition of the word *Sangita* applies to any one of the three: song, instrument, or dance. || -21 ||

<margin>Commentary by Kallinatha</margin>
Having promised the two-fold division of *Sangita* into *Marga* and *Deshi*, he provides their definitions based on their etymology, starting with "The Path (*Marga*)..." etc. It is called *Marga* because it was "sought out" <note>The word Marga comes from the root 'mrg', meaning to hunt or seek</note>. This seeking was done by Brahma and others, who said, "I shall create this Veda <note>The Fifth Veda or Natya Veda</note> known as Drama, along with its history..."

<insert>2. By that which is expressed</insert>

# Chapter 1: The Chapter on Notes (Svaras)

->Vocal music, instrumental music, and dance—this triad is called *Deshi* <note>The 'regional' or 'popular' style</note>. Dancing follows the instrument, and the instrument follows the vocal song.<-

->Therefore, because vocal music is the primary element, it is explained here first. The Grandfather <note>The Creator God, Brahma</note> gathered this art of singing from the *Sama Veda*.<-

"I shall explain," he promises, having searched through the four Vedas to create this work. The term *Margita* <note>original: "मार्गित"</note> is a form derived from the verbal root *marg* meaning 'to seek' or 'to search.' The term *Marga* <note>The 'Classical' or 'Ancient' path</note> is likewise derived from that same root. Regarding *Deshi*: the word 'country' or 'region' refers to the people living there; this is a technical name given by the teachers to the activities of singing and so on as performed by people according to their own tastes. 

Since all three—singing, playing, and dancing—are presented without distinction as being named 'Music' <term>Sangita: the unified art of vocal music, instrumental music, and dance</term> and as being limbs of the dramatic arts, the question arises as to which should be treated first. Because it is said that "one should perform the movements of the limbs according to the measure of the singing and the instruments," and "singing is born from and colored by the four types of instruments," singing is established as the primary element because the other two depend upon it. Thus, he promises its priority by stating: *Dancing follows the instrument...* (Verses 22–24).

<insert>(Sudhakara commentary)</insert> Having stated the two-fold nature of music through the categories of *Marga* and *Deshi*, he explains the definition of *Marga*: *That which was sought...* It was sought, searched for, and seen. By this, the etymology of the word *Marga* is indicated. He then gives the definition of *Deshi*: *In the region...* He provides the reason for describing vocal music first: *Dancing...* (Verses 22–24).

<insert>(Kallinatha commentary)</insert> He demonstrates the worthiness of vocal music by showing its Vedic origin, as it was gathered from the *Sama Veda*: **From the Sama Veda, this...** Its nature as a collection from that Veda is due to the fact that singing also consists of seven notes <term>Svaras: musical notes or pitches</term>. In the *Saman* chants, there are indeed seven notes known as *Krushta, Prathama, Dvitiya, Tritiya, Chaturtha, Mandra,* and *Atisvarya*. Here in secular music, these same notes are given names such as *Shadja* and the rest. The intent is that even when Brahma extracted this from the Vedas to compile it, his purpose was to make it accessible to all castes. (Verse 25).

<note>The author explains that while Vedic chanting used one set of names for the seven notes, the musical system uses another (Shadja, Rishabha, etc.), but they represent the same fundamental harmonic truth.</note>

<summary>This page defines the three components of Sangita (vocal, instrumental, and dance) and justifies why vocal music is studied first. It also traces the divine origin of music back to the Sama Veda, compiled by the god Brahma for the benefit of all.</summary>
<keywords>Sangita, Marga, Deshi, Sama Veda, Brahma, Svara, Shadja, Vocal Music, Dance, Music Theory</keywords>

Who is capable of praising the greatness of this Music? It is the one and only means for attaining the four goals of life: Virtue, Wealth, Pleasure, and Liberation <term>Purusharthas: the four-fold aims of human existence: Dharma, Artha, Kama, and Moksha</term>. (30)

This is what he says starting with "By singing..." (26–29)

<page-num>17</page-num>
<header>—Compendium 1] First Chapter: On Notes</header>

## In this first chapter concerning notes, the following are presented:
## The body, the manifestation of sound, the locations of resonance, and the microtones. || 31 ||
## Then the seven pure notes and the twelve modified ones;
## Their lineages, castes, colors, continents, seers, and presiding deities. || 32 ||

Regarding this: The fact that music is a means to achieve <term>Dharma</term><note>Righteousness or religious merit</note> is established by the Vedic scripture in the section on the Horse Sacrifice, which states: "Two Brahmins, singers of the lute, shall sing; one Brahmin shall sing." It is further proven by the inclusion of singing as an integral part of the worship of the gods. Its role as a means to achieve <term>Artha</term><note>Material wealth or prosperity</note> is observed in the world. Its role as a means to achieve <term>Kama</term><note>Desire or pleasure</note> is established both by the Vedas—"Therefore, women desire one who sings"—and by worldly experience. Its role as a means to achieve <term>Moksha</term><note>Liberation from the cycle of rebirth</note> is confirmed by:

> "One who knows the truth of lute playing, who is expert in microtones and melodic types,
> and who knows rhythm, reaches the path of liberation without effort."

This is from the *Law Code of Yajnavalkya* <note>original: "Yajnavalkya-smriti"</note>. Furthermore, regarding songs such as the *Madraka* in the section on Shiva's praise, it is said: "The Creator ordained these for the sake of liberation." || 30 ||

(Sudhakara Commentary) Regarding "Dharma, etc.": Music sung for the purpose of worshipping the Supreme Lord is a cause of religious merit. As will be stated later regarding the correct application of melodic types <insert>Jatis</insert> and other elements: "These melodic types purify even one guilty of the sin of killing a priest." It is a means of wealth for those who live by music. It is a means of pleasure because it serves as a stimulus for the erotic sentiment. The fact that the *Madraka* and other song forms lead to liberation will be explained later. || 30 ||

(Kallinatha Commentary) Wishing to summarize the contents of each chapter in this *Ocean of Music* <note>original: "Ratnakara"</note> consisting of seven chapters, the author first vows to present the topics of the body and other subjects in the Chapter on Notes, beginning with the words **In this chapter concerning notes**. The plan is that this specific collection of subjects is to be explained.

<header>The Ocean of Music [Subject Matter]</header>

->The poetic meters and the applications; the microtones and their classes;<-
->The scales, the melodic modes, and the note-sequences—both pure and <insert>1</insert>complex—along with their total counts;<-
->The permutations, the "Mountain of Fragments" <note>original: "Khandameru"; a mathematical grid used to calculate musical permutations</note>, and the methods for finding lost or specific sequences;<-
->The overlapping of notes and the overlapping of melodic types;<-
->The proper application of the sharp Seventh and the sharp Fourth <note>original: "Kakali" and "Antara"; these refer to specific sharpened variations of the notes Ni and Ga</note>; the characteristics of melodic movement;<-
->The sixty-three types of ornamentation; and then the thirteen-fold<-
->Characteristics of melodic types, including the starting and dominant notes; the "Skull" songs and the "Blanket" songs;<-
->And the various types of song-compositions: such is the summary of the subject matter. (Verses 33–36)<-

**The Chapter on Musical Notes:** This refers to the chapter concerning the notes (*swaras*). The elements following the notes—such as microtones (*shrutis*), scales (*gramas*), modes (*murchanas*), sequences (*tanas*), melodic movements (*varnas*), ornaments (*alankaras*), melodic types (*jatis*), and song-forms (*gitis*)—are to be established in this chapter. 

The word "Chapter" (*adhyaya*) is derived from the root "to study" (*adhi-i*). In a grammatical sense, it is formed with the suffix *ghañ* to denote the act of study itself. Alternatively, it can denote the instrument or the location: "that by which" or "that in which" the intended meaning is studied. Or, it may be interpreted as a text that proceeds by taking the comprehension of meaning as its primary authority. 

**Objection:** Previously, it was promised that "Song" would be the first subject explained. Now, in this first "Chapter on Musical Notes," the description of the human body and other topics are given priority. Therefore, since the promise and the actual explanation cover different subjects, is there not a contradiction?

**Response:** There is no such fault. Because the body and other preliminary topics serve the "Song" through a traditional chain of causation, explaining the elements of the notes is simply another way of explaining the "Song" itself; thus, there is no contradiction. Among the thirty subject matters mentioned (starting with the body), the order of presentation is intentional for some due to the relationship of cause and effect, while for others, the order is not strictly fixed. This meaning will be further illuminated in the following sections.

# Chapter One: On Sound and Notes
## Summary of Subject Matter

> The rules for the fingers, the various divisions such as pairs and so on,
> the rotations, the tempo, the rhythmic patterns, and the formal song-compositions; || 46 ||
> The songs such as the *Chandaka*, the collection of the components of time-keeping,

> In the sixth chapter, various types of musical instruments will be described. || 48 ||

<note>Sudhakara commentary</note> He explains the summary of the contents of the fifth chapter in the section beginning with "The Chapter on Rhythm." The "Ancient Rhythms" <note>original: "marga-talas"</note> refer to patterns like *Chaccatputa*. A "unit" <note>original: "kala"</note> is a silent action of the hand. "Beats" <note>original: "pata"</note> are actions accompanied by sound. There are four "paths" <note>original: "marga"</note> starting with *Dhruva*. The "eight-unit" refers to the *Dhruvaka* and others. "Rotation" <note>original: "parivarta"</note> is the repetition of a foot or section of the rhythm. "Tempo" <note>original: "laya"</note> is the duration of time existing between the rhythmic actions. "Rhythmic flow" <note>original: "yati"</note> is the rule governing the movement of the tempo. There are seven formal "songs" <note>original: "gitaka"</note> such as *Madraka*. The "regional rhythms" <note>original: "deshi-talas"</note> number one hundred and twenty, beginning with the *Adi* rhythm. The "methods of proof" <note>original: "pratyaya"</note> are the means by which the number and nature of the rhythms are understood, such as permutation, finding a lost pattern, and identifying a specific sequence. || 44—47 ||

<note>Kalanidhi commentary</note> He states that in the sixth chapter, the four types of instruments—stringed and others—will be discussed in their many varieties: **"In the sixth, various types..."** In the seventh, he mentions the subjects to be established: **"In the seventh..."** "Dancing" <note>original: "nartanam"</note> is a general term for the movement of the limbs in drama, expressive dance, and pure dance. **"Various aesthetic flavors and emotions"** refers to the nine flavors <note>original: "rasas"</note> such as the Erotic, and the five types of emotional states <note>original: "bhavas"</note> such as the Determinants. **"In order"** means according to the sequence in which they were first mentioned. || 48, 48- ||

<note>Sudhakara commentary</note> He states the summary of the contents of the sixth and seventh chapters: **"In the sixth..."** || 48, 48- ||

# Now begins the Second Chapter: The Origin of the Human Body

->Song is composed of sound; instruments are praised for their manifestation of sound;<-
->Dance follows both of these; thus, this triad is dependent upon sound. (1)<-
->Through sound, letters are manifested; from letters, words; from words, speech;<-
->Through speech, all worldly interaction is carried out; therefore, the world is dependent upon sound. (2)<-
->Sound is said to be of two kinds: struck and unstruck.<-
->This sound is revealed within the body; therefore, the body is now described. (3)<-

<margin>(Kallinatha)</margin><note>Kallinatha was a 15th-century commentator on this text.</note> One might ask: since sound is the primary cause of song and musical notes, why should it not be explained first? Why describe the human body? Anticipating this doubt, the author responds that sound cannot be revealed without a physical body. To explain the body, he says: "Song is composed of sound..." The meaning is this: not only is the triad of song, instrument, and dance dependent on sound, but since all worldly interaction—rooted in speech—is also dependent on sound, the body which supports it must certainly be described first. || 1–3 ||

<margin>(Simhabhupala)</margin><note>Simhabhupala was a 14th-century commentator and king.</note> Having thus stated the summary of topics, the author praises sound in order to describe the body, which is the location where sound is manifested, saying: "Song..." "Composed of sound" means that sound is its <term>Atman</term> <note>The essential nature or soul</note> or its very form. Instruments, such as the <term>Veena</term> <note>A traditional Indian plucked string instrument</note>, are praised or attain beauty only through the manifestation of sound. Dance follows both of these, as it is said, "One should support the song with the limbs." Therefore, the triad consisting of song, dance, and instruments is dependent on sound—meaning it requires sound. || Not only are song, dance, and instruments dependent on sound, but the entire world is as well, as he says: "Through sound..." By sound—meaning <term>Dhvani</term> <note>Audible vibration or tone</note>—the <term>Varna</term> <note>The basic phonetic sounds or letters of the alphabet</note> such as 'ka' and others are manifested. What is this "sound"? That which reaches the path of the ear from a distance before a specific letter is recognized, and which imparts qualities like softness or loudness to the letters—that is called <term>Dhvani</term>. From letters come <term>Pada</term> <note>Words</note> such as "pot" and so on. From words come <term>Vachas</term> <note>Speech or sentences</note>, which are a collection of words—

...inheritance. This worldly activity is based on words, which come from sentences. Therefore, the entire world is dependent on Sound <note>Nada</note>. This has also been stated by the sage Matanga in his work, the *Great Compendium on Regional Music* <note>original: "Bṛhaddeśī"</note>—

> "There is no song without Sound, nor are there musical notes without Sound.
> There is no dance without Sound; therefore, the world is composed of Sound.
> Brahma <note>the Creator</note> is remembered as the form of Sound; Vishnu <note>the Preserver</note> is the form of Sound.
> The Supreme Goddess <note>Shakti</note> is the form of Sound, and the Great Lord <note>Shiva</note> is the form of Sound.
> Regarding what is called the 'Abode of Brahma' and what is known as the 'Knot of Brahma' <note>a psychic center in the body</note>—
> Within that center resides the Vital Breath <note>Prana</note>; from the Vital Breath, fire is born <gloss>1. birth</gloss>.
> From the union of fire and air, Sound is produced.
> From Sound, the Point <note>Bindu; the seed of manifestation</note> is born, and from that, all <gloss>2. from Sound, all</gloss> speech and literature arise."

He describes the two-fold nature of Sound: the "Struck" <note>Ahata; physical sound</note> and the "Unstruck" <note>Anahata; celestial sound</note>. Both types of Sound are manifested within the physical body <note>Pinda</note>. || 1—3 ||

(Kallinatha's Commentary) That body is dependent on the past actions <note>Karma</note> of the individual soul. Since that soul, desiring knowledge, requires the Absolute <note>Brahman</note> as its own basis, the author defines the nature of the Absolute: "There exists the Absolute." It is Consciousness-Bliss, meaning its nature is knowledge and happiness. It is self-luminous, meaning it shines by its own light. It is stainless, meaning it is untainted. It is the Lord, meaning it is independent. It is the "Sign" <note>Linga</note> because the universe dissolves into it. It is without a second, meaning it lacks any other entity similar to itself. It is unborn, meaning it is free from birth. It is all-pervading, meaning it is omnipresent. It is changeless, meaning it is free from the six states of being: birth, existence, growth, transformation, decay, and destruction...

# Sangitaratnakara [The Origin of the Body]

->Just as sparks arise from a fire, conditioned by beginningless ignorance,<-
->so too are souls divided by various conditions such as wood, through their beginningless actions. (Verse 6)<-

<note>The author uses the classic analogy of fire and sparks to explain how individual souls (jivas) relate to the supreme Brahman.</note>

Free from modifications; without form; the Lord of all and creator of the entire universe; imperishable; possessing all powers—namely the powers of will, knowledge, action, and enjoyment; all-knowing, the perceiver of all objects in the past, future, and present. Such is the **Brahman** described in the Upanishads <note>The philosophical texts forming the end of the Vedas</note>. Having described the nature of Brahman, the author now defines the individual souls as being identical with It and explains their connection to the body with the phrase: **"Its parts."** These are the measures or portions of that Brahman. || 4, 5 ||

(Sudhakara Commentary) Having promised to name the body, the author now explains its root cause with the word "Exists." It exists always and everywhere; it is eternal and all-pervading. It is called **Brahman** because of its greatness or its power to make things grow. It is of the nature of Consciousness and Bliss, as the Scripture <note>original: "shruti"</note> says: "Brahman is knowledge and bliss." It is self-luminous, meaning it shines by its own light; as the Scripture says: "When He shines, everything shines after Him; by His light, all this is illuminated." It is "unstained" <note>original: "niranjana"</note>, meaning free from the smear of ignorance, since ignorance resides in the individual soul. Even in the view where ignorance resides in Brahman, the term "unstained" indicates that it does not delude its own substrate. It is the "Lord" <note>original: "ishvara"</note>, capable of doing, not doing, or doing otherwise. It is the "Cause" <note>original: "linga"</note>. It is "non-dual," free from differences of its own kind, different kinds, or internal parts. It is "unborn," having no cause itself. It is "all-pervading" <note>original: "vibhu"</note> or "capable." It is "without modification," meaning it is free from the six changes of state mentioned by the grammarian Yaska: birth, existence, growth, transformation, decay, and destruction. It is "formless," not limited by any physical shape. It is the "Lord of all," the ruler even of gods like Brahma. It is "imperishable." It possesses "all power," meaning the power called Maya, which is the cause of the entire universe, exists within it. It is "all-knowing," possessing direct perception of all objects. **"Its parts"** means they are non-different from It, just as sparks are non-different from the fire in their essence as fire. Alternatively, following the aphorism "The soul is a part, because of the mention of variety," the author accepts the view of the relationship between the part (soul) and the whole (Supreme Self). || 4–5 ||

(Kallinatha Commentary) **"Conditioned by beginningless ignorance."** Beginningless ignorance refers to the root-ignorance, which is the lack of knowledge regarding the true nature of the underlying Reality. Conditioned or limited by that ignorance, they are called "living souls" <note>original: "jiva"</note>. For an entity whose nature is Truth, Consciousness, Bliss, and All-pervasiveness, the condition of ignorance—

# [The Origin of Sound] 2] First Chapter: On Musical Notes

->Controlled by the forms of merit and demerit, which bestow pleasure and pain,<-
->they attain, in every birth, a body endowed with a specific caste <note>original: "jati"; here referring to species or social station</note>, a lifespan, and experiences born of their past actions. || 7 ||<-

->For these beings, there exists another subtle body, known as the "Linga-sharira" <note>The "subtle body" or "sign-body" that accompanies the soul through transmigrations</note>, which is considered imperishable until final liberation. || 8 ||<-

->The wise know this subtle body to be composed of the subtle elements, the senses, the vital breaths, and the internal states. The Unborn Lord creates this entire universe for the enjoyment and experience of these individual souls. || 9 ||<-

->That Supreme Soul <note>original: "Paramatma"</note> then withdraws the universe into Himself for the sake of rest. This cycle of creation and dissolution is accepted as beginningless in its flow. || 10 ||<-

---

The meaning is that the designation of "individual soul" <note>original: "jiva"</note> is a product of ignorance <note>original: "avidya"</note>, caused by the superimposition of attributes such as limited knowledge, sorrow, and finitude upon that which is actually pure existence and omniscience. He provides an illustration for this: "Just as from a fire..." The word "sparks" is implied here. Just as sparks are designated as parts of the fire (which is of the nature of light) when they are limited by external conditions such as wood, grass, $^1$ or jewels, so it is with the soul. "By those actions..." refers to those individual souls. They are governed by actions in the form of merit and demerit which, in due course, bestow pleasure and pain. That meritorious action bestows pleasure is known from the Scripture <note>original: "Sruti"</note>: "He indeed makes him perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead upward from these worlds." That sinful action bestows pain is known from the Scripture: "He indeed makes him perform bad deeds whom He wishes to lead downward." "By the beginningless..." means that since ignorance—the condition for the soul-hood of the Self who identifies as the "doer"—is beginningless, the actions performed by the soul are also beginningless when viewed as a continuous flow, according to the logic: "Individuals colored by those mental impressions share a common origin." Being "controlled" means being bound. They "attain" or reach, in every single birth, a body joined with a specific species (such as being human), a lifespan, and experiences born of their past actions. By stating that they are "controlled by actions," it is established that the souls' acquisition of a body, and the nature of that body itself, are produced by their past deeds without exception.

<margin>Footnote: $^1$ ...grass, leaves...</margin>

It uses the metaphor of fire and sparks to explain how the one Supreme Soul appears as many individual souls due to ignorance.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discussion regarding the nature of the soul (Jiva) and its relationship to the physical and subtle bodies, following the metaphor of sparks from a fire.</meta>

# The Ocean of Music [Section on the Body]

The qualification "born of action" regarding enjoyment is used here to state that the agency of individual souls is indeed fixed even toward actions performed in this life that yield visible results, such as agriculture and the like. <note>The author argues that even mundane work is governed by the soul's karmic trajectory.</note> *They possess it*—meaning that for those individual souls bounded by the gross physical body, there exists another body, different from the gross one, which is the subtle, unmanifest "sign-body" <term>Lingasharira: the subtle body that carries karmic imprints between incarnations</term>. This is established by sacred texts such as "The Person the size of a thumb" <note>original: "Angushthamatrah Purushah" from the Upanishads</note>. And that subtle body is considered by the scriptures to be imperishable until liberation—that is, until the final realization of one's true nature—because the impressions of one's own ignorance have not yet been severed.

This subtle body consists of the state of the subtle elements, the senses, and the vital breaths. "Elements" refers to earth and the rest; "senses" refers to the eyes and the rest; "vital breaths" refers to the five winds, Prana and the others. It is described as such because its nature is the collective state of these subtle, unmanifest forms along with the internal sense, the mind.

Some maintain the eternity of the world merely as a continuous flow, claiming "the world was never unlike this." To refute that view, the author describes the Supreme Self's agency in the creation and destruction of the world for a specific purpose: *For the individual souls...* For the enjoyment—the experience of pleasure and pain—of the individual souls who identify with the two aforementioned bodies, the world (consisting of elements and elemental objects) is created. The "Unborn" <note>Aja: a title for the Eternal Divine</note> is the Supreme Self. This is the connection. The "supremacy" of the Self means it has attained the status of Lordship in comparison to the lower individual souls. "That Self" refers back to the previously mentioned Brahman. The word "and" is placed differently in the sequence: it connects to "and He withdraws." Then, after the created world has endured for a time, He withdraws it *for the sake of rest*—it should be added here: "for the individual souls"—since both creation and destruction are for the sake of the soul in the manner described. To highlight the beginninglessness of the individual souls, he describes the beginninglessness of the flow of those two: *That very thing...* "Creation and destruction" <note>Srishti-samharam</note> is a compound treated as a singular neuter noun. *Beginningless in its flow*—this means that while individual instances have a beginning, the continuity as a series is without beginning. || 6–10 ||

(Su. <note>Commentary by Simhabhupala</note>) One might object: "The illustration is unequal, because sparks are different from the fire due to the association of contradictory qualities like grossness and subtleness." To this, he says: *Like wood, etc.* By the word "etc.," he includes the single underlying identity of fire found in water-fuel or electricity. Therefore, the difference in sparks and such is due to external conditions <term>Upadhi: a limiting adjunct or condition that makes one thing appear as another</term> and is not ultimate. He explains how those individual souls are bound by actions: *They, through actions...* Now, if Brahman...

<summary>This page discusses the "Lingasharira" (subtle body) that persists through transmigrations and explains that the universe is cyclically created and destroyed by the Supreme Self to provide souls with experience and rest.</summary>
