# First Chapter: On Musical Notes
<meta>—Origin 2]</meta>

->These individual souls are not distinct from the Self, nor is the world distinct from the Self.<-
->Creating through His power, He remains non-different, like gold is to an earring. || 11 ||<-
->Others say He creates through ignorance, just as a rope appears to be a snake.<-

To answer how distinct souls are bound by their actions <term>karma: the law of cause and effect</term>, the text says: "Through beginningless [actions]." These individual souls, in every birth, attain a body, a lifespan, and experiences associated with specific classes of existence—such as being human or bovine—which are produced by the activity of their past actions. Now, if souls are tied to a physical body, how can they undergo many births when the physical body is clearly seen to perish? To this, the text says: "They possess another [body]." This lasts until liberation <term>moksha: release from the cycle of rebirth</term>. If one asks what kind of "subtle body" <term>linga-sharira: the transmigrating entity consisting of mind and senses</term> this is, the text says: "Subtle." It consists of sixteen parts: the five subtle elements and the eleven senses. Now, what is the purpose of the Supreme Lord in the creation and destruction of the world? To this, it says: "For the sake of the souls." Since this process is beginningless, one cannot question its origin; thus it says: "This very thing." The combination of creation and destruction is accepted as a beginningless flow. || 6—10 ||

**(Kallinatha's Commentary)** Asserting the non-difference between the Self and individual souls through the relationship of "part and whole," the author now explains the non-difference between the Self and the world through the relationship of "cause and effect." Following the doctrine of "difference-in-non-difference" <term>bhedabheda: a school of philosophy suggesting the world is both different and non-different from God</term>, he provides an illustration: *These individual souls...* This Self, creating the world through His inherent power of action, is non-different from it. (The word "world" should be connected here by shifting the grammatical case). It is just like the identity between gold and a golden earring. As it is said:
> "In the form of the effect, there is plurality; in the form of the cause, there is non-difference.
> Just as there is non-difference in the nature of gold, but difference in the nature of earrings and such."

Taking the position of the primary Vedantists <note>referring to the Advaita or Non-dualist school</note>, he says: *He creates...* "Others" refers to these Vedantists. *Through ignorance* means through the lack of knowledge of the underlying substratum. The illustration for this is: *as a rope appears to be a snake.* By this, it is shown that the world is a "superimposition" <term>vivarta: an appearance that does not change the essence of the source</term> of the Absolute, as the world is a transformation of reality into an unreal form. || 11, 11- ||

# The Ocean of Music
## [The Origin of the Body]

> ->First from the Self came Space; from Space, Air; from Air, Fire. || 12 ||<-
> ->From Fire came Water; from Water, the Earth was born.<-
> ->These are the Great Elements, and they form the body of the Radiant Creator. || 13 ||<-

**(Sudhakara Commentary)** In response to the question of whether the Supreme Lord is different or non-different from the world, the author says: *Like light.* In creating the world through His power, He is not separate. This is the Supreme Lord. By what kind of power? A power that is both different and non-different from the Self, just like light. For example, light is spoken of as different from the sun when we say "the light of the sun," yet it is also described as non-different when we say "the sun is light." He gives another example: *Gold.* Gold is non-different from an earring in its essence as gold, yet different in its form as an earring. Following the view of the Vedantins <note>Followers of Vedanta philosophy who emphasize the non-duality of reality</note>, he explains the world's nature as a product of ignorance: *He creates.* Just as a rope, through one's own ignorance, "creates" a snake when one imagines "this is a snake," so too does the Supreme Lord—through the ignorance of His own nature as the underlying substratum—create the world starting with Space and the other elements. || 11, 11- ||

**(Kallinatha Commentary)** He describes the physical body <term>Pinda: the microcosm or individual body</term> along with its divisions, following the order of the creation of the elements, starting with the words: *First from the Self.* From the Self, which is the ultimate cause, *first*—meaning prior to Air and the others—Space was produced. The word *then* refers back to Space; from Space as the cause, Air was produced. In the phrase *then Fire,* it means Fire was born from Air. Thus says the Scripture <note>referring to the Taittiriya Upanishad</note>: "From the Self, Space was manifested; from Space, Air," and so on. *These* refer to Space and the rest of the Great Elements <term>Mahabhutas: the five primary elements of ancient Indian physics</term>. The connection is that *this* is the *body of the Radiant Creator* <note>Viraj: the first manifestation of the Absolute in the form of the entire physical universe</note>, the Vast One who is conditioned by these Great Elements. The word *this* points to what is right before us, because the collection of elements is perceptible to all people. Regarding the term *Radiant Creator*: the Self, having created the Great Elements and entered into them, is called the "Radiant One" (Viraj) because He identifies with them. In the phrase *these [elements] are this [body]*, the pronouns take different genders to establish the identity between the elements being described and the body they represent. || 12, 13 ||

<summary>This page explains the cosmological process of creation where the five elements (Space, Air, Fire, Water, Earth) emerge from the Supreme Self to form the physical body of the universe. It uses analogies like the sun's light and the rope-snake illusion to explain the relationship between the Creator and the material world.</summary>

> The Supreme Spirit created the Creator-God and, having delivered the Vedas to him, caused the material world to be created from the words of the Vedas. || 14 ||
> By His command, the Creator-God created the Lords of Creatures through thought alone. From them, the "seminal creation" of bodies is described. || 15 ||
> Bodies are of four types based on their cause: sweat-born, sprout-born, egg-born, and womb-born. Lice and such are from sweat; plants and such are from sprouting. || 16 ||
> Humans and such are from the womb; birds and such are from the egg.

(Sudhakara's Commentary) He explains the order of creation in the verse beginning "From the Self." He states that the "Cosmic Body" is the form of the Creator-God composed of the five great elements in the verse beginning "The great elements..." || 12, 13 ||

(Kallinatha's Commentary) Regarding the verse "The Supreme Spirit created the Creator-God": <term>Brahman</term> <note>The Absolute or Supreme Spirit</note> created the <term>Brahmā</term> <note>The four-faced personified Creator-God</note> in the form of the Cosmic Body. Furthermore, that Supreme Spirit, having given the Vedas (the Rigveda, etc.) to that four-faced God, acted as the "instigating agent" while the Creator acted as the "direct agent." From the words of the <term>Vedas</term> <note>derived from the root 'vid' (to know); that by which Righteousness and Unrighteousness are known</note>—specifically from the words therein which denote forms and archetypes—He caused the material world to be created. Because these words serve as reminders of the objects from previous cosmic cycles, He caused the creation of the material world consisting of the five "grossified" elements, including bodies and sense organs. This means He directed the creation of the material realm. || 14 ||

(Sudhakara's Commentary) An objection: It is common knowledge that <term>Hiranyagarbha</term> <note>The "Golden Womb" or the first manifested deity</note> is the creator of the world; why then is it said that the Supreme Lord is the creator? To this, he says: "The Supreme Spirit..." The Supreme Lord created the Creator-God (Hiranyagarbha), and giving him the Vedas, He caused the material universe to be created—meaning He inspired the Creator-God as he was creating. The phrase "From the words of the Vedas" implies a sequence: after reminding him of the Vedic words, He caused the creation. This aligns with the Scripture: "He who fashioned the Creator-God in the beginning and who delivered the Vedas to him." Therefore, the direct agency belongs to the Creator-God, while the instigating agency belongs to the Supreme Lord. || 14 ||

(Kallinatha's Commentary) He describes the sequence of material creation from the direct agent, the four-faced God, in the verse "By His command." By the command of that Cosmic Being. From those Lords of Creatures comes the <term>seminal</term> <note>original: "raitasī"</note> creation, which takes the form of the transformation of seed.

<summary>This page describes the hierarchical creation of the universe, where the Supreme Spirit inspires the Creator-God (Brahmā) to manifest the physical world using the eternal words of the Vedas as a blueprint. It categorizes biological life into four types based on their origins: sweat, sprouts, eggs, and wombs.</summary>

(Kallinatha Commentary) Among the four types of bodies mentioned, the human body alone is useful for Sound <term>Nada: the sacred primordial sound and musical vibration</term>. This is determined by the process of elimination: plants and such are unconscious; lice and such are too microscopic; birds and others lack a complete system of elements <term>Dhatu: the seven fundamental tissues of the body</term> and channels <term>Nadi: energy or physical conduits</term>. Even among those born from a womb, such as animals, although they possess a complete system of tissues and channels, they lack the power of articulate speech due to their horizontal posture. Therefore, the origin of the human body alone is described here. Thus, he says: "Therefore..." || 17 ||

(Sudhakara Commentary) He gives the reason for specifically describing the human body among all those types of bodies: "Therefore..." || 17 ||

(Kallinatha Commentary) Regarding the creation of that human body from semen, he describes the soul's transition into the womb through a succession of elements starting with the ether, beginning with the verse "The Knower of the Field..." and ending with "it enters the uterus." The "Field" is the body; he who knows it—either as "I am" or "this is mine"—is the "Knower of the Field," the individual soul. As the Blessed Lord <note>Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita</note> said:

> "This body, O son of Kunti <note>Arjuna</note>, is called the Field.
> Those who know this call him who knows it the Knower of the Field."

# The Origin of the Body
## Chapter 1: On Sound and Tone — Page 31

> Nourished by the sacrificial offering and having absorbed the essence of the earth through its rays in the summer, the Sun deposits that watery essence into the clouds; then the cloud <note>original: "balāhaka," a specific term for a rain-cloud</note> releases it. || 19 ||
> When it rains, the individual soul <note>original: "jīva," the living spark or life-force</note> descends to the earth along with the rainfall and, remaining unobserved, enters into the trees and medicinal herbs that grow there. || 20 ||
> From those plants, food is produced; that food, when consumed by men, is transformed into semen <note>original: "śuklatā," literally 'whiteness' or 'purity'</note>. This is then discharged into the "temple of Love" <note>the womb or vaginal tract</note> of a woman who possesses pure menstrual blood. || 21 ||
> If that semen is pure and joins with the menstrual blood within the womb...

Thus it is said. A "cloud" <note>original: "abhra"</note> is a collection of smoke, light, and air; when it contains water, it is called a "rain-cloud" <note>original: "megha"</note>. Regarding the phrase *nourished by the offering*: an "offering" <note>original: "āhuti"</note> refers to substances like sacrificial wood, food, or clarified butter thrown into the fire by a sacrificer with the recitation of mantras for the sake of the deities. The Sun, having been satisfied by this and having "absorbed the essence" (taken the sap or moisture from the earth) via its rays in the summer, creates the "watery essence" or rain. The soul then enters the "trees and medicinal herbs" grown from the earth. Because it is not visible to the eye, it is said to be "unobserved." From those herbs comes "food"—that which is eaten, such as cooked rice. When this food is eaten by men, it becomes the seed. 

Regarding the "woman with pure menstrual blood": "menstrual blood" <note>original: "ārtava"</note> is defined as that which "resembles the color of lac-dye or rabbit's blood and does not stain a cloth permanently when washed." If it is pure, and if the semen is also pure—described in texts as "strong, white, heavy, oily, sweet, and abundant, resembling the appearance of ghee, honey, or oil"—then it is fit for conception. 

*The Action of the Soul:* The semen does not begin the formation of an embryo simply by entering the womb. Rather, it must be "impelled by the soul's karma." This means it is driven by the accumulated past actions of the individual soul that is about to take on a new body. Only when joined with the impulse of these actions, which initiate the process of physical formation, does it begin to develop into an embryo. Here, the term "embryo" refers to the union of semen and blood that has entered the womb as the material cause of the body. || 18–22 ||

---

An "abhra" is a fragment of a cloud that does not rain, while a "megha" is a cloud that does rain. Now, one might ask how water gets into the cloud...

# The Ocean of Music [Chapter on the Body]

->Driven by the soul's past actions <note>Karma</note>, the embryo begins its formation. || 22 ||<-
->In the first month, it becomes a liquid substance called *kalala* <note>a jelly-like or mucus-like state</note>.<-
->In the second month, it becomes a solid mass <gloss>1</gloss>, a fleshy muscle, or a bud-like tumor. || 23 ||<-
->These are the respective early stages for males, females, and the third gender.<-

It is said—"By the offering": By the offering <note>sacrifice</note> prescribed in rituals and the like, the Sun is nourished or satisfied. The Sun, having absorbed the essence <note>water</note> with its rays, deposits that dense essence into the clouds. Regarding the entry of the soul into plants and such through the rain from the clouds, it says—"from that cloud." Regarding the soul's entry into the womb from plants via food and semen, it says—"from those." || 18—22 ||

**Kallinatha's Commentary:** In the manner described, he shows the different states of the embryo in the womb month by month, starting from the first month—"liquid state," etc. "Called *kalala*" means that which has the name *kalala*. *Kalala* refers to the liquid state of the union of semen and blood before it has acquired firmness. "In the second month": A solid mass <term>Pinda: a dense, rounded shape</term> is the early stage of a male to be born; a fleshy muscle <term>Peshi: an oblong or quadrangular shape</term> is the early stage of a female to be born; and a slightly firm bud-like tumor <term>Arbuda: shaped like a silk-cotton flower bud</term> is the early stage of a third-gender person to be born—this is the sequence. "Solid" implies firmness; "fleshy muscle" is quadrangular and mostly flesh; "slightly firm" is so called because it shares characteristics of both the solid mass and the muscle. *Arbuda* is shaped like the bud of a silk-cotton tree, as they say:

> "A fleshy muscle (*peshi*) is known to be quadrangular; a solid mass (*pinda*) is known to be round and dense.
> Physicians know the *arbuda* to be shaped like the bud of a silk-cotton tree."

"In the third month": From the aforementioned solid mass and the rest, the "hands, feet, and head"—the two hands, the two feet, and the head—emerge. Because these are parts of a living being, they are referred to collectively in the singular.

# Chapter on the Path to Heaven
## Section 1: The Origin of the Body
### Page 33

->At that time, the divisions of the major and minor limbs exist simultaneously in subtle form,<-
->excluding the beard, teeth, and such, which appear only after birth.¹ [Verse 25]<-
->This is the natural state; any other is considered a deformity by the wise.<-
->In the fourth month, the distinctness of these parts and their mental dispositions² arises. [Verse 26]<-
->It is said that the dispositions of men are courage and the like, while those of women are timidity and such;<-
->for those of the third gender, these traits are said to be mixed. [Verse 27]<-

Regarding the "sprouts": The limbs are called sprouts because they are just beginning to form, like a head, hands, and feet. This terminology is used to imply the future whole from the present part, following the "logic of the thread and the cloth" <note>original: "sūtra-śāṭaka-nyāya"; a philosophical rule where one refers to a cause (threads) by the name of the effect (cloth) even before the effect is fully realized</note>. This happens simultaneously during the sprout stage.

**The divisions of the major and minor limbs:** In the sprout of the head, there are the divisions of the neck, eyes, nose, ears, etc. In the sprouts of the hands, there are the divisions of the shoulders, elbows, wrists, fingers, etc. In the sprouts of the feet, there are the divisions of the thighs, knees, shins, ankles, toes, etc. These are "subtle," meaning they exist in an unmanifest form.

**This is the natural state:** The production of these major and minor limb divisions in subtle form during the sprout stage—excluding the beard, teeth, and so on which appear after birth—is the "nature" <term>Prakriti: the normal or fundamental state of development</term>. This is the common nature of viviparous <note>womb-born</note> creatures.

**Any other is a deformity:** "Other" refers to a "deformity" <term>Vikriti: a deviation from the natural form</term>, such as the beard or teeth appearing at the same time as the limbs, or the failure of certain limbs to develop, or their development in the wrong place, or having too few or too many fingers and toes.

**In the fourth month:** The "distinctness" of those major and minor limbs refers to their manifestation as separate entities. There is also the manifestation of "dispositions" <note>bhāva</note>, such as courage and other qualities of the self which were previously latent. [Verses 23–27]

By the phrase "beard, teeth, and such," the word "such" implies...

# Ocean of Music [Chapter on the Body]

The heart of this fetus, which is derived from the mother, begins to long for sensory objects. Therefore, one should fulfill the desires of the mother's mind to ensure the prosperity of the fetus. (28)

Wise men call such a woman "the one with two hearts" <note>Sanskrit: *dauhridini*</note>. From the failure to grant these "two-heart longings" <note>Sanskrit: *dohada*</note>, deformities and other defects may arise in the fetus. (29)

Whatever sensory object the mother fails to obtain, the son will be born lacking or pained in that regard. However, if the mother gazes upon a King during her pregnancy longings, the fetus will grow to be wealthy and a seeker of pleasure. (30)

If she longs for ornaments, the child will be charming; if she visits a hermitage of ascetics, the child will be righteous. Upon seeing a deity, the child becomes a devotee; but upon seeing a snake, the child becomes violent. (31)

If she eats the flesh of a monitor lizard, the child will be sleepy; if she eats beef, the child will be strong. By eating buffalo meat, she gives birth to a son with blood-red eyes like a hog and a hairy body. (32)

<column-break/>

Regarding women, the development of breasts and other features should be understood as occurring after birth, as stated in the reasoning. In the fourth month, it is said that the "states of being" <term>bhava: internal dispositions or emotions</term> become manifest. He explains these states by dividing them: "Of men..." (23–27)

<insert>(Commentary by Kallinatha)</insert> **"Derived from the mother..."** The heart of this fetus is born from the mother; and by the use of the word "and," the mother's heart is also implied. Because both of these long for sensory objects, they are connected. The meaning is this: because the heart of the fetus is connected to the heart of the mother, it is the fetus itself that desires these objects. Therefore, one who desires the prosperity of the fetus must certainly fulfill the mother's wishes. **"The one with two hearts..."** The combination of two hearts is "two-heartedness." The state of having this is called *dauhrida* <note>a grammatical derivation from the Sanskrit roots for 'two' and 'heart'</note>. Because of this connection, the fetus is also called *dauhrida*. She who possesses this longing is called *dauhridini*. He describes the fault in not fulfilling these desires: **"From the failure to grant..."** Regarding the *dohridanas*—**longing** <note>original: *dohada*</note> refers to the desire of the pregnant woman; the objects of those desires are also called *dohridanas*. He then describes the excellence or degradation of the child born according to those specific longings: **"The fetus will be..."** and so on. If the pregnant woman sees a King...

->In the fifth month, the mind becomes awakened; there is nourishment of flesh and blood.<-

Through the fulfillment of the mother's longings <note>original: "dohada" — the specific cravings of a pregnant woman believed to reflect the fetus's needs</note>, the child to be born becomes wealthy and a seeker of enjoyment. This should be understood similarly for the subsequent stages. (28-32)

**Sudhakara’s Commentary:** Regarding the phrase "born of the mother": The heart, which is connected to the mother, desires its favorite objects. Alternatively, the connection should be made such that the "mother-born" heart is formed from the mother's own physical components. He explains the term "the woman with two hearts" <note>original: "dauhadini" — a pregnant woman, possessing both her own heart and that of the fetus</note>. Regarding the danger of not fulfilling these cravings: "From non-giving," he mentions the risk of deformity. Deformity includes being one-eyed, blind, or lame. By the word "etcetera," one should understand weakness, lack of energy, and so on. He describes the specific results in the fetus based on specific cravings: "The fetus would be..." Regarding "Buffalo-meat": If a pregnant woman craves buffalo meat, she gives birth to a son with red eyes like a parrot and a hairy body. (28-32)

**Kallinatha’s Commentary:** Regarding "In the fifth": "Awakened" means that the internal faculty <note>original: "antah-karana" — the mind or psyche</note>, which was previously dormant, now becomes inclined toward activity. Regarding "In the sixth": Sinews are fine vessels; "head-hair" refers to hair on the head; "body-hair" refers to hair growing on the limbs. "Strength and complexion": Strength refers to vital energy <note>original: "sattva"</note>, and complexion refers to fairness and so on. Regarding "In the seventh": "With hands tucked between his thighs." "Thigh" <note>original: "pali"</note> is defined as the lap or a fold; thus, the hands are covered or hidden by the thighs. By saying "covering the ear-holes," the text describes the body being contracted with the head facing downwards. "Distressed" means frightened. "Confined within the uterus" means the body is enveloped by the afterbirth <note>original: "jarayu" — the placenta or fetal membrane</note>. Regarding "intent on practice": Here, "practice" refers to...

<page-num>36</page-num>
<header>The Ocean of Music [Embryology-</header>

->Meditating on the means of liberation <note>Moksha</note>, the soul remains intent on spiritual practice.<-
->In the eighth month, the skin and memory are formed, as is the Ojas <note>vital essence</note> residing in the heart. || 36 ||<-
->This essence is pure, slightly yellowish-red, and is considered the cause of life.<-
->It moves restlessly, flowing back and forth between the mother and the fetus. || 37 ||<-
->Therefore, one born in the eighth month does not survive, being deprived of Ojas.<-
->Any brief period of survival is merely due to residual momentum, like a severed limb. || 38 ||<-
->The time for birth occurs in the ninth month or thereafter.<-
->Another vessel, known as the 'Para', is connected to the mother's nutrient-carrying channel. || 39 ||<-

The desire to leave the cycle of rebirth <note>Samsara</note> leads to repeated reflection on the Self. Regarding the phrase "In the eighth [month]": it is said that "skin and memory are formed." Although skin and memory exist even in the seventh month, here it means the skin becomes dense and memory becomes capable of discernment. One should infer that Ojas is also formed. Ojas is the essence of the bodily fluids. This Ojas resides in the heart; it is "pure," meaning unaffected by corrupted humors like wind <note>Vata</note>; it is "slightly yellowish-red" in color; and it is "considered the cause" or the instrumental reason for sustaining life. 

This Ojas is "restless," meaning it does not stay in one place, but runs repeatedly between the mother and the fetus. As the teacher Vagbhata <note>A famous ancient physician</note> said: "In the eighth month, the Ojas moves sequentially between the mother and son." Because the Ojas is unstable in the eighth month, it follows that one born then does not live. This does not refer to the entire duration of the month, but rather means that if the birth occurs at the moment the Ojas has left the fetus to enter the mother, the child does not live because it is "deprived of Ojas." 

Conversely, if the Ojas has left the mother to enter the fetus, the mother may not survive the birth. If birth happens exactly while the Ojas is in transit, neither survives because the essence is not settled in either. Now, one might ask: "In the world, we sometimes see a fetus deprived of Ojas survive for a short time after birth; how can you say they do not live?" To answer this doubt, the author provides a reasoned explanation with an analogy: "For a short time..." This is due to "momentum"—the residual impression of the Ojas's movement. It is like a "severed limb," which [continues to twitch even after being cut off].

# The Origin of the Body
## Chapter 1: Section on Notes (Svaragatādhyāya)

->The umbilical cord, situated at the navel, carries the essence of the mother's food to the fetus. With hands folded and placed against its forehead, the fetus remains positioned against the mother's back. <-

->With its limbs contracted, it stays in the womb on the right side <note>Ancient Ayurvedic texts often associated the right side with a male fetus</note>. A female fetus stays on the left side, and a neuter one is considered to be in the middle. <-

->Then, by the powerful winds of labor <term>Sūti-māruta: the downward-moving vital air or Apāna Vāyu that facilitates childbirth</term>, the infant is turned head-downwards and pushed out through the mechanical opening <note>the birth canal</note>, its body aching from the passage. <-

->Immediately upon birth, the infant seeks the mother's milk. This occurs due to the mental impressions and knowledge from previous births; thus, the eternal nature of the soul is established. <-

***

The term "that limb" is a compound. It means that just as a severed limb is seen moving in the subsequent moment due to the residual impression of the flow of life-breath, so too is this state. **Regarding "In the ninth and so on":** The word "and so on" is used to show that delivery may occur in the ninth month, sometimes in the tenth, or even in the eleventh.

**(Subhaṅkara's Commentary):** In the fifth month, the mind is awakened, meaning the fetus becomes conscious. "Distinctness" refers to becoming clearly manifest through differentiation. "Nourished" means having attained growth. "Covered by the lobes": The ears are covered by the hands being separated by the <term>Karṇapālī: the lobes of the ears</term>. "Distressed" means having attained detachment from the world. "Womb-meditation" refers to the intense meditation and self-reflection within the womb. "Endowed with that": experiencing the pains <note>Yātanā</note>. "Contemplating the means of liberation": thinking of the tools for spiritual freedom. "Devoted to practice": intent on self-realization. He describes the state of the eighth month: "In the eighth..." "Hearing" refers to the perception of external sound, not the sense organ of hearing itself, because the ear—being of the nature of space—is eternal and not "produced" in the usual sense. <term>Ojas: the vital essence or vigor that sustains life</term> is a specific bodily constituent. It is "pure," meaning stainless. It is said that *Ojas* is the cause of life; he explains this further: "Again to the mother..." Regarding how the fetus is nourished, he says: "From the mother..." "Connected to the cord" means mixed with it. "Facing the mother's back" indicates the orientation. By the direction "on the right side," it is understood to be a male.

**(Kallinātha's Commentary):** "By the winds of labor" refers to the vital airs known as *Apāna*. "Through the mechanical opening" means the vaginal opening. "Of that born child..." "Soft" means possessing the quality of softness. "Spleen..." the soul—

"With a body pained," meaning the body is squeezed. "Through the opening of the machine," meaning through the narrow birth canal which acts like a mechanical press. "Habituation" <note>Saatmya</note> refers to a specific impression formed by long-term familiarity. He explains the maternal components: "The soft..." Soft parts are those regions endowed with tenderness. The spleen and liver are specific pieces of flesh located near the heart. "Heart and navel" is a compound term. According to the rules of grammar, this compound is treated as a singular unit because it refers to parts of a living being. || 42 — 46 ||

### First Chapter: On the Nature of Heaven

Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, merit, demerit, and mental impression;
Effort, knowledge, lifespan, and the senses—these are considered the offspring of the Self. || 48 ||
The organs of knowledge are hearing, touch, and sight,

Speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and procreating are, in order,

Some say the senses are born from the Absolute <note>original: "Brahma-yoni"</note>; others claim they are composed of the material elements.

Sight refers to the eye. Taste refers to the tongue. || 49 || He explains the organs of action and their activities: "Speech..." etc. || 50 || Relying on the view of the Vedantins <note>Followers of the Vedanta school of philosophy</note>, he explains the two internal instruments: "Mind and Intellect." Determination is its specific function. || 52 || He describes the cause of the senses according to different schools of thought: "Born from the Absolute..." etc. The Vedantins say the senses have the Absolute as their cause, because the entire world is a transformation of the Absolute. Alternatively, the Samkhya <note>One of the oldest schools of Indian philosophy, emphasizing dualism between spirit and matter</note> thinkers believe they are born from the Absolute and are non-material. Others, the Vaisheshikas <note>The school of atomism and logic</note>, say they are material.

He describes the states born of Habituation <note>original: "satmyajan"</note>: "Clarity..." etc. Health is the state of being free from disease. He divides the elemental qualities within the body: "The body..." etc. Composed of the elements means it is begun by the five great elements <note>Space, Air, Fire, Water, Earth</note>. Even if a body is primarily started by one element, the supporting presence of the other elements certainly exists || 56 ||. Porosity <note>original: "sushirata"</note> is the state of having small holes. Distinctness <note>original: "vaiviktyam"</note> is the state of being separate, existing apart so as to provide the body's individual nature. Subtle intellect is the effortless understanding of even difficult meanings. A "cavity" <note>original: "bilam"</note> is a large opening, whereas "porosity" is small—this is the distinction. He describes the qualities of Air in the body: "From Air..." etc. Touch is the quality. The organ of touch is the skin...

### The beard, hair, nails, teeth, bones, and other hard parts [are derived from the earth element]. There are also constitutions based on the humors like wind (Vata), and constitutions based on the elements like space (Vyoma). || 71 ||

Regarding "from the earth": Stability means being slow to act. Fortitude means remaining unconfused even in times of calamity. Heaviness is the quality that serves as the non-inherent cause of falling. || 70 || He describes other bodily distinctions: "Wind and others" refers to the three humors: Wind (Vata), Bile (Pitta), and Phlegm (Kapha). "Space and others" refers to Space, Air, Fire, Water, and Earth. || 71 || The Pure (Sattvic) body of Brahma and the others is of seven types; the Passionate (Rajasic) body of the Fiends and others is of six types; and the Ignorant (Tamasic) body of animals and others is of three types. To the question of why their specific characteristics are not mentioned, he replies: "Because of [fear of length]" || 72-74 ||

<note>The following section appears to be the commentary by Kallinātha, indicated by (Ka.).</note>

> "The moisture within the receptacles of the tissues, cooked by its own internal heat and covered by phlegm, sinews, and membranes, is called *Kala*, like the pith of wood."

The description of being "covered by sinews" and so on should be understood as applying to both the skin layers and the *Kalas*. These skins and <term>Kalas</term> exist between the tissues; that is, they act as boundaries between the seven tissues (skin, etc.), ensuring that the tissues do not become mixed together. "The first" refers to the first skin and *Kala* named *Mamsadhara*. The other six skins and *Kalas* support blood and the other substances. || 75—78 ||

To the question of where the veins and others originate, he says: "In the flesh." The *Dhamanis* are specific types of veins. The <term>Snayu</term> is a specific binding of the flesh, resembling a thread. Regarding what the other skins and *Kalas* hold, he says: "Blood..." etc. || 75—78 ||

-> When the senses dissolve but the mind remains awake in the heart, that is called the Dream State. <-
-> If the mind also dissolves into the vital breath, then the Self enters Deep Sleep. (85) <-
-> Because the Self drinks in the Supreme Self during sleep, it is traditionally called "the sleeper." <-

<note>The text here provides a philosophical commentary on the physiological states of consciousness.</note> ...and so on. The "abode of consciousness" refers to the place where the Immutable Absolute <note>original: "Kutastha-Brahman"</note> manifests itself. Here, the word "consciousness" does not refer to the individual soul <note>original: "Jiva"</note>. Why? Because that would contradict the sacred scriptures. For the scripture <note>the Chandogya Upanishad</note> states: "Now, this city of Brahman..." and describes the lotus-shaped structure as the dwelling place of the Absolute. Similarly, in the *Bhamati* <note>a famous commentary on the Brahma Sutras</note> under the section regarding the "Small Space" <note>original: "Daharadhikarana"</note>, it begins: "Now, that which is this city of Brahman, a small, subtle, cave-like lotus-dwelling..." and cites the scripture: "All these creatures go day after day to this world of the Absolute, yet they do not find it." This extensive passage argues against the "Small Space" referring merely to the physical sky or the individual soul, and instead establishes it as the Supreme Absolute. Therefore, one should understand that the "Consciousness" presiding over the heart-lotus is indeed the Absolute.

Regarding the phrase "In this...": When this Consciousness (the Absolute) is covered or veiled by darkness—that is, by beginningless ignorance <note>original: "avidya"</note>—and when that heart-lotus closes like a bud, then the Self (the individual soul) sleeps. When that lotus blooms, then the soul wakes and perceives "I am." The word "also" is used in the sense of "and." The point is this: even though the soul exists in a state of individuality due to ignorance of its true nature, it undergoes the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, which are the reasons for the designations "Universal," "Illuminated," and "Cognitive" <note>original: "Vishva, Taijasa, Prajna" — the three technical names for the soul in different states of consciousness</note>. "In two ways": Sleep is general slumber, and its two specific forms are Dreaming and Deep Sleep. (83-85)

When this [lotus] closes, the Self sleeps; when it blooms, the Self wakes. After stating that sleep is of two kinds, he defines them: "In two ways..." The "Citta" is the mind; it remains awake...

When the breath is made to enter there, and the Knots of Brahma, Vishnu, and Rudra are sequentially pierced, the *Kundalini* abandons her natural crookedness and attains straightness. **Bestows immortality**: then, by her own straightness, the *Kundalini* [reaches] the Opening of the Absolute...

# The Jewel Mine of Music
## [The Body]

> The *Svadhisthana* <note>The "Self-Abiding" center</note> is the second chakra, located at the base of the genitals, possessing six petals. || 122 ||
> In the petals starting from the East, the following results are said to occur in sequence:
> Humility, cruelty, the destruction of pride, and then stupor; || 123 ||
> Disrespect, and finally, distrust. This is the abode of the power of desire.

By emerging and piercing the thousand-petaled lotus <note>The Sahasrara chakra at the crown of the head</note>, which is the reservoir of nectar, with the tip of its own tail, it causes the nectar to flow. || 120-121 ||

**(Sudhakara Commentary)** Having thus described the major and minor limbs, the author begins to describe the chakras, starting with "between the anus and the genitals." Between the anus and the genitals lies the chakra known as the *Adhara* <note>The Muladhara or "Root Support" center</note>, which has the form of a four-petaled lotus. He describes the results of these four petals: "Supreme," etc. In the Northeast petal is Supreme Bliss; in the Southeast petal is Natural Bliss; in the Southwest petal is Heroic Bliss; and in the Northwest petal is the Bliss of Yoga. From this, it is understood that the four petals of the Root Lotus are situated in the intermediate directions. "There is," he says: The power of Brahman <note>The ultimate reality</note> called *Kundalini* <note>The "Coiled One," representing dormant spiritual energy</note> resides in the Root Lotus, so called because it is the cause of attaining Brahman. When this energy is led straight up to the aperture of Brahman <note>The Brahmarandhra at the top of the head</note>, it bestows nectar and liberation. || 120-121 ||

**(Kallinatha Commentary)** Regarding the *Svadhisthana*: Above the Root Chakra, at the base of the genitals, is the second chakra named *Svadhisthana*, having six petals. He describes the results such as humility in the petals starting from the East: "And of this," etc. "There would be disrespect"—this instruction is oriented toward spiritual practice. || 122-123 ||

**(Sudhakara Commentary)** He describes the chakra known as *Svadhisthana*: It has the form of a six-petaled lotus. He describes the results of these six petals: "And of this," etc. Humility (modesty) is the result of the petal located in the East. This means the soul situated there becomes humble. Cruelty is the intent to perform evil deeds. Pride is the feeling of self-exaltation; its destruction is the next result. Stupor is an excess of delusion. Disrespect is disregard for others. Distrust is being suspicious of everything or a lack of confidence. This *Svadhisthana* chakra is the home and support of the power that produces desire. || 122-123 ||

(Simhabhupala) <note>Another major commentator on the Sangita Ratnakara</note> He describes the *Manipura* wheel: **In the navel**. He then describes the fruits of its petals starting from the east: **Deep sleep**, etc. "Deep sleep" (*sushupti*) is the state where the external senses and the mind cease their activity. "Thirst" (*trishna*) is desire. "Envy" (*irshya*) is the inability to tolerate the virtues of others. "Slander" (*pishunata*) is pointing out the faults of others, whether real or imagined. "Shame" and "fear" are well-known. "Disgust" (*ghrina*) is the desire to avoid the suffering of others <note>often interpreted here as a sensitive aversion</note>. "Delusion" (*moha*) is the lack of awareness of objects even in the waking state. "Impurity" (*kashaya*) is having a clouded or stained disposition. "Despondency" (*vishada*) is sorrow accompanied by anxious thought. That *Manipura* wheel is the "house" or abode of the vital breath named *Bhanu* (the Sun). || 124-125 || He then describes the *Anahata* wheel: **In the heart**. It is the place of worship for Shiva who has the form of the *Pranava* (the syllable Om); the meaning is that one should worship the Supreme Lord by meditating on Him residing there. He describes the fruits of the Self residing in the twelve petals starting from the east: **Instability**, etc. "Instability" (*laulya*) is the state of being fickle...

# The Ocean of Music
## [The Origin of the Body]

->The Vishuddhi Chakra<-

In the throat lies the seat of Bharati <note>The Goddess of Speech, Saraswati</note>, known as the *Vishuddhi* <note>The "Pure" center</note>, which possesses sixteen petals. || 129 ||

The sixteen fruits or effects experienced by the soul when residing in the petals (starting from the East) are:
1. The Sacred Syllable *Om* (*Pranava*)
2. The Chanted Hymn (*Udgiṭha*)
3. The sound *Hum-phat* <note>A mantra used in rituals for protection or driving away obstacles</note>
4. The exclamation *Vashat* <note>Used when making an offering to deities</note>
5. The exclamation *Swadha* <note>Used when making offerings to ancestors</note>
6. The exclamation *Swaha* <note>Used when making offerings to gods</note>
7. The salutation *Namah*
8. Nectar (*Amrita*)
9. The seven musical notes (Shadja and the others)
10. Poison <note>Representing the dualities of existence found in the throat center</note>
|| 130 ||

Thus are the sixteen fruits in the soul located on the petals starting from the East. In the uvula <note>the small fleshy piece hanging above the throat</note> is the chakra named *Lalana*, which has twelve petals. || 131 ||

The fruits in the *Lalana* chakra, located on the petals starting from the East, are:
Intoxication, pride, affection, sorrow, suffering, greed,
discontent, agitation, the "waves" <note>The six physical and mental urges</note>, faith, satisfaction, and obstruction. || 132 ||

---

<margin>Commentary on the psychological states</margin>

The destruction of that [state] is "stillness." "Manifest" is used as an adjective for "deliberation." Deliberation is the consideration of which of two options should be accepted. "Remorse" is the state of having regret. "Embrace" is the desire for attainment. "Radiance" is the absence of hiding one's form. "Anxiety" is mere pondering. "Effort" is the desire to avoid the undesirable. "Equanimity" is viewing all things without a sense of superiority or inferiority. "Hypocrisy" is performing rituals without faith merely to gain public approval. "Frailty" is instability. "Discernment" is performing actions after proper reflection. "Egoism" is the determined will to do a task even if it is impossible. || 126-128 ||

<gloss>Kallinatha's Commentary</gloss>
Regarding the "Chanted Hymn" (*Udgiṭha*): it is the second part of a Samavedic chant. Indeed, there are five parts to a chant—the Prelude (*Prastava*) is the first, the Chanted Hymn (*Udgiṭha*) is the second, the Response (*Pratihara*) is the third, the Withdrawal (*Upadrava*) is the fourth, and the Conclusion (*Nidhana*) is the fifth. The "Sacred Syllable" (*Pranava*) is the syllable *Om* to be used at the beginning of the *Udgiṭha*. "In the uvula" means at the root of the tongue. The "waves" (*urmi*) are the six waves: hunger, thirst, sorrow, delusion, old age, and death. || 129-132 ||

<gloss>Simhabhupala's Commentary</gloss>
He describes the chakra named *Vishuddhi*: "In the throat..." It is the "Seat of Bharati," meaning the residence or refuge of the Goddess Saraswati. The meaning is that the Goddess of Speech, when meditated upon there, bestows the wealth of eloquence. He describes the sixteen fruits of the soul situated on the petals of this chakra starting from the East: "Therein..." The *Pranava* is the syllable *Om*. By meditating on the *Pranava* in the eastern petal, the soul attains spiritual welfare. The *Udgiṭha*...

# First Chapter on the Nature of Sound

->Between the eyebrows is the three-petaled wheel known as the Command Center (*Ajna-chakra*); its fruits are:<-
->The manifestations of Purity, Passion, and Ignorance, considered in their respective order.<-
->Beyond that is the Mind-Wheel (*Manas-chakra*), which has six petals; its fruits are:<-
->Dreaming, the enjoyment of taste, smelling, the perception of form,<-
->Touching, and the awareness of sound, located in the petals starting from the East.<-

<note>The text describes the "Ajna" chakra as having three petals corresponding to the three Gunas or qualities of nature: Sattva (purity/light), Rajas (activity/passion), and Tamas (darkness/inertia).</note>

Regarding the specific divisions of the Samavedic chants: This means one should meditate on the *Udgitha* <note>The principal part of a Samavedic chant</note> located on the second leaf as part of the worship of the *Udgitha*. *Hum-phat* is an indeclinable word used when offering oblations. So too is *Vashat*. *Svadha* is the word used when offering oblations to the Ancestors. *Svaha* is used for the Gods. *Namah* is the word for salutation. These are to be meditated upon in their respective petals. "Nectar" refers to *Amrita* <note>The drink of immortality</note>. The soul situated in that petal becomes happy, as if bathed in nectar. The seven notes are *Shadja* and the others: *Shadja, Rishabha, Gandhara, Madhyama, Panchama, Dhaivata,* and *Nishada*. Their respective petals are the locations for meditation. "Poison" should be explained as the opposite of nectar; the soul situated in the "poison-petal" becomes miserable.

He now describes the wheel called *Lalana*: It is located at the uvula <note>The small fleshy part hanging above the throat</note>. He describes the fruits of its petals: Pride, which is intoxication. Arrogance, which is the failure to distinguish between what should and should not be done due to a sense of superiority. Affection, which is tenderness. Grief, which is sorrow with a known cause. Distress, which is sorrow without a known cause. Greed, which is an excess of desire. Dissatisfaction, which is agitation even in the presence of the means of happiness. Agitation, which is sudden impulse. The "Six Waves" are well-known in the *Agama* scriptures:

> "Hunger and Thirst; Sorrow and Delusion; Old Age and Death.
> These are the six waves residing in the breath, the intellect, and the body."

Faith is the belief in the existence of the divine. Contentment is self-explanatory. Courtesy is consideration for others.

(Kallinatha's commentary): "Tears of meditation" refers to tears born from the intensity of meditation.

(Simhabhupala's commentary): He describes the three-petaled Command Center (*Ajna-chakra*): It is between the eyebrows. He describes its fruits: The manifestations. In the first petal, the manifestation of Purity (*Sattva*); in the second petal, the manifestation of Passion (*Rajas*)...

Above that is the sixteen-petaled Moon Cycle <note>original: "Soma-chakra"</note>. In its sixteen petals, the sixteen phases <note>original: "kala"</note> of the moon reside. (136)

"Effort" is industriousness. "Clarity" is an unpolluted mind. "Generosity" is being naturally brave in giving. "One-pointedness" is total concentration.

When the soul is situated there, it desires or attains the perfection of singing, dancing, and instrumental music. The experts in Yoga scripture know that the first and following petals are the destroyers of music. Regarding the soul's position in the <term>Brahmarandhra</term>: staying there, the soul is as if drenched in nectar, reaching a state of bliss; satisfied and free from worldly desire, it perfectly executes singing and the arts. Having thus described the petals that aid or destroy music, the author describes the neutral ones: in the remaining petals of the <term>Anahata</term><note>The heart chakra.</note>, <term>Vishuddhi</term>, and <term>Lalana</term> chakras, or in other chakras such as the <term>Manipura</term><note>The navel chakra, associated with fire and digestion.</note>, the soul remains indifferent toward the perfection of music. || 133-144 ||

> ->The bulb of the body is four finger-widths in height and breadth.<-

**The center of the body:** It is called the center of the body because it is situated midway between the upper and lower parts of the body. **From that chakra:** below the chakra at the center of the body. **The Knot of Brahma:** It is called the Knot of Brahma because it is the seat presided over by Brahma <note>the creator deity</note>. **In its center:** in the middle of the Knot of Brahma. **The Navel Chakra is twelve-spoked:** meaning it possesses twelve spokes. Because the Navel Chakra consists of a mass of energy vessels <term>Nadis: channels through which vital energy flows</term> forming a warp and woof, the analogy of a spider's web is used. **Enveloping:** making that which was not a bulb into a bulb <note>a grammatical note on the Sanskrit 'chvi' suffix indicating transformation</note>. These vessels, through their branches, cause the bulb-shaped mass to extend into the form of the body. ॥ 145-150 ॥

**(Simhabhupala's Commentary):** He describes the location of the flame of fire: **From the base.** At a distance of two finger-widths above the Base Chakra <note>Muladhara</note> and two finger-widths below the male organ, there is a space of one finger-width, gold-colored, which is the center of the body. There, a thin flame of fire resides. Nine finger-widths from that chakra—either from the center of the body or the base—is the bulb. He describes the Knot of Brahma: **Of the body.** The bulb is the cause of the body's expansion. "Height" refers to its vertical elevation. Located at the navel, it measures four finger-widths. Its name is the Knot of Brahma. **In its center:** In the middle of that Knot of Brahma, there is a chakra called the Navel Chakra with twelve petals. Like a spider <note>original: "luta"</note>, the soul wanders there. **Through the central channel:** extending from the base to the crown of the head...

->These channels are very numerous, but among them, fourteen are declared to be the primary ones:<-
->The *Sushumna*, *Ida*, and *Pingala*; then *Kuhu* and *Sarasvati*;<- 151
->*Gandhari*, *Hastijihva*, *Varuni*, and *Yashasvini*;<-

->And *Alambusa*. Among these, the first three are considered the most important.<-
->Of those three, the *Sushumna* is the most excellent; it belongs to Vishnu and leads to the path of liberation.<- 153
->It is situated in the middle of the *kanda* <note>The "bulb" or root center of the subtle body</note>. To its left is the *Ida*, and to its right is the *Pingala*.<-

->They are the causes of the passage of time; the *Sushumna* is the "Consumer of Time."<-

The *Sushumna* channel. Through it, [the breath] ascends from that [root] up to the aperture of Brahma <note>original: *brahmarandhra*; the fontanelle at the crown of the head</note> and descends from the aperture of Brahma. "Mounted on the breath" means it is embraced by the vital air. Like a "tightrope walker" <note>original: *kohalatiko*; an acrobat or dancer on a precarious path</note>. Surrounding the *Sushumna* on all sides, having embraced and pervaded the *kanda*—the knot of Brahma <note>original: *brahmagranthi*</note>—the channels extend and expand throughout the body. —149-150

(Kallinatha) **By the passage of time**: Here, the word "time" refers to the moments of the Sun's movement which cause the various states of the individual body; these are essentially the lifespan. "Passage" means their exhaustion or decay. **Consumer of Time**: Here, the word "time" refers to Death; the *Sushumna* is its "consumer" because it obstructs or prevents death. —151-155

(Simhabhupala) He declares that among those channels, fourteen are the primary ones: **These...** 150-. He gives their names: **Sushumna...** Among the fourteen, he states the importance of the three channels—*Sushumna*, *Ida*, and *Pingala*—and among those, the preeminence of the *Sushumna*: **Among these, the first...** He gives the reason for the *Sushumna's* preeminence: **Belonging to Vishnu...** "Belonging to Vishnu" means its presiding deity is Vishnu. Or, it means it is of the nature of the *Vaishnavi Maya* <note>The creative power of the Divine</note>. "Leading to the path of liberation" means it bestows final release. Or, the "path of liberation" is the Self <note>Atman</note> which is the means to release; it relates to that, meaning it is the seat or foundation of the Self.

<header>Sentiments: 3] First Chapter: On Musical Notes 63</header>

## By the worship of Sound, the gods Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva
## are surely worshipped, because they are manifestations of that Sound. || 2 ||

Sound is indeed Consciousness <note>Sanskrit: *Caitanya*</note>, because it shares the quality of illuminating all objects through the nature of "Bursting Forth" <note>The linguistic theory of *Sphota*, where meaning bursts forth from sound</note> and is thus the subject of the superimposition of consciousness. It is the Reality that appears in the form of the visible world of moving and unmoving things, though in truth it remains unchanged; this is because Sound is the substratum upon which the entire world of names and forms is superimposed, just as all speech—consisting of microtones <term>Shruti: the smallest intervals of sound</term> and letters—is reflected in it. Because this Sound manifests Bliss, the form of Bliss is superimposed upon it. It is non-dual, and because it shares the nature of the Absolute <note>Brahman</note> as the cause of the expansion of its own effects like musical notes <term>Svara: the seven notes of the scale</term>, the quality of oneness is attributed to it.

"That" is well-known to all the world. "Sound-Absolute" <note>Nada-Brahman</note> means that Sound is itself the Absolute; this is a metaphor where the identity is primary. Without denying the Sound that is the subject of this superimposition, it is treated as a complete metaphorical image possessing parts like consciousness. The phrase "We worship" uses the plural form according to the grammatical rule "of the 'I' and of the two" <note>A reference to Panini’s grammar regarding the use of the first-person plural</note>.

The underlying intention is this: Sound, which is a synonym for the Supreme Speech <note>Para-vak</note> and the power of the Absolute, is extremely close to the Absolute. By worshipping it, the attainment of the Absolute occurs, just as one who follows the light of a jewel eventually attains the jewel itself. As it has been said:

> "Therefore, through the perception of the truth of the expansion of song, microtones, and the rest,
> there may be the attainment of the Supreme Self, whose form is Truth, Consciousness, and Bliss;
> just as the attainment of a jewel happens for one who follows its light,
> because of the extreme proximity."

And also, "By the playing of the Lute..." <note>A reference to a famous verse stating that playing the Veena leads to liberation</note> and so on. Now, one might ask: while there are other well-known deities with attributes available for worship, why worship the seemingly unconscious Sound as the Absolute? To this, the author says: "By the worship of Sound..." and provides the reason: "Because they are manifestations of that." Here, "that" refers back to the Sound-Absolute. The meaning is that they are non-different from it. || 1, 2 ||

## The Ocean of Music

The Self <note>Atman; the individual soul or consciousness</note>, desiring to speak, impels the mind; the mind strikes the fire residing in the body, which in turn impels the breath. || 3 ||

Then that breath, stationed in the "Knot of Brahma" <note>Brahmagranthi; a yogic energy center located near the base of the spine</note>, moving upwards along the path, progressively manifests sound in the navel, the heart, the throat, the head, and the mouth. || 4 ||

Stationed in these five locations respectively, the sound assumes five names: the very subtle, the subtle, the developed, the undeveloped, and the artificial. || 5 ||

The syllable *na* is known as the name of breath <note>Prana</note>, and the syllable *da* is known as fire <note>Anala</note>. Because it is born from the union of breath and fire, it is called *Nada* <note>Sound</note>. || 6 ||

---

(Su.) <note>Commentary by Simhabhupala</note> Having thus described the physical body as the cause of the *Shrutis* <note>micro-tones</note> and other musical elements, and wishing to describe the *Shrutis* and notes themselves, the author performs an auspicious invocation suitable to the subject: "Consciousness..." We worship that Sound-Absolute <note>Nadabrahma</note>. It is the consciousness of all beings, or the fruit of consciousness; for without sound, what difference would there be between sentient beings and insentient things like stones? In the context of the Absolute <note>Brahman</note>, it is the consciousness or knowledge of all beings, as the scripture <note>Upanishad</note> says: "The Absolute is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinity." It is transformed into the form of the universe; because sound is famous throughout the world, it is said to be transformed into the world's form. Even in the context of the Absolute, "transformation" <term>Vivarta: an appearance that does not change the essence of the underlying reality</term> refers to the appearance of a formless state as having form. Thus, the Absolute itself transforms into the shape of the universe. It is Bliss, the means of happiness. In the other sense, it is happiness itself, as the scripture says: "He knew the Absolute as Bliss." It is non-dual, incomparable, and extraordinary. In the context of the Absolute, it is devoid of differences—whether of the same kind, different kinds, or within itself. Here, the poetic figure of speech is a "compressed metaphor" <note>Shlishta-rupaka</note>. To the question "Why is sound worshipped?", he says: "By the worship of sound..." The gods like Brahma and others are worshipped through the worship of sound, because they are composed of it. This means they are identical with sound. || 1, 2 ||

He explains the different designations of sound: **"Sound is extremely subtle,"** etc. He provides the etymological derivation of the word *Nada* <note>Nada: the primordial sound or vibration that underlies all music and creation</note> based on its components: **"The letter *Na*,"** etc. *Prana-namanam* means that which has the name *Prana* <note>Prana: the vital life-force or breath</note>. <gloss>(Sudhakara commentary)</gloss> He explains the process of the production of sound: **"The Self,"** etc. The Self, desiring to speak, impels the mind (the internal organ). That mind, impelled by the Self, strikes the digestive fire residing in the body. That fire impels the wind (breath). That wind, situated at the "Knot of Brahma" <note>Brahmagranthi: a psychic center or knot located near the base of the spine/navel area</note>, being impelled by that fire and moving upward, manifests sound through impact in the navel, heart, throat, head, and mouth. In other texts, "thick" and "thin" are named "manifest" and "unmanifest." Thus it was said by Matanga <note>Matanga: an ancient musicologist and author of the Brihaddeshi</note>:

> and the artificial in the region of the mouth; these five are to be known by the wise."

<header>The Ocean of Music [Section on Locations and Intervals]</header>

->In musical practice, this sound is threefold: it is called low in the heart,<-
->medium in the throat, and high in the head; each subsequent one being twice the pitch of the former. || 7 ||<-

By adding the primary suffix, the form *Nada* <note>Sound/Resonance</note> is established. However, Matanga <note>An ancient musicologist, author of the Brihaddesi</note> has shown the etymology as "that which resonates" (*nadyate*). Thus it has been said:

> "The letter *Na* is said to be breath (Prana), and the letter *Da* is considered fire (energy).
> This true meaning of the word *Nada* has been declared by me.
> This *Nada* comes from the root *nad* (to roar/sound), and it is of five kinds."

— verses 3-6

**(Kallinatha's Commentary)** He explains the alternative names and the differences in their nature with the phrase: *In musical practice...* "Practice" (*vyavahara*) here refers to song; it is within song that these apply. The word "but" (*tu*) distinguishes this from other contexts. It means this specific classification does not apply to the locations of the navel or the heart-space in the same way. Regarding the phrase *each subsequent one being twice the pitch*: "subsequent" means the medium is after the low, and the high is after the medium. "Twice" (*dviguna*) refers to the effort of articulation; that which has two parts of effort is "double." The meaning is this: the same note (such as *Shadja* <note>The tonic or first note of the scale, 'Sa'</note>) located in the medium register requires twice the effort of articulation compared to the same note in the low register. In terms of ascending the scale from a previous position, it refers to the eighth note <note>The octave</note>. Although the text refers to "sound" in general here, the doubling is intended for sound in the form of musical notes (*Svaras*), as these are useful in practice. If one were referring to sound in the form of micro-intervals (*Shrutis*), then the twenty-third interval would be the double. || 7 ||

**(Simhabhupala's Commentary)** He explains the practical utility of the three types of sound: *In musical practice...* In the practice of singing—whereas in the practice of naming objects like "pot" or "cloth," even sounds produced in the mouth are useful. The sound produced in the heart is called low (*Mandra*); that produced in the throat is medium (*Madhya*); and that in the head is high (*Tara*). He describes their measurement as *twice the pitch*: the medium is twice the low, and the high is twice the medium. As stated in the *Sangita-samaya-sara* <note>The Essence of the Music of the Times</note>:

> "Briefly, there are three locations: the heart, the throat, and the head.
> Within each of these, there are twenty-two varieties <note>Referring to the 22 Shrutis or micro-tones in each register</note>."

# The Ocean of Music
## Chapter 1: Sound and Pitch

The third pitch is slightly higher than the second, as indicated by the comparative suffix <note>original: "tarap-prayoga"</note>. This relationship should be understood similarly between the third and fourth microtones, and so on. Thus, the principles explained for the first location <note>the heart</note> are applied to the next two locations—namely, the throat and the head.

<insert>Sudhakara Commentary</insert> Now, the author explains the divisions of that sound. There are twenty-two distinct divisions of sound, and these are called <term>Shrutis</term> <note>literally "that which is heard"; the smallest audible intervals of pitch in Indian music</note>. He explains the etymology: they are called Shrutis because they are heard. As stated by the sage <term>Matanga</term> <note>an ancient musicologist, author of the Brhaddeshi</note>:

> "By applying the suffix 'ktin' to the verbal root meaning 'to hear,' 
> those learned in language establish the word 'Shruti' 
> as a term for the action of hearing."

Regarding whether Shruti is one or many, there is great scholarly disagreement. <term>Matanga</term> argues that sound, impelled by human effort through the union of the body’s space and breath, rises upward from the navel through the ether. Like smoke rising or someone climbing a staircase, it ascends in various ways according to the will of the breath. It appears divided into categories—such as the four-microtone interval—due to the internal fulfillment of the listener's perception.

However, the authority <term>Vishvavasu</term> spoke of a twofold nature of Shruti. He says:

> "Because it is perceived by the sense of hearing, sound itself is Shruti. 
> It is one, yet known as twofold based on the intervals between notes. 
> Because they are sung in the seven song-forms based on fixed positions, 
> those who know Shruti recognize them as belonging to the notes. 
> The intermediate microtones existing between notes are considered 'internal' Shrutis."

Some scholars claim there are three types of Shrutis due to their connection with the three registers <note>chest, throat, and head</note>. Some say there are twenty-two. Others say sixty-six. Still others claim they are infinite. As <term>Kohala</term> <note>another foundational ancient music theorist</note> says:

> "Some experts in the investigation of microtones cite twenty-two; 
> others say they are divided into sixty-six; 
> while others still assert their infinity."

In that regard, the distinction between them is established in reality because of the presence of opposing qualities, such as being low, sharp, or extra-sharp. As it is said: "This very thing is the difference, or the cause of difference: the presence of opposing attributes and the difference in causes." However, because we recognize the same Shrutis and the same <term>Swaras</term> <note>musical notes</note> in the low, middle, and high registers, the idea of absolute difference is not established. Therefore, the position that there are twenty-two Shrutis is the most correct.

<summary>This page discusses the definition and count of 'Shrutis' (microtones), citing ancient authorities like Matanga, Vishvavasu, and Kohala to debate whether musical intervals are singular, twenty-two, sixty-six, or infinite.</summary>

# Chapter One: On Musical Notes
<page-num>69</page-num>
<sig>-2 Sa: 3]</sig>

->To make these clear, we shall provide a demonstration on two lutes. || 10 ||<-
->Two lutes should be made identical so that their sound is exactly the same.<-
->On each of them, there should be twenty-two strings; among these, the first || 11 ||<-
->should be made to have the lowest possible sound, and the second slightly higher.<-
->There should be no gap between the two microtonal intervals, as no other sound should be heard between them. || 12 ||<-

Thinking thus, he stated there are twenty-two <term>Shrutis</term> <note>microtonal intervals or "audible sounds"</note>. He gives the reason for this specific number: "In the heart." In the heart, there is the upward-flowing channel called the <term>Sushumna</term> <note>the central energy channel in yogic anatomy</note>; attached to it are twenty-two transverse <note>horizontal</note> channels. Through the contact of the vital breath <note>Prana or Maruta</note> with these channels, exactly that many sounds are produced. He demonstrates the progression of these sounds: "Higher and higher." They are characterized by being progressively higher and even higher. This means the first sound is the lowest, the next is high, the one after that is higher, and the one after that is the highest. Having explained the method of microtonal production in the heart, he applies the same principle to the throat and the head. || 8-9 ||

(Kallinatha's Commentary) Since the arrangement of the specific number of channels in each location of the body and the production of microtones therein is imperceptible to the senses, there might be doubt regarding their existence. To dispel such doubt and to provide a demonstration through direct perception, he begins the section starting with "To make these clear." "Identical" means identical in form. "So that their sound is exactly the same"—the two lutes should be constructed such that, by virtue of their identical shape, their sound becomes identical. This implies that the identical shape, characterized by lightness and other qualities, is the cause for the equality of sound. "Among these"—meaning among the twenty-two strings on each of the two lutes. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> is used to include the strings of the second lute. "The first" refers to the first string, meaning the one closest to the performer. "The lowest possible sound" <note>original: "mandratama-dhvana"</note>—even though each preceding string is lower than the succeeding one, the superlative suffix is used here because this one is the lowest of all. This extremely low sound is achieved by making the string very loose. It should be made just loose enough so that the resonant sound is still possible. The second string should be made to have a "slightly higher sound." He defines what "slightly higher" means: "There should be no gap." Between the preceding and succeeding microtones...

### 13. Those notes produced from the strings, becoming progressively higher and sharper, are considered Shrutis. On two Vinas <note>The Vina is a traditional Indian stringed instrument used here as a scientific tool for measurement</note>, the notes should be established; among them, Shadja <note>The tonic or first note, similar to 'Do'</note> consists of four Shrutis.

Between two sounds produced from a string, if no other distinct sound is heard—meaning a sound that is different from the preceding or succeeding microtone, slightly higher than the former and slightly lower than the latter—then that interval is established. The reason for this is the "non-hearing" <note>original: "ashruti"</note> of any intermediate sound. By making the non-hearing of an intermediate sound the criterion, the strings should be slightly tightened to produce a marginally higher sound so that the microtones are continuous. Here, continuity is spoken of regarding the sounds themselves, not the physical positions of the strings on the crossbar or neck of the instrument. Therefore, even if a physical space is seen between the strings on the neck, one should not doubt the possibility of an intermediate sound.

The mention of the "second" string is illustrative. By this, it is meant that the third and subsequent microtones should also be produced by progressively tightening the strings to create slightly higher sounds relative to the preceding ones. When done this way, those strings become "lower and lower" in physical position but "sharper and sharper" <note>original: "adharadhara-tivra"</note> in pitch. It should be understood that just as microtones are produced in the human body as progressively higher pitches, they are produced on the Vina in the same ascending manner. The sound <term>Nada: the primordial musical sound</term> produced by striking those strings is recognized as a <term>Shruti: the smallest interval of pitch that the human ear can detect</term>.

Regarding the etymology of the word "Shruti" and the various opinions on whether Shrutis are one or many, the sage Matanga has shown different viewpoints. For example:

> "When the suffix 'ktin' is properly attached to the verbal root meaning 'to hear,' this word 'Shruti' is established by grammarians as an object of action."

That which is heard is a Shruti. Is it one or many? Some say Shruti is only one. To explain: first, through the union of the body's internal space and breath, impelled by human effort, the sound rises upward from the navel into the space of the throat. Like smoke, it ascends in various ways according to the movement of the breath, like a flight of stairs. Because it fulfills the sense of completing a scale, it appears divided into four Shrutis and so on; this is my own view. Others, however, believe Shruti to be of two types. How? Based on the division between different musical notes. Thus said the celestial musician Vishvavasu:

The note <term>Rishabha</term><note>The second note of the scale, often abbreviated as 'Ri'</note>, possessing three micro-tones, should be established on the fourth string. Then, the note <term>Gandhara</term><note>The third note of the scale, abbreviated as 'Ga'</note>, possessing two micro-tones, should be established on the third string from the fifth. || 14 ||

> "Sound itself becomes a <term>Shruti</term><note>original: 'shruti'; the smallest audible interval of pitch or a 'micro-tone'</note> because it is perceived by the sense of hearing.
> It is known as one, yet is of two types based on the division between musical notes.
> Because they reside in fixed micro-tonal positions, the seven notes are sung in songs.
> Therefore, those who know micro-tones should understand them as being inherent to the notes."

This means they take the form of pure notes.

> "The intermediate micro-tones are considered to exist between the notes."

This means they take the form of modified <insert>chromatic</insert> notes. The use of the plural "micro-tones" is due to the frequency of their use in practice.

> "The variation in these also arises from the division of performance and the scales."

Some believe the <term>Shruti</term> is of three types due to its connection with the three registers <note>lower, middle, and upper</note>. Others believe the <term>Shruti</term> is of three types due to the "deficiency of the senses." This sensory deficiency is threefold: innate, caused by humoral imbalance, or caused by external injury. Here, the "sense" refers to the mind. In this context, "innate" is associated with the quality of purity <note>Sattva</note>, "imbalance" with passion and ignorance <note>Rajas and Tamas</note>, and "injury" refers to being impaired by tastes such as sourness. Still others have asserted that the <term>Shruti</term> is of four types, distinguished by the humors: wind, bile, phlegm, and their combination. As <term>Tumburu</term><note>A celestial musician and ancient authority on music</note> says:

> "A very high and harsh sound is known by the wise to be born of wind <note>Vata</note>.
> A deep, thick, and resonant sound is known to be born of bile <note>Pitta</note>.
> A smooth, delicate, and sweet sound is born of phlegm <note>Kapha</note>.
> A sound possessing the qualities of all three is known to be born of their combination <note>Sannipata</note>."

These, however, will be discussed as varieties of sound. Other sages, such as Venu and others, believe the <term>Shruti</term> is of nine types. For instance—

# The Ocean of Music
## [Chapter on Microtones and Notes]

From the eighth <note>referring to the finger-hole or position</note> to the second, the **Madhyama** <note>the fourth note, F</note> is produced, consisting of four microtones. From the tenth to the fourth, the **Panchama** <note>the fifth note, G</note> is produced, also consisting of four microtones. From the fourteenth to the fourth, the **Dhaivata** <note>the sixth note, A</note> is produced, consisting of three microtones.

> "The application of notes—whether they consist of two, three, or four microtones—should be performed by the wise through the finger-holes of the flute."

As was also stated by **Bharata** <note>the legendary author of the Natyashastra</note>:

> "The notes produced on the flute should be understood as having two, three, or four units. These notes are produced by fingers that are trembling, half-covering the hole, or fully uncovering it. Thus, I have correctly explained these nine microtones."

It should be understood that these six aforementioned opinions were put forward by accepting the identity <note>non-difference</note> between the note and the microtone. However, these views are not entirely accurate because they deny the distinction between the note and the microtone, which actually possess different forms—one being the manifester and the other being the manifested.

On this subject, some scholars whose intellects are strengthened by **Mimamsa** <note>the school of Vedic hermeneutics and logic</note> believe there are twenty-two microtones. Others, however, say that the microtones are divided into sixty-six varieties. Still others describe the microtones as being infinite. As **Kohala** <note>an ancient musicologist</note> said:

> "Some experts in the investigation of microtonal knowledge cite twenty-two microtones. Some say they are divided into sixty-six, while others maintain their infinity."

Regarding that:

> "The wise suggest the infinity of microtones just as there is an infinity of distinct sounds within the belly of the sky. The succession of waves arising from the mass of water tossed by high winds cannot be reduced to a specific number."
