<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of musical intervals (shrutis) and their relationship to notes (swaras), specifically addressing the debate between the 22-interval system and the 66-interval system.</meta>

<page-num>73</page-num>
<header>-0r Sa: 3] First Chapter: On Swaras (Notes) 73</header>

## On the eighteenth [string], the third [interval] is Nishada; then, on the twenty-first, the second. || 16 ||
## On the twenty-first, the second; here, one Veena shall be the fixed (Dhruva) instrument.

Thus, the infinite nature of <term>shrutis</term> <note>microtonal intervals</note> is demonstrated. In this view, even if one accepts a distinction between <term>shruti</term> and <term>swara</term> <note>the musical note itself</note> as being characterized by the initial strike (<term>ranana</term>) and the subsequent resonance (<term>anuranana</term>), the resonant sounds are also called <term>shrutis</term>. Both types are produced like the "law of waves and ripples" <note>the way sound propagates in successive circles</note>. By imagining extremely subtle divisions of these sounds, and intending to show the multitude of sound-atoms that make up each echo, infinity is suggested. However, it must be understood that this view is untenable. Although sound capable of being heard is composed of parts—much like a <term>trasarenu</term> <note>the smallest visible mote of dust in a sunbeam</note>—and these parts are inferred by the fact that the sound is grasped by the senses, they are not themselves perceptible to the ear. Just as the atoms within a mote of dust are only reachable through logic or implication, these sub-divisions do not directly manifest the <term>swara</term> (note) and therefore cannot be considered <term>shrutis</term>.

In the theory of twenty-two <term>shrutis</term> and the theory of sixty-six <term>shrutis</term>, the distinction between <term>shruti</term> and <term>swara</term> is accepted equally. However, there is a difference: in the twenty-two <term>shruti</term> theory, the twenty-two intervals of the <term>mandra-sthana</term> <note>lower register/octave</note> are simply repeated in the other registers by doubling the frequency. In the sixty-six <term>shruti</term> theory, those intervals are not repeated across the three registers but are considered distinct from one another. If one accepts this non-repetition theory, then the notes like <term>Shadja</term> <note>the tonic or 'Sa'</note> would also not repeat, and the fourteen notes of the middle and high registers would have to be given entirely different names. But that is not how music is practiced.

Therefore, among the nine theories shown by <term>Matanga</term> <note>an ancient musicologist, author of Brihaddeshi</note> and others, the theory of twenty-two <term>shrutis</term> is the most essential. It does not deny the distinction between <term>shruti</term> and <term>swara</term> experienced through strike and resonance, and it accounts for the practical use of only seven <term>swaras</term> (notes) across different registers through repetition. Having determined this, the author [Sarngadeva], without hesitation, establishes the seven notes—<term>Shadja</term> and the rest—starting from the fourth <term>shruti</term> according to the scriptures, by demonstrating the preceding and succeeding boundaries on the two <term>Veenas</term> <note>lutes used for tuning demonstrations</note>. He does this with the verse beginning "The two Veenas..."

Regarding the term <term>Chatuh-shruti</term> <note>four-interval note</note>: this refers to a note that has four <term>shrutis</term> as the cause of its manifestation. The same logic should be applied to terms like <term>Tri-shruti</term> <note>three-interval note</note> and so on. || 10 - 16 ||

# Sangita Ratnakara: [Chapter on Shruti]

(Commentary by Simhabhupala) These specific distinctions of sound are difficult to understand without a practical illustration, and they are impossible to demonstrate through the human voice alone. Therefore, the author promises to provide an illustration using two <term>Vinas</term><note>The Vina is a traditional Indian stringed instrument; here it refers to a stick-zither used for acoustic experiments.</note> by saying "for the sake of manifestation." This means to show them clearly. As stated in the *Sangita-samaya-sara*:

> "Those twenty-two sounds cannot be clearly manifested 
> by the human voice. Therefore, their demonstration 
> is shown upon the Vina."

The author explains the promised method: "Two Vinas." These should be "alike," meaning identical. He explains that physical similarity is necessary here so that "the sound produced is exactly the same." As it is said:

> "Two Vinas should be made equal in all their parts, 
> so that to the listener, the two appear as if they 
> were a single instrument."

On each of these, twenty-two strings are to be fixed. Among these, the first string should be tuned to the lowest possible pitch (<term>mandra-tama</term>). That pitch is considered the "lowest" if no other pleasing sound lower than it can be produced. The second string should have a pitch slightly higher than the first. By saying "slightly," he clarifies the meaning: "so that no other intermediate sound is heard between them." The continuity must be maintained such that no distinct, dissimilar sound can arise in the middle. As it is said:

> "The second string is then tuned to a sharper sound, 
> such that between the two, a third distinct 
> sound cannot be produced."

These strings become progressively sharper in sound as one moves down the series. The sound produced from these strings is called a <term>Shruti</term><note>Literally 'that which is heard'; the smallest perceptible interval in Indian music theory.</note>. The standard of measurement for a Shruti was stated by the sage Matanga: "Now, what is the measure of a Shruti? It is said that the note <term>Panchama</term><note>The fifth note of the scale, equivalent to 'So' in solfège.</note> is well-known in the world as existing in two scales. <gloss>1</gloss>The interval resulting from the heightening or lowering of that note—due to its softness or tension—is the measure of one Shruti." In the *Sangita-samaya-sara*, the names of the sixty-six Shrutis across the three registers are given:

> "Mandra (Low), Atimandra (Very Low), Ghora (Terrible), Ghoratara (More Terrible), 
> Mandana (Adorning), Saumya (Gentle), Sumana (Pleasant), Pushkara (Lotus-like), 
> Shankhini (Conch-like), Nila (Blue), Utpala (Water-lily), Anunasika (Nasal), 
> Ghoshavati (Resonant), Linanada (Dissolved Sound), Avartanti (Revolving), and others..."

## 18. Then, compared to the notes of the fixed vina, the notes on this shifting vina
## become lowered by one interval; the other tunings follow the same process.¹

The author explains the tuning process <term>sarana; the systematic shifting of pitch to demonstrate intervals</term> on the shifting vina <term>chala-vina; an experimental instrument with adjustable strings</term> with the phrase: *on that one*. The instruction is to shift the strings. The word "but" is used here to show the distinction between this and the fixed vina <term>dhruva-vina; the reference instrument kept at a constant pitch</term>. To "shift" means to perform the tuning process; specifically, it means to move the notes residing on their respective strings away from their original interval positions and bring the strings to different interval positions. 

Lest one think this shifting is random, the rule for the intervals in the first and subsequent tunings is given: *to its own penultimate [string]*. This refers to the first tuning. One might ask: "By reaching a different interval, does the note not become a different note entirely?" To this, he says: *compared to the notes of the fixed vina*. Because the notes—such as Shadja <note>the tonic or 'Do'</note> and others characterized by having four intervals—are the same as those on the fixed vina, even when they reach a different interval, they are perceived only as being lowered by one interval <term>shruti; the smallest audible unit of pitch</term>. Since they are only perceived as lower versions of themselves, they do not become entirely different notes. He applies this same method to the subsequent tunings with the word: *In this way*. In this context, "the other" means taking the notes that were lowered by one interval in the previous tuning as the new starting point and bringing them to the next penultimate string. || 17-18 ||

(Sudhakara commentary) Here, of the two vinas, one is shifting and one is fixed. The one whose notes are lowered from their original positions is the shifting vina; the one whose notes are not lowered is the fixed vina. To determine the nature of the intervals, he describes what must be done on the shifting vina: *on that one*. On that shifting vina, one should shift or lower the strings. He describes the method for the first tuning: *to its own penultimate*. On that shifting vina, the "final" strings are those where the seven notes were originally placed; the "penultimate" are those immediately preceding them. The seven notes should be brought to and established on those. What happens when this first tuning is performed? He says: *the fixed vina*. On this shifting vina, those notes—Shadja and the rest—become lowered by one interval compared to the notes of the fixed vina. In this very same way...

# Chapter One: On Sound and Notes
<sig>-Sa. 3]</sig>
<term>Shruti (Microtone)</term>, <term>Sarana (Shift/Tuning process)</term>, <term>Chala-vina (Movable lute)</term>, <term>Dhruva-vina (Fixed lute)</term>, <term>Shadja (Do)</term>, <term>Nishada (Ti)</term>, <term>Gandhara (Mi)</term>, <term>Rishabha (Re)</term>, <term>Dhaivata (La)</term>, <term>Svara (Musical note)</term>

->**The Verses**<-

By the loss of two microtones in this [second shift], the notes <term>Gandhara</term> and <term>Nishada</term> on the movable lute || 19 ||
Enter respectively into the notes <term>Rishabha</term> and <term>Dhaivata</term> located on the fixed lute.
In the third shift, <term>Rishabha</term> and <term>Dhaivata</term> enter into <term>Shadja</term> and <term>Panchama</term> [the fifth] || 20 ||
In the fourth shift, <term>Shadja</term>, <term>Madhyama</term> [the fourth], and <term>Panchama</term> enter into <term>Nishada</term>, <term>Gandhara</term>, and <term>Madhyama</term> respectively.
Thus, through these four shifts, the twenty-two microtones are demonstrated || 21 ||

Regarding how the second, third, and fourth shifts are to be performed, he says: "Thus..." In each shift of the notes, a further reduction of one microtone at a time must be performed. || 17-18 || <note>The commentator refers back to the cumulative process of lowering the pitch.</note>

->**The Commentary (Kallinatha)**<-

(Ka.) He demonstrates what is to be understood in the second and subsequent shifts with the words: "By the loss of two microtones..."
In this **second shift**, on the **movable lute**—meaning the notes situated on their respective penultimate strings—the notes **Gandhara** and **Nishada** enter into the **Rishabha** and **Dhaivata** of the **fixed lute** (which remain on their original base microtones). Specifically, Gandhara merges into Rishabha, and Nishada into Dhaivata. This happens because of the "loss of two microtones," meaning they have abandoned two of their own microtones. "Enter" means they become absorbed or merged; they achieve the same form because their sounds become identical. One should observe the entry of other notes in the third and fourth shifts in the same way.

Now, a question arises: In the fourth shift, it is said that the low-register **Shadja** enters into **Nishada**. How is this possible? Since the process begins from the very first microtone of Shadja with the instruction "the lowest possible sound should be made," there is no sound preceding it, and thus no "penultimate string" exists for it to move back to. It is true that because no lower sound exists, there is no physical string; however, in the cycle of the low octave, because Shadja and Nishada are adjacent, one can conclude the entry by imagining the base microtone of Nishada as the penultimate position. Alternatively, since that same Shadja recurs in different registers, its entry into the preceding Nishada can be observed there.

He states the result of these shifts: "Thus, through the twenty-two microtones..." One might argue that according to certain theories, the determination of the twenty-nine <note>original: "ekonavimshati" - likely a scribal error or specific theory regarding total microtonal intervals</note> microtones of all seven notes could be achieved even with five shifts. This is not so. Notes are essentially the resonance of the microtones. These notes, such as Shadja and the rest...

# 78 Sangita Ratnakara [Chapter on Shrutis and Notes]

When the notes are merged into the fixed <term>shrutis</term><note>The smallest audible intervals of pitch</note>, their precise quantity becomes clearly known. Beyond this point, no further lowering of pitch should be performed, as it would destroy the <term>rakti</term><note>The inherent melodic beauty or "pleasingness" of a note</note>. || 22 ||
From these <term>shrutis</term> arise the <term>svaras</term><note>Musical notes</note>: <term>Shadja</term>, <term>Rsabha</term>, <term>Gandhara</term>, and <term>Madhyama</term>.

In both common practice and scientific theory, these notes are established as being manifested on the fourth and subsequent <term>shrutis</term> through their correspondence with the sounds of the peacock and other animals. If one were to continue shifting them to the fifth <term>shruti</term> and beyond according to the aforementioned method, that specific resonance would be lost. Furthermore, because the higher and lower positions of the chest and throat registers would overlap, the distinction between high and low pitches would vanish, thereby destroying the melodic beauty. With this intention, it is said: "Beyond this point..." || 19-22 ||

<gloss>(Commentary by Simhabhupala)</gloss> He explains what is achieved when the second <term>sarana</term><note>The process of tuning/shifting pitch</note> is performed: **"By two shrutis..."** When this second tuning shift is performed on the <term>chala-veena</term><note>The "mobile" or variable veena used for the experiment</note>, due to the lowering by two <term>shrutis</term>, the notes <term>Gandhara</term> and <term>Nishada</term> present on the <term>chala-veena</term> enter into (align with) the <term>Rsabha</term> and <term>Dhaivata</term> of the <term>dhruva-veena</term><note>The "fixed" reference veena</note>. He says "in order," meaning: <term>Gandhara</term> becomes <term>Rsabha</term>, and <term>Nishada</term> becomes <term>Dhaivata</term>. "Enter into those two" means they become identical in sound. He then describes the result of the third tuning: **"In the third..."** <term>Rsabha</term> and <term>Dhaivata</term> enter into <term>Shadja</term> and <term>Panchama</term>. Specifically, <term>Rsabha</term> enters <term>Shadja</term>, and <term>Dhaivata</term> enters <term>Panchama</term>. In the fourth tuning, the middle <term>Shadja</term> enters the lower <term>Nishada</term>, the <term>Madhyama</term> enters <term>Gandhara</term>, and the <term>Panchama</term> enters <term>Madhyama</term>. He concludes: **"In the twenty-two shrutis..."** Thus, through these four tuning shifts, when all are merged into the fixed <term>shrutis</term>, the exact quantity—the number twenty-two—is realized. In the second tuning, four <term>shrutis</term> are gained; in the third, six; and in the fourth, twelve. One might ask if the lowering should continue; he replies: **"Beyond this..."** No further lowering should be done. Why? Because it is **"destructive to beauty."** If lowered further, the notes lose their ability to color the mind, and their very nature as "notes" is destroyed, for it will be said later: "That which colors the heart of the listener by itself is called a <term>svara</term>." || 19-22 ||

<gloss>(Commentary by Kallinatha)</gloss> Having thus determined the quantity, he describes the manifestation of the notes from these <term>shrutis</term>: **"From the shrutis arise the notes..."** From four, three, and two [shrutis respectively]...

# First Chapter: On Notes
<page-num>79</page-num>

->The fifth is Pañcama, then Dhaivata, and Niṣāda; these are the seven.<-
->Their other recognized names are Sa, Ri, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, and Ni.<-

The meaning is that the seven notes <note>swaras</note> arise from the twenty-two microtones <note>shrutis</note> as appropriate. Here, five distinct viewpoints <note>pakṣas</note> are possible regarding their relationship:

1.  **Identity:** Since both are perceived by the single sense of hearing and lack distinct tactile qualities, the note and the microtone are identical, much like a universal class and an individual instance.
2.  **Reflection:** The notes are reflections <note>vivarta</note> of the microtones, like a face reflected in a mirror.
3.  **Causality:** Just as a pot is the product of a lump of clay and a staff, the notes are the effects produced by the microtones.
4.  **Transformation:** The microtones transform into the form of notes, just as milk turns into curd.
5.  **Manifestation:** The notes are manifested by the microtones, just as a lamp reveals a pot sitting in the darkness.

The first view is incorrect because notes and microtones are perceived by different mental processes and have a relationship of "container and contained." Furthermore, even in the case of a class and an individual, a distinction is established by the maxim: "There is no universal without particularity." 

The second view is also incorrect; if they were merely reflections, the notes would be an illusion <note>bhrānta</note>. This is not the case, as we see they are the cause of consistent musical practice. 

The third view also fails under scrutiny. It is not right to say there is no evidence for the existence of microtones apart from the notes. Their existence is proven either by "presumption" <note>arthāpatti; a method of logical postulation</note>—since the resonant quality of a note cannot exist without an initial strike—or by "inference" <note>anumāna</note>: "This note is preceded by a strike, because it possesses resonance, like the ringing sound of a victory bell struck by a rod." 

True, while there is a perception of cause and effect with a clear sequence, there is a difference here. In the case of clay, the material cause is not perceived separately once the pot is made; however, the microtones *are* perceived during the production of a note. Therefore, they are not "causes" in the sense of raw material. 

The fourth and fifth views, being free from flaws, are accepted by authorities such as Matanga <note>An ancient musicologist, author of the Brhaddeshi</note>. Now, the author enumerates the pure notes by their well-known meaningful names, starting with Ṣaḍja. The meaningful nature of the name Ṣaḍja and others was stated by Matanga:

> "Because it is the parent of the six notes, or is produced by six notes, 
> or is born from six parts of the body, it is called Ṣaḍja <note>literally 'born of six'</note>."

# The Ocean of Music [Chapter on Notes]

Because it generates or illuminates the other six notes, the term **Shadja** <note>The first note of the scale, corresponding to 'Do' or 'C'</note> is formed from the root *jan* (to give birth) with a causative sense, applying the grammatical rule "seen in others as well" to add the suffix *da* and dropping the final syllable. Alternatively, **Shadja** is so named because it is produced or illuminated by the other six notes entering into it as subordinate parts. The formation of the word is the same as before. Or, it is called **Shadja** because it is born from the six places of articulation: the nose, throat, chest, palate, tongue, and teeth, following the rule "born from the fifth case" to add the suffix *da*.

> "It reaches the heart more quickly than any other, thus it is known as Rishabha. 
> Just as a great bull stands out and shines among a herd of cows, 
> so does this note, Rishabha, stand out within the village of notes."

It is called **Rishabha** <note>The second note, 'Re' or 'D'</note> because it "goes" (*rishati*) to the heart faster than other notes; the form is derived from the root *rish* (to go) with the grammatical suffix *abhach*. Just as a bull is the strongest in a herd of cattle, this second note is the strong one in the collection or "village" of notes. Alternatively, it is called Rishabha because it bellows like a bull.

> "Because it holds the speech that consists of song, it is named Gandhara."

Because it holds (*dhatte*) speech (*vacham*) which is composed of song (*ga*), the form **Gandhara** <note>The third note, 'Ga' or 'E'</note> is derived from the root *dhri* (to hold) with the word *gau* (speech) as the object, using the suffix *an*. This follows the linguistic group of "spotted-belly" words or general usage where the elision does not occur. Or, it is called Gandhara because it is the cause of the pleasure found in the *Gandharva* <note>Celestial music or the art of the Gandharvas, the divine musicians</note>.

> "Because of its position in the middle of the notes, it is desired as the Madhyama note."

Because it is the fourth note among the seven and stands in the center, the form **Madhyama** <note>The fourth note, 'Ma' or 'F'</note> is derived from the word *madhya* (middle) with the suffix *ma* signifying "being therein." Alternatively, it is *maddhvama*, meaning "the sickness of my intellect," or rather, when heard among the seven notes, it "afflicts" the mind with the suspicion of its extreme beauty.

> "That which measures the expansion of the other notes is Panchama.
> Or, it is the fifth by count according to the order of recitation."

# Chapter One: On the Nature of Musical Notes
<sig>11</sig>

The term **Panchama** <note>The fifth note of the musical scale, corresponding to 'So' in solfège</note> is derived from the root *paci* meaning "to expand." By adding the suffix *ghañ* to denote the state of being, and then applying the rule "a suffix *ka* is added to a root ending in *ā* when there is no prefix," we arrive at the form *Panchama*, meaning "that which measures out a five-fold expansion." Other grammatical derivations involving the suffixes *aṇ* and *yuk* are set aside here as this is a formal name. Alternatively, through phonetic variation <term>pṛṣodarādi; a category of words in Sanskrit grammar that undergo irregular changes</term>, the augment and the elision of vowels occur. It is called the "Fifth" either because it is the fifth in the sequence of notes or because it is produced from the fifth station of breath.

->“Because it belongs to the one who possesses wisdom (*dhīvān*), it is known as **Dhaivata**.”<-
->Alternatively, “Because it is held in the sixth position, it is considered **Dhaivata**.”<-

The one who has wisdom (*dhī*) is called *dhīvān*; that which pertains to him is *Dhaivata* <note>The sixth note, corresponding to 'La'</note>. This "pertaining to" can be characterized in several ways: as the relationship between the definer and the defined, the enjoyer and the enjoyed, or the cause and the effect. Because its microtones <term>shrutis; the smallest intervals of pitch</term> are blended with the subsequent note, it is difficult for those of dull intellect to discern; since it can only be truly perceived by those of subtle wisdom (*dhīmat*), it is called *Dhaivata*. Or, it is called *Dhaivata* because it is held in the sixth station, which is the forehead.

->“Because all the notes settle (*niṣīdanti*) within it, it is called **Nishada**.”<-

From the root *ṣadlṛ* meaning "to settle" or "to dissolve," the form **Nishada** <note>The seventh note, corresponding to 'Ti'</note> is derived using the rule "the suffix *ghañ* is used in senses other than the agent," meaning the note in which the others reach their conclusion. Regarding the rule that there are exactly seven notes, one should consider the reasoning given by the sage Matanga <note>An ancient musicologist, author of the Brhaddeshi</note>, which links them to the seven constituent elements of the body <term>dhatus</term> or the seven energy centers <term>chakras</term>.

For the sake of ease in musical practice, the author provides alternative names by extracting their initial syllables. The method of extraction favored by Matanga for the syllables *Sa, Ri, Ga*, etc., is as follows: There are eight groups of consonants <note>The Varga system of the Sanskrit alphabet</note>. From the eighth group, take the third letter and join it with the seed-syllable of Hari <note>The vowel 'a'</note> to extract the first note. From the seventh group, take the second letter and join it with the seed-syllable of Kama <note>The vowel 'i'</note> to extract the second note. From the second group, take the third letter and join it with the seed-syllable of Hari to extract the third note. From the sixth group, take the fifth letter joined with 'a' to <gloss>1</gloss> extract the fourth note. From the sixth group, take the first letter—

<note>The verse defines 'Swara' (musical note) as a sound that possesses inherent aesthetic beauty, distinguishing it from the 'Shruti' (microtone) which is the foundational unit of sound.</note>

...one should extract the fifth note <note>Panchama</note> combined with the syllable 'Ka'. From the fifth, one should extract the sixth note combined with the fourth 'A' syllable. **(Sudhakara Commentary)** Having thus described the microtones <term>Shruti: the smallest audible intervals of pitch</term>, he now describes the notes <term>Swara: the seven primary notes of the scale</term>—starting with "From the microtones..." He provides alternative names for the purpose of practical usage, using the first letters of Shadja, Rishabha, and the others—starting with "Of those..." These names—Sa, Ri, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni—are the subsequent designations derived from the first syllables of the primary notes. Although it would be proper to announce the names as Shadja, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni, the reading "Sa-Ri-Ga" is a simplified vernacular form. || 23, 23- ||

**(Kallinatha Commentary)** He states the general definition of the notes and the etymology of the word 'Swara'—starting with "Immediately following the microtone..." **Immediately following the microtone** means it has the nature of appearing after the microtone (such as the fourth microtone), which is the first sound produced by the striking of the internal air. **Pleasing** means not harsh, capable of being heard from a distance. **Resonant** means having the nature of an echo or an after-sound. **By itself** means without depending on any other auxiliary cause, it **charms the mind of the listener**, making it feel colored with emotion. From the root *ranj* (to color/charm), combined with the prefix *swa* (self), the form 'Swara' is established through grammatical derivation <note>The commentator explains the linguistic root of Swara as 'that which shines or charms by itself'</note>. || -24, 24- ||

**(Sudhakara Commentary)** He explains the definition and the etymology of the note—starting with "Immediately following the microtone..." It is called 'following the microtone' because it occurs after the microtone. When a string is first struck, the sound produced that is devoid of resonance is the **microtone** <insert>Shruti</insert>; however, that which is heard immediately after as a resonant sound is the **note** <insert>Swara</insert>. Why is it called a note? He says: **By itself**. Because it charms the mind of the listener by itself, without needing anything else, it is etymologically called a 'Swara'. How does it possess this **charming quality** <note>Ranjakatvam: the power to affect the emotions</note>? For this reason...

<page-num>-0 Rasa: 3] 83</page-num>
<header>Chapter One: On Sound and Notes</header>

The adjective "resonant" <note>original: "snigdha," literally meaning oily, smooth, or cohesive</note> is used here. Although resonance is technically a property of the element of Water—as it is said, "Viscosity is a specific quality of Water"—and is not strictly something perceivable by the sense of hearing, it is applied to musical notes in a metaphorical sense.

On this subject, there are many conflicting opinions. Some describe an identity <term>tādātmya: the state of being the same essence</term> between the note and the microtone. As they say:

> "Because they lack a specific tactile quality and are both perceivable by the sense of hearing, there is an identity between the note and the microtone, much like the relationship between a universal class and an individual instance."

Others claim a relationship of reflection <term>vivarta: an appearance or illusory transformation</term> between the note and the microtone. As they say:

> "Just as the faces of men are reflected in mirrors, the notes appear as reflections within the microtones themselves."

Some speak of a cause-and-effect relationship between the note and the microtone. As they say:

> "Some indeed say that notes are the effects of microtones, just as a pot is the effect of a lump of clay and a potter's staff."

Others favor the theory of transformation <term>pariṇāma: a literal change from one state to another</term>. As they say:

> "The microtones undergo a transformation into the form of the note, just as milk turns into curd in every respect."

Still others accept the theory of manifestation <term>abhivyakti: revealing something already present</term>. As they say:

> "The seven notes, beginning with Shadja <note>the first note of the scale, 'Sa'</note>, are always manifested by the microtones, just as a lamp reveals a pot or other objects sitting in the darkness."

Among these views, Matanga <note>an ancient musicologist, author of the Brihaddeshi</note> accepted only the theories of transformation and manifestation. As he said:

> "The distinction between their individual characteristics is established generally, just as with other objects. Without these specific distinctions, the concept would be as empty as a flower growing in the sky. Because they are perceived by different cognitions, there is a difference between the note and the microtone. Furthermore, because of the distinction between the container and the contained, how could a total identity be established?"

# Ocean of Music <note>original: "Sangita Ratnakara"</note> [Chapter on the Classes of Notes]

> "The claim that notes are merely a transformation <note>original: "vivartatvam"; a philosophical term suggesting an illusory appearance or modification</note> is inconsistent. If notes were merely transformations, it would lead to the fallacy of illusory knowledge. Furthermore, the causal relationship of the microtones <term>Shrutis: the 22 subtle intervals of sound that form the basis of notes</term> would be impossible. For a cause is not perceived while its effects are fully present. Just as when a clay pot exists, the original lump of clay is no longer perceived; therefore, the theories of transformation, manifestation, or inherent existence are the accepted views."

Thus it is said. However, the sage Matanga has derived the word for 'note' <term>Svara: a musical note</term> differently. As he said:

> "From the verbal root *rajṛ*, meaning 'to shine,' preceded by the prefix *sva* (self). Because it shines by itself, it is known as *Svara* (self-shining)."

The etymological definitions of the notes beginning with *Shadja* have been stated by the author of the *Essence of the Ocean of Music* <note>original: "Sangitasamayasara"</note>:

> "Because it is produced from six locations—the nose, throat, chest, palate, tongue, and teeth—it is known as **Shadja** <note>literally: 'six-born'</note>.
>
> Because the air rising from the navel, striking the throat and the head, bellows like a bull <note>original: "rishabha"</note>, it is called **Rishabha**.
>
> The air rising from the navel, striking the throat and the head, becomes the cause of delight for the celestial musicians <note>original: "Gandharvas"</note>; for that reason, it is **Gandhara**.
>
> The air rising from the navel and striking the heart is called **Madhyama**, because it originates from the middle position <note>original: "madhya-sthana"</note>.
>
> The air rising from the navel and striking the five locations of the lips, throat, head, and heart is called **Panchama** <note>literally: 'the fifth'</note> because it is produced from five places.
>
> Because the air rising from the navel is held in the various locations of the throat, palate, head, and heart, it is considered **Dhaivata**.
>
> When the air rises from the navel and is struck in the throat, palate, and head, all the other notes 'settle down' <note>original: "nishidanti"</note> within it; therefore, it is called **Nishada**."

# Chapter 1: On Notes
## Section 3: Microtones and Sentiments

One might ask: if the fourth microtone <note>shrutis are the 22 microtonal intervals that make up an octave</note> and its equivalents are the cause of a note, then how can the preceding three microtones be considered causes? || 25 ||

We reply: the third microtone and those preceding it are determined by their desire for the fourth. Therefore, the preceding microtones are also causes here. There are five "families" <note>jati: categories of emotional resonance</note> of microtones: the Radiant, the Extended, the Compassionate, the Soft, and the Intermediate. || 26–27 ||

Their arrangement within the notes is as follows: In the note *Shadja* <note>the tonic or 'Do'</note>, there are the Radiant, Extended, Soft, and Intermediate. In *Rishabha* <note>the second note, 'Re'</note>, there reside the Compassionate and the Intermediate. In *Gandhara* <note>the third note, 'Mi'</note>, there are the Soft and the Radiant. In *Madhyama* <note>the fourth note, 'Fa'</note>, there are the Extended, the Soft, and the Intermediate. || 28–29 ||

In *Panchama* <note>the fifth note, 'Sol'</note>, there reside the Soft, the Intermediate, the Extended, and the Compassionate. In *Dhaivata* <note>the sixth note, 'La'</note>, there are the Compassionate, the Extended, and the Intermediate. In the seventh note, *Nishada* <note>the seventh note, 'Ti'</note>, there are the Radiant and the Intermediate. Now we shall describe the subdivisions of these families. || 30–31 ||

The Radiant family is said to be fourfold: Sharp, Terrible, Thunderous, and Fierce. The Extended family has five divisions: Lily-like, Wrathful, Spreading, Kindling, and Rising. || 31–32 ||

---

(Commentary by Kallinatha) If it is argued that only the fourth microtone (and its equivalents) should be the cause of a note, and not the ones preceding it, the author raises this objection with the phrase "One might ask." Regarding the phrase "the third and so on": this refers to the third microtone onwards. In this grammatical usage, even when the suffix is dropped, the meaning remains. The author resolves this by saying, "We reply." The third microtone is identified by its relation to the fourth. For the notes *Shadja*, *Madhyama*, and *Panchama*, the defining microtone is the fourth; for *Rishabha* and *Dhaivata*, it is the third; and by the use of the word "and so on," for *Gandhara* and *Nishada*, it is the second. These are determined by their "desire for the preceding"—the word "preceding" should be understood distributively to mean each preceding microtone is required to define the pitch of the note that follows.

<summary>This page explains how the 22 microtones (shrutis) are grouped into five emotional categories and assigned to the seven primary musical notes. It also clarifies the philosophical argument that all preceding microtones contribute to the identity of a final musical note.</summary>

# The Ocean of Music [Chapter on Notes and Microtones]

->Dayavati, Alapini, and Madantika: these three are the variations of the **Compassionate** category. There are four variations of the **Soft** category:<-

->Manda, Ratika, Priti, and Kshiti. The **Intermediate** category is six-fold: Chhandovati, Ranjani, Marjani, Raktika,<-

->Ramya, and Kshobhini. Now, we shall describe the placement of the notes within these. Tivra, Kumudvati, Manda, and Chhandovati are located in **Shadja** <note>The first note, 'Sa', corresponding to the tonic</note>.<-

->Dayavati, Ranjani, and Raktika reside in **Rishabha** <note>The second note, 'Ri'</note>. Raudri and Krodha are in **Gandhara** <note>The third note, 'Ga'</note>. Vajrika, Prasarini,<-

->Priti, and Marjani—these microtones are supported by **Madhyama** <note>The fourth note, 'Ma'</note>. Kshiti, Rakta, Sandipani, and Alapini are in **Panchama** <note>The fifth note, 'Pa'</note>.<-

->Madanti, Rohini, and Ramya—these three reside in **Dhaivata** <note>The sixth note, 'Dha'</note>. Ugra and Kshobhini are the two microtones dwelling in **Nishada** <note>The seventh note, 'Ni'</note>.<-

The meaning is that because each preceding element creates an expectation for the next, they are determined by designations such as "fourth" and so on. In order to recognize the nature of the <term>shrutis</term> <note>microtones; the smallest audible intervals of pitch</note> without confusing them with one another, and to achieve a pleasing quality through their natural affinity and association, the author demonstrates the arrangement of the <term>jatis</term> <note>classes or families of microtones</note> along with their sub-variations within the notes—starting with "Brilliant" (Dipta), "Extended" (Ayata), and so forth. Although these microtone-classes were mentioned after the application of the notes, their description here is appropriate due to the logical connection in analyzing the relationship between microtones and notes. The mention of them out of the original order is intended to show that, in some instances, the specific sequence is not strictly intended. By this, one should understand that the sequence starting with "Families, classes..." is not mandatory. || 25–38 ||

---

(Sudhakara commentary) It has been stated that "Notes arise from microtones." In the phrase "from microtones," the use of the ablative case <note>original: "shrutibhyah"</note> indicates, according to the grammatical rule "the source of the creator is the material cause," that the microtones are the cause of the notes. Furthermore, because it is said "this note has four microtones, this one has three, and this one has two," it is understood that all of them serve as causes.

# Chapter One: On Musical Notes

It is perceived, and then an objection is raised—"But wait." But wait, if the <term>Svara</term> <note>the fundamental musical note</note> is established on a specific <term>Shruti</term> <note>the smallest audible interval or microtone</note>, such as the fourth, etc.—namely the 4th, 7th, 9th, 13th, 17th, 20th, and 22nd <term>Shruti</term>—let these be the cause of the <term>Svaras</term> like <term>Shadja</term> <note>the first note, 'Sa'</note> and the others, either by manifesting them or transforming into them. But how can the preceding three <term>Shrutis</term> be the cause of a note? By the phrase "the three, etc.," it is meant: what is the use of the three preceding <term>Shrutis</term> for <term>Shadja</term>, <term>Madhyama</term>, and <term>Panchama</term>; the two for <term>Rishabha</term> and <term>Dhaivata</term>; and the one for <term>Gandhara</term> and <term>Nishada</term> toward the production of the note?

The answer is given—"We say this." The fourth, third, etc., <term>Shruti</term> is determined only in relation to the preceding ones. The designation that "this is the fourth, this is the third, this is the second" is a convention that depends on the previous <term>Shrutis</term>. If the preceding <term>Shrutis</term> did not exist, in relation to what would this designation of "fourth" and so on occur? Therefore, to establish the identity of the fourth and subsequent positions, the causality of the preceding <term>Shrutis</term> is also proven.

Now, the author classifies the <term>Shruti-Jatis</term> <note>families or "castes" of microtones based on their emotional/tonal quality</note>—"Brilliant, Extended, etc." There are five <term>Jatis</term> of <term>Shrutis</term>: <term>Dipta</term> (Brilliant), <term>Ayata</term> (Extended), <term>Karuna</term> (Compassionate), <term>Mridu</term> (Soft), and <term>Madhya</term> (Intermediate). Regarding which <term>Jati</term> resides in which <term>Svara</term>, he says—"And among them..."

In <term>Shadja</term> <note>the note 'Sa'</note>, there are four <term>Shruti-Jatis</term> beginning with <term>Dipta</term>: the first <term>Shruti</term> is <term>Dipta</term>, the second is <term>Ayata</term>, the third is <term>Mridu</term>, and the fourth is <term>Madhya</term>. In <term>Rishabha</term> <note>the note 'Re'</note>, the first <term>Shruti</term> is <term>Karuna</term>, the second is <term>Madhya</term>, and the third is <term>Mridu</term>. In <term>Gandhara</term> <note>the note 'Ga'</note>, the first <term>Shruti</term> is <term>Dipta</term> and the second is <term>Ayata</term>. In <term>Madhyama</term> <note>the note 'Ma'</note>, those same <term>Dipta</term>, <term>Ayata</term>, <term>Mridu</term>, and <term>Madhya</term> are situated; thus, <term>Madhyama's</term> first <term>Shruti</term> is <term>Dipta</term>, the second is <term>Ayata</term>, the third is <term>Mridu</term>, and the fourth is <term>Madhya</term>. In <term>Panchama</term> <note>the note 'Pa'</note>, the first <term>Shruti</term> is <term>Mridu</term>, the second is <term>Madhya</term>, the third is <term>Ayata</term>, and the fourth is <term>Karuna</term>. In <term>Dhaivata</term> <note>the note 'Dha'</note>, the first <term>Shruti</term> is <term>Karuna</term>, the second is <term>Ayata</term>, and the third is <term>Madhya</term>. In the seventh, <term>Nishada</term> <note>the note 'Ni'</note>, the first <term>Shruti</term> is <term>Dipta</term> and the second is <term>Madhya</term>.

Having promised to explain the sub-varieties of these <term>Jatis</term>, he says—"And of those..." <term>Dipta</term> is of four types: <term>Tivra</term> (Sharp), <term>Raudri</term> (Terrible), <term>Vajrika</term> (Thunderbolt-like), and <term>Ugra</term> (Fierce). There are five divisions of <term>Ayata</term>: <term>Kumudvati</term> (Moon-lotus), <term>Krodha</term> (Anger), <term>Prasarini</term> (Spreading), <term>Sandipani</term> (Kindling), and <term>Rohini</term> (Rising). <term>Karuna</term> has three divisions: <term>Dayavati</term> (Merciful), <term>Alapini</term> (Conversational), and <term>Madantika</term> (Intoxicating). Of <term>Mridu</term>, there are four divisions: <term>Manda</term> (Slow/Low), <term>Rati</term> (Delight), <term>Priti</term> (Affection), and <term>Kshiti</term> (Earth). <term>Madhya</term> is of six types: <term>Chhandovati</term> (Metrical), <term>Ranjani</term> (Pleasing), <term>Marjani</term> (Cleansing), <term>Raktika</term> (Reddening/Passionate), <term>Ramya</term> (Beautiful), and <term>Kshobhini</term> (Agitating). The word "but" <note>original: 'tu'</note> indicates that this has more divisions than the previous ones.

Having promised to explain the placement of these <term>Jatis</term> within the notes, he says—"Now, of these..." Among these <term>Shruti-Jatis</term>, those belonging to <term>Shadja</term> are the four <term>Jatis</term> starting with <term>Tivra</term>. Thus, in <term>Shadja</term>, the first <term>Shruti</term> is <term>Dipta</term> pervaded by the <term>Tivra</term> sub-type; the second is <term>Ayata</term> of the <term>Kumudvati</term> sub-type; the third is <term>Mridu</term> of the <term>Manda</term> sub-type; and the fourth is <term>Madhya</term> of the <term>Chhandovati</term> sub-type. In <term>Rishabha</term>, the first <term>Shruti</term> is of the <term>Dayavati</term> sub-type...

These <note>the seven notes</note> are considered to be of three types based on the difference in their registers: low, middle, and high.
These same notes are explained as having twelve modified states. || 39 ||
The note *Shadja* <note>the tonic or 'Sa'</note>, when modified to possess only two microtones, becomes twofold: "fallen" and "not-fallen."
This occurs during the "overlapping" <term>Sadharana: a state where notes share microtonal space</term> and when the note *Nishada* <note>'Ni'</note> takes the *Kakali* <note>sharp</note> form. || 40 ||
When the note *Rishabha* <note>'Re'</note> takes a microtone from *Shadja* during this overlapping state,
it then attains a four-microtone status and thus becomes one of the modified forms. || 41 ||

...the first is Compassionate; the second is *Ranjani*, of the Intermediate class; the third is *Rati*, of the Soft class. In *Gandhara* <note>'Ga'</note>:
the first microtone is *Raudri*, of the Brilliant class; the second is *Krodha*, of the Extended class. In *Madhyama* <note>'Ma'</note>:
the first microtone is *Vajrika*, of the Brilliant class; the second is *Prasarini*, of the Extended class; the third is
*Priti*, of the Soft class; the fourth is *Marjani*, of the Intermediate class. In *Panchama* <note>'Pa'</note>: the first microtone is
*Kshiti*, of the Soft class; the second is *Rakta*, of the Intermediate class; the third is *Sandipani*, of the
Extended class; the fourth is *Alapini*, of the Compassionate class. In *Dhaivata* <note>'Dha'</note>: the first microtone is *Madanti*, of the
Compassionate class; the second is *Rohini*, of the Extended class; the third is *Ramya*, of the Intermediate class. In *Nishada* <note>'Ni'</note>:
the first microtone is *Ugra*, of the Brilliant class; the second is *Kshobhini*, of the Intermediate class. Now, what is the
purpose of defining these classes of microtones? It is said—by hearing a microtone of a particular class, a corresponding
state is produced in the mind, matching the name of that class; this is the reason for defining the microtone classes.
Therefore, upon hearing a "Brilliant" <note>Dipta</note> microtone, the mind becomes as if brilliant; upon hearing an "Extended" <note>Ayata</note> microtone,
it becomes as if extended; the same should be understood for "Compassionate" <note>Karuna</note> and the others. || 27-38 ||

(Ka.) <note>Commentary by Kallinatha</note> Having discussed the classes of microtones in context, the author now describes their threefold nature based on register, while referring back to the natural notes—"These low," etc. One might ask: should the "fallen" notes and others be considered separate notes? Why categorize them as *Shadja* and others in a different state? To this he says—"These same," etc. "Twelve" refers to...
He defines the modified notes in the order they appear in relation to the two scales <note>the Shadja-grama and Madhyama-grama</note>—"Fallen, not-fallen," and so on. *Shadja*, which normally has four microtones, becomes twofold—"fallen" and "not-fallen"—when it is modified to have only two. This "falling" occurs during its own overlapping state, and when *Nishada* becomes *Kakali*...

The term "Achyuta" <note>immovable/fixed</note> is seen here. In the phrase "In <term>Sadharana</term> it consists of <term>three shrutis</term>," it specifically means <term>Madhyama-sadharana</term>. In the phrase "In the state of <term>Antara</term> it consists of <term>four shrutis</term>," it should be specified as its own internal variation. Regarding "<term>Madhyama</term> is like <term>Shadja</term>": here, "like <term>Shadja</term>" means that just as <term>Shadja</term> becomes a <term>two-shruti</term> modified note through the distinction of being "fallen" <note>Chyuta</note> or "not fallen" <note>Achyuta</note>, so too does <term>Madhyama</term>. In the phrase "In <term>Kaishika</term> and <term>Kakali</term> states," it means in <term>Kaishika</term> (the <term>Shadja-sadharana</term> state) it has <term>three shrutis</term>, and in its own <term>Kakali</term> state it has <term>four shrutis</term>. || 39--45- ||

(Commentary by Simhabhupala) Thus, having explained the <term>shrutis</term>, the <term>classes of shrutis</term>, <gloss>1</gloss> and the <term>origin of notes</term> from the classes of shrutis, he now describes the <term>variations of notes</term>—"These," etc. Those notes, <term>Shadja and the others</term>, are of three kinds or three types. Why three types? He says: because of the distinction of <term>registers</term> <note>Sthana</note> known as <term>low</term> <note>Mandra</note>, <term>middle</term> <note>Madhya</note>, and <term>high</term> <note>Tara</note>. Therefore, there is no fundamental difference in their essence, but rather a difference imagined by their <term>register</term>. Just as a single man named Devadatta, staying on the first floor, second floor, or third floor of a three-story palace, <gloss>2</gloss> appears as if he were different, so too do the notes appear different due to their specific <term>register</term>. # The Ocean of Music [Section on Notes]

->Page 90<-

A fundamental difference is perceived specifically in this way; just as there is a difference between the notes Shadja <note>The tonic or first note, 'Sa'</note> and others located in the low, middle, and high registers, why is it that here [in the case of the seven notes] a merely conceptual difference is accepted? We reply: because of **recognition**. In all three registers, the very same notes are perceived. That very same Shadja which exists in the low register is perceived in the middle and high registers as well; this recognition, witnessed by all people, cannot be disregarded. However, among the seven notes—Shadja, Rishabha, and the rest—there is not even a trace of such recognition <note>meaning 'Sa' is fundamentally recognized as 'Sa' across octaves, but 'Sa' is never recognized as 'Ri'</note>; this is the great distinction.

Thus, having described the seven pure notes, the author now describes the twelve modified <term>Vikrita|Notes that have deviated from their natural pitch or interval</term> notes by classifying them, saying: **"These very same..."** Those seven pure notes themselves, when they reach a state of modification, become twelve in number. || 39 ||

He demonstrates that very modification, saying: **"Fallen..."** The two-microtone <term>Shruti|The smallest audible unit of pitch</term> Shadja becomes modified in two ways, called "fallen" <note>Chyuta</note> and "unfallen" <note>Achyuta</note>. Among these, the "fallen" one has dropped from the fourth microtone where it was originally established. The "unfallen" one remains on that same microtone, but becomes modified by the loss of its preceding microtones. When does it possess such modifications? He says: **"In overlap..."** In the case of its own overlap <note>Sadharana</note> and when Nishada <note>The seventh note, 'Ni'</note> becomes Kakali <note>A sharp variety of Nishada</note>, both types of modification occur.

> "If Nishada takes refuge in the first microtone of Shadja,
> and Rishabha takes the last, that is called Shadja-overlap."

In this "Shadja-overlap" which will be described later, Shadja falls from its own place on the fourth microtone and stays on the third microtone, thus becoming modified.

> "If Nishada takes two microtones of Shadja,
> it is called Kakali; if Gandhara takes two from Madhyama, it is Antara."

In the case of Nishada becoming Kakali, as described later, Shadja becomes "unfallen" because it remains in its own place on the fourth microtone, yet it is modified because it has lost its two preceding microtones. Now, one might ask: if it stays in its own place, even if it loses two preceding microtones, how can it be modified if there is no change in sound? It is replied: although there is no change in sound because it stays in that position, when Nishada is in its own place, Shadja is "extended" because it possesses four microtones. When Nishada becomes Kakali and stays on the second microtone of Shadja, then Shadja is perceived as "unextended" because it possesses only two microtones. Therefore, it is indeed modified. || 40 ||

He describes the modification of Rishabha <note>The second note, 'Ri'</note>, saying: **"In overlap..."** In the case of Shadja-overlap, Rishabha takes the last microtone of Shadja; then, possessing four microtones, it becomes modified. || 41 ||

He describes the two modified types of Gandhara <note>The third note, 'Ga'</note>, saying: **"In overlap..."** In the case of overlap—specifically Madhyama-overlap—

# The peacock, the skylark, the goat, the heron, the cuckoo, and the frog, || 46 ||
# And the elephant—these seven utter the notes starting from Shadja in order.

<note>This verse links the seven musical notes to the sounds of animals: Shadja (peacock), Rishabha (skylark), Gandhara (goat), Madhyama (heron), Panchama (cuckoo), Dhaivata (frog), and Nishada (elephant).</note>

The note Gandhara <term>Gandhara: the third note of the scale</term> takes the first microtone <term>Shruti: the smallest interval of pitch a human ear can detect</term> of Madhyama. At that time, it becomes a modified note of three microtones. <insert>1. But the intermediate note</insert> Gandhara takes the first two microtones of Madhyama; then, having four microtones, it becomes modified. || 42 ||
He explains the two modified variations of Madhyama <term>Madhyama: the fourth note, the "middle" note</term>—saying "Madhyama." Just as Shadja <term>Shadja: the first note, the tonic</term> was said to be modified in two ways by falling or not falling from its pitch, and in the "overlapping" <term>Sadharana: a state where two notes share microtones</term> of the note Nishada becoming Kakali, similarly in the overlapping of Madhyama, when Gandhara becomes the intermediate note, Madhyama also becomes modified in two ways.

> "The overlapping of Madhyama is also considered to belong to Gandhara and Panchama."
> "...the Gandhara of Madhyama is the intermediate note."

And the intermediate nature of Gandhara in the overlapping of Madhyama will be discussed later. || 42- || He explains the two-fold modification of Panchama <term>Panchama: the fifth note</term>—saying "Panchama." When the fifth note is situated on the third microtone, it is called the "Middle Scale" <term>Madhyama-grama: one of the two ancient standard scales</term>. In that Middle Scale, the three-microtone Panchama becomes modified. Furthermore, in the "hair-fine" <term>Kaishiki: a subtle variation of a note</term> overlapping of Madhyama, by taking the final microtone of Madhyama, it becomes a modified note of four microtones. || -43, 43- || He explains the single modification of Dhaivata <term>Dhaivata: the sixth note</term>—saying "Dhaivata." In the Middle Scale, because the Panchama is situated on the third microtone, the final microtone of Panchama enters Dhaivata. It then becomes a modified note of four microtones. || -44 || He explains the two-fold modification of Nishada <term>Nishada: the seventh note</term>—saying "Kaishiki." In the Kaishiki overlapping of Shadja, when Nishada stays on the first microtone of Shadja, it is modified with three microtones; but when it becomes "Kakali" <term>Kakali: a sharp variety of the seventh note</term> by taking two microtones of Shadja and becomes four microtones, it is also modified. Thus, there are twelve modified variations. Including the pure notes, there are nineteen variations in total, as he says—"by these." || 45, 49- ||

(Kallinatha's Commentary) In order to recognize the nature of Shadja and the other notes from the world, he mentions the sounds of specific animals like the peacock as an illustration—saying "Peacock etc." Having spoken of the differences in the nature of the notes themselves, he now shows their four-fold classification by different methods of practice for the purpose of performance—

## The Ocean of Music

### Notes are of four kinds: the Sonant, the Consonant, and the Dissonant, || 47 ||
### As well as the Assonant. The Sonant is the note used most frequently in performance.
### Those two notes which have an interval of either twelve or eight || 48 ||
### Microtones between them are mutually Consonant. Nī and Gā are Dissonant to others, || 49 ||
### Or perhaps Ri and Dha are Dissonant to each other, or Nī and Gā are Dissonant to Ri and Dha.

Regarding "four kinds": The **Sonant** <note>Sanskrit: *Vādī*, literally "the speaker"</note> is so called because it "speaks." One might ask: "Speaking is a property of living beings; how can it belong to inanimate musical notes?" True, but by "speaking" we mean the capacity to manifest the melodic character <note>Sanskrit: *Rāga*</note>, not literal speech; thus, there is no error. The **Consonant** <note>Sanskrit: *Samvādī*</note> is so called from "speaking in harmony." This harmony means sustaining the melodic essence produced by the Sonant note. The **Dissonant** <note>Sanskrit: *Vivādī*</note> comes from "speaking against." This means destroying the aesthetic delight <note>Sanskrit: *Rakti*</note> produced by the Sonant and other notes. The **Assonant** <note>Sanskrit: *Anuvādī*</note> comes from "speaking after." This means following and supporting the delight produced by the Sonant and Consonant notes.

The author defines them in order, starting with "The Sonant is...": In a performance of a melodic type <note>Sanskrit: *Jāti*, the precursor to the modern Raga</note>, it is the note that is "frequent," meaning it is repeated again and again through its roles as the starting, central, or final note.

To understand the definition of Consonance, one should first draw a "Circular Diagram" <note>Sanskrit: *Maṇḍala-prastāra*</note> or a "Lute Diagram" <note>Sanskrit: *Vīṇā-prastāra*</note>. The Circular Diagram is made as follows: draw six vertical lines, leaving the ends slightly extended at the top and bottom, and draw five horizontal lines in the middle, also leaving the ends extended. This results in twenty-two line-ends around the perimeter <note>representing the 22 *Shrutis* or microtones</note>. For the Lute Diagram: simply draw twenty-two horizontal lines. There will be twenty-two line-ends on the left or right.

On one such microtonal circle, one should mark the natural and modified notes—Sa, Ri, Ga, etc.—according to their respective number of microtones. Among these, when the microtones situated in the interval between two notes—excluding the microtones upon which the notes themselves rest—are seen to be either twelve or eight, those two should be understood as mutually Consonant.

Regarding "Nī and Gā are Dissonant to others": This means they are Dissonant to (or enemies of) the other five notes. Now, it is stated that Nī and Gā are Dissonant toward all five other notes; however, this seems inconsistent, as we observe a Consonant relationship between a natural Ma and a natural Nī. Due to this dissatisfaction...

->The remaining notes are called "Assonants" (Anuvadi). The "Sonant" (Vadi) is sung here as the King.<-
->The "Consonant" (Samvadi), because it follows the King, is called the Minister.<-
->The "Dissonant" (Vivadi), because of its contrary nature, is called the Enemy by the brave.<-

He states another view: *Or specifically of Ri and Dha.* <note>Referring to the notes Rishabha and Dhaivata.</note> The initial general statement regarding "others being dissonant" was made according to the view that consonance only occurs between notes with an equal number of micro-tones (Shrutis). Therefore, it is established that the definition of a Consonant note is simply being separated by an interval of twelve or eight micro-tones. *Those two of those two:* Those two, Ri and Dha, are the Dissonants of those two, Ni and Ga. <note>Nishada and Gandhara.</note> By this, the definition is indicated that notes separated by a single micro-tone are mutually Dissonant. Even regarding the statement by Matanga <note>An ancient musicologist, author of the Brhaddeshi</note> that "Dissonance is due to a two-interval gap," the meaning is actually a single-micro-tone interval, because he intends the two intervals to include the micro-tone base of one of the notes. Similarly, Matanga’s definition of Consonance as "an interval of thirteen or nine" actually means an interval of twelve or eight <note>Matanga counts the starting note, whereas the present system counts the intervals between them</note>. Thus, just as there is mutual dissonance between Ri-Ga and Dha-Ni in their natural state, one should observe dissonance between Ga-Ma and Ni-Sa in their modified states. The intention is this: even if the Sonant, Consonant, and Assonant notes are used with their positions swapped, the character of the *Jati* <note>melodic classification</note> or *Raga* <note>musical mode</note> is not destroyed; however, the use of a Dissonant note would destroy the *Jati* or *Raga*. *Of the remaining:* of those lacking the characteristics of Sonant, etc. Now, he demonstrates the hierarchy of the Sonant and others in practice, using an analogy: *The Sonant is the King,* etc. || 46-51 ||

<note>Su. refers to Sudhakara, a commentary by Simhabhupala on the Sangita Ratnakara.</note>

(Su.) To understand the nature of these notes, he names the unique creatures that utter them: *The Peacock,* etc. The peacock utters the note *Shadja* (Sa), the *Chataka* bird <note>a mythical bird that drinks only raindrops</note> utters *Rishabha* (Ri), the goat utters *Gandhara* (Ga), the heron utters *Madhyama* (Ma), the cuckoo utters *Panchama* (Pa), the frog utters *Dhaivata* (Dha), and the elephant utters *Nishada* (Ni). || -46, 46- || He explains the fourfold nature of notes: *Four kinds,* etc. He gives the definition of the Sonant: *The Sonant,* etc. In practice, such as in a *Jati* or *Raga*, that which is uttered frequently (in abundance) is the Sonant, which is another name for the *Amsha* <note>the predominant or tonic note</note>. Now, one might ask: "Sonant" (Vadi) means "one who speaks"; speaking is a property of living beings, so how can it apply to inanimate notes? True; but "speaking" here is intended to mean "demonstrating the Raga." Therefore, they are "Sonants" because they speak or demonstrate the "Raga-ness" of the Ragas. || -47, 47- || Consonant—

# Page 94
## Definition of Musical Intervals

He explains the definition: "The microtones" <note>original: "shrutis"</note>. When twelve or eight microtones exist between two notes, they are mutually **consonant** <note>term: Samvadi - notes that harmonize perfectly together, like a fifth or a fourth</note>. 

But wait—Matanga <note>An influential early musicologist, author of the Brhaddeshi</note> stated that consonance occurs when there is an interval of thirteen or nine microtones; as he said: "Consonant notes are to be understood as those having equal microtonal measures and an interval of thirteen or nine between them." Dattila <note>Another ancient authority on music theory</note> also said:

-> "Those with an interval of thirteen or nine between them are known as mutually consonant." <-

So why is it said here, "where twelve or eight microtones fall in between"? The explanation is this: if you exclude the two microtones upon which the two notes actually sit and count only the microtones *staying in the middle*, there are twelve or eight. This is the intention behind the statement. Matanga and others, however, included the starting note's position in the count, arriving at thirteen and nine. Thus, there is no contradiction.

Therefore:
*   For **Shadja** <note>The tonic or 'Sa'</note>, the consonants are **Madhyama** <note>the fourth</note> and **Panchama** <note>the fifth</note>.
*   For **Rishabha** <note>'Ri'</note>, it is **Dhaivata** <note>'Dha'</note>.
*   For **Gandhara** <note>'Ga'</note>, it is **Nishada** <note>'Ni'</note>.
*   For **Madhyama** <note>'Ma'</note>, it is **Shadja**.
*   For **Panchama** <note>'Pa'</note>, it is **Shadja**.
*   For **Dhaivata**, it is **Rishabha**.
*   For **Nishada**, it is **Gandhara**.

One might ask: what is the practical use of this consonance? We reply: In a song, if **Madhyama** is played in the place of a **Shadja** that was intended as the dominant note <note>term: Amsha - the most important, soul-note of a melody</note>, it does not destroy the character of the *Jati* <note>melodic classification</note> or the *Raga*. Or, if through the progression of the scale <note>term: Murchana</note> a **Shadja** is used where a **Madhyama** was intended, the melody is not ruined. Similarly, swapping **Shadja** and **Panchama**, or **Rishabha** and **Dhaivata**, or **Gandhara** and **Nishada** does not cause the loss of the musical character.

He then gives the definition of **dissonance** <note>term: Vivadi - notes that clash or sound 'discordant'</note>: "Ni and Ga." **Nishada** and **Gandhara** are dissonant to all other notes. He offers an alternative view: "Regarding Ri and Dha." These two (Ni and Ga) are dissonant specifically to **Rishabha** and **Dhaivata**. He gives a third view: "Of those two." Meaning **Rishabha** and **Dhaivata** are dissonant to **Nishada** and **Gandhara**. Matanga, however, defined dissonance by an interval of two microtones; as he said, "Two notes with an interval of two are dissonant." 

What is this "dissonance"? We say: it is the quality of destroying the established melodic identity—whether that identity was created by the dominant, sub-dominant, or assonant notes. Thus, when **Gandhara** is used in the place of **Rishabha**, or **Rishabha** in the place of **Gandhara**, the character of the *Jati* and *Raga* is destroyed.

He explains the definition of **assonance** <note>term: Anuvadi - 'neutral' notes that follow the melody without being primary consonants or dissonants</note>: "Of the remaining." Those notes which are neither mutually consonant nor dissonant are assonant. Matanga, however, defined it as being short of one microtone...

### Because it follows the King and the Minister, the Anuvadi is like a servant. || 51 ||
### Born of the lineage of the Gods are Shadja, Gandhara, and Madhyama.

The nature of the *Vadi* <note>The 'sonant' or melodic king-note</note> has been stated. Now, what does the *Anuvadi* <note>The 'assonant' or neutral note</note> note "repeat" or "follow"? That which establishes the melodic character of a Raga through the *Vadi* is what is meant by the term *Anuvaditva* (the state of being an Anuvadi). Consequently:

Using *Rishabha* in the place of *Shadja*, or *Shadja* in the place of *Rishabha*, does not destroy the *Jati* <note>The melodic prototype or parent scale</note> or the Raga. Using *Dhaivata* in the place of *Panchama*, or *Panchama* in the place of *Dhaivata*, does not destroy the Raga. Using *Dhaivata* in the place of *Shadja*, or *Shadja* in the place of *Dhaivata*, does not destroy the Raga. Likewise, using *Rishabha* in the place of *Panchama*, or *Panchama* in the place of *Rishabha*, does not destroy the Raga. Using *Rishabha* in the place of *Madhyama*, or *Madhyama* in the place of *Rishabha*, as well as using *Madhyama* in the place of *Dhaivata*, or *Dhaivata* in the place of *Madhyama*, does not destroy the *Jati*. 

Between *Rishabha* and *Gandhara*, because they are separated by only one *Shruti* <note>The smallest audible microtonal interval</note>, they might seem to be *Anuvadi*, but because they are actually two intervals apart, they are considered *Vivadi* <note>Dissonant</note>. 

Such is the consideration of *Vadi* (sonant), *Samvadi* (consonant), *Vivadi* (dissonant), and *Anuvadi* (assonant) in the **Shadja-grama** <note>The primary scale starting on the note 'Sa'</note>. In the **Madhyama-grama** <note>The secondary scale starting on the note 'Ma'</note> as well, because the *Panchama* note is situated on the third *Shruti*, this same consideration should be understood with slight modifications. 

In that context:
The consonant of <term>Shadja (Sa)</term> is <term>Madhyama (Ma)</term>; 
of <term>Rishabha (Ri)</term> are <term>Dhaivata (Dha)</term> and <term>Panchama (Pa)</term>; 
of <term>Gandhara (Ga)</term> is <term>Nishada (Ni)</term>; 
of <term>Madhyama (Ma)</term> are <term>Shadja (Sa)</term> and <term>Nishada (Ni)</term>; 
of <term>Panchama (Pa)</term> is <term>Rishabha (Ri)</term>; 
of <term>Dhaivata (Dha)</term> is <term>Rishabha (Ri)</term>; 
and of <term>Nishada (Ni)</term> are <term>Gandhara (Ga)</term> and <term>Madhyama (Ma)</term>. 

The dissonance (*Vivadi*) remains the same in both *Gramas* (scales). 
The assonants (*Anuvadi*) of *Shadja* are *Panchama*, *Dhaivata*, and *Rishabha*. 
For *Rishabha*, they are *Shadja* and *Madhyama*. 
For *Gandhara* and *Nishada*, because they are dissonant to all, there is no "assonance." 
For *Madhyama*, they are *Rishabha* and *Dhaivata*. 
For *Panchama*, they are *Madhyama* and *Dhaivata*. 
For *Dhaivata*, they are *Madhyama* and *Panchama*. This is how it should be known.

Regarding the primary and secondary qualities of these <term>Vadi and others</term>, it is said: "The Vadi is the King." Just as a King is the principal figure, so is the <term>Vadi</term>, because all others follow it. The <term>Samvadi</term> is like the King's chief minister (principal person). Why? Because it follows and acts in concert with the King; hence it is called *Amatya* <note>Minister</note>, meaning "one who sits/dwells nearby." The <term>Vivadi</term> is like an enemy because of its contrary nature—meaning it does not follow the others. The <term>Anuvadi</term> is like a servant; if the King is the *Vadi* and the Minister is the *Samvadi*, the servant follows both of them. || 46 — 51 ||

# The Jewel Mine of Music [Lineage, Sages, and Meters]

The note *Panchama* <note>The fifth note, 'Pa'</note> is born from the lineage of the Ancestors. *Rishabha* and *Dhaivata* <note>The second and sixth notes, 'Ri' and 'Dha'</note> are born from the lineage of the Sages. || 52 ||
*Nishada* <note>The seventh note, 'Ni'</note> is born from the lineage of the Demons. The notes *Shadja*, *Madhyama*, and *Panchama* <note>1st, 4th, and 5th</note> are of the Brahmin <note>priestly</note> caste. *Rishabha* and *Dhaivata* are known as Kshatriyas <note>warriors</note>, while *Nishada* and *Gandhara* <note>3rd</note> are considered Vaishyas <note>merchants</note>. || 53 ||
The two notes *Antara-gandhara* and *Kakali-nishada* <note>sharpened variations of the 3rd and 7th notes</note> are Shudras <note>laborers</note>. Now, I shall describe their colors in order:
The luster of a lotus <note>reddish</note>, reddish-yellow, the color of gold, the brilliance of a jasmine flower <note>white</note>, black, || 54 ||
yellow, and variegated. Now I shall speak of their birthplaces.
In the continents of Jambu, Shaka, Kusha, Krauncha, Shalmali, Shveta, || 55 ||
and Pushkara—in these lands, the notes starting with *Shadja* were born respectively.
The Sages Agni <note>Fire</note>, Brahma <note>the Creator</note>, the Moon, Vishnu <note>Lord of Lakshmi</note>, and Narada || 56 ||
beheld the five notes starting with *Shadja*; Tumburu beheld *Dhaivata* and *Nishada*.
Agni, Brahma, Saraswati, Shiva, Vishnu, Ganesha, || 57 ||
and the Sun are declared to be the presiding deities of the notes starting with *Shadja*.
The meters *Anustubh*, *Gayatri*, *Tristubh*, *Brihati*, || 58 ||
*Pankti*, *Usnik*, and *Jagati* are said to belong to the notes starting with *Shadja*.
*Shadja* and *Rishabha* are used in the Heroic, Marvellous, and Furious sentiments. *Dhaivata* is used in the Odious and Terrible sentiments. || 59 ||
*Gandhara* and *Nishada* are used in the Pathetic sentiment, while *Madhyama* and *Panchama* are used in the Humorous and Erotic sentiments.

->**Commentary (by Simhabhupala)**<-

Now he describes the lineages of the notes starting with *Shadja*: "Divine," etc.
*Shadja*, *Gandhara*, and *Madhyama* are born of the divine lineage; *Panchama* is born of the lineage of the Ancestors; *Rishabha* and *Dhaivata* are born of the lineage of the Sages; *Nishada* is of the demonic lineage. Now he describes the specific castes such as Brahmin: "Brahmins," etc. *Shadja*, *Madhyama*, and *Panchama* are Brahmins; *Rishabha* and *Dhaivata* are Kshatriyas; *Nishada* and *Gandhara* are Vaishyas; *Antara* and *Kakali* are Shudras. He will explain the characteristics of those two in the section on *Murchanas* <note>scales/modes</note>. || 51-53 || Now he describes the specific colors such as white: "Lotus-lustered," etc. *Shadja* is lotus-lustered, which means red; *Rishabha* is *pinjara*, meaning slightly yellow; *Gandhara* is gold-colored, meaning very yellow; *Madhyama* is jasmine-colored, meaning white; *Panchama* is *asita*, meaning black...

# Chapter 1: On Notes (Svaras)

-> Section 3: The Flavors (Rasas) <-

**Dhaivata** is yellow in color; **Nishada** is of a variegated or dappled color. || 54 ||

Now, having promised to explain the birthplaces of these notes, the author states: "This is the birthplace." The origin of **Shadja** is in *Jambudvipa* <note>The "Rose-apple Island," representing the central continent in ancient Indian cosmology</note>; **Rishabha** in *Shakadvipa*; **Gandhara** in *Kushadvipa*; **Madhyama** in *Kraunchadvipa*; **Panchama** in *Shalmalidvipa*; **Dhaivata** in *Shvetadvipa*; and **Nishada** in *Pushkaradvipa*.

One might ask: of what use is this description of their origin in these continents? We reply that it is to establish the certainty that there are exactly seven notes. As was said by **Matanga** <note>An ancient musicologist, author of the Brihaddeshi</note>: "How is the rule of seven notes established? It is said—just as there are seven constituent elements of the body (*dhatus*) such as the juices and so on, so too says **Sushruta** <note>The famous ancient Indian physician and father of surgery</note>:"

> "Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the seven elements."

Thus, by being based on the seven chakras <note>Energy centers in the subtle body</note> or based on the seven continents, there are exactly seven notes. 

But then, since the notes **Kakali** and **Antara** <note>Sharpened versions of Nishada and Gandhara respectively</note> also exist, how is the rule of "only seven" proven? One should say there are nine notes. Not so; because these two lack the status of being "tonic" or "fundamental" (*anshatva*), they are not considered separate notes. **Kakali** is merely a modified form of **Nishada**, and **Antara** is a modified form of **Gandhara**. As was said by **Dattila** <note>An early authority on music theory</note>:

> "Nishada becomes known as Kakali by being raised by two *shrutis* <note>The smallest audible units of pitch</note>.
> Gandhara becomes the 'Intermediate' (Antara) note in the same way.
> Because they lack the status of a primary note, they are not called separate notes.
> Therefore, the ancients declared these to be forms of Nishada and Gandhara."

|| 55, 56- ||

Now he names the Seers (*Rishis*) who "saw" or discovered the notes: **Agni** (Fire) is the Seer of **Shadja**; **Brahma** (the Creator) of **Rishabha**; **Chandra** (the Moon) of **Gandhara**; **Vishnu** (the Preserver) of **Madhyama**; **Narada** of **Panchama**; and **Tumburu** <note>A celestial musician or Gandharva</note> is the Seer for both **Dhaivata** and **Nishada**. || -56, 56- ||

He names the Deities: **Agni**... || -57, 57- ||

He names the poetic meters: starting with **Anushtubh** in order. 

Now, one might ask: what is the use of describing the colors of the notes (like "lotus-colored"), their Seers, Deities, and meters? Know that it is for the **Worship of the Notes** (*Svaropasana*). When the notes **Shadja** and the rest are worshipped using their seed-syllables (*bijas*), then their Seers, Deities, and meters must be remembered, and their colors must be meditated upon. For this very reason, the seed-syllables of the notes were spoken of by **Matanga**:

> "By taking the eight groups of letters from 'A' to 'Ha', 
> and combining them with the vowel-marks, 
> one should extract the seven notes."

The expert in musical notes should carefully extract the first note <note>Shadja</note> from the third of the eighth group, combined with the seed-syllable of Vishnu <note>Hari-bija</note>.
From the second of the seventh group, combined with the seed-syllable of Desire <note>Kama-bija</note>, one should always extract the beautiful note of the Bull <note>original: "Saurabheya," referring to the note Rishabha</note>. <margin>The commentary *Sudha* notes: "Saurabheya means Rishabha."</margin>
From the third of the second group, combined with the seed-syllable of Vishnu, one should extract the third note <note>Gandhara</note>, which is elegant and supreme.
The final of the sixth group, joined with the first, should be known as the indestructible and excellent middle note <note>Madhyama</note>.
Know that the beautiful note <note>Panchama</note> is joined with the first of that group, combined with the number of the sky <note>zero or the void</note>, and produced from the position of the lips.
From the fourth of the fifth group, adorned with the first, one should extract the excellent note <note>Dhaivata</note> produced from the two bows <note>referring to the shape of the eyebrows or a specific yogic posture</note>.
One should extract the final of the fifth group, distinguished by the end of the letter 'A', produced from the seat of Brahma <note>the crown of the head</note> and endowed with a very high-pitched sound <note>Nishada</note>.
Thus, the extraction of notes as found in the sacred traditions <term>Agamas: ancient scriptures detailing ritual and technical knowledge</term> has been demonstrated.

Thus ends the section. Now, the rule for the manifestation of sentiments <term>Rasas: the emotional essence or "flavor" of a performance</term> by the notes is stated: *Sa-Ri* and so on.
The notes Shadja and Rishabha are used in the Heroic, the Wondrous, and the Furious sentiments; Dhaivata is used in the Loathsome and the Terrifying; Gandhara and Nishada are used in the Compassionate; Madhyama and Panchama are used in the Comic and the Erotic.
