# Now begins the section on the Scales, Melodic Ranges, and Tonal Sequences

->The Scale is a collection of notes, the foundation for Melodic Ranges and other forms.<gloss>1</gloss><-
->On this earth, there are two such scales; the first is the Scale of the First Note (Ṣaḍja).<- ॥ 1 ॥
->The second is the Scale of the Fourth Note (Madhyama). Their characteristics are now described.<-
->The Scale of the First Note occurs when the fifth note (Pañcama) is established on its own fourth microtone (Śruti).<- ॥ 2 ॥

(Commentary) Having thus defined the individual notes, the author recognizes that isolated notes do not serve a purpose for either worldly enjoyment or spiritual merit. To achieve those goals, one must define the Melodic Ranges <term>Mūrcchanā: the sequential rise and fall of seven notes</term> and other forms which consist of specific arrangements of all the notes. Since these depend on the Scales <term>Grāma: the basic collection of notes from which scales are derived</term> as their foundation and organizing principle, the author first provides the general definition: **The Scale**. A Scale is like a village <note>The word 'Grāma' literally means village; just as a village is a collection of people, a musical Grāma is a collection of notes</note>. Just as in common usage a collection of people is called a village, here a collection of notes is intended to be a Scale. If one were to say only "a collection of notes is a Scale," the definition would be too broad, as it would apply to the groups of tones found in ordinary speech or Vedic chanting. To prevent this, the qualification **the foundation for Melodic Ranges and other forms** is added. Here, the word "and others" includes Tonal Sequences <term>Tāna</term>, Melodic Patterns <term>Varṇa</term>, Ornaments <term>Alaṃkāra</term>, and Parent Modes <term>Jāti</term>. In the general definition, "Scale" is used in the singular to denote the category; however, while all seven notes are part of a scale, the author specifies the particular characteristics of the scales as they exist in the world, saying **On this earth, there are two**. If one asks why there are only two scales on earth when any group of seven notes could theoretically be called a scale, the answer is: because of the two ways notes are used in their pure and modified forms, and because of the Sage's <note>Referring to Bharata Muni, the author of the Nāṭyaśāstra</note> decree:

> "Two scales are famous in the world, known as the Scale of the First Note and the Scale of the Fourth Note."

Thus, the Scale of the First Note (Ṣaḍjagrāma) is considered the first because it is the basis for pure notes, and the Scale of the Fourth Note (Madhyamagrāma) is second because it involves modified notes. Regarding the phrase **established on its own fourth microtone**: its own—

# The Ocean of Music [Scales and Modes]

->When the [note Panchama] is situated on its own penultimate microtone, it is considered the Madhyama scale.<-
->Alternatively: in the Shadja scale, Dhaivata has three microtones, but in the Madhyama scale, it has four. (3)<-
->If Gandhara takes one microtone each from Rishabha and Madhyama,<-
->And if Nishada takes one microtone from Dhaivata, and Dhaivata takes one from Panchama and one from Shadja, (4)<-
->Then the Sage Narada declares that to be the Gandhara scale.<-
->That scale exists in the heavenly realm, but not on this earth. (5)<-

When [the note Panchama] is situated on the seventeenth microtone <note>named Alapini, of the Karuna class</note>, it is the Shadja scale. Regarding the phrase "situated on its own penultimate microtone": this refers to it standing on the sixteenth microtone <note>named Sandipani, of the Ayata class</note>. Here, the word "own" is used in both cases to avoid confusion. If one simply said "situated on the fourth microtone" or "situated on the penultimate microtone," a misunderstanding could occur regarding the Madhyama scale. In the Madhyama scale, due to the overlap of notes, the Panchama—which usually has four microtones—might appear to be on its third or second microtone. By specifying "its own," the author clarifies that the shift is an internal structural change of the note's position within the scale system, not just a relative change. 

The phrase "Alternatively" introduces a secondary perspective. Why? Because the distinction between the scales is fundamentally established by the change in the note Panchama <term>Panchama: the fifth note, similar to 'So' in solfege</term>. The variation in the note Dhaivata <term>Dhaivata: the sixth note, 'La'</term> is mentioned because it depends on the Panchama. Dhaivata does not change the scale on its own; rather, by becoming four-microtones wide (modified) or three-microtones wide (pure), it serves as an indicator of which scale is being used.

<insert>(Sudhakara Commentary)</insert> To define the "Grama" <term>Grama: literally 'village', here meaning a fundamental scale or collection of notes</term>, the author says: "A Grama is a collection of notes." A group of musical notes is called a Grama. But why use the word "village" for a group of notes? It is explained: because it is the foundation or "shelter" for the *Murchanas* <term>Murchana: the expansion of a scale into modes</term> and other melodic structures. Just as a village is a shelter for people, the Grama is the shelter for notes. As stated by the sage Matanga—

# Chapter One: On Notes
## Section 4: Sequential Tones (Kramatanas)

> "Just as all members of a family live together in unity, that is called a 'Village' <note>original: 'Grama'; in music, this refers to a fundamental scale or collection of notes</note> where there is a permanent, organized residence for all people."

Thus it is said. Alternatively, if a mere collection of notes were called a Village, then even notes uttered without any systematic order would be a Village. To prevent this misunderstanding, it is stated that a Village is "the substratum for melodic movements <note>original: 'Murchanas'</note> and the like." The meaning is that only that collection of notes which serves as the basis for melodic movements is designated by the word Village, not a collection of notes uttered randomly. And so it has been said by the author of the *Compendium of the Essence of Music* <note>original: 'Sangita-Samayasara'</note>:

> "A Village is desired as a collection of notes consisting of melodic movements, sequences, parent scales, and dominant notes, which are indeed established upon fixed micro-tones <note>original: 'Shrutis'</note>."

He states the divisions of that Village: "They are two." But is it not well known that there are three Villages? Why is it said there are only two? To this he replies: "On this earth." Among those, the first and primary is the **Sa-scale** <note>original: 'Shadjagrama'</note>. The second is the **Ma-scale** <note>original: 'Madhyamagrama'</note>. Therefore, it was said by the sage Matanga:

> "Between the two Villages, which one is considered primary? The primacy of the Sa-scale is understood from the words of the Sage."

Having promised to define them, he describes them: "Of the two..." When the fifth note <note>original: 'Panchama' or 'Pa'</note> remains in its own fourth micro-tone—the position where it is traditionally established—and is thus "unmodified," it is the **Sa-scale**. Although in the Sa-scale other notes like the tonic <note>original: 'Shadja'</note> are also unmodified, the reason for specifically mentioning the fifth note as unmodified is to demonstrate its distinction from the Ma-scale, where the fifth note becomes "modified."

He describes the definition of the **Ma-scale**: "By its penultimate..." When this fifth note stands upon the third micro-tone, which is near its own penultimate micro-tone, it becomes the Ma-scale. Although the first micro-tone of the sixth note <note>original: 'Dhaivata'</note> is also near the final micro-tone of the fifth, it is not "its own" <insert>belonging to the fifth note</insert>; therefore, the word "own" is used to exclude that. He explains this same definition in another way: "Or rather..." The sixth note <note>original: 'Dha'</note> has three micro-tones in the Sa-scale, but in the Ma-scale, it gains the final micro-tone of the fifth note and thus has four micro-tones. The meaning remains the same. However, previously the definition of both was given by emphasizing the fifth note—

# Sangitaratnakara [Scales and Modes]

->The Shadja <note>The first note, 'Sa'</note> is primary because it is the first, and because of its many 'ministers' <note>referring to its many consonant relationships</note>.<-
->In its scale, the Madhyama <note>The fourth note, 'Ma'</note> is the leader because it is never omitted. (6)<-
->Because he is born of this lineage, Gandhara <note>The third note, 'Ga'</note> is also a leader in the heavens.<-
->In the three scales, the presiding deities are Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva respectively. (7)<-
->Those seeking prosperity should sing them in the Winter, Summer, and Rainy seasons,<-
->In the morning, at midday, and in the afternoon respectively. (8)<-

...was stated; however, this is in regards to the prominence of Dhaivata <note>The sixth note, 'Dha'</note>. <gloss>1</gloss> The definition previously mentioned regarding the prominence of Dhaivata seems inconsistent, but that is according to the views of others, not the author's own view. For this very reason, the author will later explain that in "crooked" melodic sequences <term>Kuta-tana</term> <note>non-sequential note patterns</note> lacking the fifth note (Panchama), repetition occurs precisely because the distinguishing fifth is absent, not because of the absence of the sixth (Dhaivata). Even though the <term>Gandhara-grama</term> <note>The scale starting on the third note</note> is not in practical use on earth, the treatise describes its characteristics because the science of music must cover all subjects. Regarding the notes Ri and Ma: <term>Gandhara</term> becomes a four-microtone note by leaning on the final microtone <term>Shruti</term> of Rishabha and the first microtone of Madhyama. Dhaivata leans on the final microtone of Panchama. Nishada <note>The seventh note, 'Ni'</note>, taking the final microtone of Dhaivata and leaning on the first microtone of Shadja, also becomes a four-microtone note. At that time, the sage Narada declared it the Gandhara-scale. The mention of Narada is for the sake of authority, not to suggest a difference in the author's own opinion. (1–5)

(Kallinatha's Commentary) Now, one might object: "Since scales depend on the use of notes, there should only be two scales here; why distinguish them as <term>Shadja-grama</term> and <term>Madhyama-grama</term> when other notes exist?" Anticipating this, he provides the reasoning: "The Shadja is primary." "Because of its many ministers" means because of the abundance of its consonant notes <note>Samvadi-svaras</note>. The connection is that it is primary within the scale. Regarding "because it is never omitted": the non-omission of the Madhyama note is based on the view that <term>Consonance</term> <note>Samvada</note> is the sounding together on a string of pairs—the lower notes (Sa, Ri, Ga) and the upper notes (Pa, Dha, Ni) respectively. According to this view, since the lone Madhyama has no consonant partner, it remains as a fixed boundary and its omission is not desired; this is the opinion of some. For others, however, in the context of pure melodic structures...

## The ascent and descent of the seven notes in order.

At the time of defining characteristics, authorities such as Bharata <note>Bharata Muni, the legendary author of the Natyashastra</note> and others have prescribed the omission of notes like Shadja, Rishabha, Nishada, and Panchama to create hexatonic <term>Shadava (six-note scales)</term> and pentatonic <term>Auduva (five-note scales)</term>. However, because the note Madhyama is never omitted, it is considered "indestructible" or permanent. || 6—8 ||

<margin>(Sudhakara)</margin> Now, one might ask: why are only Shadja, Madhyama, and Gandhara designated as the basis for "Gramas" <note>Grama: the fundamental scales or "villages" of notes</note> and not the other notes? To this, he says: "Shadja." Shadja is the first of all notes, and therefore it is the leader or the primary one. He gives another reason for its primacy: "due to the abundance of ministers." The "ministers" are the <term>Samvadins (consonant notes)</term>; their abundance is relative to other notes. For other notes, there is only one consonant note each, but for Shadja, there are two consonant notes: Madhyama and Panchama. Madhyama is also a leader in the Grama system and shares the designation of the scale. The reason given is "due to its non-omissibility." In the formation of six-note or five-note scales, the Madhyama is never dropped. Therefore, it too is primary. Because Gandhara is born in the same divine lineage as Shadja and Madhyama, it is considered the leader of notes in the heavenly world and also receives the designation of a Grama. Thus it was said by Matanga <note>An influential musicologist, author of Brihaddeshi</note>: "How is it that the Gramas are named after the notes Shadja and Madhyama? It is said: they are named after them due to their extraordinary nature. Their extraordinary nature comes from being born of a divine family." The non-omissibility of Madhyama was also stated by Dattila <note>An ancient sage and music theorist</note>:

> "In the Madhyama-grama, the Panchama is non-omissible; in the Shadja-grama, the Dhaivata. But one should know that the Madhyama is non-omissible everywhere."

He then names the presiding deities of the three Gramas with the word "In order." He explains the rules for singing according to the seasons with "Hemanta" <note>Early Winter</note>. Even within specific seasons, he regulates the singing to specific times like the forenoon with "In the forenoon." Since the result is stated to be for "those seeking prosperity," the rule implies a benefit, but there is no sin in its non-observance. The purpose of defining the Gramas was stated by Matanga: "The purpose is to establish the system for notes, intervals, scales, melodic movements, and modes." || 6—8 || Thus ends the section on Gramas.

<margin>(Kallinatha)</margin> Regarding the definition of Gramas, he now gives the general definition of <term>Murchanas (scales/modes)</term>, which were mentioned first as being dependent on the Gramas, with the phrase: "Of the seven notes in order." The word "in order" is used to exclude <term>Kuta-tanas (irregular or scrambled note sequences)</term>. Of the seven...

<header>The Jewel Mine of Music [Scales of the Gramas]</header>

->A scale is defined as such; in the two systems, there are seven in each. (9)<-

->In the Shadja system, the first is Uttaramandra, then Rajani, Uttarayata,
Shuddhashadja, <insert>Matsarikrita</insert>, Ashvakranta, and Abhirudgata. (10)<-

->In the Madhyama system, there is Sauviri, then Harinashva,
followed by Kalopanata, Shuddhamadhya, Margi, Pauravi, (11)<-

->and Hrishyaka. Now, their specific characteristics are explained.<-

---

The phrase "of the notes" <note>original: "svaranam"</note> is used to exclude the "pure melodic fragments" <term>shuddha-tana: simplified melodic units used in ancient practice</term>. The phrase "ascent and descent" is used to exclude the two types of melodic ornamentation <term>alankara</term> that consist only of ascending or descending movements. **Scale** <note>original: "murchana"</note>: This term is derived from the root *murch*, meaning "to thicken/pervade" or "to faint/faint with joy." It is called a scale because it is the means by which a melody <term>raga</term> is expanded or pervaded, or because the listener is "enchanted" <note>literally "made to faint" with pleasure</note> by it. Although authorities like Matanga and Nandikeshvara have mentioned twelve-note scales to cover the three registers in practice, they are not mentioned separately here. This is because, in practice, one usually sees a combination of the two systems <term>gramas</term>, which naturally covers the three registers. He shows the specific types in both systems for practical use, by name and form, starting with the number: **In the two systems**, etc. Although "scale" was introduced in the singular to denote the category, the use of the plural "they" <note>original: "tah"</note> is appropriate as it refers to the specific types to be described. The first scale, Uttaramandra, begins with the note Shadja <note>the tonic or 'Do'</note> in the middle register. Why this rule? Because it was regulated by ancient sages like Bharata. As Bharata said: "The indication of the scale on the flute is by the middle note," and Matanga also said: "The indication of the scale should be made using the middle septet <term>saptaka: octave</term> to achieve the lower and higher registers." (9–11)

---

(Sudhakara commentary) He defines the scale: **In order**, etc. The ascent and descent of the seven notes is called a scale <note>murchana</note>. By the words "ascent and descent," the notes endowed with those movements are meant.

Therefore, the seven notes in ascending and descending order are designated by the term <term>Murchana</term>. The etymology of the word <term>Murchana</term> is explained by the sage Matanga:

> "The word <term>Murchana</term> is derived from the roots meaning 'fainting' or 'increasing/swelling.' That by which a <term>Raga</term><note>A melodic framework or 'color' of the mind.</note> is allowed to swell or manifest is called a <term>Murchana</term>."

The quality of being a <term>Murchana</term> belongs to the notes themselves, and not merely to the action of ascending and descending; this too was stated by him:

> "The collection of seven notes in the sequence of ascent and descent should be understood by the experts as being designated by the term <term>Murchana</term>."

The mention of "seven notes" is an informal description, as Matanga has also established <term>Murchanas</term> consisting of twelve notes. He now describes their divisions: "In the two <term>Gramas</term><note>Parent scales or 'villages' of notes.</note>." In the <term>Shadja-grama</term>, there are seven <term>Murchanas</term>, and in the <term>Madhyama-grama</term>, there are seven. He states their names: In the <term>Shadja-grama</term>, the first scale is <term>Uttaramandra</term>, the second is <term>Rajani</term>, the third is <term>Uttarayata</term>, the fourth is <term>Shuddhashadja</term>, the fifth is <term>Matsarikrita</term>, the sixth is <term>Ashvakranta</term>, and the seventh is <term>Abhirudgata</term>. In the <term>Madhyama-grama</term>, the first is <term>Sauviri</term>, the second is <term>Harinashva</term>, the third is <term>Kalopanata</term>, the fourth is <term>Shuddhamadhya</term>, the fifth is <term>Margi</term>, the sixth is <term>Pauravi</term>, and the seventh is <term>Hrishyaka</term>. || 9-11 ||

# The Ocean of Music (Sangitaratnakara)
## [Scales and Modes]

It should be understood from the context that these are produced by the notes residing in their proper registers. This means that one should sound the notes of the *Rajani* scale—<note>original: "ni sa ri ga ma pa dha"</note>—using the same physical positions as the notes of the *Uttaramandra* scale—<note>original: "sa ri ga ma pa dha ni"</note>. Regarding the *Harinashva* and subsequent scales: here too, starting from the middle-register *Madhyama* note, one should sound the notes of the *Harinashva* scale—<note>original: "ga ma pa dha ni sa ri"</note>—within the same positions as the *Sauviri* scale—<note>original: "ma pa dha ni sa ri ga"</note>. In both cases, the phrase "and so on" implies that the starting notes of the respective scales must begin within the registers of the *Shadja* and *Madhyama* <term>gramas (fundamental scales)</term>. || 12–14 ||

(Commentary by Sudhakara) To ensure the listener's attention and to highlight the distinctions between them, the author declares their characteristics: "Now, regarding those..." The first scale of the *Shadja-grama*, called *Uttaramandra*, begins with the *Shadja* note located in the middle register. One must perform an ascent from *Shadja* to the seventh note, and a descent from the seventh note back to *Shadja*. The other scales, such as *Rajani*, should be performed by starting from the six notes below that middle-register *Shadja*—namely the lower-register *Nishada*, *Dhaivata*, and so on, down to the lower-register *Rishabha*.

He then defines the scales of the *Madhyama-grama*: "The middle Madhyama..." Starting from the *Madhyama* note in the middle register, *Sauviri* becomes the first scale of the *Madhyama-grama*. The other six, such as *Harinashva*, are performed by starting from the notes situated progressively lower than that middle-register *Madhyama*—namely *Gandhara*, *Rishabha*, and so on, down to the lower-register *Panchama*.

The nature of the scales is as follows—<note>In the written notation, a note with a dot above the head is to be known as a lower-register (mandra) note, while those with a vertical line above the head are high-register (tara) notes, as will be stated later: "The lower note has a dot head; the high note has a vertical line in writing."</note> Only the ascending order is written here; the descending order should be understood by reversing from the final note.

<header>Sequential Tones: 4] First Chapter: On Notes</header>

## One should move the notes starting from Shadja and Madhyama upward in succession. || 15 ||
## These are fourfold: purely "Shuddha," <note>original: "śuddhā"</note> those with the Kakali note,
## those with the Antara note, and those with both. Thus, fifty-six are described. || 16 ||

Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma — Hṛṣyakā || 7 || Just as before, this variation of the Pure Shadja scale is distinguished by the fifth note.
He states the definition of these according to another school of thought: **"In the place of Shadja..."** By placing notes starting with Nishada in the position of Shadja, the scales Rajani and others are formed. When Nishada is placed in the position of Shadja, it is Rajani || 2 ||.
When Dhaivata is placed there, it is Uttarāyatā || 3 ||. When Panchama is placed there, it is Śuddha-ṣaḍjā || 4 ||.
When Madhyama is placed there, it is Matsarīkṛtā || 5 ||. When Gandhara is placed there, it is Aśvakrāntā || 6 ||. When Rishabha is placed there, it is Abhirudgatā || 7 ||.
Similarly, by placing Gandhara and others in the position of Madhyama, Hāriṇāśvā and others are formed. When Gandhara is placed in the position of Madhyama, it is Hāriṇāśvā || 2 ||. When Rishabha is placed there, it is Kalopanatā || 3 ||.
When Shadja is placed there, it is Śuddhamadhyā || 4 ||. When Nishada is placed there, it is Mārgī || 5 ||. When Dhaivata is placed there, it is Pauravī || 6 ||.
When Panchama is placed there, it is Hṛṣyakā || 7 ||. Thus. || 12—14 ||

(Kallinātha's Commentary) Now, a doubt arises: if Nishada, Gandhara, and other notes are simply used in the positions of Shadja and Madhyama, how is there any mutual distinction between scales like Uttaramandrā and Rajanī in the Shadja-scale (Grāma), or between Sauvīrī and Hāriṇāśvā in the Madhyama-scale? To resolve this doubt, he says:
**"Starting from Shadja and Madhyama..."** and **"Upward from that..."** In scales like Rajanī (where Nishada is in the Shadja position) or Hāriṇāśvā (where Gandhara is in the Madhyama position), one should "move" or slide the subsequent notes—Shadja, Madhyama, etc.—upward. This means one should reach the other microtones <term>Śruti: the smallest audible interval of pitch</term> by carefully considering the specific number of microtones belonging to each note.
**"In succession"** means the following order: in Uttarāyatā, when Dhaivata is placed in the Shadja position, the note above it is Nishada; in Kalopanatā, when Rishabha is placed in the Madhyama position, the note above it is Gandhara, and so on. Therefore, he shows that each of the scales has four variations based on being "Pure" (Shuddha) or modified: **"Fourfold..."** This refers to the fourteen scales (Mūrchanās) mentioned in the two parent scales (Grāmas).

# Page 108
## [The Gramas and Murchanas]

The **Pure** <note>Shuddha: the unmodified or natural state of the notes</note> notes in the <term>Shadja-grama</term> <note>The primary scale starting on the note 'Sa'</note> are those devoid of any alterations. However, in the <term>Madhyama-grama</term> <note>The secondary scale starting on the note 'Ma'</note>, the notes are considered "pure" even when they exclude the alterations of <term>Panchama</term> <note>The fifth note, 'Pa'</note>—which defines the difference between the two scales—and the <term>Dhaivata</term> <note>The sixth note, 'Dha'</note> which characterizes it. In that context, the "purity" is intended to mean that these two notes remain in their fixed positions specific to that scale. 

Now, one might ask: even if the fifth note (Panchama) serves its purpose by distinguishing the scales, and even if the second (Rishabha) and sixth (Dhaivata) notes have no independent power to distinguish scales (as their changes depend on the changes of the first and fifth notes), how can we be certain there are only four types of scales when other variations are possible through the overlapping of the first and fourth notes? Why is it determined to be four types solely by resorting to the <term>Kakali</term> <note>A sharp Seventh</note> and <term>Antara</term> <note>A sharp Third</note> notes? 

This is true: although the first and fourth notes (Shadja and Madhyama) could potentially distinguish scales when they overlap, the <term>Kakali and Antara</term> notes are already included within those overlapping categories, and thus do not create separate distinctions. As the sage Matanga says: "The two overlapping notes are the Seventh (Nishada) and Third (Gandhara); all other alterations are included within them." Furthermore, when describing the different types of <term>overlapping scales (Murchana-sadharana)</term> in the two Gramas, the overlapping of the first and fourth notes is not utilized as it is restricted to specific scales. As Bharata stated: "In the Shadja-grama, use the Shadja-overlap; in the Madhyama-grama, use the Madhyama-overlap." Therefore, the teacher’s secret—that there are four types—is difficult to grasp for those who do not know the oral tradition.

> The ocean of arts, Kallinatha, who knows the true measure of <term>intervals (Shrutis)</term> and <term>notes (Svaras)</term>, 
> has thus established the fourfold nature of the <term>scales (Murchanas)</term> here. || 15, 16 ||

(Commentary by Simhabhupala): Now, if the Seventh (Nishada) and others, or the Third (Gandhara) and others, are placed in the <term>position of the first note (Shadja)</term> or the <term>position of the fourth note (Madhyama)</term>, where do the original first and fourth notes go? He answers: "The Shadja and others..." One should shift the notes like Shadja, Rishabha, and Gandhara, or Madhyama, Panchama, and Dhaivata, upwards; that is, place them in the positions of the higher notes. For example, when the Seventh (Nishada) is placed in the position of the first (Shadja), then the first (Shadja) moves to the position of the second (Rishabha), and the second (Rishabha) moves to the position of the third (Gandhara), and so on. Similarly, when the sixth (Dhaivata) is in the first (Shadja) position, the seventh (Nishada) moves to the second (Rishabha) position, and the first (Shadja) to the third (Gandhara) position—this should be inferred by the reader. 

But how can one note occupy the place of another? We say: this is not a primary literal usage, but a metaphorical or technical one. Alternatively, it is stated this way because it was accepted by ancient authorities like Dattila. Indeed, Dattila says that one may, by one's own will, start on any <term>microtone (Shruti)</term>...

# Chapter 1: On Notes (Swaras)

One should establish the <term>Shadja</term><note>The fundamental note, similar to 'Do' in Western solfège</note> as the starting point, and in relation to that, one should establish the other notes according to the rules of <term>Shrutis</term><note>Microtonal intervals; the smallest audible pitch differences</note>. As it has been said:

> "Whichever sound is taken as the <term>Shadja</term> in the <term>Shadja-grama</term><note>The primary scale or 'grama' of ancient Indian music</note>, the third note above it will certainly be <term>Rishabha</term>.
> Two steps from there is <term>Gandhara</term>, and four steps from that is <term>Madhyama</term>.
> Likewise, the fifth note from <term>Madhyama</term> is <term>Panchama</term>, and three steps from there is <term>Dhaivata</term>.
> From there, the second is <term>Nishada</term>, and the fourth from that returns to <term>Shadja</term>."

This is explained in the commentary on Dattila known as *Prayoga-stabaka*: "Whichever specific sound is grasped—meaning imagined or intellectually established—as the <term>Shadja</term> note in the scale called <term>Shadja-grama</term>, the third interval above that specific sound is <term>Rishabha</term>." With this very intention, the sage Dattila spoke of the identity between the <term>Murchanas</term><note>Scales or modes derived by shifting the tonic</note> of the <term>Shadja-grama</term> and the <term>Madhyama-grama</term> through a slight modification. As he said:

> "If one makes <term>Gandhara</term> into <term>Dhaivata</term> by raising it by two <term>Shrutis</term>,
> and accordingly adjusts <term>Madhyama</term> and the others, and <term>Nishada</term> and the others as they stand,
> then a particular <term>Murchana</term> of the <term>Shadja-grama</term>
> becomes that same numbered <term>Murchana</term> of the <term>Madhyama-grama</term>.
> Conversely, by lowering <term>Dhaivata</term> by two <term>Shrutis</term> to make it <term>Gandhara</term>,
> one should contemplate the <term>Shadja-murchanas</term> as before."

By accepting the placement of <term>Shadja</term> according to one's own will, authorities like Dattila and Daksha-Prajapati accepted <term>Avadhana</term><note>Focused attention or musical mindfulness</note> as a limb of <term>Gandharva</term><note>Sacred celestial music</note>. As Dattila said:

> "A collection of notes residing in words, well-measured by rhythm (<term>Tala</term>),
> and performed with focused attention (<term>Avadhana</term>), is called <term>Gandharva</term>."

Daksha-Prajapati also stated:

> "In <term>Gandharva</term>, focused attention comes first, followed by notes, words, and the rest.
> Without the excess of focused attention, the three-fold musical art cannot be realized."

<summary>This page discusses the mathematical relationship between notes in ancient Indian scales and explains how shifting the fundamental note (Shadja) allows for the transformation of one scale into another. It emphasizes that sacred music (Gandharva) requires not just technical precision in pitch and rhythm, but also intense mental focus (Avadhana).</summary>

<keywords>Shadja-grama, Madhyama-grama, Murchana, Dattila, Daksha-Prajapati, Gandharva, Avadhana, Shruti, musical intervals, ancient Indian music theory</keywords>

# Ocean of Music [Scales and Modes]

...so he said. <term>Concentration (Avadhana)</term> <note>original: "avadhana"</note> refers to the one-pointed focus of the mind, intellect, memory, and the senses. <term>Shadja (The Tonic)</term> <note>The fundamental note 'Sa' from which all other notes are measured.</note> is established, and in relation to that alone, the other notes are pronounced. If the notes were not established according to one's will, then concentration would serve no purpose. Even <term>Sharngadeva</term> <note>The 13th-century author of the Sangita Ratnakara.</note> accepted this view to some extent in his description of the shifting lute (chala-vina), stating: "The seven notes are to be brought forth by the wise from the penultimate string of that instrument." In the world, we see lute players establishing notes according to their own will; let us leave it at that. However, <term>Matanga</term> <note>An earlier influential musicologist, author of Brihaddeshi.</note> spoke of <term>twelve-note modes (murchanas)</term>:

->“Now I shall describe the twelve-note modes.”<-

Here, the <term>designation of modes</term> is intended to achieve a range across three registers <note>low, middle, and high</note>; thus, modes consisting of twelve notes should be understood. <term>Nandikeshvara</term> <note>A legendary figure in Indian arts and musicology.</note> also stated:

> “The wise should understand modes as being composed of twelve notes.
> This is for the sake of establishing the melodic types (Jatis) and languages,¹ and for the mastery of the high and low registers.”

These are as follows: Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga — <term>Uttaramandra</term> (1). Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma — <term>Rajani</term> (2). Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa — <term>Uttarayata</term> (3). Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha — <term>Shuddhashadja</term> (4). Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni — <term>Matsarikrita</term> (5). Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa — <term>Ashvakranta</term> (6). Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri — <term>Abhirudgata</term> (7). These are in the <term>Shadja-grama</term> <note>The primary scale starting on the note Sa.</note>. In the <term>Madhyama-grama</term> <note>The secondary scale starting on the note Ma.</note>, it is the same: ²Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa — <term>Sauviri</term> (1). Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha — <term>Harinashva</term> (2). Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni — <term>Kalopanata</term> (3). Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa — <term>Shuddhamadhya</term> (4). Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri — <term>Margi</term> (5). Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga — <term>Pauravi</term> (6). Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma — <term>Hrishyaka</term> (7).

He explains the fourfold nature of all fourteen modes: "fourfold." Those fourteen modes are each of four types: pure, <term>with Kakali-Ni</term> <note>using a sharp 7th note</note>, <term>with Antara-Ga</term> <note>using a sharp 3rd note</note>, and <term>with both Kakali and Antara</term>. Thus, there are fifty-six variations in total. || 19, 16 ||

<page-num>111</page-num>
<header>Kramatana 4] First Chapter: On Notes</header>

->**If the note Nishada takes for itself two microtones of Shadja, then it is called Kakali; likewise, if Gandhara takes two microtones of Madhyama, it is called the Antara note. || 17 ||**<-

(**Kallinatha**) <note>Kallinatha is a 15th-century commentator on this text.</note> He explains the nature of the *Kakali* and *Antara* notes, which have been introduced because they create variations in the *Murchanas* <note>The ancient scales or melodic frameworks</note>. Regarding the phrase "If [it takes] two microtones of Madhyama," the previous words "if it takes two microtones" should be applied here as well. Since the *Kakali* and *Antara* notes are useful for differentiating scales, he mentions the concepts of <term>Pravesha (Entrance)</term> and <term>Nigraha (Restraint)</term> as taught by the sage Matanga. Specifically: the practice of *Tanas* <note>melodic patterns</note> is twofold, through Entrance and Restraint. <term>Entrance</term> is also twofold: by the "pulling away" of the preceding note and the "softening" of the succeeding note. In this context, regarding the note Shadja <note>the tonic 'Do'</note> which is lower than Rishabha <note>the second note 'Re'</note> and is meant to be omitted, "pulling away" means pressing or pushing it toward Rishabha. Conversely, for that same Shadja when it is higher than Nishada <note>the seventh note 'Ti'</note>, "softening" means loosening it, or bringing it toward Nishada. <term>Restraint</term> is the total abandonment of the succeeding note, meaning it is not touched at all. As Bharata <note>the legendary author of the Natyashastra</note> says:

> "The action of the *Tana* on the strings is twofold: through Entrance and through Restraint."

In that context, Entrance is defined as either the pulling away of the lower note or the softening of the higher note. Restraint is the non-touching of the note. Dattila <note>another ancient music authority</note> has also said:

> "The action of the *Tana* on the strings is twofold: through Entrance and through Restraint. Entrance is the merging of sounds, while Restraint is the lack of contact."

|| 17 ||

(**Simhabhupala**) <note>Another major commentator on the text.</note> It was previously mentioned that scales can include the *Kakali* and *Antara* notes; in response to the question of what these notes are, he says: "If the note Nishada..." If Nishada <note>the 7th note</note> takes two microtones <note>Shrutis</note> from Shadja <note>the 1st note</note>—that is, if it stands on the second microtone of Shadja and thus becomes a note of four microtones—it is called <term>Kakali</term> <note>a sharp 7th</note>. And if Gandhara <note>the 3rd note</note> takes two microtones of Madhyama <note>the 4th note</note> and becomes a note of four microtones, it is called <term>Antara</term> <note>a sharp 3rd</note>. It was stated previously that Nishada and Gandhara are the only notes that become *Kakali* and *Antara*; they are not entirely different notes from the basic seven. || 17 ||

# The Ocean of Music [Scales and Melodic Progressions]

In whichever position the notes *Shadja* <note>The tonic or first note, 'Sa'</note> and *Madhyama* <note>The fourth note, 'Ma'</note> appear respectively within the two scales <note>The Shadja-grama and Madhyama-grama</note>, that specific scale-variant is designated by that same number by the author Nishanka <note>A title for the author, Sharngadeva, meaning 'The Doubtless One'</note>. || 18 ||

Starting from the first note and so on, each scale-variant becomes sevenfold. In these, one should pronounce the final notes and then the preceding ones in a regular sequence. || 19 ||

These are the *Kramas* <note>Sequential permutations of notes</note>; their total number is three hundred and ninety-two. The Yakshas, Rakshasas, Narada, Brahma, the Nagas, the Ashvins, and Varuna— || 20 ||

—these are the presiding deities of the scales in the *Shadja-grama* <note>The scale starting on the tonic</note> in their respective order. Brahma, Indra, Vayu, the Gandharvas, the Siddhas, Shiva, and the Humans— || 21 ||

—these are the deities of the *Madhyama-grama* <note>The scale starting on the fourth note</note> scales in order. The sage Narada has provided alternative names for these. || 22 ||

In the *Shadja-grama*, the first is *Uttaramandra*, followed by *Abhirudgata*, *Ashvakranta*, *Sauviri*, *Hrishyaka*, *Uttarayata*, || 23 ||

and *Rajani*; these are known as the seven scales of the Sages. *Apyayani*, *Vishvakrita*, *Chandra*, *Hema*, *Kapardini*, || 24 ||

*Maitri*, and *Chandramasi*—these are the ancestral scales in the *Madhyama* scale. *Nanda*, *Vishala*, *Sumukhi*, *Chitra*, *Chitravati*, *Sukha*, || 25 ||

and *Alapa*—these are the seven scales in the *Gandhara-grama* <note>The third ancient scale, believed to have been lost to heaven</note>. These are to be performed in the celestial realms; they are not described here in detail. || 26 ||

**Commentary (by Kallinatha):** He explains the method for recognizing the numerical order (first, second, etc.) among the scales with the verse beginning "In whichever..."

Regarding the phrase "In whichever position" <note>original: "yāvatithau"</note>: The word is formed from "yāvat" with a suffix indicating ordinal position. In whichever scale of the two *gramas* the notes *Shadja* and *Madhyama* occupy a certain ordinal position, that scale is known by that number. Here, according to the grammatical rule... <note>The commentator begins a technical grammatical explanation of the Sanskrit suffixing used to denote the numerical position of the notes.</note>

# Sequential Variations (Kramas): 4] First Chapter on Notes

<page-num>113</page-num>

Now, in connection with the scales (<term>murchanas</term>—the foundational melodic structures), the author defines the "sequences" (<term>kramas</term>—ordered successions of notes) which consist of only ascending notes and form a part of those scales. These are determined in a specific quantity for each scale to be used in the permutation of "complex sequences" (<term>kuta-tanas</term>). He defines them starting with the phrase: **"From the beginning of the first note..."**

This means starting from the first note of whichever scale is being used. By including the other six notes through a grammatical convention of grouping, we arrive at the seven notes starting from the first. **"Each one"** refers to each of the fifty-six scales previously mentioned (divided into pure and other types). In these scales, one should pronounce the notes in order up to the final note, and then—applying the word "sequentially" repeatedly—one should pronounce the "preceding" notes. "Preceding" here means those notes situated below the starting note.

In this definition of seven-note sequences, the instruction to "pronounce the preceding notes" may not apply to the very first sequence of a scale (which starts on the first note), but it applies to the second sequence and those following. For example, in the scale called *Uttaramandra*:
1. The first sequence is: Do, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La, Ti <note>original: Sa, Ri, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni</note>.
2. The second is: Ti, Do, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La <note>original: Ni, Sa, Ri, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha</note>.
3. The third is: La, Ti, Do, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol <note>original: Dha, Ni, Sa, Ri, Ga, Ma, Pa</note>.
4. The fourth is: Sol, La, Ti, Do, Re, Mi, Fa <note>original: Pa, Dha, Ni, Sa, Ri, Ga, Ma</note>.
5. The fifth is: Fa, Sol, La, Ti, Do, Re, Mi <note>original: Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni, Sa, Ri, Ga</note>.
6. The sixth is: Mi, Fa, Sol, La, Ti, Do, Re <note>original: Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni, Sa, Ri</note>.
7. The seventh is: Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La, Ti, Do <note>original: Ri, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni, Sa</note>.

Because these are pronounced in this specific order, they are given the technical name "Sequence" (<term>krama</term>). The verses mentioning "Yakshas and Rakshasas" <note>mythological beings associated with specific musical patterns</note> are clear in their meaning. || 18-26 ||

<note>The following is the Sudhakara commentary by Simhabhupala on the work of Sharngadeva.</note>

**(Su.)** The author provides an easy method for recognizing the number of the scale: **"In which..."**
Between the two parent scales (<term>gramas</term>), the position of the notes "Do" (<term>Shadja</term>) and "Fa" (<term>Madhyama</term>) determines the number of the scale. This was stated by Sharngadeva, who is adorned with the title "The Fearless" (<term>Nishanka</term>). 

In the scales of the *Shadja-grama* (the Do-scale system):
- If "Do" is the first note, it is the 1st scale.
- If "Do" is the second note, it is the 2nd scale.
- If it is the third, then the 3rd; if fourth, the 4th; if fifth, the 5th; if sixth, the 6th; and if seventh, the 7th.

Similarly, in the scales of the *Madhyama-grama* (the Fa-scale system):
- If "Fa" is the first note, it is the 1st scale.
- If it is the second, the 2nd; if it is the third, the 3rd, and so on. || 18 ||

He demonstrates that each of the fifty-six scales has seven variations: **"Starting with the first..."**
Each single scale becomes sevenfold based on starting from the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh note. One might ask: how can there be seven notes if one starts from the second note or later? To this he replies: **"In those..."** In those scales, after pronouncing up to the final note, one then pronounces the preceding notes...

# The Ocean of Music [Scales and Melodic Lines]

One should perform them. Now, an objection might be raised: if there is no regular ascent and descent, would the nature of the <term>Murchana</term><note>A murchana is a sequential scale or "mode" produced by starting a seven-note scale on different degrees.</note> be violated? To this, the author says:
**By sequence.** Even if there is no strict sequence in the ascent and descent themselves, the nature of the scale is preserved because the underlying sequence of the notes remains present. || 19 || These variations of the scales are referred to by the term "sequence." Their total number should be known as three hundred and ninety-two. However, the sages Matanga and Dattila have described a fourfold classification of scales in a different manner. As Matanga said: "There, the seven-note scale is of four types: Complete, Hexatonic, Pentatonic, and Overlapping." Among these, when sung with seven notes, it is **Complete** (<term>Purna</term>). When sung with six notes, it is **Hexatonic** (<term>Shadava</term>). When sung with five notes, it is **Pentatonic** (<term>Auduvita</term>). When sung with the auxiliary notes <term>Kakali</term><note>The sharp 7th</note> and <term>Antara</term><note>The sharp 3rd</note>, it is **Overlapping** (<term>Sadharani</term>). Dattila also says:

> "Whatever position the notes Shadja and Madhyama hold in the two basic scales,
> That same position determines the scale in those two systems.
> All of these are remembered as being made through five, six, full, or overlapping notes."

The hexatonic nature of scales is explained according to the method of hexatonic <term>Tanas</term><note>A Tana is a melodic fragment or a specific permutation of notes.</note> to be described later. The pentatonic nature is explained according to the method of pentatonic melodic fragments to be described later. Through these two, the hexatonic and pentatonic states are achieved. Furthermore, the distinction between a scale (<term>Murchana</term>) and a melodic fragment (<term>Tana</term>) was established by Matanga. As he said: "Now, what is the difference between a scale and a melodic fragment? It is said: Vishakhila holds that there is a difference in meaning between the two. This is not inconsistent, as the difference between scales and melodic fragments has been established in the summary verses. How so? We say: a collection of notes possessing a sequence of both ascent and descent is called a **Murchana**, whereas a **Tana** occurs only by the sequence of ascent; this is the difference." || 19- ||

The author now names the presiding deities of the scales: **The Yakshas** <note>Nature spirits</note>, **the Rakshasas** <note>Protective or fierce spirits</note>, **Narada** <note>The divine sage of music</note>, **the Lotus-born Brahma** <note>The Creator</note>, **the Nagas** <note>Serpent deities</note>, **the Ashvins** <note>Divine twin physicians</note>, and **the Noose-bearer Varuna** <note>God of the waters</note>. || -20, 20- ||

He then names the deities of the scales belonging to the <term>Madhyama Grama</term><note>The basic scale starting on the fourth note, F</note>: **Brahma**, and so on. The purpose of stating the deities is to indicate that by singing a particular scale, that specific deity is pleased. He then gives alternative names for the scales according to the view of Narada: **Of those...** "Known by the names of the Sages," meaning they were named by the ancient seers. He then gives the names of the scales of the <term>Gandhara Grama</term><note>The "Celestial Scale," believed to have been lost to the heavens/earthly practice</note> according to Narada's view: **Nanda**, etc. Now, why are the characteristics of the Gandhara-scale not described? To this, he says: **And those...** A "characteristic" (<term>Lakshana</term>) is that which distinguishes or differentiates something from others of its own kind or different kinds. The meaning is that he has not provided a formal definition for them here. || -21—26 ||

# Tanas are pure Murchanas that have been made hexatonic or pentatonic.
# If the seven scales starting from Shadja <note>the first note, 'Sa'</note> are deprived of Sa, Ri, Pa, and Ni <note>the 1st, 2nd, 5th, and 7th notes</note> in sequence, || 27 ||
# then there are twenty-eight Tanas. In the Madhyama scale <note>the scale starting on the 4th note, 'Ma'</note>, if Sa, Ri, and Ga <note>1st, 2nd, and 3rd notes</note> are omitted,
# there are seven each in sequence, then there are twenty-one. || 28 ||
# Both of these together are considered the forty-nine hexatonic <term>Shadava: a scale of six notes</term> Tanas.
# By omitting Sa and Pa, and the two-microtone notes Ri and Pa, seven each are excluded; || 29 ||
# in the Shadja-grama <note>the primary scale system</note>, there are twenty-one distinct pentatonic <term>Auduva: a scale of five notes</term> Tanas.
# In the Madhyama-grama <note>the secondary scale system</note>, by omitting the two-microtone notes Ri and Dha, || 30 ||
# there are only fourteen; thus, they total thirty-five.
# All together, the hexatonic and pentatonic Tanas combined are eighty-four. || 31 ||

(Kallinatha’s Commentary) Having discussed the sequences in context, the author now defines the "Pure Tanas" which were mentioned immediately after the Murchanas, as they represent a partial form of a Murchana. Regarding the phrase <term>Tanas are...</term>: The word <term>Tana</term> <note>original: "tāna"</note> is derived from the root *tan* (to stretch or extend). By applying the grammatical rule "In senses other than the agent..." <note>referring to Panini's Sanskrit grammar</note>, the form *tana* is derived in the passive sense (that which is stretched), similar to the words for "gift" or "gain." 

The meaning is: "Pure <term>Murchanas</term> <note>the basic seven-note scales</note> having been made <term>hexatonic or pentatonic</term> become pure Tanas." The word "pure" applies to both terms. If "pure" were only connected to the word "Tana," then because "Murchanas" are the general subject at hand, it would imply that all fifty-six Murchanas <note>including those from the celestial realms</note> are included. If each of those were made hexatonic and pentatonic in the manner to be described, the total number of Tanas would reach 336. This would contradict the authoritative statement of the sage Bharata <note>author of the Natyashastra</note> who said, "There are eighty-four Tanas." 

Furthermore, in the subsequent sentences, the mention of "seven in the Shadja scale" and "seven in the Madhyama scale" would be illogical. Therefore, the connection must be made as "pure Murchanas." Now, if the word "pure" were only connected to "Murchana," then <term>Kutatanas</term> <note>fragmentary or non-sequential melodic patterns</note> might also be perceived as the target of this definition, since the word "Tana" is used generally. To prevent this—

# The Ocean of Music
## [Scales and Melodic Patterns]

The connection must be made in both cases. Here, the "purity" of <term>murchanas</term> <note>the basic seven-note scales</note> refers to the absence of the <term>kakali</term> <note>sharp seventh</note> and <term>antara</term> <note>sharp fourth</note> notes. However, the purity of <term>tanas</term> <note>melodic fragments or variations</note> should be understood as being free from those same notes, as well as being free from notes played out of their natural sequence. 

Regarding the phrase **"transformed into hexatonic and pentatonic"**: By omitting one specific note from the seven, it becomes <term>shadava</term> <note>hexatonic/six-note</note>. By omitting two specific notes from the seven, it becomes <term>auduvita</term> <note>pentatonic/five-note</note>. What was previously not hexatonic becomes hexatonic; what was previously not pentatonic becomes pentatonic. The compound term "hexatonic-pentatonic-transformed" is used here. Since the omission of one or two notes could technically apply to any note, the author regulates the omission according to the views of Sage Bharata and others, starting with the phrase **"The Shadja-grama..."** 

One might ask: "In certain pure tanas, if the <term>Panchama</term> <note>the fifth note, which distinguishes the two primary scales</note> is omitted, how can we distinguish between the two <term>gramas</term> <note>fundamental scale systems</note>?" It is explained: because these tanas lacking specific notes are named only in reference to a particular grama, the identity of the tana itself serves to distinguish the grama, even if the distinguishing fifth note is absent. || 27-31 ||

---

->(Sudhakara Commentary)<-

He defines the <term>tanas</term>: **"The tanas are..."** Pure murchanas become tanas. What kind of murchanas? Those made into six-note and five-note structures by the subtraction of one intended note or two intended notes. He explains that specific subtraction: **"In the Shadja-grama..."** 

When the murchanas of the <term>Shadja-grama</term> <note>the scale starting on the tonic 'Sa'</note> are deprived of the note <term>Shadja</term>, there are seven tanas. When deprived of <term>Rishabha</term>, there are seven. When deprived of <term>Panchama</term>, there are seven. When deprived of <term>Nishada</term>, there are seven. Thus, in the Shadja-grama, there are twenty-eight hexatonic tanas. 

In the <term>Madhyama-grama</term> <note>the scale starting on the fourth note 'Ma'</note>, when the seven murchanas are left without <term>Shadja</term>, there are seven tanas. When left without <term>Rishabha</term>, there are seven. When left without <term>Gandhara</term>, there are seven. Thus, in the Madhyama-grama, there are twenty-one hexatonic tanas. Combined in both gramas, there are forty-nine hexatonic tanas. || 27-28 ||

He then defines the pentatonic tanas: **"By Sa and Pa..."** When the Shadja-grama murchanas are divested of <term>Shadja</term> and <term>Panchama</term> <note>the 1st and 5th notes</note>, there are seven pentatonic tanas. When divested of the two-microtone notes <term>Gandhara</term> and <term>Nishada</term> <note>the 3rd and 7th notes</note>, there are seven. When deprived of <term>Rishabha</term> and <term>Panchama</term> <note>the 2nd and 5th notes</note>, there are seven. Thus, in the Shadja-grama, there are twenty-one pentatonic tanas. 

In the Madhyama-grama, when the seven murchanas are deprived of <term>Rishabha</term> and <term>Dhaivata</term> <note>the 2nd and 6th notes</note>, there are seven pentatonic tanas. When deprived of the two-microtone notes <term>Gandhara</term> and <term>Nishada</term>, there are seven. Thus, in the Madhyama-grama...

## When the notes of the scales—whether incomplete or complete—are sounded in a non-sequential order,
## they become "Kūṭatānas" <note>literally "crooked" or "perplexing" melodic patterns</note>. We shall now state their total number. || 32 ||
## In each individual scale, there are five thousand and forty complete Kūṭatānas, including the sequential ones. || 33 ||

There are fourteen pentatonic <note>five-note</note> permutations. Across the two Gramas <note>the basic parent scales of ancient Indian music</note>, the pentatonic patterns total thirty-five. All hexatonic <note>six-note</note> and pentatonic patterns together total eighty-four. Matanga <note>an ancient musicologist, author of the Brhaddesi</note> stated that the application of these permutations is twofold. As he said—if one asks how these permutations are to be applied, it is explained: the application of permutations is twofold, by "entry" <term>Pravesha: a subtle tonal transition</term> and by "restraint" <term>Nigraha: skipping a note</term>.

"Entry" is the stretching or pressing of the lower note, such as the Shadja <note>the tonic, 'Sa'</note>, in relation to the Rishabha <note>the second note, 'Ri'</note> which is to be omitted; it means bringing it toward the pitch of Rishabha. This is entry by stretching. Alternatively, by softening: the softening or loosening of that same Shadja when it is higher than the Nishada <note>the seventh note, 'Ni'</note>; it means bringing it toward the pitch of Nishada. Thus, entry is of two kinds.

"Restraint," however, is the abandonment or non-touching of the subsequent note. An example of the practice is: *Sa-Sa-Ga-Ri-Pa-Pa-Ma-Ri*. Bharata <note>the legendary author of the Natyashastra</note> says the same: "The action of permutations on the strings is twofold: entry and restraint. Here, entry is defined by the stretching of a lower note and the softening of a higher note. Restraint is the lack of contact." Dattila <note>another foundational music theorist</note> also says:

> "The action of permutations on the strings is twofold: through entry and through restraint.
> Entry is the equalization of sound; restraint is the lack of contact."

Now, a question arises: in the first and seventh scales, if the Shadja is omitted, the form *Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha-Ni* remains the same in both; so what is the distinction? Truly, there is no difference in the notes themselves, but a distinction certainly exists based on the low <note>Mandra</note> and high <note>Tara</note> registers. One might ask: since scales are useful in the performance of Jatis, Ragas, and Bhashas <note>various categories of ancient melodic modes</note>, their description is appropriate; but where are these permutations used? It is explained: Matanga stated that the use of permutations is to demonstrate the distinctiveness of the Jati-singing in the two Gramas. || 29—31 ||

---

(Kallinatha's Commentary) He defines the Kūṭatānas which follow in sequence: **"Whether incomplete..."** etc. The connection is that all four types of scales, whether complete or incomplete, become Kūṭatānas if the notes are sounded in a non-sequential order. "Complete" means possessing seven notes. "Incomplete" refers to those ending with six notes down to a single note, following the omission of each successive final note. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> implies an alternative. Non-sequential sound—

<meta>catchword: Non-sequential sound—</meta>

<keywords>Kūṭatāna, melodic permutations, Pravesha, Nigraha, Matanga, Bharata, Dattila, musical theory, ancient Indian music, scales</keywords>

# Ocean of Music [Scales and Modes]

-> When the full permutations are applied across the fifty-six modes, <-
-> they are numbered as two hundred eighty-two thousand, two hundred <-
-> and forty. (34) <-
-> Now we shall explain the incomplete ones. <-
-> By removing the final note one by one, six variations like the six-note scale arise. (35) <-
-> Although the single-note scale has no variations, it is mentioned to establish the "lost" and "found" methods. <-
-> The regular sequences are mentioned because they are useful within those permutations, even if they are not "complex" themselves. (36) <-

Regarding the "ordered notes," a <term>Krama</term><note>A regular, ascending sequence of notes.</note> is simply the ascent of notes in their natural order. Any alteration of the order among those notes is called <term>Vyutkrama</term><note>Inverted or disordered sequence.</note>. Even in a descent, if the natural order is reversed, it lacks the quality of a "Krama" and is instead considered a <term>Kuta-tana</term><note>A "complex" or "crooked" melodic fragment formed by permuting notes.</note>. The definition of "crookedness" (<term>Kutatvam</term>) is the quality of notes being pronounced out of their natural order.

Now, across the fifty-six <term>Murchanas</term><note>Basic scales or modes.</note>, for each of the seven types (starting from the "complete" seven-note scale), the author begins a formal declaration to show the specific number of <term>Kuta-tanas</term> resulting from the <term>Prastara</term><note>The process of mathematical permutation/tabulation.</note> process, starting with the phrase: **"The complete ones are five thousand..."** and so on.

Regarding the phrase **"By removing the final note one by one"**: this means by abandoning the last note of each scale. By repeating the word "final," it implies a sequence: in the complete scale of the <term>Uttaramandra</term> mode, the final note is <term>Nishada</term> <note>The 7th note, 'Ni'.</note>; by abandoning it, a six-note sequence is formed. In that sequence, the final note is <term>Dhaivata</term> <note>The 6th note, 'Dha'.</note>; by abandoning it, a five-note sequence is formed. In this way, six "incomplete" variations are to be observed.

For example:
*   *Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa-Dha* is the six-note variation.
*   *Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma-Pa* is the five-note variation.
*   *Sa-Ri-Ga-Ma* is the four-note variation.
*   *Sa-Ri-Ga* is the three-note variation.
*   *Sa-Ri* is the two-note variation.
*   *Sa* is the one-note variation.

The same six variations should be understood for every other mode as well. The term **"without variations"** (<term>Nirbheda</term>) refers to the single-note scale, which lacks internal sub-variations because no permutation (<term>Prastara</term>) is possible. Regarding the phrase **"to establish the 'lost' and 'found' methods"**: the word "and so on" includes the calculation of the total number. Since the single-note <term>Tana</term> is used in the rule "combined with the original single digit," its inclusion is necessary for the success of those mathematical proofs.

Regarding **"useful within those"**: the regular sequences are mentioned because they serve as the "root cause" or basis for the <term>Kuta-tanas</term>. The idea is that a disordered sequence (<term>Vyutkrama</term>) inherently depends upon a regular sequence (<term>Krama</term>). // 32-36 //

# Sequential Permutations: 4] First Chapter on Notes

<page-num>119</page-num>

(Su. <note>Referring to the commentator Simhabhupala</note>) He explains the **Irregular Permutations** <term>Kuta-tana: non-sequential melodic patterns used in improvisation</term>—starting with "The incomplete ones," and so on. Those **scales** <term>Murchana: the foundational seven-note scales of ancient Indian music</term> which are incomplete and those which are complete, when their notes are sounded in a non-sequential order, become **Irregular Permutations**. Having promised to state the number of complete permutations for each scale, he says: "That number..." || 32 ||

For each individual scale, there are five thousand and forty (5040) complete **Irregular Permutations**.

Now, a doubt is raised: Matanga <note>An ancient musicologist, author of the Brhaddesi</note> stated the number of permutations per scale to be five thousand and thirty-three (5033), as he said: "Five thousand and thirty-three irregular permutations are produced." Dattila <note>Another foundational sage of music theory</note> also said:

-> "The complete ones are five thousand and thirty-three in number; <-
-> they are stated for each parent-scale; now the method of calculation is given." <-

To resolve this contradiction, he says: "Including the sequences." When the **permutation-table** <term>Prastara: a mathematical process to show all possible arrangements of notes</term> is made for each scale, seven **natural sequences** <term>Krama: notes in their straight ascending or descending order</term> are produced. The meaning is that including those seven, the total becomes five thousand and forty. Dattila and others, however, specified the number of **Irregular Permutations** by excluding the natural sequences; thus, there is no contradiction. || 33 ||

Having stated the number of permutations for a single scale, he now states the total number for all scales: "Fifty-six," and so on. Five thousand and forty must be multiplied by fifty-six <note>There are 7 notes, and 8 scales per grama (system), totaling 56 variations across the two primary systems</note>. By this calculation, the number two hundred eighty-two thousand, two hundred and forty (282,240) is produced.

Having promised to explain the incomplete permutations, he says: "Now the incomplete ones..." There are six variations of sequences and permutations, such as the six-note patterns and so on. In response to the question of how they arise, he says: "By the omission of each successive final note." In the complete scales of the two **primary systems** <term>Grama: the Shadja-grama and Madhyama-grama, the two fundamental tuning systems</term>, by removing the last note, the six-note variations arise; by removing the last two notes, the five-note variations; by the absence of the last three notes, the four-note variations; by the loss of the last four notes, the three-note variations; by the loss of the last five notes, the two-note variations; and by the loss of the last six notes, the single-note variation. || 34, 35 ||

One might object: since there is no "permutation" possible for a single note, there are no variations; why then are they mentioned here? To this, he says: "The single note..." The single-note variations are mentioned for the sake of perfecting the **lost and found** <term>Nashtoddishta: a mathematical method to find the sequence of a specific permutation or its rank in a list</term> calculations. The meaning is that if one excludes the single-note patterns, it would be impossible to understand the "lost and found" calculations in the **Khandameru** <term>A tabular diagram used to calculate musical permutations</term> even when placing two-note patterns and others.

But then, since the **natural sequences** are not "irregular permutations," why are they mentioned here? To this, he says: "The sequences..." Although the sequences are not irregular permutations, they are useful in the **permutation-table** which will be described later with the rule "the note should be placed after setting down the sequence," because without the sequences, it is impossible to know the irregular permutations. || 32-36 ||

It emphasizes that even single notes and natural sequences are included in the theory to facilitate complex mathematical calculations like the Khandameru.</summary>

# Sangita Ratnakara [Grama-Murchana Section]

There are seven hundred and twenty variations for the hexatonic <term>Shadava; six-note scales</term> series. For the pentatonic <term>Auduva; five-note scales</term> series, one hundred and twenty variations are recognized. || 37 ||

For the <gloss>1</gloss> <insert>of the melodic patterns</insert> <term>Kuta-tanas; non-sequential note permutations</term> consisting of four notes, twenty-four variations are stated. Those with three notes have six variations; those with two notes have two; and the single-note form is considered to have only one. || 38 ||

Archika, Gathika, Samika, and Swarantara: these are the four names given to the melodic patterns starting from one note up to four notes respectively. || 39 ||

<gloss>2</gloss> These are stated to be of four types, including the "pure" <note>Shuddha</note> varieties and others. Following the primary order, they are considered to be of two kinds based on the omission of one note from each. || 40 ||

**(Kallinatha's Commentary):** Regarding the phrase *syuḥ ṣāḍavānām* (there are [variations] of the hexatonic): Here, "hexatonic-ness" is intended simply as the state of possessing six notes, not necessarily the state of possessing six notes capable of being used in a specific performance. The same should be understood for the pentatonic <note>Auduva</note> forms. Regarding *ārcikaḥ*: Because the Rigvedic hymns <note>Rics</note> used in sacrificial rituals rely on a single note, that form is called Archika due to that connection. Similarly, the two-note form is Gathika due to its connection with the Gatha <note>ancient verse chants</note>. The three-note form is Samika due to its connection with the Samaveda. Although the Samavedic chants may use seven notes, they are called Samika here in reference to the three registers <note>low, middle, and high</note>. Because the four-note melodic pattern falls in the middle of the seven types of patterns (starting from one note), it is given the name Swarantara <note>literally "between notes"</note>. Regarding *uktāḥ śuddhādibhedena* (stated by the divisions of pure, etc.): Here, the word "etc." includes those patterns joined with the <term>Kakali; the sharp seventh note</term> and <term>Antara; the sharp third note</term>, or both. || 37-40 ||

**(Simhabhupala's Commentary):** He states the number of hexatonic "knotted" permutations <note>Kuta-tanas</note> along with their sequential orders: *syuḥ ṣāḍavānām*. When the permutation <term>Prastara; a mathematical process of listing all possible combinations</term> of a hexatonic sequence is performed, seven hundred and twenty (720) variations are produced. In the permutation of the pentatonic forms, there are one hundred and twenty (120) variations for each <term>Murchana; the foundational seven-note scale</term>. In the permutation of four-note forms, there are twenty-four variations. In the permutation of three-note forms—

# Krama-tanas 4] First Chapter: On Notes (Svaragatadhyaya)

->The two beginning with Shadja and the two beginning with Madhyama are each of two kinds.<-
->The others are of four kinds; these permutations total forty-eight. (41)<-
->The previously mentioned seven hundred and twenty, when multiplied by these permutations,<-
->become thirty-four thousand, five hundred and sixty. (42)<-

There are six (6) variations. In the permutation of two notes, there are two (2) variations. In the permutation of one note, there is one (1) variation. (37, 38) He states the specific names of the permutations starting from one note: *Archika*, and so on. A single-note sequence is called *Archika*. Two notes are *Gathika*. Three notes are *Samika*. Four notes are *Svarantara*. He will later describe the five-note sequence as *Auduva* and the six-note sequence as *Shadava*. Seven notes are *Sampurna* (complete), as there are no sequences exceeding seven notes. As Narada <note>A legendary sage and celestial musician often cited as an authority in musicology</note> said:

> ‘Archika, Gathika, Samika, and Svarantara;
> Auduva, Shadava, and the seventh is Sampurna.
> The use of a single note is indeed called Archika.
> Gathika is known as two notes, and three notes are Samika.
> The use of four notes is called Svarantara.
> Auduva consists of five, and Shadava consists of six notes.
> Sampurna is to be known by singers as consisting of seven notes.’

Thus (39). Having thus stated the number for each *Shadava* <note>six-note scale</note> and others, he explains the calculation for the *Shadava* permutations: "Stated by the divisions of pure, etc." In the two *Gramas* <note>the basic scales of ancient Indian music: Shadja-grama and Madhyama-grama</note>, there are fourteen *Murchanas* <note>modes or scales derived by shifting the tonic</note>. When *Shadava* sequences are created by dropping one note at a time from the end, the variations involving *Nishada* and *Gandhara* <note>the 7th and 3rd notes of the scale</note> are of four types: Pure, with *Kakali* <note>a sharp 7th</note>, with *Antara* <note>a sharp 3rd</note>, and with both. When one of those two (*Nishada* or *Gandhara*) is missing, they are of two types: without *Nishada* (Pure or with *Antara*), and without *Gandhara* (Pure or with *Kakali*). (40)

<insert>(Commentary by Kallinatha)</insert> **The two beginning with Shadja and the two beginning with Madhyama**: In the *Shadja-grama*, the *Uttaramandra* sequence begins with *Shadja*; in the *Madhyama-grama*, the *Shuddhamadhyama* begins with *Shadja*—these are the two beginning with *Shadja*. In the *Madhyama-grama*, the *Sauvira* sequence begins with *Madhyama*; in the *Shadja-grama*, the *Matsarikrita* sequence begins with *Madhyama*—these are the two beginning with *Madhyama*. Together, these four are "each of two kinds."

->Thus is the calculation for the hexatonic <term>Shadava; hexatonic scales consisting of six notes</term> sequences; now I shall speak of the five-note sequences.<-

->In the two-note sequences, there are two types again: those starting with Ri, Ga, Dha, and Ni are eight in number, while the others are pure.<-
->These twenty-two, when multiplied by two, result in forty-four.<-

<note>The author is calculating "Kuta-tanas," which are the total possible permutations of notes in a scale. The math relies on factorials: 5 notes = 120 permutations (5!), 4 notes = 24 permutations (4!), etc.</note>

This means that Ni and Ga are each omitted one by one. The "other ten" have four variations because they include both Ni and Ga <note>which can be modified into "Kakali Ni" or "Antara Ga"</note>. The same logic should be applied to the sequences starting with Ga, Dha, etc. || 41-48 ||

<margin>Commentary by Simhabhupala</margin>
(Su.) Regarding the question of which among the fourteen are of four types and which are of two types, he says: "Those starting with Shadja," etc. In the <term>Murchanas; melodic scales</term> of the two <term>Gramas; fundamental scales (Sa-grama and Ma-grama)</term>, the two starting with Shadja (Sa) have two variations because they lack Nishada (Ni); these are the "Pure" and "with Antara" <note>Antara is a sharped version of the third note, Gandhara</note>. The two starting with Madhyama (Ma) also have two variations because they lack Gandhara (Ga); these are "Pure" and "with Kakali" <note>Kakali is a sharped version of the seventh note, Nishada</note>. The other ten variations are four-fold: Pure, with Antara, with Kakali, and with both. Thus, there are forty-eight hexatonic (<term>Shadava</term>) sequences. For each sequence, there are seven hundred and twenty permutations (720). These multiplied by forty-eight result in thirty-four thousand, five hundred and sixty (34,560) total hexatonic <term>Kuta-tana</term> variations. Now he counts the five-note (<term>Panchasvara</term>) sequences: "Those starting with Ga," etc. In the two Gramas, there are two starting with Gandhara, two with Dhaivata, and two with Nishada. Thus, these six pentatonic (<term>Auduva</term>) variations lack Nishada and Gandhara...

<header>The Ocean of Music [Scales and Modes—</header>

->These twelve result from three-note patterns, while two result from two-note patterns.<-
->There is one single-note pattern; these sixty-three are associated with the Uttaramandra mode. (51)<-
->Again, certain patterns are considered repetitions; following the sequence of the Margi mode and others,<-
->there are four hundred patterns consisting of five notes. (52)<-
->There are four hundred and eighty patterns of four notes, and ninety-six of others.<-
->Twelve in the pair of three-note patterns, and four in the pair of two-note patterns. (53)<-
->There is one single-note pattern; thus, this total of five hundred<-
->and ninety-three patterns are identical to those found in the Rajani mode. (54)<-

Because they are beneficial. "Original" means existing at the root, signifying they are "pure" <note>shuddha</note>. There are exactly fourteen; this restriction is made here to exclude other combinations. This is the intention: even though <term>Nishada and Gandhara</term> <note>the 7th and 3rd notes</note> can cause variations in the <term>Murchana</term> <note>a sequential scale or mode</note> by taking on the states of <term>Kakali</term> <note>sharp 7th</note> and <term>Antara</term> <note>sharp 3rd</note>, nevertheless, because the subtle internal difference of those two individual notes cannot be perceived without the union of another note, the calculation is based only on the pure notes, not on the Kakali or Antara variations.

When, however, in the <term>Shadja-grama</term> <note>the scale starting on the tonic 'Sa'</note>, the <term>Rajani</term> and other <term>Murchanas</term> are formed by starting with <term>Nishada</term> <note>the 7th note</note> and so on, right at the position of the middle-register <term>Shadja</term>; and similarly in the <term>Madhyama-grama</term> <note>the scale starting on the 4th note 'Ma'</note>, the <term>Harinashva</term> and other <term>Murchanas</term> are formed by starting with <term>Gandhara</term> <note>the 3rd note</note> and so on, right at the position of the middle-register <term>Madhyama</term>—in that view, even in the absence of the <term>Panchama</term> <note>the 5th note</note> which distinguishes the two scales, there is no repetition of the <term>Kuta-tanas</term> <note>complex melodic permutations</note> because a difference in pitch-register exists.

But when one adopts the view that the <term>Murchanas</term> of both scales start on notes situated progressively lower and lower, then the patterns belonging to the <term>Shuddhamadhyama, Margi, and Pauravi</term> modes of the <term>Madhyama-grama</term> would lack a difference in pitch-register when compared to the six-note patterns of the <term>Uttaramandra, Rajani, and Uttarayata</term> modes of the <term>Shadja-grama</term>. Since the distinguishing <term>Panchama</term> is absent, repetition is certain. In that case, having established the first-mentioned patterns of the <term>Shadja-grama</term> as the primary basis in the calculation, the author now enumerates the repeated patterns of the <term>Madhyama-grama</term> in order to set them aside, starting with the words: "From the Shadja, of the Shuddhamadhyama..."
