---

If one plays the notes above and below the second note of the subsequent unit, that is the ornament called *Prasada*. || 32–32 ||
He defines *Vyavrtta*: "Four-note..." In this, the pattern has four notes. Its first, third, second, and fourth notes should be sounded in that order. By abandoning the first note, three other patterns are formed in the same way; where this occurs, it is the ornament called *Vyavrtta*. || 33–34 ||
He defines *Skhalita*: "A pattern..." Using the first, third, and second notes of the ornament starting from the lower register, and sounding the fourth (higher) note twice, if one then sounds them in a descending order, that eight-note pattern is the ornament called *Skhalita*. || 35 ||
He defines *Parivartaka*: "A note..." Leaving out the second note, the first pattern consists of three notes: the first, third, and fourth. Starting from that skipped second note, where other such patterns follow, that is the ornament called *Parivartaka*. || 36 ||
He defines *Akshepa*: "Three-note..." Three-note patterns formed by abandoning the preceding ones and moving to the higher notes...

(46) He defines **Sannivrtta-pravrttaka**: Where one sings the first and fifth notes and then sings three notes in descent starting from the fourth note, that is one unit. The greatest devotee of Shiva <note>referring to the author Sarngadeva</note> describes the ornament called *Mandra-tara-prasanna* <note>literally "low-high-clear"</note>:

Singing the first note, then the second, then the first again—each twice—and then singing the second and the first once each within a rhythmic unit (*kala*) constitutes the ornament *Avartaka* <note>meaning "revolving" or "repetitive"</note>. (58)
-> Sa Sa Ri Ri Sa Sa Ri Sa | Ri Ri Ga Ga Ri Ri Ga Ri | Ga Ga Ma Ma Ga Ga Ma Ga | Ma Ma Pa Pa Ma Ma Pa Ma | Pa Pa Dha Dha Pa Pa Dha Pa | Dha Dha Ni Ni Dha Dha Ni Dha. (3) <-

When this same rhythmic unit is sung while omitting the final two notes, the wise recognize it as the ornament *Sampradana* <note>meaning "bestowal" or "handing over"</note>. (59)
-> Sa Sa Ri Ri Sa Sa | Ri Ri Ga Ga Ri Ri | Ga Ga Ma Ma Ga Ga | Ma Ma Pa Pa Ma Ma | Pa Pa Dha Dha Pa Pa | Dha Dha Ni Ni Dha Dha. (4) <-

If a pair of notes separated by one interval is used, and similarly a pair starting from the omitted note is used twice each, it is the ornament *Vidhuta* <note>meaning "shaken" or "tremulous"</note>, approved by the learned. (60)
-> Sa Ga Sa Ga | Ri Ma Ri Ma | Ga Pa Ga Pa | Ma Dha Ma Dha | Pa Ni Pa Ni. (5) <-

If, in a rhythmic unit, a pair of the first two notes is followed by a pair of the third and second notes... (61)

**Commentary:**
He defines *Mandra-tara-prasanna*: If, after singing the eighth note from the base note <note>the upper octave</note>, seven notes are sung in descending order, it is the ornament called *Mandra-tara-prasanna*. (57)

He defines *Avartaka*: If one sings the first note, then the second, and the first again—each twice—and then sings the second and first once, it is the ornament called *Avartaka*. (58)

He defines *Sampradana*: If the rhythmic units of this *Avartaka* are sung while leaving out the last two notes, it is the ornament called *Sampradana*. (59)

He defines the ornament *Vidhuta*: A pair of notes separated by one interval is sung twice; then, starting from the note that was skipped, another pair separated by one interval is sung twice. This five-unit pattern of four notes is the ornament called *Vidhuta*. (60)

He defines *Upalola*: If the pair of the first two notes is sung twice, and then the pair of the third and second notes is sung twice...

When a pattern is used twice by those who know the art, it is called **Upalola** (The Moving Pattern).
**Sa-Ri-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ri-Ga-Ri | Ri-Ga-Ri-Ga-Ma-Ga-Ma-Ga | Ga-Ma-Ga-Ma-Pa-Ma-Pa-Ma | Ma-Pa-Ma-Pa-Dha-Pa-Dha-Pa | Pa-Dha-Pa-Dha-Ni-Dha-Ni-Dha.** (6) <note>These are solfège syllables representing the notes of the scale: Sa (C), Ri (D), Ga (E), Ma (F), Pa (G), Dha (A), Ni (B).</note>

Thus, I have described sixty-three famous ornaments.
Because they are infinite in number, they cannot be fully recounted in this scripture.
The gain of melodic beauty, the knowledge of notes, and the variety of the components of melodic movements—

He concludes the general statement on all ornaments: "Thus..." (63) He states the purpose of the <term>Alankara</term>:
"The gain of beauty." The knowledge of the pleasing quality of notes, the understanding of their true nature, and the variety of the <term>Sthayi</term> <note>The four types of melodic movement: standing, ascending, descending, and circling</note> and other melodic patterns are the purposes for defining ornaments. # Now, the Seventh Section: On the Jatis

->There are seven Pure Jatis, named after the notes starting with Shadja:<-
->Shadji, Arshabhi, Gandhari, Madhyama, and Panchami,<-
->Dhaivati, and Naishadi. Now, the characteristics of the Pure Jatis are described:<-
->Those whose namesake note serves as the Ending Note, the Secondary Ending, the Dominant, and the Starting Note,<-
->and which are devoid of an Ending Note in the high register and are complete in notes, are considered "Pure."<-

(Kallinatha's Commentary) After defining the Melodic Movements <term>varna: the functional act of singing</term> and Ornamentation <term>alankara: specific melodic patterns</term>, the author now intends to explain the characteristics of the Jatis <note>Jatis are the ancient melodic frameworks that preceded the modern Raga system</note>, which appear as the primary structures to be adorned. He begins by defining the Jatis and their divisions with the words: **"There are seven Pure..."** and so on. Regarding the term "Jatis": they are called Jatis because they are born <note>Sanskrit: jayante</note> from the two parent scales <term>gramas: the Shadja-grama and Madhyama-grama</term> as appropriate. Therefore, even if a single universal definition is lacking, they are called Jatis because they persist across many individual songs, much like the "cowness" <note>the universal essence of a cow</note> persists in individual cows. Alternatively, according to authorities like Matanga, they are called Jatis because the "collection of songs" <note>gita-jatam</note> or their aesthetic coloring is born from them. 

There are seven "Pure" Jatis, endowed with the characteristics of purity to be described. They are "named after the notes starting with Shadja." This means their names are derived from the names of the notes (Shadja, Rishabha, etc.) which serve as their basis. He lists them specifically: **"Shadji..."** and so on. 

To the question "What constitutes their purity?", he replies: **"The characteristics of the Pure..."** For these Jatis (Shadji, etc.), the namesake note (e.g., Shadja for Shadji) must function in the roles of:
1. <term>Nyasa: the final note of a composition</term>
2. <term>Apanyasa: the note ending an intermediate section</term>
3. <term>Amsha: the dominant, most frequent note</term>
4. <term>Graha: the starting note</term>

Furthermore, they must be "devoid of an Ending Note in the high register." This specific prohibition implies that the Ending Note is permitted in the low and middle registers as appropriate. Even though the sage Bharata <note>author of the Natyashastra</note> stated that "In the Pure Jatis, the Ending Note should be in the low register," this should be understood as a prohibition of the high register. Otherwise...

<page-num>170</page-num>
<header>The Ocean of Music [On Jatis—</header>

# Modified forms are those lacking these characteristics, except for the final note. || 3 ||

The view stated by Matanga <note>An ancient musicologist, author of the Brihaddesi</note> regarding the Shadji Jati having the middle Shadja as its final note would contradict musical practice. "Complete" means possessing all seven notes. "Named after the pure" means they bear the designations of the pure forms. || 1-2 ||

(Sudhakara's Commentary) He defines the Jatis: "They are pure." There are seven pure Jatis. In response to the question of what their names are, he says: "They are named after the notes beginning with Shadja." The seven notes—Shadja and the rest—are the basis for their names. He lists those note-related names: Shadji, and so on. Having promised to define the pure state, he explains: "Pure..." Those Jatis in which the note they are named after serves as the final note <term>Nyasa: the note that ends a phrase or composition</term>, the intermediate final note <term>Apanyasa</term>, the predominant note <term>Amsha</term>, and the starting note <term>Graha</term>, and where the final note is not in the high register—these are to be known as the Pure Jatis. He will explain the definitions of Nyasa and the others later. || 1-2 ||

(Kallinatha's Commentary) "These" refers to the pure Shadji and the others. **"Lacking these characteristics, except for the final note"**: Among the five characteristics stated for the purity of Jatis—namely, that the namesake note must be the final, intermediate final, predominant, and starting note, and that the scale must be complete—if one sets aside the rule regarding the final note <note>Nyasa</note>, and the Jati lacks the other fixed characteristics (intermediate final, predominant, starting note, and completeness), it is modified. The meaning is this: one should keep the namesake note as the final note, but may make other notes the intermediate final and so on. If done this way, they become "Modified" <term>Vikrita</term>; they reach a modified state, but they do not lose their identity or become entirely different Jatis like those born from mixtures. Here, abandoning the rule of the final note is not desired; if even that were abandoned, the essential components that distinguish them from other Jatis would be lost, and one would not recognize them as variations of that specific pure Jati. || 3 ||

(Sudhakara's Commentary) He describes the modified Jatis: "Modified." Those lacking the stated characteristics, excluding the final note, are modified. Does "lacking the characteristic of the final note" mean having a high-register final note? Is that not possible for modified forms? No. As stated by Matanga: "In the pure Jatis, the namesake final note is restricted to the lower register; in the modified Jatis, there is no such restriction that the namesake note must be in the lower register." Among the pure...

<meta>catchword: Among the pure</meta>

# Chapter 7] The First Chapter on Musical Notes 171

> Through the omission of one at a time among the four characteristics—namely, full complement of notes <term>Sampurnatva: the use of all seven notes in a scale</term>, the starting note <term>Graha</term>, the predominant note <term>Amsha</term>, and the secondary final note <term>Apanyasa</term>—four variations arise. When two are omitted, six variations are recognized. || 4 ||
> When three are omitted, there are four variations; and when all four are omitted, there is one. These fifteen variations of the *Shadji* <note>The first and primary melodic mode</note> have been described by the wise. || 5 ||
> Among those, eight are lacking the full complement of notes, while seven are devoid of the others. Those lacking the full complement are of two types: six-note <term>Shadava</term> and five-note <term>Auduva</term> variations. || 6 ||
> Therefore, in the modes starting from *Arshabhi* and others which include five-note variations, there are eight additional types. Thus, in each of the other six modes, twenty-three variations are declared. || 7 ||

The *Jatis* <note>The fundamental melodic frameworks or "parent scales" of Indian classical music</note> possess a dual nature: purity <term>Shuddhatva</term> and modification <term>Vikritatva</term>. However, for the eleven *Jatis* such as *Shadja-kaishiki* and others, they exist only in a modified state, not a pure one. The etymology of the word *Jati* is explained by the sage Matanga: "They are called *Jatis* because they are born from the collection of micro-tones <term>Shruti</term>, notes <term>Svara</term>, and scales <term>Grama</term>; or, they are called *Jatis* because they arise from the starting notes and others. Alternatively, they are *Jatis* because the realization of aesthetic flavor <term>Rasa-pratiti</term> is born from them. Or, they are *Jatis* because they are the cause of birth for all musical melodies <term>Ragas</term>. Or finally, just as among men there are castes <term>Jatis</term> such as Brahmins and others, which are either pure or mixed, so too are these." || 3 ||

---

<insert>(Commentary by Kallinatha)</insert> Regarding the four characteristics—full complement of notes and the rest, excluding the final note <term>Nyasa</term>—the author enumerates the variations produced in *Shadji* and other modes by the omission of one, two, or more characteristics, as far as possible, starting with the phrase: **Through the omission of one at a time.** By "omission of one at a time," the inherent nature of the full complement of notes and the others is not being negated—as that would result in the non-existence of the *Jati* itself—but rather, through the exclusion of certain fixed notes, the application of other notes is understood. 

**Four variations arise:** When the full complement of notes is omitted, there is one variation possessing the starting note, predominant note, and secondary final note. When the starting note is omitted, the second variation possesses the full complement, the predominant note, and the secondary final note. When the predominant note is omitted, the third variation possesses the full complement, the starting note, and the secondary final note. When the secondary final note is omitted, the fourth variation possesses the full complement, the starting note, and the predominant note. Thus, there are four variations. 

**When two are omitted, six are recognized:** By omitting the pairs of (1) full complement and starting note, (2) full complement and predominant note, (3) full complement and secondary final note, (4) starting note and predominant note, (5) starting note and secondary final note, and (6) predominant note and secondary final note, six variations are formed.

# Variations of the Shadjya Mode

There are variations. By omitting three [characteristics], four variations arise. These four variations are formed by omitting: 1. Fullness, the starting note, and the predominant note; 2. Fullness, the starting note, and the final note; 3. Fullness, the predominant note, and the final note; and 4. The starting note, the predominant note, and the final note. When all four characteristics are omitted, there is one variation. Thus, these fifteen variations of the *Shadjya* <note>The melodic mode based on the note Shadja (C)</note> have been described.

To explain the sub-variations of those lacking "fullness" <term>Sampurnatva: the use of all seven notes in a scale</term>, the author divides them: "Among them, eight." Among those fifteen, eight variations are "lacking fullness," meaning they are devoid of the complete seven-note scale. The other seven are "devoid of others." This means while they possess fullness, they are devoid of one, two, or three of the other characteristics—the starting note <term>Graha</term>, the predominant note <term>Amsha</term>, or the final note <term>Apanyasa</term>—as applicable.

The eight variations lacking fullness are of two types: hexatonic <term>Shadava: six-note scales</term> and pentatonic <term>Auduva: five-note scales</term>. This results in sixteen variations. Now, if one asks: "Since variations lacking fullness could also include those with only four notes, why are only two types mentioned?" The answer is: Although terms like "lacking fullness" could imply four-note scales, by the principle of "exclusion of the dissimilar," only the hexatonic and pentatonic are accepted here because they possess a likeness to the full scale in their ability to produce *Jati-Ragas* <note>The melodic precursors to modern Ragas</note>. The use of four-note scales was mentioned by the sage Bharata <note>Author of the Natyashastra</note> only in the context of the *Apakrishta Dhruva* <note>A specific type of theatrical song</note>. The use of three-note scales and others is to be seen in songs other than the chanting of the Sama Veda <margin>¹ Among the singers of the Sama Veda</margin> <gloss>¹ See the singers of the Sama Veda</gloss>.

Regarding the six other *Jatis* starting with *Arshabhi* <note>The mode based on the note Rishabha (D)</note>, the author shows an increase in variations compared to *Shadjya*: "Therefore, eight." In *Shadjya*, there are fifteen variations (eight hexatonic variations lacking fullness, plus seven variations possessing fullness but lacking other traits). In the other six modes like *Arshabhi*, the pentatonic states are also applicable. Therefore, eight additional pentatonic variations are added. For this reason, those six modes (*Arshabhi*, etc.) are each said to have twenty-three variations. Thus, across the seven primary modes, the total number of modified variations combined is one hundred and fifty-three. || 4 — 7 ||

(Sudhakara Commentary) He counts the modified variations: "Fullness," etc. The pure modes have four characteristics: 1. Having the name-note as the starting note; 2. Having the name-note as the predominant note; 3. Having the name-note as the final note; and 4. Fullness (using all seven notes). By omitting fullness, there is one modified variation; by omitting the starting note, one; by omitting the predominant note, one...

It calculates a total of 153 modified variations across the seven primary musical scales.</summary>

## Through the combination of the modified forms, eleven are known to be born.
## These are: Shadjakaishiki, Shadjodichyava, and Shadjamadhyama; || 8 ||
## Gandharodichyava, Rakshatagandhari, and likewise Kaishiki;
## Madhyamodichyava, Karmaravi, and Gandharapanchami; || 9 ||
## As well as Andhra and Nandayanti. I shall now describe their origins.
## From the union of Shadji and Gandhari, Shadjakaishiki is produced. || 10 ||

<note>The text is describing the "Samsargaja" or hybrid Jatis, which are created by mixing the primary parent scales.</note>

By omitting the <term>Apanyasa</term><note>A secondary note for ending a musical phrase, slightly less important than the final note.</note>, one variation is formed; thus, by omitting each characteristic one by one, four types are created. By omitting <term>Sampurnatva</term><note>The quality of being "complete," using all seven notes of the scale.</note>, one variation; by omitting the <term>Amsha</term><note>The dominant or "soul" note of the scale.</note>, one variation; by omitting both completeness and the secondary ending, one variation; by omitting the starting note (<term>Graha</term>) and the dominant note, one variation; by omitting the starting note and the secondary ending, one variation; by omitting the dominant note and the secondary ending, one variation. In this way, by omitting two characteristics at a time, six modified variations are produced. 

By omitting three characteristics—completeness, the starting note, and the dominant note—one variation; by omitting completeness, the starting note, and the secondary ending, one variation; by omitting completeness, the dominant note, and the secondary ending, one variation; by omitting the starting note, the dominant note, and the secondary ending, one variation. Thus, by omitting three characteristics, four modified variations are produced. By omitting all four characteristics, there is only one variation. 

In this manner, there are fifteen variations of the <term>Shadji</term> Jati. Among them, eight are lacking completeness, and seven are lacking other characteristics. In Shadji, incompleteness is due to <term>Shadavatva</term><note>The hexatonic state, where only six notes are used.</note>. For the others, the author says "they are of two kinds" to explain the increase in variations due to both hexatonic and <term>Auduvitatva</term><note>The pentatonic state, where only five notes are used.</note> (five-note) structures. Therefore, in the six Jatis starting with <term>Arshabhi</term>, there are eight additional modified variations. Consequently, for each of those, there are twenty-three modified variations. Combined, the total number of modified variations for these is one hundred and fifty-three. || 4—7 ||

---

(Kallinatha's Commentary) Having stated the names of the modified Jatis born from the combination of the aforementioned modified variations, he gives their number: **"Through the combination of the modified..."** The word "but" (<note>original: "tu"</note>) indicates a distinction in the sequence—those born from the combination of modified forms. The previously mentioned "modified" forms were merely different states of the pure Jatis; however, these [eleven] are not the same because they are born from the mixture of those modified states. This is the meaning of the word "but." To identify them, he shows the combination of Shadji and others that have attained a modified state as the cause: **"These are Shadjakaishiki..."**

<vocab>
Modified (Vikrita): A variation of a basic musical scale.
Combination (Samsarga): The mixing of two or more parent scales to create a new one.
Shadjakaishiki: A hybrid scale born from Shadji and Gandhari.
Apanyasa: The intermediate stop or penultimate note in a melody.
Sampurnatva: Fullness; the use of all seven notes in a scale.
Graha: The starting note of a composition.
Amsha: The most important, frequently used note (the "tonic" or "dominant").
Shadavatva: A six-note scale.
Auduvitatva: A five-note scale.
Arshabhi: A Jati based on the note Rishabha (Re).
</vocab>

# Chapter 7] The First Chapter on Notes 175

->The four modes beginning with Shadja, along with Naishadi, Dhaivati,<-
->and Arshabhi—these seven are the *Jatis* <note>melodic modes or parent scales</note> of the *Shadja-grama* <note>the scale starting on the tonic C</note>. || 17 ||<-

From Naishadi, Madhyama, and Panchami comes Rakshagandhari. From Shadji, Gandhari, Madhyama, Panchami, and Naishadi comes Kaishiki. || 8 — 16 ||

---

(Kallinatha) <note>The commentator Kallinatha, son of Sodhala</note> Now he demonstrates the division of all the *Jatis* according to their respective *Gramas* <note>scales</note>—starting with the verse "The four..." and so on. Among the eighteen *Jatis*, he describes their similarities based on their "fullness" and other qualities—using the phrase "Now, their fullness..." and so on. By the word "fullness" (and the "etc." implied in the original Sanskrit), we should also understand *Shadava* <note>hexatonic, or six-note scales</note> and *Auduva* <note>pentatonic, or five-note scales</note>. 

*Nitya-purna* means "always complete"; the meaning is that these never transition into hexatonic or pentatonic states. *Sampurna-shadava* means they can be both complete and hexatonic. Having analyzed the opinions of authorities like Bharata, it is stated as a rule that these four modes—Shadji, Nandayanti, Andhra, and Gandharodichyava—are fixed as being either complete or hexatonic. 

This being the case, when a singer wishes to make them hexatonic, the hexatonic state must be seen as fixed according to the following characteristics: in Shadji by dropping the note *Nishada* <note>the 7th note, B</note>, in Nandayanti and Andhra by dropping *Shadja* <note>the tonic, C</note>, and in Gandharodichyava by dropping *Rishabha* <note>the 2nd note, D</note>. Regarding the phrase "The remaining ten": the ten that remain are those distinct from the four "always complete" modes and the four "complete-hexatonic" modes—

<header>Ocean of Music [Jatis]</header>

## In the Jatis known as Panchami, Madhyama, and Shadjamadhyama,
## The overlap of notes <term>Svara-sadharana; a technique where a note shifts slightly toward its neighbor</term> was taught by the Sage Bharata and others. || 21 ||

The Jatis are: Arshabhi, Gandhari, Madhyama, Panchami, Dhaivati, Naishadi, Shadjo-dichyava, Shadjamadhyama, Rakta-gandhari, and Kaishiki. These ten possess the states of being complete <term>Sampurna; seven notes</term>, hexatonic <term>Shadava; six notes</term>, and pentatonic <term>Auduvita; five notes</term>. This means these ten can be performed in any of these three states depending on the omission of specific notes. For example:
* **Arshabhi** becomes hexatonic by omitting Shadja <note>the 1st note, C</note>, and pentatonic by omitting both Shadja and Panchama <note>the 5th note, G</note>.
* **Gandhari, Rakta-gandhari, and Kaishiki** become hexatonic by omitting Rishabha <note>the 2nd note, D</note>, and pentatonic by omitting Rishabha and Dhaivata <note>the 6th note, A</note>.
* **Madhyama and Panchami** become hexatonic by omitting Gandhara <note>the 3rd note, E</note>, and pentatonic by omitting Nishada <note>the 7th note, B</note> and Gandhara.
* **Dhaivati and Naishadi** become hexatonic by omitting Panchama, and pentatonic by omitting Shadja and Panchama.
* **Shadjo-dichyava** becomes hexatonic by omitting Rishabha, and pentatonic by omitting Panchama and Rishabha.
* **Shadjamadhyama** becomes hexatonic by omitting Nishada, and pentatonic by omitting Nishada and Gandhara. || 17—20 ||

<term>(Sudhakara Commentary)</term> Regarding the question of how many of these belong to which scale <term>Grama</term>, the author says: "Four..." Among these Jatis, the four containing the word 'Shadja'—namely Shadji, Shadja-kaishiki, Shadjamadhyama, and Shadjo-dichyava—along with Naishadi, Dhaivati, and Arshabhi, these seven are born from the **Shadja-grama** <note>The primary scale starting on C</note>. The remaining eleven are born from the **Madhyama-grama** <note>The secondary scale starting on F</note>. 

Having promised to explain the completeness, hexatonic, and pentatonic natures of the Jatis, he states: Karmaravi, Gandhara-panchami, Shadja-kaishiki, and Madhyamodichyava are **only** complete; they are never hexatonic or pentatonic. Shadji, Nandayanti, Andhra, and Gandharodichyava possess both completeness and hexatonic forms, but never pentatonic. The remaining ten Jatis possess all three states: complete, hexatonic, and pentatonic. || 17—20 ||

<term>(Kallinatha Commentary)</term> Here, he demonstrates the rule regarding the use of "note overlap" <term>Svara-sadharana</term> as taught by Bharata and others in certain Jatis. By this statement, in the three Jatis—Panchami, Madhyama, and Shadjamadhyama—when either the Shadja, Madhyama, or Panchama notes act as the dominant <term>Amsha; the primary melodic pivot</term>, or when another note acts as the dominant, the overlap of notes is applied. This rule is meant to restrict the application of overlap specifically to these contexts...

<header>Chapter 7] First Chapter: On Notes (Svaras)</header>

## In the case of the Aṃśas <note>The dominant or "soul" note of a melody</note> being Sa, Ma, or Pa, this occurs according to their respective rules.
## Kambala, Aśvatara, and others state that this applies to those scales where Ni and Ga are weak. (22)
## That is also the opinion regarding Ragas and Bhashas <note>Melodic categories</note> where the two-shruti notes are weak. However, this does not occur in the Ṣaḍjamadhyamā scale when Ni and Ga are the Aṃśas. (23)
## Even there, they are only modified notes based on the overlapping of notes (Svara-Sādhāraṇa).

---

The author enumerates the overlaps: **In the case of the Aṃśas being Sa, Ma, or Pa.** This refers to the overlapping of notes (*Svara-Sādhāraṇa*). **According to their respective rules** means without violating the rules previously stated, such as "having sounded the note Sa, one should employ..." and so forth.

Here is the arrangement: In the *Pañcamī* scale when Pa is the Aṃśa, and in the *Madhyamā* and *Ṣaḍjamadhyamā* scales when Sa, Ma, or Pa are the Aṃśas, the use of overlapping is prescribed. **Kambala, Aśvatara, and others** <note>Legendary serpent-sages associated with the origins of music theory</note> say this overlapping of notes is for the purpose of knowing the *Kākalī* <note>Sharp Ni</note> and *Antara* <note>Sharp Ga</note> notes. **In those where Ni and Ga are weak** refers to the scales named *Pañcamī*, *Madhyamā*, and *Ṣaḍjamadhyamā* where the notes Niṣāda (Ni) and Gāndhāra (Ga) are omitted or diminished.

The meaning is as follows: When either Niṣāda or Gāndhāra is the Aṃśa (dominant note), the other cannot be omitted because they are consonant with each other; therefore, the use of *Kākalī* and *Antara* should not be performed. **Where the two-shruti notes are weak** means where Niṣāda and Gāndhāra are to be omitted. **In Ragas and Bhashas also**: Here, the word "Raga" encompasses all three types—Grāmarāga, Uparāga, and Rāga. The word "Bhasha" encompasses the three types—Bhāṣā, Vibhāṣā, and Antarabhāṣā. By the word "and others," the fourfold group of Rāgāṅga, Bhāṣāṅga, Kriyāṅga, and Upāṅga is included, thus covering the entire tenfold expansion of Ragas.

The word "also" in that context highlights that this is not only in scales (Jatis) where the two-shruti notes are weak, but everywhere in Ragas and similar forms where those notes are weak. That opinion on the overlapping of *Kākalī* and *Antara* is the accepted view of Bharata <note>The foundational sage of Indian dramaturgy and music</note> and others.

Strengthening the stated meaning by providing a counter-example, he says: **When Ni and Ga are the Aṃśas.** This refers to those scales mentioned according to the view of Bharata (the *Pañcamī* and *Madhyamā* scales) and according to the view of Kambala, Aśvatara, and others (the scales where Ni and Ga are weak).

---

<term>Kākalī/Antara</term>: Specific sharpened variations of the notes Niṣāda and Gāndhāra.

# Sangita Ratnakara [Jatis]

-> Nandayanti, Madhyamodichyava, and Gandharapanchami have only one dominant note (Amsha). || 24 || <-

-> Dhaivati, Gandharodichyava, and Panchami are said to have two dominant notes. || 25 || <-

Regarding the four Jatis—Panchami, Madhyama, Shadjamadhyama, and Shadji—since Shadjamadhyama is born from a mixture of modified notes <note>original: "vikrita-samsargajatvena"</note>, it is considered purely modified. Even though the other three could potentially use overlapping notes <term>Svara-sadharana: a technique where a note partakes in the character of its neighbor</term> in both their pure and modified states, the rule is established: they use them only when modified. "In those also" refers to the three: Panchami, Madhyama, and Shadji. The intent is this: in the pure state of Shadji and the others, the use of modified notes is not permitted. || 21—23- ||

**(Sudhakara Commentary)** Regarding "Panchami" etc.: Sage Bharata and others have stated that the overlapping note technique should be employed in the Panchami, Madhyama, and Shadjamadhyama Jatis. || 21 || Regarding "In the dominant notes": This overlapping technique must be strictly performed when Shadja, Madhyama, or Panchama are the dominant notes. How? By not overstepping their respective positions. When Shadja is the dominant note, use Shadja-overlapping; when Madhyama or Panchama are dominant, use Madhyama-overlapping. Kambala and Ashvatara <note>Ancient authorities on music often cited as a pair</note> say this occurs in Jatis where the notes Nishada and Gandhara are weak. It is the opinion of Kambala, Ashvatara, and others that this technique should also be used in Ragas and Bhashas <note>categories of melodic compositions</note> where Nishada and Gandhara are weak. || 22, 22- || Regarding "Ni and Ga": When Nishada and Gandhara are the dominant notes in the Shadjamadhyama Jati, this overlapping technique should not be used. Generally, only the modified forms of the Jatis employ these overlapping notes. || - 23, 23- ||

**(Kalanidhi Commentary)** Now, among the eighteen Jatis, the author determines the total number of dominant notes <note>original: "Amsha"</note>—ranging from one to seven—by describing their specific characteristics. From "Nandayanti..." until the end of the section on the eighteen Jatis: "Single-dominant" <note>original: "Ekansha"</note> refers to those having only one note as the dominant. According to the characteristics to be described, Nandayanti, Madhyamodichyava, and Gandharapanchami each have Panchama (the 5th note) as their dominant. "Two-dominant" <note>original: "Dvyansha"</note> refers to Dhaivati, Gandharodichyava, and Panchami. In Dhaivati, the dominants are Rishabha and Dhaivata; in Gandharodichyava, they are Shadja—

# The Ocean of Music
## [On Jati—]

->The Graha, Amsha, Tara, and Mandra; the Nyasa and Apanyasa;<-
->Also the Sannyasa and Vinyasa; then Bahutva and Alpatva;<-
->Along with the Antaramarga, these are the characteristics of Jatis;<-
->Including the hexatonic and pentatonic variations, they are said to be thirteen.<-

According to Matanga <note>An influential 9th-century musicologist, author of the Brihaddeshi</note>:
> “Seven more than forty [47] are to be applied in the hexatonic form. The meaning is this: when the hexatonic <term>Shadava: a scale using six notes</term> rule is applied, there are forty-seven Amshas <note>The dominant or 'soul' notes of a scale</note>. How? From the sixty-three total Amshas, nine belonging to the four Jatis that are always 'complete' (septatonic) must be subtracted. When these nine are removed, fifty-four remain. From those, seven specific Amshas belonging to the Shadjamadhyama, Shadji, Shadjodichyava, Kaishiki, and Rakshagandhari Jatis are exceptions and must also be removed. After removing those seven, forty-seven Amshas remain.”

In the pentatonic <term>Auduvita: a scale using five notes</term> rule, there are thirty Amshas. As stated by Matanga:
> “Likewise, excluding the exceptions, there are thirty in the pentatonic form. The meaning is as follows:”

As before: when sixteen are subtracted—specifically the twelve from those that are always complete or hexatonic, and five others that are exceptions—there remain thirty Amshas in the pentatonic form. Thus Bharata <note>The legendary sage and author of the Natyashastra, the foundational text of Indian performing arts</note> says:
> “The pentatonic form is to be understood as having five notes by those skilled in the ten-fold practice. Its characteristics are established in thirty varieties as previously mentioned.”

Furthermore, Bharata mentions the use of even four-note scales in the context of the *Apakrishta Dhruva* <note>A specific type of song used in ancient drama, often associated with sorrow or despondency</note>:
> “There is the use of six notes, and likewise of five notes; there is even the use of four notes in the Apakrishta Dhruva songs.”

***

(Kallinatha's Commentary) Now, regarding the mention of the “thirteen-fold characteristics of Jati,” at this stage of defining the Jatis, the author defines the thirteen components starting with Graha in order: *The Graha, Amsha, Tara, Mandra, etc.* Regarding the phrase *hexatonic and pentatonic variations*, this refers to those Jatis other than the ones that are "always complete" (septatonic), as appropriate. Although authorities like Bharata and Matanga consider *Sannyasa* and *Vinyasa* to be included within *Apanyasa* because they depend on the *Vidari* <note>A musical phrase or section</note>, and consider *Antaramarga* to be a subset of the *Amsha*...

# Chapter 7]          First Chapter on Notes

->Page 181<-

> The note placed at the beginning of a song or musical composition is called the **Graha** <note>The "take-off" or starting note</note>. In cases where only one of either the **Aṃśa** <note>The dominant or "soul" note</note> or the **Graha** is mentioned, both should be understood as the same note. || 31 ||
> That which manifests melodic beauty in the song, and whose consonant and assonant notes are frequent in the *Vidārī* <note>A section or phrase of a composition</note>, and from which the arrangement of high and low registers is determined; || 32 ||
> Which is itself the starting point, and whose consonant and assonant notes function as the **Nyāsa** <note>Final note</note>, **Apanyāsa** <note>Intermediate stop</note>, **Vinyāsa** <note>Phrase ending</note>, **Saṃnyāsa** <note>Ending of the first part of a verse</note>, and **Graha**; || 33 ||
> That note which is used most frequently in performance is the **Vādī** <note>The "king" note</note> or **Aṃśa**, due to its inherent suitability. This abundance in performance is the pervasive characteristic of the **Aṃśa**. || 34 ||

---

Since the mutual relationship of these characteristics is established through their connection to the **Aṃśa** and others, a separate listing was not strictly required, and thus it was said that there are ten characteristics of a *Jāti* <note>The melodic prototypes preceding the modern Raga system</note>. However, because **Saṃnyāsa** and **Vinyāsa** are distinct components, and because the "internal path" (*Antaramārga*) is essential—as a performance cannot be accomplished without it even if the **Aṃśa** and other components are present—the author has listed them separately to state that there are thirteen characteristics.

Regarding the verse "Placed at the beginning of a song": Among those thirteen, the note placed at the beginning—that is, at the commencement of the song (the melodic arrangement that creates beauty)—is the **Graha**. It is called **Graha** <note>literally "the seizer"</note> because the song is "grasped" or started by it.

Regarding the phrase "In cases where only one of either the **Aṃśa** or **Graha** is mentioned": This refers to the definition of a song's performance. Where only the **Aṃśa** is specified and not the **Graha**, or where only the **Graha** is specified and not the **Aṃśa**, then "both are taken" (both the **Graha** and **Aṃśa** are understood to be that same note). The meaning is this: in the definition of a song, whichever note is designated as the **Aṃśa** and no other is named as the **Graha**, that same note is also the **Graha**. Conversely, if a note is named as the **Graha** and no other as the **Aṃśa**, it is also the **Aṃśa**. By this, it is stated that in any particular *Jāti*, however many **Aṃśas** there are, there are exactly that many **Grahas**. This means that across all *Jātis*, there are sixty-three **Grahas**. As was stated by **Bharata** <note>The legendary sage and author of the Natyashastra</note>:

> "Sixty-three **Aṃśas** are to be known, and the **Grahas** of those [Jātis] are exactly like the **Aṃśas**."

<summary>This page defines the Graha (starting note) and Aṃśa (dominant note) within the ancient Indian Jāti system, explaining that they are often identical and totaling sixty-three across all melodic types. It also justifies why the author lists thirteen musical characteristics instead of the traditional ten.</summary>

<keywords>Graha, Aṃśa, Jāti, Bharata, musical theory, Vādī, melodic characteristics, Sanskrit musicology</keywords>

--- Page 212 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of musical theory from the Sangitaratnakara, specifically focusing on the definition and characteristics of the 'Amsha' (dominant note) within the 'Jati' (melodic classification) system.</meta>

<page-num>182</page-num>
->### Sangitaratnakara: [On Jatis]<-

Matanga also stated— "That <term>Amsha</term><note>The 'Amsha' is the most important, dominant note of a musical scale, similar to a tonic or key-note in Western music, but with more functional roles.</note> should be understood as having sixty-three distinct variations." Regarding the definition of the Amsha as "that which produces <term>Rakti</term>"<note>Rakti refers to melodic beauty, charm, or the capacity to please the ear of the listener.</note> and so on: that note which possesses qualities such as manifesting melodic beauty is designated as the Amsha in a song, because it is the primary constituent of the music. If one were to say only "that which manifests beauty," it would apply to other notes as well, as all notes possess some inherent beauty. Therefore, the qualification "in a song" is intended here to mean the manifestation of a *specific* beauty tied to a particular melodic arrangement. This is similar to how a word, while expressing its own literal meaning, manifests the intended sentiment (<term>Rasa</term>) of a whole sentence in the context of "undifferentiated suggestion" <note>original: "asaṃlakṣyakrama-dhvani"; a term from Sanskrit poetics where the transition from literal meaning to aesthetic suggestion is so fast it is unnoticeable.</note>.

"Whose <term>Samvadi</term> and <term>Anuvadi</term>..."<note>Samvadi is a consonant note (like a perfect fifth); Anuvadi is an assonant or 'attendant' note.</note> refers to that note which is intended to be defined as the Amsha. In this definition, the word "which" in every sentence refers to the Amsha note being established. Its Samvadi and Anuvadi notes (defined previously) are "abundant" or frequently used within the <term>Vidari</term> <note>A section or phrase of a song.</note>. From this note, the arrangement of the high (<term>Tara</term>) and low (<term>Mandra</term>) registers is determined; taking this note as the limit, the high register is established by ascending to higher notes, and the low register by descending to lower notes.

The Amsha is its own Samvadi—meaning, the note which bears the designation of "Vadi" (the speaker/tonic) can sometimes act as its own consonant. Here, the word "and" implies "only"—it is only a Samvadi to itself. However, the Anuvadi is always a "different" note; a note is never its own Anuvadi. This is like a King in the world who, due to necessity, may perform the duties of a Minister, but never the duties of a servant.

Furthermore, the note that becomes "abundant" in performance through its roles as <term>Nyasa</term> (final note), <term>Apanyasa</term> (intermediate stop), <term>Vinyasa</term> (phrase-ending note), <term>Samyasa</term> (final note of a section), and <term>Graha</term> (starting note) is the Amsha. Its assumption of these forms (Nyasa, etc.) is the cause of its frequency in usage. That "Vadi" (sonant note) becomes the Amsha by virtue of its "fitness." "Fitness" here means deserving the aforementioned definition, such as being the manifestor of melodic beauty. As Bharata said:

> "That in which the <term>Raga</term> <note>The melodic framework or 'color' of the music.</note> resides and from which it proceeds;
> That which is perceived as the leader of the high and low registers;
> That which is followed through the combination of the starting note (<term>Graha</term>), 
> intermediate stops (<term>Apanyasa</term>, <term>Vinyasa</term>, <term>Samyasa</term>), and the final note (<term>Nyasa</term>);
> That note here shall be the Amsha, possessing the ten characteristics of an Amsha."

<note>1. Intended / desired to be expressed.</note>

<summary>This page defines the 'Amsha' (dominant note) in Indian classical music theory, explaining its role as the melodic center that determines registers and governs other functional notes like the starting and ending tones. It cites authorities like Matanga and Bharata to establish the Amsha's ten essential characteristics, including its ability to create aesthetic beauty (Rakti).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of musical theory from the first chapter on notes (Svaragatadhyaya), specifically focusing on the characteristics of the 'Amsha' (the dominant note) and 'Graha' (the starting note) within the 'Jati' (melodic framework) system.</meta>

# Chapter 7] First Chapter on Notes: Page 183

Thus. Now, if one asks: "Since Bharata <note>The legendary sage and author of the Natyashastra, the foundational text on Indian performing arts</note> has ordained that 'the starting note is the dominant note' (*graha* is *amsha*), and therefore the starting note possesses all the characteristics of the dominant note, what then is the distinction between the starting note (*graha*) and the dominant note (*amsha*)?"

It is said in response: By the extension of the dominant note's characteristics to the starting note, it is not only the quality of being the 'sonant' <term>vadi: the primary melodic protagonist or 'king' note</term> that is obtained, but rather all four melodic functions <note>The four functions are Vadi (sonant), Samvadi (consonant), Anuvadi (assonant), and Vivadi (dissonant)</note>. This is their distinction. As stated by Matanga <note>An influential musicologist, author of the Brihaddeshi</note>: "The dominant note (*amsha*) is strictly the sonant (*vadi*) only, but the starting note (*graha*) is fourfold, divided by the distinctions of sonant and the rest."

Because the ten characteristics [of Jatis] manifest in sixty-seven ways, the "constant abundance" is the fixed definition of the dominant note (*amsha*). Thus he says: **Abundance**. The connection is that abundance in performance is the comprehensive characteristic of the dominant note. **Comprehensive** means that whatever is the dominant note is necessarily abundant, due to their invariable concomitance. || 29—34 ||

(Sudhakara Commentary) He divides the thirteen-fold characteristics of the *Jati* <term>Jati: the ancient melodic prototypes that preceded the modern Raga system</term>: **Starting note, dominant note...** and so on. Regarding the phrase **"In the hexatonic and pentatonic [scales] somewhere"**: this means excluding the four Jatis like Karmaravi, which are always "full" (heptatonic).

He explains the definition of the starting note (*graha*): **The beginning of the song...** The note that is employed at the very beginning of a song or a Jati is called the *graha*. **Therein**: because of the rule that "the note which is the dominant (*amsha*) is the same as the starting note (*graha*)," by mentioning one, both are understood.

Now, if that is so, what is the difference between the starting note and the dominant note? It is said: The dominant note is only the sonant (*vadi*), whereas the starting note is fourfold, distinguished by the sonant and others. Furthermore, the dominant note is primary because it generates the *Raga* (aesthetic color), while the starting note is secondary. This is their distinction. || 29—31 ||

He explains the definition of the dominant note (*amsha*): **That which manifests beauty...** That which expresses the quality of pleasingness in a song, and whose consonant (*samvadi*) and assonant (*anuvadi*) notes are abundant in the *vidari*.

Now, what is meant by the word *vidari*? A *vidari* is that by which the song or the verse is "split" or partitioned <note>A musical phrase or section break</note>. It is of two types: the song-partition (*gita-vidari*) and the word-partition (*pada-vidari*). This will be specifically described in the Chapter on Rhythm (*Taladhyaya*).

[The dominant note is also] that which serves as the limit for the arrangement of the lower (*mandra*) and higher (*tara*) registers; or that which, along with its consonant and assonant notes, attains the status of the final note (*nyasa*), the intermediate final (*apanyasa*), the medial final (*vinyasa*), the initial final (*sannyasa*), and the starting note (*graha*). That which has abundance in the performance of Jatis and the like is called the dominant note and its consonant.

**By virtue of fitness**: because of its importance, it is called by the word "beginning" (*adi*), and by other characteristics, it is called by the word "dominant" (*amsha*). He states that abundance in performance is the primary characteristic of the dominant note by saying: **Abundance**.

Now, why is it called by the word *amsha* (part/portion)? The word *amsha* signifies a "part." This note is called *amsha* because it causes the division of Jatis, Ragas, and so on—treating the cause as the effect. || 32—34 ||

<summary>This page defines and distinguishes between the 'Amsha' (dominant note) and 'Graha' (starting note) in ancient Indian music theory, emphasizing that while they often coincide, the Amsha is the primary melodic driver characterized by its frequent repetition.</summary>
<keywords>Amsha, Graha, Vadi, Jati, Vidari, Bharata, Matanga, Indian music theory, sonant, melodic registers</keywords>

# The Jewel Mine of Music [On Jatis]

->The dominant note should be in the middle octave; from that note, when it is situated in the high register,<-
->one may ascend four notes further; this is the supreme limit of the high register.<-
->Below that, one may act according to desire; even a note omitted in the high register is counted.<-
->In the *Nandayanti* melody, the ascent is proclaimed to reach up to the high Shadja.<-

<gloss>Kallinatha's Commentary</gloss> Now he explains the arrangement of the high register (*tara*) <note>The high register or octave</note> with the verse beginning "The dominant note should be in the middle octave."
In the middle octave—meaning among the seven notes beginning with *Shadja* <note>The tonic or first note, 'C'</note> situated in the middle register—there should be the *Amsha* <note>The dominant or 'soul' note of a melody</note>. Because of the importance and strength of the *Shadja-grama* and *Madhyama-grama* <note>The two primary parent scales of ancient Indian music</note>, whichever note with four *shrutis* <note>Micro-tonal intervals</note>—either *Shadja* or *Madhyama*—becomes the dominant in its respective scale, one may ascend four notes beyond that note when it is doubled in the high register. 

In the *Madhyama-grama* scale, regarding the phrase "from that," referring to the high *Madhyama*: the grammatical fifth case is used here to mean "starting from that." Therefore, including that note, one should ascend four notes: *Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni* <note>F, G, A, B</note>. 
In the *Shadja-grama* scale, however, "from that" refers to the high *Shadja*; the fifth case here indicates a limit. From there, one should ascend four notes: *Ri, Ga, Ma, Pa* <note>D, E, F, G</note>. 
This is the "limit of the high register"; this described method is the supreme, absolute limit. Why? Because in the *Madhyama-grama*, a note higher than the high *Nishada* <note>B</note> simply does not exist in this system; whereas in the *Shadja-grama*, even though the notes *Dhaivata* and *Nishada* <note>A and B</note> are possible above the high *Panchama* <note>G</note>, and the singer might have the power to reach them, they are not used because they lack "redness" <note>Rakti: melodic beauty or emotional appeal</note>.

Regarding "Below that, one may act according to desire": if the limit is less than the aforementioned high *Nishada* or *Panchama*, and ends on any lower note in the high register, it is a matter of "free will"—proceeding according to the singer's capability or whim. 
Regarding "Even a note omitted is counted": in the context of the high register arrangement, when it is said "one should ascend four," if one note is omitted due to the specific characteristics of the performance, it is still included in the count of the ascent. 
Because the *Nandayanti* jati <note>A specific melodic type or proto-raga</note> also belongs to the *Madhyama-grama* scale, its high register limit should technically begin from the high *Madhyama*. However, as an exception, the high *Shadja* is prescribed as the upper limit according to the school of Bharata <note>Author of the Natyashastra</note> and as the starting limit according to Rudrata and others. Keeping this in mind, he says with dual meaning: "Up to the high Shadja." In the sense of an upper limit, it means "up to..."

<summary>This page defines the permissible upper limits for melodic ascent in the two primary ancient Indian scales, explaining that the high register typically extends four notes beyond the dominant note of the middle octave. It also notes exceptions for specific melodic types like Nandayanti and discusses the aesthetic reasons for these limits.</summary>
<keywords>octave, dominant note, high register, Shadja-grama, Madhyama-grama, Nandayanti, Bharata, musical aesthetics, melodic ascent</keywords>

# Chapter 7: The First Chapter on Notes

The ascent is proclaimed by authorities such as Bharata <note>Bharata Muni, the legendary author of the Natyashastra, the foundational text on Indian performing arts</note> to extend from the tonic <term>Shadja: the first note of the scale, similar to 'Do'</term> up to the higher tonic. As Bharata said:

> "In the movement of the high register, one should never exceed the higher tonic."

However, regarding the lower limit of that range, the ascent generally reaches the fourth note starting from the higher tonic. This general rule is proclaimed by Rudrata and others. As Matanga <note>An influential musicologist, author of the Brihaddesi</note> stated: the high register movement reaches only as far as the tonic, because the fourth note <term>Madhyama: the fourth note, similar to 'Fa'</term> is also in consonance here and is not omitted; thus, Rudrata’s assignment of the high register movement to the fourth note is not a flaw. The intention is this: in the melody <term>Nandayanti: a specific ancient melodic structure or Jati</term>, because it is associated with the *Hrishyaka* scale-type <term>Murchana: a melodic scale or mode</term> and lacks the fifth note, and because it pervades the lower register, the teachers have restricted the high register movement. The general arrangement of the high register, however, was stated by Bharata as follows:

> "One should know the high register movement starts from the dominant note <term>Amsha: the primary or 'soul' note of a melody</term> up to the fourth note; or it may extend to the fifth or seventh note, but beyond that is not desired here."

The term *Tara* <note>High register/pitch</note> is derived from the causative form of the root *tr* (to cross); it is formed in the passive sense, referring to the sound produced in the head which can be heard from a distance. || 35, 36 ||

(Simhabhupala's Commentary) He explains the definition of the high register: *In the middle...* From whatever note is situated in the middle octave, one should perform an ascent up to the fourth note situated in the high octave. This is stated as the maximum limit of the ascent. One should not ascend beyond that. Below that limit, the movement in the high register is according to one's desire. Even a note omitted in other contexts may be taken in the high register. Bharata stated the high register movement extends to the fourth, fifth, or seventh note. As he said:

> "One should know the high register movement starts from the dominant note up to the fourth note; or it may extend to the fifth or seventh note, but beyond that is not desired here."

Regarding the phrase *up to the high tonic*: in the *Nandayanti* melody, the ascent should only be performed up to the higher tonic. This is an exception to the previously stated rule. || 35, 36 ||

<header>The Ocean of Music [On Jatis]</header>

->From the tonic note situated in the middle register, one may descend to the tonic in the lower register.<-
->Or, one may descend as far as the lower final note, or even to the notes Re and Dha situated below that. (37)<-
->This is the limit of the lower movement; within that range, one may move as one pleases.<-
->The conclusion of a song is the final note, and that is of twenty-one varieties. (38)<-

(Kallinatha's Commentary) **From the tonic note situated in the middle register** means starting from the <term>Amsha</term><note>The dominant or "soul" note of a scale, often acting as the tonic</note>—either Shadja or Madhyama depending on the <term>Grama</term><note>The basic scale system; either the Shadja-grama or Madhyama-grama</note>. Here, the grammatical case implies "starting from the tonic." **To the tonic in the lower register** means descending as far as the Shadja or Madhyama located in the lower register, according to the respective scale. The prefix "a-" here indicates "including the limit." One should descend. By this, it is understood that the performance of a <term>Jati</term><note>The melodic prototypes that preceded the modern Raga system</note> generally begins with the tonic in the middle register. This is one position regarding the arrangement of the lower register in Jati practice.

**Or, as far as the lower final note** means up to the note designated as the "final" (<term>Nyasa</term>) in the lower register. Again, the prefix indicates "including the limit." In this context, the word "final" refers to the boundary notes of the two scales—Gandhara and Nishada—rather than the note that concludes a specific song. By a process of reversal, in the practice of the Shadja-grama, the lower Gandhara is the limit; in the Madhyama-grama, the lower Nishada is the limit. These constitute the lower boundaries of the two scales. The evidence for this second position is seen in the fact that even in the Shadja-grami and Shadja-kaishiki Jatis, the lower Gandhara is observed to act as a limit.

**Or even to the notes Re and Dha situated below that** is the third position. The word "even" here implies an alternative: "either Re or Dha." The word "that" refers back to the previously mentioned scale-limits, Gandhara and Nishada. By saying **the Re and Dha situated below them**, the text shows the reversal of the two limits according to the specific scale intended. As stated by the sage Bharata:

> "The movement in the lower register is threefold: ending at the tonic, ending at the final, or ending at the intermediate final.
> 
> There is no lower movement beyond the tonic; however, in the case of the final, two notes are established.
> By the evidence of the Gandhara-limit, the use of Rishabha is observed."

This constitutes the **limit** or boundary of the **lower movement** (the descent of notes into the lower register) based on any of these three positions. **Within that range**—meaning anything less than that stated limit—there is **freedom of movement** according to the singer's desire or capability.

# Chapter 7: The First Chapter on Notes

->For the seven Jatis starting with Shadjī, the final note is the note for which they are named.<-
->For Shadjamadhyamā, two notes—Shadja and Madhyama—are considered the name-giving finals. || 39 ||<-
->The three Udichyavā Jatis end in Madhyama; Kaishikī ends in Nishada, Panchama, or Gandhara.<-
->Kārmāravī ends in Panchama; the remaining five are remembered as ending in Gandhara. || 40 ||<-

...or the lack of progression. The word *Mandra* <note>original: "मन्द्र"</note> is derived from the root *mad* (to rejoice/gladden) with a causative suffix, meaning "that which gladdens." This term is assigned to a sound that is pleasing and deep. Now, regarding the **Nyasa** <note>the "final" or "cadence" note</note>: it is that which brings the song to a conclusion. In the performance of *Jatis* <note>melodic frameworks that preceded the modern Raga system</note> and other forms, the *Nyasa* is the note that creates a sense of completion and independence. It is called *Nyasa* (from the root meaning "to set down") because it is the note by which the song is set down or concluded. In the eighteen *Jatis*, this occurs in twenty-one ways, as will be explained. || 37, 38 ||

**(Sudhakara's Commentary)** He defines the *Mandra* <note>lower register</note>: "From the middle register..." One should perform a descent from the notes in the middle register down to the lower Shadja, or down to the lower *Nyasa* note, or down to the lower Rishabha and Dhaivata—these are the three views. This is stated as the furthest limit of the lower movement. Within that limit, the movement in the lower register is according to one's desire. He then states the definition of *Nyasa*: "In the song..." That which concludes the song, standing at the end of the *Jati* and so on, is called the *Nyasa*. It is the note in which or by which the song is "set down" (finished). It is of twenty-one types. || 37, 38 ||

**(Kallinatha's Commentary)** He explains this further with the verse beginning "For the seven Jatis starting with Shadjī..." For the seven—including both the pure and the modified forms—the "name-giving" note is the final; for example, in *Shadjī* the final is Shadja, in *Arshabhī* it is Rishabha, and so on. The word "but" <note>original: "तु" (tu)</note> implies "none other." Regarding "The three Udichyavā Jatis": the triad of Shadjudichyavā, Gandharudichyavā, and Madhyamudichyavā ends in Madhyama. The "remaining five" are Shadja-kaishikī, Rakta-gandharī, Gandhara-panchamī, Andhrī, and Nandayantī. "Remembered" means as recorded by Bharata <note>the legendary sage and author of the Natyashastra</note> and others. || 39, 40 ||

**(Sudhakara's Commentary)** He clarifies the twenty-one types: For the seven starting with Shadjī, the seven notes they are named after are the finals. For Shadjamadhyamā, both Shadja and Madhyama are the finals...

# Sangitaratnakara [Chapter on Jatis]

The <term>Apanyasa</term> <note>A secondary resting note or medial cadence that marks the end of a musical phrase within a larger composition</note> is that note which concludes a <term>Vidari</term> <note>A specific section or phrase of a song, similar to a musical line or verse</note>. In the *Karmaravi*, *Naishadi*, *Andhri*, and the two *Madhyama* Jatis, as well as in the *Arshabhi* Jati, those notes which serve as the <term>Amsha</term> <note>The dominant or melodic soul-note</note> are also designated as the Apanyasas. ॥ 41 ॥

In the three *Udichyava* Jatis, the Apanyasas are *Shadja* and *Dhaivata*. In *Raktagandhari*, the Apanyasa is *Madhyama*. In *Gandhari*, they are *Shadja* and *Panchama*. In *Shadjakashiki*, they are *Shadja*, *Nishada*, and *Panchama*. In *Panchami*, they are recorded as *Nishada*, *Rishabha*, and *Panchama*. ॥ 42-43 ॥

In *Gandharpanchami*, they are *Rishabha* and *Panchama*. In *Shadji*, they are *Gandhara* and *Panchama*. In *Dhaivati*, they are said to be *Rishabha*, *Madhyama*, and *Dhaivata*. In *Nandayanti*, *Madhyama* and *Panchama* are intended. ॥ 44 ॥

In *Kaishiki*, six notes are used, excluding *Rishabha*; however, others say all seven notes may serve as Apanyasas. Regarding the *Shadjamadhyama* Jati, they say all seven notes function as Apanyasas. ॥ 45 ॥

Here, the final Apanyasas <note>referring to the primary set</note> are nineteen; the others are thirty-seven, totaling fifty-six. If one accepts the view of seven Apanyasas in *Kaishiki*, they are known to be fifty-seven. ॥ 46 ॥

In *Shadja-udichyava*, *Gandhara-udichyava*, and *Madhyama-udichyava*, the <term>Nyasa</term> <note>The final note of a composition; the tonic cadence</note> is *Madhyama*. In *Kaishiki*, the Nyasas are *Nishada*, *Panchama*, and *Gandhara*. In *Karmaravi*, it is *Panchama*. For the remaining five Jatis, *Gandhara* is the Nyasa. Thus, there are twenty-one Nyasas. ॥ 39, 40 ॥

<gloss>Commentary by Kallinatha:</gloss> Now, the Apanyasa is defined. From the phrase "The Apanyasa note is that..." until "they are known to be fifty-seven," the explanation is clear. An Apanyasa is that by which the musical performance is "set down" <note>original: *apanyasyate*</note> or paused. While it lacks the finality of a Nyasa, it creates an intermediate division and thus appears like a conclusion. ॥ 41-46 ॥

<gloss>Commentary by Simhabhupala:</gloss> He defines the Apanyasa: "The Apanyasa..." etc. That note which concludes a *Vidari* (a limb or segment of a song) is the Apanyasa. As Matanga also stated: "Where the music seems to have ended..."

->The *Sannyasa* <note>a note used to end the first section of a melody</note> is a note that does not conflict with the *Amsha* <term>Amsha: the primary or "soul" note of a musical composition</term> and marks the conclusion of the first *Vidari* <term>Vidari: a melodic phrase or structural division of a song</term>. (47)<-
->The *Vinyasa* <note>a note used to end a smaller phrase within a section</note> is described similarly as non-conflicting with the *Amsha*; however, it is said to be that which stands at the end of the words that form the parts of a *Vidari*. (48)<-
->Abundance <note>original: *Bahutva*</note> is considered to be of two types: through non-skipping <note>frequent usage</note> and through repetition. This abundance resides in the alternate *Amsha* notes and also in the "sonant" and "consonant" notes. (49)<-

The note through which the song shines forth is the *Apanyasa* <note>a secondary ending note</note>. It occurs in the middle of a *Vidari*; this means within the body of the song. He enumerates the *Apanyasas* in the *Karmaravi* and other modes: In the modes *Karmaravi*, *Naishadi*, *Andhri*, *Madhyama*, and *Arshabhi*, the *Amsha* notes themselves serve as the *Apanyasas*. In *Shadjodichyava*, *Gandharodichyava*, and *Madhyamodichyava*, the notes *Shadja* <note>the first note, 'Sa'</note> and *Dhaivata* <note>the sixth note, 'Dha'</note> are the *Apanyasas*. In *Raktagandhari*, the *Madhyama* <note>the fourth note, 'Ma'</note> is the *Apanyasa*. In *Gandhari*, *Shadja* and *Madhyama* are the *Apanyasas*. In *Shadjakashiki*, the notes *Shadja*, *Panchama* <note>the fifth note, 'Pa'</note>, and *Nishada* <note>the seventh note, 'Ni'</note> are used. In *Panchami*, they are *Nishada*, *Rishabha* <note>the second note, 'Ri'</note>, and *Panchama*. In *Gandharapanchami*, they are *Rishabha* and *Panchama*. In *Shadji*, they are *Gandhara* <note>the third note, 'Ga'</note> and *Panchama*. In *Dhaivati*, they are *Rishabha*, *Madhyama*, and *Dhaivata*. In *Nandayanti*, they are *Madhyama* and *Panchama*. In *Kaishiki*, six notes are *Apanyasas*, excluding *Rishabha*; however, some are of the opinion that all seven notes can be used. In *Shadjamadhyama*, all seven notes are used. Here, the *Amsha* notes themselves are the *Apanyasas*. These total nineteen. Others total thirty-seven. Combined, they are fifty-six. If seven *Apanyasas* are counted in *Kaishiki*, then there are fifty-seven *Apanyasa* notes. (41–46)

(Kallinatha's Commentary) Now, regarding *Sannyasa* and *Vinyasa*: "Non-conflicting with the *Amsha*" means it is a consonant note that does not oppose the primary note used in that specific performance. "Marks the conclusion of the first *Vidari*" means it completes the first section. By this, it should be understood that the *Apanyasa* <note>mentioned previously</note> concerns the remaining sections of the *Vidari*. "The *Vinyasa* is described": the word "that" refers to what is about to be said. Its non-conflicting nature with the *Amsha* has already been stated. "At the end of the words that form the parts of a *Vidari*": the parts of a *Vidari* are like the words of a sentence, consisting of the components of a *Raga* <note>melodic framework</note> endowed with *Varna* <term>Varna: melodic movement</term> and *Alankara* <term>Alankara: musical ornamentation</term>. The connection is to that note which stands at the end of such clusters of notes. Because all notes except the "dissonant" ones <note>original: *vivadi*</note> can potentially serve as *Sannyasa* or *Vinyasa*, their specific number is not stated. Now, regarding "Abundance" <note>original: *Bahutva*</note>: "Through non-skipping"—skipping <note>original: *langhana*</note> means a slight touch, a reduction in the nature of a note caused by its position or the effort of pronunciation.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of musical characteristics (laksana) from the Sangitaratnakara, specifically focusing on the concepts of Alpatva (scarcity) and Bahutva (abundance) of notes, as well as structural pause-notes like Sanyasa and Vinyasa.</meta>

# The Ocean of Music [On Jatis]

->**Scarcity and Abundance of Notes**<-

Scarcity <note>Sanskrit: *Alpatva*</note> is said to be of two kinds: from non-repetition and from skipping. Non-repetition is generally desired in notes that are not the "tonic" <note>Sanskrit: *Anamsha*, notes other than the primary melodic center</note> and even in those notes that are subject to omission. || 50 ||

Skipping <note>Sanskrit: *Langhana*</note> is a slight or glancing touch of a note; it generally occurs with notes that are to be omitted. The experts in song also desire this occasionally even for notes that are not the tonic. || 51 ||

The absence of skipping is "non-skipping," which means touching the note in its entirety. This is one form of abundance <note>Sanskrit: *Bahutva*</note>. The other is from practice, meaning repetition. Repetition is the sounding of a note again and again, whether continuously or with intervals. This is the second type of abundance. This twofold abundance should be applied to the alternate tonics <note>Sanskrit: *Paryayansha*</note>, or to notes other than the primary tonic, and it also resides in the "sonant" <note>Sanskrit: *Vadi*</note> and "consonant" <note>Sanskrit: *Samvadi*</note> notes.

Now, regarding scarcity: it is defined by the opposites of the characteristics of abundance—namely, non-repetition and skipping. Non-repetition, which is the scarcity taking the form of sounding a note only once without repeating it, is desired in non-tonic notes (those distinct from both the primary and alternate tonics). It is also frequently desired in notes that are omitted when forming hexatonic <note>Sanskrit: *Shadava*, six-note scales</note> or pentatonic <note>Sanskrit: *Auduva*, five-note scales</note> melodies. The text "a slight touch" <note>referring to verse 51</note> is self-explanatory. || 47–51 ||

**[Commentary by Sudhakara]**
He defines the "Intermediate Pause" <note>Sanskrit: *Sanyasa*</note>: A note that is not discordant with the tonic and which concludes the first section <note>Sanskrit: *Vidari*, a phrase or melodic unit</note> of a musical composition is the *Sanyasa*. Matanga <note>An ancient musicologist</note> has also said: "If a note that is not discordant with the tonic is used at the end of the first melodic section, it is called *Sanyasa*."

He defines the "Phrase-Ending Pause" <note>Sanskrit: *Vinyasa*</note>: A note that is not discordant with the tonic and stands at the end of the individual words or parts that make up a melodic section is the *Vinyasa* note. Matanga has also said: "When this same *Sanyasa* note is placed at the end of a word-phrase, it is a *Vinyasa*." Therefore, it is said that a note consonant or assonant with the tonic occurs at the end of a phrase-section.

He explains abundance: Abundance is of two kinds, from non-skipping and from repetition. This abundance belongs to the sonant and consonant notes. That note which has abundance through non-skipping is the sonant <note>*Vadi*</note>; that which has it through repetition is the consonant <note>*Samvadi*</note>.

Regarding scarcity: Scarcity is also of two types, from non-repetition and from skipping. Non-repetition is desired by Bharata <note>The legendary author of the Natyashastra</note> and others for notes other than the tonic, and sometimes even for notes that are to be omitted. It was mentioned that scarcity comes from skipping; here, one might ask what this "skipping" entails...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of musical characteristics (lakshanas) from the previous section of the Sangita Ratnakara, specifically focusing on the subtle transitions between notes and the definition of six-note scales.</meta>

<page-num>191</page-num>
<header>Chapter 7] First Chapter on Notes</header>

### Leaving aside the positions of the final note and others, the connection of notes possessing "fewness" with the dominant note and others in the middle of a melody, which creates variety— ## 52 ##

### —is called the "Internal Path" (Antaramarga), created sometimes by non-repetition and sometimes solely by skipping. It occurs mostly in the modified melodic types. ## 53 ##

### Those notes which maintain a performance of six are considered "hexatonic" (Shadava). Because it is born from those six notes, the song is called hexatonic. ## 54 ##

<note>The author explains:</note> A slight touch. Skipping is defined as pronouncing a note only once. This generally occurs with notes that are meant to be omitted. According to some opinions, skipping can also occur on notes other than the dominant note. ## 47—51 ##

(Kallinatha) Now, regarding the Internal Path (**Antaramarga**): **"Leaving aside the positions of the final note and others."** This means leaving aside or abandoning the positions of the <term>Nyasa</term> (final note), <term>Apanyasa</term> (intermediate stop), <term>Vinyasa</term> (phrase ending), <term>Sannyasa</term> (ending of the first part), <term>Graha</term> (starting note), and <term>Amsha</term> (dominant note)—essentially the specific regions of the song. **"In the middle"** is repeated to indicate the spaces between each of these various functional notes. Thus, it refers to the space between any two of the aforementioned notes. There, the **"connection with the dominant and others"** refers to the notes possessing the two types of "fewness" <note>Alpata: either by skipping or non-repetition</note> being joined with the dominant, starting, or intermediate notes through ascending or descending patterns. This creates **"variety,"** meaning a unique beauty in the melodic structure. This is produced sometimes solely by non-repetition and sometimes by skipping, depending on the aesthetic delight of the particular style. This is the "Internal Path." It occurs mostly in the **"modified melodic types"** (<term>Vikrita Jatis</term>), meaning it is only occasional in the pure melodic types. ## 52, 53 ##

(Simhabhupala) He defines the Internal Path: **"Leaving aside the positions..."** Abandoning the positions of the final, intermediate, phrase-ending, part-ending, starting, and dominant notes, the connection made with the dominant and others—which creates a special melodic curve for the "few" notes in the middle, sometimes through non-repetition and sometimes through skipping—is called the Internal Path (**Antaramarga**). This is generally found within the modified melodic types. ## 52, 53 ##

(Kallinatha) Now, regarding the hexatonic (**Shadava**): **"Those which maintain six."** Those six notes, whether pure or modified, which "maintain" or protect the performance of a melodic type (<term>Jati</term>), are called *Shadavas*.

<summary>This page defines "Antaramarga" (the internal melodic path) as the artistic connection of minor notes between structural pillars of a melody, and introduces the definition of "Shadava" (hexatonic) scales. It highlights how subtle techniques like skipping notes create melodic variety in Indian classical music theory.</summary>
<keywords>Antaramarga, Shadava, Nyasa, Amsha, Alpata, musical theory, Sangita Ratnakara, hexatonic, melodic variety, Jati</keywords>

# Sangitaratnakara [Chapter on Jatis]

> The stars move and go within it; thus, the wise call the sky *Uduva* <note>original: "uduvam". A poetic term for the firmament or ether</note>.
> Among the elements, it is the fifth; from this, the number five is derived. || 55 ||
> That which possesses this "five-ness" is called *Auduvi*. The notes belonging to it are considered *Auduva* <note>Pentatonic</note>.
> The song in which these notes are produced is called *Auduvita*. || 56 ||
> Because of this connection, the wise know the five-note scale as *Auduva*.

The term *Shadava* <note>Hexatonic/six-note scale</note> is derived from the root *av* (to protect) with the suffix *ach*. It is a compound meaning "six" and "protected." Because it is produced from these six protected notes, the six-note song is called *Shadava*. This is the interpretation: when one note is omitted from the seven notes according to the rules <term>Lakshana; the theoretical rules governing musical composition</term>, the song produced through the expansion of the remaining six notes receives the designation *Shadava*.

Now, regarding *Auduvita* <note>Pentatonicism</note>: The text says "they move." This refers to the root *va* (to move or to smell), indicating motion. Because the stars (*uduvah*) move or go within it, the word *Uduvam* is used to mean the sky or ether <note>Akasha</note>. Among the elements <term>Mahabhutas; the five great elements: Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether</term>, this *Uduva* (Ether) is the fifth when counting in the reverse order of creation: Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether. 

The number five, being dependent on the substance (Ether) produced therein, is called *Auduvi*. This form is derived from the word *Uduva* with a suffix indicating "produced there." When two specific notes are omitted according to the rules, and that "five-ness" belongs to the remaining notes that perform the melody, those five notes are considered *Auduva*. 

The word "but" (*tu*) in the verse implies that these are specifically the five notes intended by the rules, not just any five notes occurring by chance (as in the logic of "fifty within a hundred"). When these *Auduva* notes are fully realized in a song, that song is called *Auduvita*. This is derived from the word *Auduva* using the suffix meaning "that which is produced in it."

<vocab>Sangitaratnakara, Shadava, Auduva, Panchasvara, Uduva, Mahabhuta, Svara, Lakshana</vocab>
