->The qualities of being "small" and "smaller" belong respectively to the notes that create hexatonic and pentatonic scales. ॥ 57 ॥<-
->These occur during the state of completeness; however, in the *Panchami* scale, the opposite is true.<-

<note>The author is explaining the grammatical derivation of musical terms.</note> This does not mean the suffix *itach* is applied here. "Because of that connection": this song has five notes; because of that connection—the word "that" refers to the pentatonic scales—belonging to those pentatonic scales. In the sense of "belonging to that," the suffix *an* is used to derive the term *Auduva* <note>Pentatonic</note> ॥ 54—56 ॥

**(Simhabhupala's Commentary)** He defines the hexatonic (*Shadava*): Those that protect (*avanti*). The six notes which, joining together, protect the performance, the class (*jati*), and so on, are the *Shadavas*. That which is produced from the six is *Shadava*. The suffix *an* is used in the sense of "produced therein." He defines the pentatonic (*Auduva*): They move (*vanti*). The *Uduvas* are the stars; that in which they move is the *Uduva*, meaning the sky. Among the elements, the sky is the fifth. Therefore, the number five is indicated. Those notes which possess the number five are *Auduva* notes. The song in which those five notes are produced is called *Auduvita*. Here, the suffix *itach* is used in the sense of "produced therein." Because of that connection to the five notes, the wise ones, such as Bharata <note>The legendary sage of Indian dramaturgy and music</note>, know it as *Auduva* ॥ 54—56 ॥

**(Kallinatha's Commentary)** Previously, the two types of "smallness" (*alpatva*) were described generally as being related to notes that can be omitted. Now, he shows the specific arrangement of those omissible notes: "In order," etc. "Small" and "smaller" are the two notes; their states are "smallness" and "smaller-ness." Here, the suffix *tal* <note>indicating a state of being</note> at the end of the compound applies to each: smallness and smaller-ness. Smallness means non-repetition; smaller-ness means skipping over the note. In the "state of completeness" (*sampurnatva*)—for those musical classes (*jatis*) where the three states (complete, hexatonic, and pentatonic) are possible—it is only in the state of completeness that these two qualities belong to the hexatonic-forming and pentatonic-forming notes respectively. The "smallness" belongs to the note that would be dropped to make it hexatonic, and "smaller-ness" belongs to the note dropped to make it pentatonic. However, for those classes that only have two states (complete and hexatonic), there is only smallness for the hexatonic-forming note; since there is no pentatonic-forming note, there is no "smaller-ness." For those that are eternally complete, since there are no omissible notes, smallness applies only to the non-tonic notes. He shows an exception to this rule of smallness: "But in the *Panchami*..."

<page-num>194</page-num>
<header>The Ocean of Music (Sangita-Ratnakara)</header>

# A rule is a "Vidhi" when it establishes scarcity or abundance where they were not previously obtained. || 58 ||
# It is "Parisankhya" (Exclusion) when, out of two possibilities, one is specified for the sake of excellence.

The word "but" is used here to highlight the distinction from other *Jatis* <note>melodic modes</note>. "Reversal" means a change in the usual state. This is what is being said: In the *Panchami Jati*, which possesses three states <note>complete, hexatonic, and pentatonic</note>, the definition of completeness states "Sa, Ga, and Ma are considered scarce." Because of this, the scarcity of Shadja and Madhyama—which would not normally be established since they are the notes dropped to make the mode hexatonic or pentatonic—is established here. Furthermore, since the note Gandhara is dropped to make the mode hexatonic, and Nishada is dropped to make it pentatonic, scarcity is expected there. However, by the rule stating "Rishabha, Panchama, and Nishada are the *Apanyasas* <note>secondary tonal centers</note>," the abundance of Nishada is established, overriding the usual restriction. 

This is similar to how the rule "One should eat facing East" is overridden in the *Lakshmi-Vrata* by the specific instruction "One desiring wealth should face West." 

Now, one might ask: how can there be a reversal of the scarcity that is fixed for all *Jatis* in the case of *Panchami*? To this, the author says: **A rule is a Vidhi.** In this context of *Panchami*, when the tonal properties of scarcity and abundance are not otherwise obtained—specifically, the scarcity of Shadja and Madhyama (the notes that make it hexatonic/pentatonic) and the abundance of Nishada (the note that makes it pentatonic)—the statement itself creates the rule. 

The statement by the sage Bharata, "Scarcity is to be known here in Shadja, Gandhara, and Madhyama," directly establishes scarcity for Shadja and Madhyama. Similarly, the statement "Nishada is an *Apanyasa*" indicates abundance for Nishada. This is a *Vidhi* <note>an original injunction</note>, much like the command "One should perform the morning twilight devotions." The word *Vidhi* is derived from the root meaning "that by which something is enjoined."

But if the statement of scarcity for Shadja and Madhyama is a *Vidhi*, and the statement of abundance for Nishada is also a *Vidhi*, why is scarcity prescribed again for Gandhara, when it was already expected because Gandhara is the note dropped in the hexatonic form? To answer this, the author says: **Parisankhya.** When two things—here, Gandhara and Nishada—are both candidates for a property (scarcity), but the rule specifies only one of them (Gandhara) for the sake of "excellence" <note>heightened aesthetic beauty or *Rakti*</note>, that is called *Parisankhya* <note>exclusive specification</note>. Because the relationship between "that" and "which" is eternal...

## Now, the characteristics of each of these musical modes (Jatis) are described. || 59 ||

The word "that" should be supplied here to complete the sense. An example of "exclusive specification" <term>Parisankhya; a logical rule where mentioning one thing implies the exclusion of others</term> is as follows: "They took this rope of the cosmic order," thus he takes the horse's halter. In the context of the Fire Altar ritual, the mantra "They took this..." refers to the halters of both the horse and the donkey. However, because the donkey is considered inferior—as stated in the text "Therefore the donkey and mule are inferior to the horse"—the horse's halter is superior. To emphasize the excellence of that one alone, the scriptural statement "he takes the horse's halter" acts as an exclusive specification. Just as such a specification results in the exclusion of others, here too, the result is the prohibition of the "diminished" status for the note *Nishada* <note>The seventh note of the scale, 'Ni'</note>. || 57-58 ||

(Sudhakara's Commentary) Regarding the phrase "in order": The two notes that cause a mode to become hexatonic <term>Shadava; a six-note scale</term> or pentatonic <term>Auduva; a five-note scale</term> should be understood as "diminished" and "further diminished" respectively when the scale is in its full seven-note state. Specifically, the note whose omission makes a scale hexatonic is "diminished" in the full state; the note whose omission makes it pentatonic is "further diminished." However, in the fifth *Jati* <note>musical mode</note>, the reverse is true: the note for hexatonic reduction is "further diminished," and the note for pentatonic reduction is "diminished." Regarding the "statement": The rule "diminished and further diminished in order" is a mandatory injunction <term>Vidhi</term> because it provides information not otherwise obtainable. When two options are possible, the statement of one is an "exclusive specification" <term>Parisankhya</term>. That statement serves to highlight the excellence of one. The definitions of Injunction and Exclusive Specification were stated by the Great Teacher <note>referring to the philosopher Kumarila Bhatta</note>:

> "An Injunction applies when something is completely unknown; a Restrictive Rule applies when something is partially known;
> When something is applicable both here and elsewhere, it is sung as an Exclusive Specification."

Thus. || 57-58 ||

(Kallinatha's Commentary) Having defined the nature of the thirteen characteristics of *Jatis*—such as the starting note <term>Graha</term> and others—according to their literal meanings, he now describes them as they occur in the eighteen *Jatis*. These include the seven pure modes beginning with *Shadjia* and the eleven modes arising from their mutual combinations, such as *Shadja-kaishiki*, in order and as they are applicable—

# The Jewel Mine of Music [On the Jatis]

The notes used as the primary melodic centers <term>Amsha: the dominant note or "soul" of a musical mode</term> in the *Shadji* mode are five, excluding the notes *Nishada* (B) and *Rishabha* (D). By omitting *Nishada*, a six-note scale <term>Shadava: a hexatonic scale</term> is formed; in its complete seven-note form, the *Kakali* <note>a sharp or "ornamental" variety of the note B</note> is occasionally used. || 60 ||

In this mode, there is a frequent association between the notes *Shadja* (C) and *Gandhara* (E), as well as between *Shadja* (C) and *Dhaivata* (A). The note *Gandhara* (E) is used abundantly. When *Gandhara* is the dominant note, *Nishada* (B) is never omitted. The melodic scale <term>Murchana: a structured sequence of notes similar to a scale</term> begins with the note *Dhaivata* (A). || 61 ||

To demonstrate this with its full expansion, the author says: "Now, for each..." and so on. "Each" means one by one. In this *Shadji* mode, the five notes—*Shadja* (C), *Gandhara* (E), *Madhyama* (F), *Panchama* (G), and *Dhaivata* (A)—serve as the dominant notes <term>Amsha</term>. This means they function alternately as the melodic center and the starting note <term>Graha</term>. By omitting *Nishada* (B), a six-note usage is to be performed. That *Nishada*, in the complete state of the *Shadji* mode, occasionally becomes *Kakali* <note>the "refined" B</note> in a modified state when *Shadja* (C) is the dominant. Regarding the "association between C and E, and C and A": here, *Shadja* is linked according to taste with *Gandhara* and *Dhaivata*, which are separated by one interval, such as "C-E-C-E-C-A" or "E-C-E-C-A-C." The note *Gandhara* (E) is "abundant." 

<margin>The author explains why E is used frequently despite certain rules.</margin>

Even though *Gandhara* (E) might not normally be frequent because it can be "discordant" <note>original: "vivadi"</note> with certain notes, it is prescribed here as abundant based on the Sage's <note>referring to the ancient authority Bharata Muni</note> words: "And there is an abundance of Gandhara." When *Gandhara* is the dominant note, there is no omission of *Nishada* (B). This is because *Nishada* is "consonant" <note>original: "samvadi"</note> with *Gandhara*, and a note consonant with the dominant cannot be omitted. By this rule, even though this mode has two states <note>six-note and seven-note</note>, when *Gandhara* is the dominant, the omission of B is prohibited; thus, it exists only in the complete seven-note state. Therefore, in the other four dominants (F, G, A, and C), both states—complete and six-note—are established. 

According to the scholar Matanga, there are ten dominant variations to be understood: six in the complete state and four in the six-note state. This method of calculating dominant notes based on the state of the mode should be applied to other *Jatis* as well. The scale <term>Murchana</term> begins with *Dhaivata* (A); since this mode belongs to the *Shadja-grama* <note>the primary system of tuning based on the note C</note>, the scale is the *Uttarayata* (starting on A), not the *Pauravi* which belongs to the *Madhyama-grama* (the system based on F).

<keywords>Shadji Jati, Amsha, Gandhara, Nishada, Shadava, Murchana, Sangitaratnakara, Matanga, musical theory, Indian classical music</keywords>

# Chapter 7] First Chapter: On Notes 197

->The rhythm here is the three-fold *Panchapani*, starting with one *kala*;<-
->The *margas* are, in order: *Chitra*, *Vritti*, and *Dakshina*; the *gitis* are:<-
->*Magadhi*, *Sambhavita*, and *Prithula* in that same sequence.<-
->This is prescribed for the first performance and for the *Naishkramiki Dhruva*. || 62-63 ||<-

This explains the rules for the application of <term>Tala</term> (rhythm), <term>Marga</term> (style/tempo), and <term>Giti</term> (song-form). In this context of the *Shadji* mode, the <term>Panchapani</term> <note>original: "Shatpitaputrakah"; a specific rhythmic cycle of five or more beats</note> is three-fold: consisting of one <term>Kala</term> (unit of time), two units, or four units. This is the implied application. By the phrase "the *margas* in order," it is shown that:
1. With the one-unit *Panchapani*, the *Chitra* style and *Magadhi* song-form are used.
2. With the two-unit version, the *Varttika* style and *Sambhavita* song-form are used.
3. With the four-unit version, the *Dakshina* style and *Prithula* song-form are used.

Here, the mention of the *Shadji* mode is illustrative; this arrangement of time-units should be applied to other melodic modes (<term>Jatis</term>) and other rhythms as well, as we will state generally later with the phrase "the number of units is to be applied by us." The specific definitions of rhythm and style will be explained in their own respective chapters. Furthermore, the application is remembered as being for the "first performance" and the "exit song" (<term>Naishkramiki Dhruva</term>). "First performance" refers to the first act of a drama. Regarding the "exit song," the general definition of a <term>Dhruva</term> (stage song) was stated by Bharata <note>The legendary author of the Natyashastra</note>:

> "Those songs which are composed according to the rules of meter and poetic rhythm, 
> and which serve as the various parts of the song—such as the opening and progression—
> when they are used in a drama, they are known by the name *Dhruva*."

The specific types are:

> "The first is the Entrance song; the second is the Intervening song; 
> the third is the Pleasing song; the fourth is the Transitional song; 
> and the fifth *Dhruva* is known by the wise as the Exit song."

<page-num>198</page-num>
->Music-Jewel-Mine [Jati-<-

## The application involves twelve sections here; a section consists of eight short units.^1

From the indication of purposes such as the "entrance" and others, the meaningful nature of these names should be understood. In the "drawn-down" <note>original: "apakṛṣṭa," a slower tempo or specific melodic style</note> style, the *Tadita* and other varieties—consisting mostly of long syllables, short syllables, or both—are the three types of *Dhruva* <note>theatrical songs</note> which serve as sub-divisions of the "entrance" songs and others. The fact that these possess rhythmic meter <note>original: "satālatvam"</note> is stated regarding the lyrics: "The lyrics are bound to rhythmic meter for the purposes of the *Dhruva* songs." In that same context, it is remembered: "The syllables not bound to meter would be those such as *Tenena* and the like.^2" "There, at the end of an act, during the exit, there should be a song ending in three-beat units." The application of this for the present purpose is:

> "One should know the 'Exit Song' <note>original: "naiṣkrāmikī"</note> as having qualities suited for the departure."
> "Furthermore, for noble characters, a song ending in four-beat units should be performed;
> But for low characters, a *Dhruva* ending in three-beat units should be performed."

Regarding the Exit Song: "In the three-beat meter, the pause is after three units; in the four-beat meter, it is after four units.

> This applies to the Entrance *Dhruva* as well as the Exit *Dhruva*."

Thus, the application of the Exit *Dhruva* is fixed by those specific rhythmic meters. The connection of the lines of the *Dhruva* with the arrangement of notes mentioned for this *Jati* is for the purpose of the drama. By the word "and," it is implied that they may also be used independently for the praise of Shiva, using words spoken by Brahma or others. "It is remembered"—the words "by Bharata and others" are understood as the remainder of the thought. "Twelve sections here": In this context, the sections—specific durations of time—for the *Shadji* jati are twelve, because the *Panchapani* rhythm mentioned here consists of twelve beats in its literal form. Since the duration of time understood by the word "section" <term>Kala: a unit of musical time</term> takes many forms depending on the different paths <note>tempos/styles</note> of the *Dhruva* and others, the author asks: what measure is intended here? He says: "A section consists of eight short units." Here, by the word "short" <term>Laghu: a prosodic short syllable</term>, a duration of time equal to the utterance of five short syllables is intended. That section which has eight such short units is "eight-short." By this, it is meant that the section here follows the "Southern Path" <note>original: "dakṣiṇa-mārga," the most elaborate and slow of the three ancient musical paths</note>.

<page-num>199</page-num>

In this *Shadjī* <note>The first of the seven pure musical modes or 'jatis'</note> mode, *Shadja* <note>The tonic or 'Sa'</note> is the *nyāsa* <note>The final note or cadence</note>. *Gāndhāra* and *Pañchama* are the *apanyāsas* <note>Intermediate stopping notes</note>.
The *Varātī* <note>A specific melodic form or raga-type</note> is observed here. Its rhythmic notation is as follows:

->1 Shadjī<-
->1 Sa Sa Sa Sa Pa Ni-Dha Pa Dha-Ni<-
->Tam bha va la lā ta<- <note>Lyrics referring to the forehead of Lord Shiva</note>

It is understood thus. And so it will be said:
> "The number of *kalās* <note>Units of time</note> mentioned by us is situated in the *Dakshina* <note>Southern or sophisticated</note> style."

Therefore, in this context, one should understand two repetitions of the *Pañchapāni* <note>A specific rhythmic pattern</note> of four *kalās* each. However, when following the *Vritti* style, there are twenty-four *kalās*, consisting of four repetitions of the two-*kalā* *Pañchapāni*. Again, when following the *Chitra* style, there are forty-eight *kalās*, consisting of eight repetitions of the *Pañchapāni* according to the syllables. Other rhythmic patterns (*tālas*) should be inferred in the same way. || 59—63 ||

**(Sudhākara Commentary)** Now, he promises to describe the individual characteristics of these modes:
"Now" (*Atha*). He describes the characteristics of *Shadjī*: In *Shadjī*, the notes *Shadja*, *Gāndhāra*, *Madhyama*, *Pañchama*, and *Dhaivata* are the *amshas* <note>Dominant or melodic center notes</note>. They become the dominant notes by turns; as it will be said later:
> "When *Gāndhāra* is the dominant, there is no omission of *Nishāda*."
Matanga has also said:
> "Thus there are sixty-three dominant notes; they become dominants one by one."
Hexatonicism <note>a six-note scale</note> occurs by the omission of *Nishāda*. When that *Nishāda* is present in the complete scale, it is *Kākalī* <note>A sharped seventh</note>. There is a melodic association between *Shadja* and *Gāndhāra*, and between *Shadja* and *Dhaivata*. There is an abundance of *Gāndhāra*. When *Gāndhāra* is the dominant, hexatonicism is not possible because *Nishāda* cannot be omitted. The scale sequence (*mūrchhanā*) begins with *Dhaivata*. The rhythm (*tāla*) here is *Pañchapāni* or *Shatpitāputraka*, consisting of one, two, or four *kalās*. When it is one *kalā*, it is the *Chitra* <note>Elegant/Fast</note> style; when two *kalās*, it is the *Vārttika* <note>Professional/Medium</note> style; when four *kalās*, it is the *Dakshina* <note>Elaborate/Slow</note> style. Regarding the song-forms (*gītis*): when in *Chitra* style, it is *Māgadhī*; in *Vārttika*, it is *Sambhāvitā*; in *Dakshina*, it is *Prithulā*. It is used for the *Naishkāmika-Dhruvā* <note>An exit song in ancient drama</note> in the first performance. Here there are twelve *kalās*. In a *kalā*, there are eight long syllables (*gurus*). || 59—63 ||

The status of the <term>Nyasa</term><note>The final note or 'cadence' of a musical phrase.</note> is fixed in both the pure and modified forms of the melodies. The statement that Gandhara and Panchama <note>The third and fifth notes of the scale.</note> serve as the <term>Apanyasa</term><note>A secondary resting note or intermediate cadence.</note> is made in reference to the modified state of the melody. However, in the pure state, the <term>Apanyasa</term> is either the tonic note <note>Shadja, the first note of the scale.</note> or the note for which the melody is named.

# [Chapter 7] First Chapter on Musical Notes

### Now, the Arshabhī Mode

> In the Arshabhī mode, there are three primary notes <term>Amshas: the dominant or melodic center of a mode</term>: the Seventh <note>Nishāda</note>, the Second <note>Rishabha</note>, and the Sixth <note>Dhaivata</note>. || 64 ||
>
> There is a melodic association between the two-microtone notes <note>the Third and the Seventh</note> and the remaining notes; furthermore, the Fifth <note>Panchama</note> is skipped. || 65 ||
>
> A six-note scale <term>Shādava</term> is formed by omitting the First <note>Shadja</note>, and a five-note scale <term>Auduva</term> is formed here by omitting both the First and the Fifth. || 65 ||
>
> The scale sequence <term>Mūrchhanā</term> begins with the Fifth, and the rhythmic pattern <term>Tāla</term> is considered to be the Chatchatputa. || 66 ||
>
> There are eight rhythmic units <term>Kalās</term> here, and the ritual application is as previously stated. || 66 ||

The arrangement when the First <note>Shadja</note> is the dominant note: even when the Third <note>Gāndhāra</note> and others are dominant, the extraction of the melody should be properly considered based on the abundance of those dominant notes. The dominance of the Third and others applies only to those notes remaining in their natural positions. Making them stationary on the Vina <note>a traditional Indian lute</note> involves bringing the secondary strings into resonance with their sound—this is the secret. In all modes such as Shadjī, the emotional flavor <term>Rasa</term> should be understood as residing in the dominant note. **Thus ends the Shadjī mode.**

<insert>(Kallinātha)</insert> **Regarding Arshabhī:** The word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note> is used to highlight the distinction of this mode from Shadjī. The Seventh, Second, and Sixth are the three dominant notes <term>Amshas</term> as well as the starting notes <term>Grahas</term>. There is a connection or association of the two-microtone notes—the Third and the Seventh—with each of the five remaining notes (First, Second, Third, Fifth, and Sixth) as appropriate. By this, it is indicated that the Third and Seventh occur frequently, while the others occur rarely. There is also the "skipping" of the Fifth. Skipping means making it extremely rare. The word "and" implies that this rarity occurs in the complete seven-note version of the scale. The phrase "six-note scale by omitting the First" and so on is self-explanatory.

<insert>(Simhabhūpāla)</insert> **He defines Arshabhī:** In Arshabhī, the Seventh, Second, and Sixth are the three dominant notes. There is a melodic association of the two-microtone notes (Third and Seventh) with the other notes. There is a "slight touching" <note>original: "ishat-sparsha"</note> of the Fifth. The six-note state is achieved by the absence of the First. The five-note state is achieved by the absence of both the First and the Fifth. The scale sequence begins on the Fifth. The rhythm is Chatchatputa. There are eight rhythmic units. The application is as before, in the "Exit" <term>Naishkrāmika</term> song of a drama.

### Now, the Gadhari Mode

> In the Gadhari mode, there are five <term>Amshas</term><note>The dominant or "soul" notes of a scale</note>, excluding Rishabha (Re) and Dhaivata (Dha). The melodic movement (<term>Sangati</term>) occurs between the <term>Nyasa</term><note>The final or concluding note</note> and the Amshas, or among the other notes. One should move from Dhaivata to Rishabha. || 67 ||
>
> By dropping Rishabha and Dhaivata, the hexatonic (<term>Shadava</term>) and pentatonic (<term>Auduvita</term>) forms are produced respectively. The note Panchama (Pa) is "hostile" to the hexatonic form; likewise, Nishada (Ni), Sadja (Sa), Madhyama (Ma), and Panchama (Pa) || 68 ||
>
> as Amshas are "hostile" to the pentatonic form. Sixteen <term>Kalas</term><note>Time units or rhythmic beats</note> are prescribed. The <term>Murchana</term><note>The specific melodic sequence or scale structure</note> begins with Dhaivata, and the <term>Tala</term><note>Rhythmic cycle</note> is considered to be <term>Caccatputa</term>. || 69 ||
>
> Its application (<term>Viniyoga</term>) is in the singing of <term>Dhruva</term> songs during the third act of a play.

Here too, the number of notes should be understood from the <term>Prastara</term><note>The systematic permutation or mapping of musical variations</note> itself, and should be inferred in the permutations of other dominant notes.
Thus ends the Arshabhi mode. || 2 ||

---

(Commentary by Kallinatha) "Five Amshas," etc. In this Gadhari mode, excluding Rishabha and Dhaivata, the five notes—Sadja, Gandhara, Madhyama, Panchama, and Nishada—serve as both the Amshas and the <term>Grahas</term><note>The starting notes of a melody</note>. Regarding the melodic movement: it occurs between the Nyasa (which is Gandhara) and one of the Amshas (Sadja, Madhyama, Panchama, or Nishada), or between the other notes that are not the currently selected dominant note. This is the implied meaning. "One should move from Dhaivata to Rishabha" means that in the complete (heptatonic) state, there may occasionally be a transition between Dhaivata and Rishabha. By saying "Panchama is hostile to the hexatonic," the following is stated: when Panchama is the Amsha, only the complete (seven-note) state exists. When Nishada, Sadja, or Madhyama are the Amshas, only the complete and hexatonic states are possible. From this, it is understood that only when Gandhara is the Amsha does this mode possess all three states (heptatonic, hexatonic, and pentatonic). The reasoning for "Panchama is hostile to the hexatonic; Nishada, Sadja, Madhyama, and Panchama as Amshas are hostile to the pentatonic," as well as the teacher's <note>referring to Bharata Muni</note> instructions, will be fully explained under the "Rakta-Gadhari" mode; it should be understood from there. Regarding "Sixteen Kalas are prescribed," this refers to four repetitions of the four-beat Caccatputa rhythm in the <term>Dakshina</term><note>Southern or sophisticated</note> style. "The Murchana begins with Dhaivata" means that since this Gadhari mode belongs to the <term>Madhyama Grama</term><note>The scale system based on the F-natural equivalent</note>, its scale is the <term>Pauravi</term> Murchana.

# Chapter 7] First Chapter on Notes

In this Gāndhārī mode, the note Gāndhāra <note>the third note, 'Ga'</note> is the *Nyāsa* <term>Nyāsa: the final note or tonic cadence</term>. The notes Sadja <note>the first note, 'Sa'</note> and Pañcama <note>the fifth note, 'Pa'</note> are the *Apanyāsas* <term>Apanyāsa: intermediate stopping points or secondary cadences</term>.
The melodies Gāndhāra-pañcama, Deśī, and Velāvatī are seen to derive from this. Its notation structure is as follows:

Regarding the phrase "In the third performance, in the singing of the *Dhruvā* songs": because of the general instruction for *Dhruvā* songs, it means this should be applied appropriately in the *Prāveśikī* <note>entrance songs</note> and other stage sequences. || 67—69- ||

**(Sudhākara commentary)** He defines Gāndhārī: "The five are the *Aṃśas* <term>Aṃśa: the dominant or 'soul' note</term>." In Gāndhārī, the notes Saḍja, Gāndhāra, Madhyama, Pañcama, and Niṣāda are optionally the five dominant notes. Other notes are used in conjunction with the *Nyāsa* and *Aṃśa* notes.
One should perform the ascent from Dhaivata to Ṛṣabha. By omitting Ṛṣabha, it becomes a six-note scale (*Ṣāḍava*). By omitting both Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata, it becomes a five-note scale (*Auduvita*).
When Pañcama is the dominant note, the six-note scale is not used. When Niṣāda, Saḍja, or Pañcama are the dominant notes, the five-note scale is not used. There are sixteen *Kalās* <note>units of time</note>. The *Mūrcchanā* <term>Mūrcchanā: a specific melodic scale or sequence</term> begins on Dhaivata. The *Tāla* <note>rhythm</note> is *Cañcatpuṭa*. The application is in the singing of *Dhruvā* songs during the third performance. || 67—69- ||

**(Kalānidhi commentary)** The mention of "Saḍja and Pañcama as *Apanyāsas*" is intended to show their modified status. Regarding the phrase "Gāndhāra-pañcama, Deśī, and Velāvatī are seen": Gāndhāra-pañcama is a *Grāma-rāga* <note>a traditional melodic category</note>. They are seen...

# The Sangita Ratnakara
## [The Gandhari Mode]

Two [notes], then two [notes] of the tonic <note>original: 'sa' (Shadja)</note>, making eight short beats <term>laghus: a basic unit of time in Indian music</term> in total. The syllables are *Ra-ja-ta-gi-ri-shi-kha-ra* <note>meaning "Like the peak of the silver mountain"</note> — with *Ra-ja-ta-gi* corresponding to the notes Ri, Ga, Ma, Pa <note>Re, Mi, Fa, Sol</note> respectively; the remainder of that phrase is Dha; then with *ri-shi-kha-ra*, the notes are Ri, Ga, Sa, Sa (9). In the tenth [section], there are eight short beats of the note Ni <note>Nishada</note> in the lower register. The syllables are *Ma-ni-sha-ka-la-shan-kha* <note>meaning "Like a piece of gem or a conch shell"</note> — with *Ma-ni-sha-ka-la-sham*, there are six Ni notes; the remainder falls on the penultimate, and the syllable *kha* on the last (10). The eleventh is like the seventh. The syllables are *Va-ra-yu-va-ti-dan-ta* <note>meaning "Like the teeth of a beautiful young woman"</note> — with *Va-ra*, two Ga notes; the remainder is Ma; with *yu-va-ti*, the notes are Pa, Pa, Dha; the remainder is Pa; the syllable *dam* is Ma; the remainders are Ni and Dha; thus Ni; the remainder is Sa (11). The twelfth is like the eighth. The syllables are *Pank-ti-ni-bham* <note>meaning "resembling a row"</note> — with *Pa*, the note Ni; the remainders are Dha, Pa, Ni; with *pank-ti-ni*, two Ma notes; the remainders are Pa and Ri; with *bham*, the note Ga; the remainders are Ga notes (12). In the thirteenth, in the middle register, the notes are Ni-Ni-Pa-Ni-Ga-Ma-Ga-Sa, forming eight short beats. The syllables are *Pra-na-ma-mi Pra-na-ya* <note>meaning "I bow with affection"</note> — the fourth syllable is the remainder of the Ma note (13). In the fourteenth, in the middle register, there are two Ga-Sa, three Ga, one Ga-Ma, and two Ga, totaling eight short beats. The syllables are *Ra-ti-ka-la-ha-ra-va-nu* <note>referring to the dispelling of lover's quarrels</note>; the middle note is the remainder of Ra (14). In the fifteenth, in the middle register, two Ga-Pa, two Ma, one Ni-Dha, one Ni and high Sa, one middle Ni-Dha, and one Pa-Ni, totaling eight short beats. The syllable *dam* is Ga, and the others are the remainders (15). In the sixteenth, in the middle register, one Ma, one Pa-Ri-Ga, and six Ga, totaling eight short beats. The syllables are *Sha-shi-nam* <note>meaning "to the Moon"</note> — with *Sha-shi*, the notes Ma and Pa; the remainders are three Ri and Ga; with *nam*, the note Ga; the remainders are three Ga notes (16).

---

-> "Behold, O fair-limbed one, this moon that brings rest to the face of the smoke of night," <-
-> "Whose body has the grace of your face, stainless, soft-rayed, and born of nectar." <-
-> "Resembling the peak of the silver mountain, a piece of gem, a conch, or the row of teeth of a beautiful young woman," <-
-> "I bow to the Moon, the dispeller of the sound of lover's quarrels." <-

---

In this context, even though it is a salutation to the Moon (*Shashin*), it ultimately results in a hymn to Lord Shiva <note>Shankara</note> because of the Moon's connection to him as the one who wears the moon on his crest <note>Shashishekhara</note>. Alternatively, it should be understood as a salutation to the Moon itself, as it is one of the eight forms <note>Ashtamurti</note> of Lord Shiva. Thus ends the section on the **Gandhari** mode. // 3 //

## Now, the Madhyama Mode

> In the *Madhyama* mode <note>one of the seven pure parent scales</note>, there are five dominant notes, excluding *Gandhara* and *Nishada*. || 70 ||
> The notes *Shadja* and *Madhyama* are used frequently. *Gandhara* is used sparingly. The six-note form is created by omitting *Gandhara*.
> The five-note form is created by omitting both *Nishada* and *Gandhara*. It consists of eight rhythmic units. || 71 ||
> The scale-pattern <term>Murchana: a sequential arrangement of notes</term> begins on *Rishabha*. The rhythmic cycle is considered to be *Chanchatputa*.
> Its application is in the singing of *Dhruva* songs during the second act of a play. || 72 ||

In this *Madhyama* mode, the note *Madhyama* is the final note <term>Nyasa: the note on which a melody ends</term>. The dominant notes themselves serve as the intermediate stopping notes <term>Apanyasa</term>. The melodic variations *Choksha-Shadava*, *Deshi*, and *Andhali* are observed here. The following is its musical notation <term>Prastara</term>:

| 4 | Madhyama | | | | | | | |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 1 | Ma | Ma | Ma | Ma | Pa | Dha-Ni | Ni | Dha-Pa |
| | Pa | | | | Tu | Bha | Va | Mu |
| 2. | Ma | Pa-Ma | Ma | Sa | Ma | Ga | Ri | Ri |
| | Dha | Ja | | | | Na | Na | |

<note>The table above represents a rhythmic and melodic structure. The top rows indicate the notes (Svaras) like Ma (F), Pa (G), etc., while the bottom rows contain syllables of a song text.</note>

**Kallinatha's Commentary:** Regarding the phrase "five dominant notes": In the *Madhyama* mode, excluding *Gandhara* and *Nishada*, the five notes—*Shadja, Rishabha, Madhyama, Panchama,* and *Dhaivata*—serve as both the dominant notes <term>Amsha</term> and the starting notes <term>Graha</term>. Although *Shadja* and *Madhyama* are already included in this list, they are mentioned again to emphasize their role as primary melodic "discourse" notes <term>Vadi</term>. The instruction "Gandhara is used sparingly" applies when the mode is played in its full seven-note form. The reference to the six-note form is self-explanatory. || 70-72 ||

**Simhabhupala's Commentary:** He defines the *Madhyama* mode: The notes *Shadja, Rishabha, Madhyama, Panchama,* and *Dhaivata* are the dominant notes by turns. *Shadja* and *Madhyama* are used abundantly. *Gandhara* is used minimally. By dropping *Gandhara*, the six-note <term>Shadava</term> form is produced. By dropping both *Nishada* and *Gandhara*, the five-note <term>Auduvita</term> form is produced. It has eight rhythmic beats. The scale starts on *Rishabha*. The rhythm is *Chanchatputa*. It is applied in *Dhruva* singing during the second theatrical performance. || 70-72 ||

<insert>(Kallinatha's Commentary)</insert> **Regarding Choksha-Shadava:** This refers to the *Shuddha-Shadava* <note>A "pure six-note" melodic scale</note> which is a *Gramaraga* <note>A fundamental melodic category in ancient Indian music</note>. In the arrangement of pure notes belonging to the *Madhyama Grama* <note>The scale starting on the fourth note, Ma</note>: in the middle of the first *Kala* <note>A rhythmic unit or beat</note>, there are four *Laghus* <note>Short time-units</note> of the note Ma; one of Pa; one of Dha-Ni; one of Ni-Ri; and one of Dha-Pa. Thus, there are eight *Laghus* in total. The syllables of the text "Born from the feet" (*patu bhavam*) are distributed as follows: *Pa* is on the note Ma, followed by two Ma notes; the syllables *tu-bha-vam* are on Ma-Pa-Dha, followed by Ni; the syllable *mu* is on Ni, followed by Dha-Pa (1). 

In the middle of the second unit, there is one Ma; one Pa-Ma; and six notes consisting of Ma-Sa-Ma-Ga-Ri-Ya. Thus, there are eight *Laghus*. The syllables of the text "The face of the elephant-headed god" (*dhajanana*) are distributed as follows: the syllables *dha-ja* are on Ma-Pa, followed by Ma-Ma-Sa; the syllables *na-na* are on Ma-Ga, followed by two Ri notes (2). 

In the middle of the third unit, there are two notes, Pa and Ma; one Ri-Ma; one Ga-Ma; and four Ma notes. Thus, there are eight *Laghus*. The syllables of the text "The Crown" (*kirita*) are distributed as follows: *ki-ri-ta* are on Pa-Ma-Ri; the remaining notes follow (3). 

In the fourth unit, there is one Ma in the high register (*tara*); one Ni-Dha in the middle register; one Ni and high Sa; one Ni-Dha in the middle; one Pa-Ma; one Pa-Dha; and two Ma notes. Thus, there are eight *Laghus*. The syllables of the text "The Jewel-Mirror" (*manidarpana*) are distributed as follows: *ma-ni* are on Ma-Ni; the remaining note is Dha; *dar* is on Ni; the remaining notes are Sa-Ni-Dha; *panam* is on Pa; the remaining notes are Ma-Pa-Dha.

### Now, the Fifth Jati (Panchami)

->**In the Panchami mode, Ri and Pa are the primary notes (Amshas); Sa, Ga, and Ma are considered weak.**<-
->**The combination of Ri and Ma should be used; in the complete form, Ga and Ni are included. || 73 ||**<-

<note>The verse describes the structural rules for the Panchami Jati, identifying which notes are dominant and which are omitted in specific scales.</note>

...the syllable *nam* is on Ma; the remainder is Ma (4). In the fifth section, there are two Ni notes in the lower register, two Ri notes in the middle register, one Ni in the lower, and three notes—Ri, Ri, Pa—in the middle; thus, there are eight beats <term>laghus; short time units</term>. The syllables of the phrase *Gauri-kara-peta* are: *Gau* on Ni, the remainder is Ni; *ri* on Ri, the remainder is Ri; *kara-pai* on Ni-Ri-Ri-Pa, the remainder is Pa (5). In the sixth section, there is one Ni in the lower register, Ma and Pa together in the middle, two Ma notes, and four Sa notes; thus, eight beats. For the syllables *lvangulistvi*: *lva* is on Ni and Ma, the remainder are Pa-Ma-Ma; *gulibhyam* is on two Sa notes, the remainder is Sa; *suna* is on Sa (6). In the seventh section, Ga is in the high register, Ni in the middle, Sa and Ga in the high, Dha and Pa together in the middle, one Ma, Dha and Ni together, and one Sa in the high register; thus, eight beats. For the syllables *tejitam*: *te* is on Ga, the remainder are the next six notes; *ji* is on Dha, the remainder is Ni; *tam* is on Sa (7). In the eighth section, there is one Pa in the middle, one Sa in the high, again one Pa in the middle, Ni-Dha-Pa together, and four Ma notes; thus, eight beats. For the syllables *sukiranam*: *su-ki-rai* are on Pa-Sa-Pa, the remainder are Ni-Dha-Pa; *nam* is on Ma, and the remainder are three beats (8).

> May the beautiful rays, polished like a mirror by the jewel in the crown on Shiva's head,
> And brightened by the sprout-like fingers of Gauri's hand, protect us. || This concludes the Madhyama Jati || 4 ||

<note>This verse is a prayer (Mangala) used as a lyrical example for the musical structure described above.</note>

(Kallinatha's Commentary) **Regarding "Ri and Pa are the primary notes":** In the phrase "Sa, Ga, and Ma are considered weak," the mention of Sa and Ma being weak is a specific rule <term>vidhi</term> because they are not usually omitted in the six-note <term>shadava</term> or five-note <term>auduva</term> scales. However, since Ga is naturally subject to omission in those scales, its mention here serves as a restriction <term>parisankhya</term>. This was previously explained during the commentary on the text "But in Panchami, the reverse..." and so on. The phrase "In the complete form, Ga and Ni are included" means one should create a melodic association <term>sangati</term> between Ga and Ni. By implication, it is understood that in the six-note form (where Ga is dropped) and the five-note form (where Ni and Ga are dropped), one should not attempt this association. With Ga, or with Ni and Ga being omitted...

<header>Ocean of Music [Jati-</header>

Through the omission of Gandhara and the pair of Nishada and Gandhara, the hexatonic <note>six-note</note> and pentatonic <note>five-note</note> forms are respectively recognized.<margin>The hexatonic and pentatonic forms are recognized</margin> When Rishabha is the primary note <term>Amsha: the dominant melodic center</term>, it rejects the pentatonic form; eight beats <term>Kalas: units of time</term> are prescribed. || 74 ||
The melodic scale <term>Murchana: the starting scale</term> and other elements are as previously described; it is used in the third act of a theatrical performance.

In this Panchami Jati, Panchama is the final note <term>Nyasa: the note that ends a phrase</term>. Rishabha, Panchama, and Nishada are the intermediate pause notes <term>Apanyasas</term>. The Choksha-Panchami, Deshi, and Anthali variations are observed here. The following is its rhythmic notation:

->5. Panchami<-

| 1 | Pa | Dha-Ni | Ni | Ni | Ma | Ni | Ma | Pa |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | Ha | ra | mu | rdha | ja | | | na |
<note>The syllables in the second row represent a song fragment: "Hara-murdha-jana" (The people on Shiva's head/The Ganges).</note>

The phrase "by the omitted notes" should be supplied here by inference. Hexatonic and pentatonic forms occur in sequence: hexatonic by omitting Gandhara, and pentatonic by omitting both Nishada and Gandhara. "Rishabha as the primary note rejects the pentatonic form": in this Jati, even though there is no lack of consonance with Rishabha when Nishada and Gandhara (the notes that make it pentatonic) are present, one must consider the prohibition of the pentatonic form based on the Sage's <note>Bharata Muni, author of the Natyashastra</note> decree:

> "Rishabha in Panchami, and Dhaivata in Kaishiki;
> these twelve should always be avoided in the five-note scale."

"The melodic scale and others are as before": just as in the Madhyama Jati, the scale here begins with Rishabha. By the word "others," the Chanchatputa rhythmic cycle <term>Tala</term> is understood. The rest has already been explained. || 73—74- ||

(Commentary by Simhabhupala) He defines Panchami: In Panchami, Rishabha and Panchama are the primary notes; Shadja, Gandhara, and Madhyama are used sparingly; there is a melodic movement between Rishabha and Madhyama. In its complete form, the ascent goes from Gandhara to Nishada. By omitting Gandhara, it becomes hexatonic; by omitting Nishada and Gandhara, it becomes pentatonic. When Rishabha is the primary note, the pentatonic form is not used. There are eight beats. The scale begins on Rishabha. The rhythm is Chanchatputa. It is used in the third song-entry of a play. || 73—74- ||

# Now, the Dhaivati Jati

> In the Dhaivati Jati, the notes Rishabha <note>Re</note> and Dhaivata <note>Dha</note> are the primary notes <term>Amsha</term>. The notes Shadja <note>Sa</note> and Panchama <note>Pa</note> are to be skipped <term>Langhya</term> during the ascending scale <term>Arohin</term>. || 75 ||
> It is said to be hexatonic <term>Shadava</term> by the omission of Panchama, and pentatonic <term>Auduva</term> by the omission of both Shadja and Panchama.
> Its melodic scale <term>Murchana</term> begins with Rishabha. The rhythm <term>Tala</term>, the style <term>Marga</term>, and the song-forms <term>Gitis</term> || 76 ||
> and its ritual application <term>Viniyoga</term> are the same as those of the Shadjiji jati. Twelve time-units <term>Kalas</term> are prescribed.

The notes Pa, Ma, Dha, and Ni are four; Ni and Dha are one; Pa is three; thus there are eight short beats <term>Laghus</term>. The syllables are "Namanantam"—"Namana" corresponds to Pa-Ma-Dha; the remainder of that is Ni; "Tam" is Ni; the others are the remainder (4). In the fifth section, there are two middle-register Pa notes, and six high-register <term>Tara</term> Rishabha notes; thus eight short beats. The syllables are "Pranamami Purusha"—"Pranama" corresponds to Pa-Pa-Ya <note>likely a scribal variant for a note or rhythmic marker</note>, the remainder is Ri; the four Rishabhas correspond to "mi-pu-ru-sha" (5). In the sixth section, there is one low-register <term>Mandra</term> Ma; one combined low Ni and middle Ga; one Sa; one combined Sa and Dha; and four Nishadas; thus eight short beats. The syllables are "Mukhapadmalakshmi"—"Mukha" by Ma-Ni; the remainder is Ga; "Padma" by Sa; the remainder is Dha-Ni; "le" by Ni; the remainder is Ni; "kshmi" by Ni (6). In the seventh section, there are three high-register Sa notes, one middle Ma, and four Pa notes; thus eight short beats. The syllables are "Haramambikapatya"—"Harama" by the three Sa notes; the remainder is Ma; "Bika" by two Pa notes; the remainder is Pa; "pe" is Pa (7). In the eighth section, the middle-register notes Dha, Ma, Dha, and Ni are four; Pa notes are four; thus eight short beats. The syllables are "Timajeyam"—"Timaje" corresponds to Dha-Ma-Dha; the remainder is Ni; "Yam" is Pa; the others are the remainder (8).

> I bow to the infinite one, whose face is the hair of Shiva, the Great Lord, who paralyzed the arms of the Lord of the Immortals <note>Indra</note>.
> I bow to that Supreme Being, whose face is the beauty of the lotus, the Lord of Ambika, the unconquerable.

Thus ends the fifth section || 5 ||

---

<insert>(Commentary by Kallinatha)</insert> Regarding "In the Dhaivati": In the ascending movement <term>Arohin</term>, the notes Sa and Pa are "to be skipped" <term>Langhya</term>; this means that even in the complete <term>Purna</term> state of the scale, they should be rendered very subtly <term>Alpa</term>. By this, it is implied that in the descent <term>Avaroha</term>, Sa and Pa are also weak.

In this *Dhaivati* <note>a specific melodic mode or 'jati' centered around the note Dhaivata</note>, the note *Dhaivata* <note>the sixth note of the scale, 'A'</note> serves as the *Nyasa* <note>the final note or tonic of a composition</note>. The notes *Rishabha* <note>the second note, 'D'</note>, *Madhyama* <note>the fourth note, 'F'</note>, and *Dhaivata* are the *Apanyasas* <note>intermediate stopping points or secondary tonics</note>.
The melodies *Choksha-Kaishiki*, *Deshi*, and *Simhali* are seen to derive from this. The following is its *Prastara* <note>a formal musical notation or skeletal arrangement</note>:

### 6. Dhaivati

| | | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. | Dha Dha Ni-Dha Pa-Dha Ma Ma Ma Ma | | | |
| | Ta ru na | ma lai | du | |
| 2. | Dha Dha Ni-Dha Ni-Sa Sa Sa Sa Sa | | | |
| | Ma ni bhu | shi ta | ma | |
| 3. | Sa-Dha Dha Pa Ma-Dha Dha Ni-Dha Dha-Ni Dha | | | |
| | La shi ro | jam | | |
| 4. | Sa Sa Ri-Ga Ri-Ga Sa Ri-Ga Sa Sa | | | |
| | Bhu ja ga | dhi pai | ka | |
| 5. | Dha Dha Ni Pa Dha Pa Ma Ma | | | |
| | Kun da la vi la | sa | | |
| 6. | Dha Dha Pa Ma-Dha Dha Ni-Dha Dha-Ni Dha | | | |
| | Kr ta sho | bha | | |
| 7. | Dha Dha Ni-Sa Ni-Sa Ni-Dha Pa Pa Pa | | | |
| | Na ga su | nu la | kshmi | |

<note>The lyrics above refer to a deity, likely Shiva, adorned with the young moon, jewels, and serpents.</note>

These notes should be performed, and it is understood they should not be too weak. The text stating "hexatonic through the omission of *Panchama*" etc., is clear in its meaning. || -75 — 76- ||

(Sudhakara commentary) He defines the *Dhaivati* mode: "In *Dhaivati*..." In the *Dhaivati* mode, *Rishabha* and *Dhaivata* are the predominant notes. The notes *Shadja* <note>the first note, 'C'</note> and *Panchama* <note>the fifth note, 'G'</note>, when occurring in an ascending melodic line, are to be "leaped over" <note>original: "langhya", meaning touched upon only lightly or skipped</note>. By omitting *Panchama*, it becomes hexatonic <note>term: Shadhava - a six-note scale</note>. By omitting both *Shadja* and *Panchama*, it becomes pentatonic <note>term: Auduvita - a five-note scale</note>. The *Murchana* <note>the specific scale or sequence of notes</note> begins with *Rishabha*. The application of rhythm, path, and song style here is the same as in the *Shadji* mode. It consists of twelve *Kalas* <note>units of time or rhythmic beats</note>. || -75—76- ||

# The Naishadi Jati

### On Naishadi

> In the Naishadi Jati, the notes Nishada <note>the 7th note, B</note>, Rishabha <note>the 2nd note, D</note>, and Gandhara <note>the 3rd note, E</note> are considered the dominant notes (*Amshas*). The non-dominant notes are used frequently. || 77 ||
> The hexatonic and pentatonic forms, as well as the notes to be skipped, are as described previously. The application is the same as before. The rhythmic cycle is *Chaccatputa* consisting of sixteen beats, and the scale (*Murchana*) begins with Gandhara. || 78 ||

In this Naishadi Jati, <term>Nishada is the final note (Nyasa)</term>. The <term>dominant notes (Amshas)</term> themselves serve as the intermediate pause notes (*Apanyasas*). The musical styles *Choksha-Sadharita*, *Deshi*, and *Velavali* are seen to derive from this. The musical notation (*Prastara*) is as follows:

-> 7. Naishadi <-

1. Ni Ni Ni Ni Sa Dha Ni Ni
-> To the one worshipped by gods <- <note>This is a fragment of a hymn, likely to Shiva</note>

---

<insert>(Kallinatha’s Commentary)</insert> Regarding "In Naishadi": The dominant notes are Nishada, Rishabha, and Gandhara. The phrase "non-dominant notes are frequent" means that the notes Shadja, Madhyama, Panchama, and Dhaivata <note>1st, 4th, 5th, and 6th notes</note> are used often. If interpreted differently, it would contradict the sage Matanga’s teaching that "In the complete state, the 1st, 4th, 5th, and 6th notes are weak; in the hexatonic, the 1st, 4th, and 6th are weak; and in the pentatonic, the 4th and 6th are weak." As in the Dhaivati Jati, the hexatonic and pentatonic forms are created by skipping notes: hexatonic by dropping the 5th, and pentatonic by dropping both the 1st and 5th. The application is the same as the Shadji Jati. The rest has been explained previously. || 77, 78 ||

---

<insert>(Simhabhupala’s Commentary)</insert> He defines Naishadi: In Naishadi, the notes Nishada, Rishabha, and Gandhara are the dominant notes by variation. The notes Shadja, Madhyama, Panchama, and Dhaivata are used frequently. By dropping the 5th note, it becomes hexatonic; by dropping the 1st and 5th, it becomes pentatonic. The 1st and 5th notes are to be skipped in ascent. Its ritual application is for the <term>Exit Song (Naishkramiki Dhruva)</term> during the first act of a play. The <term>rhythmic cycle is Chaccatputa</term>. It consists of sixteen beats. The <term>melodic scale (Murchana) begins on Gandhara</term>. || 77, 78 ||

## Now, the Shadjakaishiki Jati

In the *Shadjakaishiki* <note>A specific melodic mode or 'Jati' derived from the parent scales Shadjagrama and Madhyamagrama</note>, the dominant notes (*Amshas*) are Sa, Ga, and Pa <note>Tonic, minor third, and perfect fifth</note>. The notes Ri and Ma <note>Second and fourth</note> are used sparingly, while Dha and Ni <note>Sixth and seventh</note> are slightly more prominent. || 79 ||

The rhythmic cycle used is *Chachchatputa* <note>A traditional eight-beat time cycle</note>, consisting of sixteen units (*Kalas*). It is employed in the *Praveshiki Dhruva* <note>An entrance song in ancient Sanskrit drama</note> during the second act of a theatrical performance. || 80 ||

In this *Shadjakaishiki*, the final note (*Nyasa*) is Ga. The intermediate pause notes (*Apanyasas*) are Sa, Ni, and Pa. Within this framework, one can see the shadows of the previously mentioned melodies: *Gandhara-panchama*, *Hindolaka*, *Deshi*, and *Velavali*.
The notation layout is as follows:

->8. Shadjakaishiki<-

1. Sa Sa Ma Pa Ga-Ri Ma-Ga Ma Ma
<gloss>To the God</gloss> <note>The syllable 'De' from 'Devam'</note>

2. Ma Ma Ma Ma Sa Sa Sa Sa
<gloss>...</gloss> <note>The syllable 'vam'</note>

**Kallinatha’s Commentary:** Now, regarding the first of the modified Jatis born from a mixture of scales—*Shadjakaishiki*. Regarding the phrase "the dominant notes are...": the scarcity of notes usually applied to all non-dominant notes (Ri, Ma, Dha, Ni) is here specifically restricted to Ri and Ma. The phrase "Dha and Ni are slightly more prominent" means that while they are lesser than the dominant Sa, Ga, and Pa, they should be played more frequently than the sparse Ri and Ma. The rest, regarding the *Chachchatputa* rhythm, is clear. || 79, 80 ||

**Simhabhupala’s Commentary:** He defines *Shadjakaishiki*: the dominant notes are Sa, Ga, and Pa. Ri and Ma are weak (infrequent), while Dha and Ni are somewhat more frequent. The rhythm is *Chachchatputa*. It consists of sixteen units. Its application is for the entrance song in the second act of a play. || 79, 80 ||

<term>Shadjakaishiki: A complex melodic mode derived from combining elements of the Shadjagrama and Madhyamagrama scales.</term>
<term>Amsha: The most important or "soul" note of a melody that determines its character.</term>
<term>Nyasa: The note on which a musical composition or phrase must end.</term>
<term>Dhruva: A type of structured song used in ancient Indian theater to signal character entrances or emotional shifts.</term>

(Kallinatha's Commentary) **Gandhara is the final note (Nyasa)**; as the Sage <note>Bharata Muni, author of the Natyashastra</note> stated: "Gandhara shall be the final note." By this, regarding the rule "these characteristics are lacking except for the final note," it is meant that the rule for modified Jatis <gloss>¹</gloss> does not apply to those born of combination. In the pure scale of the Shadja-grama <term>Shadja-grama: the primary ancient Indian musical scale starting on the note 'Sa'</term>: In the first unit (kala), there are two middle-register 'Sa' notes; two low-register 'Ma' and 'Pa' notes; one middle-register 'Ga' and 'Ri' combined; one 'Ma' and 'Ga' combined; and two 'Ma' notes—thus making eight short time-units (laghus). The syllable *De* falls on the first 'Sa', and the others are extensions (1). In the second unit, there are four middle-register 'Ma' notes and four low-register 'Sa' notes, totaling eight laghus. The syllable *vam* falls on 'Ma', and the others are extensions (2). In the third unit, there are two middle-register 'Dha' notes, two 'Pa' notes, two 'Dha' notes, one 'Ri', and one 'Ri-Ma' combination; totaling eight laghus. These correspond to the syllables *a-sa-ka-la-sha-shi-te-la*, with the last being an extension (3). In the fourth unit, there are two middle-register 'Ri' notes and six low-register 'Ni' notes, totaling eight laghus. The syllable *ka* falls on 'Ri', and the others are extensions (4). In the fifth unit, there are two middle-register 'Dha' notes, one 'Pa', one 'Dha-Ni' combination, two 'Ma' notes, and two 'Pa' notes, totaling eight laghus. These correspond to the syllables *dvi-ra-da-ga-ti*—*dvi-ra-da-ga* fall on 'Dha-Pa-Dha', the remainder on 'Ni'; *ti* falls on 'Ma', and the others follow (5). In the sixth unit, there are two middle-register 'Dha' notes, one 'Pa', one 'Dha-Ni' combination, two 'Dha' notes, and two 'Pa' notes, totaling eight laghus. These correspond to the syllables *ni-pu-na-ma-ti*—*ni-pu-na-ma* fall on 'Dha-Pa-Dha', the remainder on 'Ni'; *ti* falls on 'Dha', and the others follow (6). In the seventh unit, there are eight middle-register 'Sa' notes (laghus). These correspond to the syllables *mu-gdha-mu-kha-bdhi*—*mu* on 'Sa', its extension on 'Sa', *gdha* on 'Sa', its extension on 'Sa'; *mu-kha* on two 'Sa' notes, its extension on 'Sa', and *bdhi* on 'Sa' (7). In the eighth unit, there are four 'Dha-Pa-Dha' notes, one 'Dha-Ni', and three 'Dha' notes, totaling eight laghus. These correspond to the syllables *ru-ha-di-vya-kan-ti*, with the fourth, sixth, and penultimate notes being extensions (8).

In the **ninth** measure, in the middle register: three *Sa* notes, one *Ri-Ga* unit, one *Sa*, one *Ri-Ga*, and two *Dha* notes; thus making eight *laghus* <note>short rhythmic units</note>. In the **tenth** measure, in the middle register: two *Ma-Dha* units, two *Pa* notes, two *Dha* notes, and two *Ni* notes; thus eight *laghus*. The syllables are *dhi-ni-na-da-m*. *Dhi-ni-na* are set to *Ma-Dha-Pa*; the remaining is *Pa*; *da-m* is set to *Dha*; the others remain (10).

In the **twelfth** measure, in the lower register: one *Dha*, one *Ri-Sa*, one *Ri*, one *Sa-Ri*, one *Ri*, and three *Sa* notes; thus eight *laghus*. The syllables are *de-ha-rdha-mi-shri*. *De* is set to *Dha*; the remaining are *Ri-Sa*; *ha* is set to *Ri*; the remaining are *Sa-Ri*; *rdha-mi* are set to *Ri-Sa*; the remaining is *Sa*; *shri* is set to *Sa* (12).

The syllables are *ta-sha-ri-ra-m*. *Ta-sha* are set to the *Sa* notes; the remaining is *Ri*; *ri* is set to *Ri*; the remaining are *Sa-Ri*; *ra-m* is set to *Ri*; the remaining are *Ma* notes (13).

In the **fourteenth** measure, in the middle register: four *Ma* notes, one *Ni-Dha*, one *Pa-Dha*, and two *Ma* notes; thus eight *laghus*. The syllables are *pra-na-ma-mi-ta-ma-ha-m*; the fourth, sixth, and tenth units are remainders (14).

In the **fifteenth** measure, in the middle register: three *Ni-Ni-Pa* units, one *Pa-Ma*, one *Pa*, one *Pa-Ma*, one *Pa-Dha*, and one *Ri-Ga*; thus eight *laghus*. The syllables are *a-nu-pa-ma-mu-kha-ka-ma-la*; the fifth, eighth, tenth, and twelfth units are remainders (15).

-> I bow to the God who wears the crescent moon as an ornament, whose gait is like that of an elephant, <-
-> who is of profound intellect, and whose lotus-face possesses divine splendor. <-
-> To Hara <note>Shiva</note>, whose roar is like the thunder of clouds and the ocean, whose body is joined with the half-form of the daughter of the mountain, <-
-> I bow to him, whose lotus-face is incomparable. Thus ends the Shadjakaishiki melody. || 8 || <-

### Now, the Shadjodichyava Mode

> The primary notes <term>Amshas; the dominant notes that characterize a melody</term> for Shadjodichyava are declared to be Sa, Ma, Ni, and Dha <note>original: "sa-ma-ni-dha"</note>.
> These notes should be used in close association with one another; there is an abundance of the note Ga in the lower register <term>Mandra; the lower octave</term>. || 81 ||
> The notes Sa and Ri should be frequent in the high register <term>Tara; the upper octave</term>. By omitting Ri, it is considered a six-note scale <term>Shadava</term>. || 82 ||
> By omitting both Ri and Pa, it becomes a five-note scale <term>Auduva</term>. However, when Dha is the dominant note, the six-note variation is not permitted. || 82 ||
> Its rhythm and other elements are like the Shadji mode, and its scale-pattern <term>Murchana</term> begins with Ga. It is employed in the second act of a play during the singing of a Dhruva song. || 83 ||

(Kallinatha's Commentary) Regarding the phrase "The primary notes are Sa, Ma, Ni, and Dha": These notes should be mutually associated, meaning they are linked together as appropriate to create musical beauty <note>Rakti</note>. "An abundance of Ga in the lower register": even though Ga is not a dominant note <term>Amsha</term>, it occurs frequently in the lower register. This follows the Sage Bharata's teaching that "Sa, Ri, and Ga should be strong." This implies that Ga is not necessarily abundant when in other registers. "Sa and Ri should be frequent in the high register" means that their prevalence should be established specifically in the upper octave. 

In this context, regarding the rule for Ri, Matanga <note>An earlier musicologist</note> states that "in the full seven-note version, Ri and Pa are weak." This should be understood as referring to Ri in the lower and middle registers. However, the Sage's statement that "Ri should be strong" refers specifically to Ri in the high register. Thus the system is reconciled. Furthermore, while Sa is already frequent because it is a dominant note, the instruction "Sa and Ri" is given to emphasize that Sa should be even more prominent in the high register compared to the lower and middle registers. 

Regarding "when Dha is the dominant note, the six-note variation is not permitted": this is because Ri is the consonant partner <term>Samvadi</term> to Dha, and it is undesirable to omit a note that harmonizes with the dominant. If one asks how a five-note version (omitting Ri) is possible under that same dominant, it is explained that when both Ri and Pa are omitted to form the five-note scale, the responsibility for the "six-note-ness" (the first omission) rests on Pa; since Pa is not the consonant partner of Dha, there is no contradiction. The phrase "like the Shadji mode" and the rest have been explained previously. || 81—83 ||

In order to demonstrate the application of song lyrics in all musical modes <term>Jatis</term> such as Magadhi and others, the author shows the application of the *Ardhamagadhi* song style—where the Magadhi style repeats a phrase three times and the Ardhamagadhi repeats it twice, according to the characteristics to be described later—starting with the words **Shaile** and so on. The first rhythmic unit <term>kala</term> should be joined with the two syllables **Shai-le**. The second unit is joined with **sha-su-nu**; the compound is treated as a single unit, meaning it should be joined with the three syllables Shai, Su, and Nu. **With those five, the third unit is formed**: this means the third rhythmic unit should be joined with the five syllables **Shai-le-sha-su-nu**. The seventh unit is joined with the "additional syllables" <insert>adhika-akshara</insert>, namely **A-dhi-ka**. The eighth unit is joined with the word *Mukhendu*, the three syllables **Mu-khe-ndu**. The ninth unit is joined with **those six: A-dhi-ka-mu-khe-ndu**. For the other rhythmic units, the application of the song should be understood according to the defined characteristics. || 84, 84- || Thus ends the description of the Sadjodicvava mode. || 9 ||

### Now, the Shadjamadhyama Jati

> In the *Shadjamadhyama* mode, all seven notes can serve as the primary notes <note>original: "amshas"</note>, and they are mutually compatible with one another. || 85 ||
> In its complete form, the note *Nishada* <note>the 7th note, B</note> should be used sparingly, unless it is the primary note itself.
> By dropping *Nishada*, or both *Nishada* and *Gandhara* <note>the 3rd note, E</note>, the hexatonic <note>six-note</note> and pentatonic <note>five-note</note> forms are recognized. || 86 ||
> However, these two notes of two micro-tones <note>Nishada and Gandhara</note> are "opposites" in the hexatonic and pentatonic forms.
> The song-styles, rhythms, and time-units are like those of the *Shadji* mode; the scale-pattern <note>original: "murchana"</note> used here || 87 ||
> is known as *Madhyamadi* <note>starting on the 4th note, F</note>. Its application is as previously described.

(Sudhakara commentary) Regarding the rules for the syllables in the time-units <note>original: "kala"</note> of this mode: The first unit should be performed with two syllables signifying Shiva. The second with a word signifying Ganesha. The third unit with five syllables signifying both Shiva and Ganesha. The seventh unit with additional syllables. The eighth with "Mukhendu." The ninth with six syllables. || 84, 84- ||

(Kalanidhi commentary) Regarding "all seven notes are primary notes": In the complete state, <term>Nishada</term> <note>the 7th note</note> is to be made weak <note>used infrequently</note>. Regarding "unless it is the primary note": even in that state, when <term>Gandhara</term> <note>the 3rd note</note> is the primary note, the weakness of *Nishada* is not desired because of their consonance. "Without being the tonic" <note>original: "vadita"</note> means that if the note itself is the tonic, there is obviously no weakness. The two-microtone notes, *Nishada* and *Gandhara*, are "opposites" when they are primary notes in the hexatonic and pentatonic forms; this is because the hexatonic and pentatonic forms are created by dropping *Nishada* or both *Nishada* and *Gandhara*. There is a contradiction between a note being a primary note and being a note that is dropped. In such a case, the <term>hexatonic and pentatonic</term> forms do not occur. Therefore, since the notes *Nishada* and *Gandhara* must be present when they are primary notes, one should observe the seventeen primary notes mentioned by Matanga: five hexatonic primaries, five pentatonic primaries, and seven complete primaries. Regarding "song-styles, rhythms, and time-units are like *Shadji*": the song-styles are the three known as *Magadhi*, *Sambhavita*, and *Prithula*. The rhythm <note>original: "tala"</note> is the three-fold *Panchapani* with variations of one or two units. The time-units <note>original: "kala"</note> are twelve, consisting of eight short beats. The word "etcetera" refers to the musical paths known as *Chitra*, *Vritti*, and *Dakshina*...

**In this Shadjamadhyama mode, the notes Shadja <note>the tonic, 'Sa'</note> and Madhyama <note>the fourth, 'Ma'</note> are the final notes <term>Nyasa</term>. All seven notes serve as the secondary final notes <term>Apanyasa</term>. The rhythmic notation <term>Prastara</term> is as follows:**

<note>The lyrics above describe a poetic scene: "The face of the Lady Night, with eyes sparkling, like a blooming water-lily and foam..."</note>

These elements, such as the song-style, should be performed as in the Shadji mode; this is an extended application <note>atidesha</note> meaning what applies to Shadji applies here. The <term>Murchana</term> <note>the sequential scale</note> should be understood as starting from Madhyama. Since this mode belongs to the Shadja-Gramic system, the specific scale is the one known as *Matsarikrita*. The application <term>Viniyoga</term> is as before; specifically, it is used in the second act of a play during the <term>Dhruva-gana</term> <note>theatrical songs that establish mood or character</note>, similar to the Shadjo-dichyava mode.

(Sudhakara commentary) He defines Shadjamadhyama: "The seven notes are the primary notes <term>Amsha</term>." In Shadjamadhyama, all seven notes can serve as the dominant primary notes. These primary notes have a mutual relationship. The note Nishada <note>the seventh, 'Ni'</note> is <term>Alpa</term> <note>weak or used sparingly</note>. However, when Gandhara <note>the third, 'Ga'</note> is the primary note, the weakness of Nishada is not observed. Likewise, when Nishada itself is the melodic protagonist <term>Vadi</term>, it is not weak. By omitting Nishada, the mode becomes <term>Shadava</term> <note>six-toned</note>. By omitting both Nishada and Gandhara, it becomes <term>Auduvita</term> <note>five-toned</note>. When these six or five-toned versions are performed, Nishada and Gandhara act as dissonant notes <term>Vivadi</term>. The song-style, rhythm, and time-units are like Shadji. The scale starts on Madhyama. The usage is like Shadjo-dichyava.

### Now, the Gandharodicyava Mode

In the *Gandharodicyava* <note>A specific melodic mode or 'Jati' whose name suggests a northern (Udicyava) variation of the Gandhara scale</note> mode, there are two primary notes (*Amshas*): *Shadja* (C) and *Madhyama* (F). || 88 ||
By omitting the note *Rishabha* (D), it is known as a hexatonic <note>six-note scale</note> form. In its complete (heptatonic) form, the notes other than the primary ones are used sparingly. When played as a hexatonic scale, the notes *Nishada* (B), *Dhaivata* (A), *Panchama* (G), and *Gandhara* (E) are declared to be used infrequently. || 89 ||
A specific association between *Rishabha* (D) and *Dhaivata* (A) should be recognized, and the *Murchana* <note>the sequential scale or melodic progression</note> begins with *Dhaivata* (A). The rhythm (*Tala*) is known as *Caccatputa*, consisting of sixteen time-units (*Kalas*). || 90 ||
Its application is prescribed for the *Dhruva* songs <note>theatrical songs used in ancient Indian drama</note> during the fourth act of a play.

The rhythmic structure is as follows: F-G-E is one unit; G-M are two; thus there are eight short units (*Laghus*). The syllables of the prayer "I bow to the God" (*Pranamami Devam*) are arranged thus:
*Prana* corresponds to E and F; the remaining are G and F; *ma* corresponds to F; the remaining are B and A; *mi* corresponds to G.
The remaining is A; *De* corresponds to G; the remaining are E and G; *vam* corresponds to E; the remaining is F (10).
In the eleventh unit, in the middle, A is one; G-A are one; G-D are one; D-E are one; F-E are one;
D-E are one; C-A-C are one; C is one; thus there are eight short units. The syllables for "Dweller in the Night-Lotus" (*Kumudadhivasi*) are: *Kumu* corresponds to A and G; the remaining is A; *da* corresponds to G; the remaining is D;
*dhi* corresponds to D; the remaining is E; *va* corresponds to F; the remaining are E-D-E-C-A-C; *si* corresponds to C (11).
In the twelfth unit, in the middle, B-A are one; C-D are two; E-F-E are one; F consists of four;
thus there are eight short units. *Nam* corresponds to B; the others are the remaining notes (12).

->The eyes that are the play of the face of the Lady Night,<-
->Resembling the foam on the petals of the blossoming night-lotus;<-
->The delight of the eyes and hearts of those in love,<-
->I bow to the God who dwells in the night-lotus.<-
Thus ends the section on the *Shadjamadhyama* mode. || 10 ||

<insert>Commentary by Kallinatha:</insert> Regarding the phrase "In the *Gandharodicyava*": In the state of completeness (the seven-note version), there is "infrequency of others than the primary notes," meaning that other than the two primary notes (C and F), the notes D, E, G, A, and B are used sparingly. In the hexatonic state...

-> (Commentary by Simhabhupala) <-
He defines the characteristics of *Gandharodicyava*: In *Gandharodicyava*, *Shadja* and *Madhyama* are the dominant notes (*Amsha*). It is a hexatonic scale (*Shadava*) due to the omission of *Rishabha* <note>The second note, 'Ri'</note>. In its complete form, the notes other than the dominant ones are weak. In the hexatonic form, *Nishada*, *Dhaivata*, *Panchama*, and *Gandhara* are weak. There is a specific progression between *Rishabha* and *Dhaivata*. The melodic scale (*Murchana*) begins on *Dhaivata*. The rhythmic cycle (*Tala*) is *Chanchatputa*. It consists of sixteen beats (*Kalas*). It is used in the singing of *Dhruva* songs during the fourth theatrical preview. || 88—90 ||

# 240
### [Jati Section]

### Now, the Raktagandhari Mode

In the *Raktagandhari* <note>literally "Reddish Gandhari," a specific melodic type</note> mode, there are five *Amshas* <note>dominant or melodic center notes</note>, excluding the notes *Dha* and *Ri* <note>Dhaivata and Rishabha, the 6th and 2nd notes of the scale</note>. || 91 ||

By bypassing *Ri*, one should create a close melodic union between *Sa* and *Ga* <note>the 1st and 3rd notes</note>. By omitting *Ri*, it becomes *Shadava* <note>a six-note scale</note>, and by omitting both *Ri* and *Dha*, it is considered *Auduva* <note>a five-note scale</note>. || 92 ||

The notes *Ni* and *Dha* <note>7th and 6th</note> are used frequently. When the fifth note <note>Pancama or 'Pa'</note> is the dominant, the six-note variation is avoided. The notes *Sa*, *Ni*, *Ma*, and *Pa* <note>1st, 7th, 4th, and 5th</note> avoid the five-note variation. *Sa* and *Ga* are played in conjunction. || 93 ||

The rhythmic pattern used is *Pancapani*. The *Murchana* <note>the specific scale or melodic progression</note> begins with *Ri* <note>Rishabha</note>, as in the *Shadji* mode. This mode is employed in the *Dhruva* <note>theatrical song</note> of the third act of a play. || 94 ||

In the fourteenth rhythmic unit, in the high register, the notes are *Ni-Ni-Pa-Dha-Ni* (five notes) and three *Ga* notes, totaling eight short beats. The syllables are *Pra-na-ma-mi Gau-ri* <note>"I bow to Gauri"</note>; the fourth and seventh beats are the remainder (14). In the fifteenth unit, in the high register, the notes are *Ni-Ni-Dha-Pa-Dha-Pa-Ma-Pa*, eight short beats. The syllables are *Ca-ra-na-yu-ga-ma-nu-pe-tya* <note>"Having approached the pair of feet"</note> (15). In the sixteenth unit, in the high register, the notes are *Dha-Pa-Sa-Sa* (four) and four *Ma* notes, totaling eight short beats. The syllable *Ma* corresponds to *Dha*, and the rest follow (16).

> I bow to the incomparable pair of feet of the Goddess Gauri,
> Which are kissed by the divine mark on her lotus-like face,
> Resembling a fully blossomed golden lotus.
> They are the pure abode of mirrors, which are her most beautiful and radiant nails,
> And they are the ones that struck the body of the God of Love.
-> This concludes the Gandharodicyava mode. || 11 || <-

<margin>The commentary states: "The dominant notes are..."</margin> (Kallinatha's Commentary) Regarding the dominant notes: excluding *Dhaivata* and *Rishabha*, the five are *Sa, Ga, Ma, Pa, Ni*. One should perform the union of *Sa* and *Ga* by bypassing *Ri*. "Bypassing *Ri*" means without the note *Rishabha*.

"And here, the movement between *Gandhara* and *Shadja* occurs without *Rishabha*."

- **Sangitaratnakara**: "The Ocean of Music," a definitive 13th-century Sanskrit treatise on music and dance.

- **Amsha**: The primary note that defines the character of a raga or jati.
- **Shadav/Auduv**: Hexatonic (6-note) and Pentatonic (5-note) scales.
- **Murchana**: A melodic lineage or the sequence of notes in a scale.
- **Dhruva**: A type of song used in ancient Indian Sanskrit drama to enhance the mood.</note>

<page-num>241</page-num>
<header>Chapter 7] First Chapter on Musical Notes</header>
<sig>31</sig>

...as stated in the words of the Sage <note>The "Sage" refers to Bharata Muni, the legendary author of the Natyashastra</note>. Here, regarding the notes Sa and Ga <note>Sa: Shadja; Ga: Gandhara</note>, there should be "proximity" and "blending" with the other notes—Ma, Pa, Dha, and Ni—as appropriate. In this context, "proximity" refers to the immediate succession of two notes that have different short time-durations. "Blending" is intended to mean the immediate succession of two or three notes within a single short time-duration. These two actions should be performed to the best of one's ability. The term "six-toned and five-toned" <term>Shadava and Auduva: Shadava refers to a hexatonic (6-note) scale, and Auduva refers to a pentatonic (5-note) scale</term> is treated here as a compound in the singular. Regarding the "abundance of Ni and Dha": here, although Ni <note>Nishada</note> is usually designated to be used sparingly, its "abundance" is prescribed for the sake of melodic excellence. As for Dha <note>Dhaivata</note>, which causes the five-toned state, even though it is absent in the five-toned stage, its "abundance" is prescribed in the complete (seven-tone) and six-tone stages, overriding its usual scarcity.

->'In this context, Dhaivata and the seventh note (Nishada) become strong.'<-

It should be understood that this is ordained by the words of the Sage. When Pa <note>Panchama</note> is the primary note <term>Amsha: the dominant or "soul" note of a melody</term>, it "hates" (forbids) the six-toned state. The meaning is that when Panchama itself becomes the primary note, it does not tolerate the six-toned state produced by the omission of Ri <note>Rishabha</note>, because in the *Madhyama Grama* <note>The "Middle Scale," one of the two ancient fundamental tuning systems</note>, there is a consonance between Panchama and Rishabha. Sa, Ni, Ma, and Pa "hate" the five-toned state; meaning that when Sa, Ni, Ma, or Pa are the primary notes, they do not tolerate the five-toned state produced by the omission of Ri and Dha. Only one primary note, Ga <note>Gandhara</note>, tolerates the five-toned state. Here, the refusal to accept the five-toned state when Ni and Dha are not in consonance with the primary note Sa should be understood from the Sage's words:

> 'In the melodies Gandhari and Rakshagandhari, the notes Shadja, Madhyama, and Panchama,
> as well as the seventh (Nishada), should be known; in these, the five-toned state shall not occur.'

Therefore, in the *Jatis* that can be six-toned, the prohibition of the six-toned state in certain cases is fixed because the omission of a note consonant with the primary note is not accepted. As stated by the Sage:

->'Because of the omission of a consonant note, these seven are excluded from the six-toned states.'<-

It should be observed that in the *Jatis* that can be five-toned, the prohibition of the five-toned state—even when it might otherwise occur—is sometimes due to the omission of the primary note and sometimes simply due to the scriptural injunction itself. Regarding the phrase "Sa and Ga are joined"...

The melodic association <term>Sangati: the pairing or proximity of notes</term> between Shadja <note>C</note> and Gandhara <note>E</note> has been described as occurring through proximity, blending, or both, excluding the note Rishabha <note>D</note>. (Sudhakara) <note>This is a commentary by Simhabhupala</note> He defines the Rakta-Gandhari mode: "The tonic notes shall be..." In Rakta-Gandhari, five notes are used as the tonic <term>Amsha: the predominant or 'soul' note of the mode</term>, excluding Dhaivata <note>A</note> and Rishabha <note>D</note>. There is a melodic pairing of Shadja and Gandhara without overstepping into Rishabha. By omitting Rishabha, it becomes a six-note scale <term>Shadava</term>. By omitting both Rishabha and Dhaivata, it becomes a five-note scale <term>Auduvita</term>. The notes Nishada <note>B</note> and Dhaivata <note>A</note> are used frequently. When Panchama <note>G</note> is the tonic, the six-note variation is not used. When Shadja, Nishada, Madhyama, or Panchama are the tonics, the five-note variation is not used. There is a pairing of Shadja and Gandhara. The melodic progression <term>Murchhana</term> begins with Rishabha. The allocation of time-units <term>Kala</term> and other elements is similar to the Shadji mode. || 91–94 ||
