<header>The Ocean of Music [Jatis]</header>

### Now, the Kaishiki Jati

In the *Kaishiki* mode, all notes except for *Rishabha* (Re) can serve as the *Amsha* <note>The dominant or melodic center of the mode</note>. When *Nishada* (Ni) and *Dhaivata* (Dha) are the dominant notes, then *Panchama* (Pa) alone must be the *Nyasa* <note>The final note or cadence</note>. In other cases, the two-shruti notes <note>Ni and Ga</note> are considered the final notes. || 95 ||

Others, however, maintain that when *Ni* and *Dha* are the dominant notes, the final notes can be *Ni*, *Ga*, or *Pa*. By omitting *Ri* or both *Ri* and *Pa*, the hexatonic <term>Shadava (six-note scale)</term> and pentatonic <term>Auduvita (five-note scale)</term> forms are achieved. || 96 ||

In this mode, *Ri* is used sparingly, while *Ni* and *Pa* are used frequently. The dominant notes should transition into one another. In the hexatonic and pentatonic forms, *Panchama* and *Dhaivata* are prescribed as the final notes respectively. || 97 ||

The rhythmic structure follows the *Shadji* style, using the *Panchapani* <note>a specific time-measure</note> and similar patterns. The *Murchana* <note>the melodic scale/progression</note> begins on *Gandhara* (Ga). This mode is to be employed in the *Dhruva* songs of the *Panchama-prekshana* <note>a specific type of dramatic performance</note>. || 98 ||

The notes are joined with the syllable *Sa*. The lyrics are "Vadanaravi..."; the remaining notes are the fourth, seventh, and eighth. (8).
In the ninth section, there are eight short beats of *Pa* in the middle register. The first syllable is "de-", followed by the others. (9).
In the tenth section, the notes are *Ri-Ga-Sa-Sa-Ri-Ga-Ga-Ga* over eight short beats. The lyrics are "Pritikaram"; here, the *Ga* notes are the remainder. (10).
In the eleventh section, in the high register, there are two *Ga*s, one *Pa*, one *Dha-Ma*, one *Dha*, one *Ni-Dha*, and two *Pa*s, totaling eight short beats. All are remainders. (11).
In the twelfth section, in the high register, there are three *Ma-Pa-Ma*, one *Pa-Ri-Ga*, and four *Ga*s; thus eight short beats. All are remainders. (12).

> I bow to Him, who is adorned with the young moon as a crest-jewel and smeared with sacred ash;
> Who brings joy to the lotus-like face of the Goddess Gauri.
> — Thus ends the *Raktagandhari* mode. || 12 ||

<margin>Commentary by Kallinatha</margin>
Regarding the *Kaishiki*: "Except for Rishabha" means the six notes *Sa, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni* are the dominant notes (*Amshas*). When *Ni* and *Dha* are the dominants, then *Pa* alone is the final note (*Nyasa*). As it is said:

-> "When Dhaivata or Nishada are the dominant notes, the final note is desired to be Panchama." <-

# 13. Kaishiki

->In this Kaishiki mode, the notes Gandhara, Panchama, and Nishada are the <term>Nyasa</term> (final notes). Excluding Rishabha,<-
->the remaining six or seven notes serve as <term>Apanyasa</term> (intermediate pauses). Its notation is as follows:<-

1.  Pa Dha-Ni Pa Dha-Ni Ga Ga Ga Ga
    Ke  li      ha       ta
    <note>This is a rhythmic notation example: Pa (5th), Dha (6th), Ni (7th), Ga (3rd).</note>

This is regulated by the words of the Sage <note>referring to Bharata Muni, the author of the Natyashastra</note>. This means that at other times, when the <term>Amsha</term> (dominant notes) are other than Nishada and Dhaivata, the notes Sa, Ri, Ga, Ma, and Pa can all be pauses. The two-microtone notes Nishada and Gandhara are accepted as final notes. However, others like Matanga <note>author of the Brihaddeshi</note> and his followers understand all three—Nishada, Gandhara, and Panchama—to be final notes when Nishada and Dhaivata are the dominant notes; for Matanga stated, "When Dhaivata and Nishada are dominant, Panchama is also a final note." This view also results in the rule that Panchama is a final note only when Nishada and Dhaivata are dominant. The phrase "by the omission of Ri and Dha" is treated as a single concept. The note Rishabha is weak even in the "complete" (seven-note) state. Regarding the "abundance of Ni and Pa," it should be understood that although these two are dominant and thus naturally frequent, the Sage's statement "the final note and the fifth are strong" ordains their extreme abundance compared to other dominant notes. When Panchama and Dhaivata become dominant, the hexatonic <note>six-note</note> and pentatonic <note>five-note</note> forms are indicated respectively. The order is: Panchama leads to hexatonic, Dhaivata to pentatonic. In the <term>Madhyama Grama</term> (the Middle Scale), because Rishabha is the consonant of Panchama, it cannot be omitted when Dhaivata is the dominant. The phrase "like Shadji" is easy to understand. || 95—98 ||

(Sudhakara commentary) He defines Kaishiki: In Kaishiki, the six notes other than Rishabha are the dominant notes. When Nishada and Dhaivata are dominant, then Panchama alone is the final note; otherwise, it is Nishada and Gandhara. Some others, however, consider Nishada, Gandhara, and Panchama as final notes when Nishada and Dhaivata are dominant. It is hexatonic through the omission of Rishabha, and pentatonic through the omission of Rishabha and Dhaivata. Rishabha is weak. There is an abundance of Nishada and Panchama. There is mutual consistency among the dominant notes. When Panchama is the dominant, the hexatonic form is not used. When Dhaivata is the dominant, the pentatonic form is not used. The rhythm is the <term>Shatpitaputrakatala</term>, etc., similar to the Shadji Jati. The <term>Murchana</term> (scale) begins with Gandhara. Its application is in the <term>Dhruva</term> songs during the "Panchama-prekshana" <note>a specific stage of a dramatic performance</note>. || 95-98 ||

<summary>This page defines the technical characteristics of the Kaishiki Jati, including its dominant, final, and omitted notes, while reconciling the views of Bharata Muni and Matanga. It specifies how the mode changes from seven notes to six or five depending on which note is dominant.</summary>

# Chapter 7: The First Chapter on Notes

->(Commentary) Six or seven notes may serve as the secondary tonal center <term>Apanyasa: a note that concludes a section of a melody</term>, excluding the second note <term>Rishabha: the second note of the scale, abbreviated as 'Ri'</term>.<-

> "The second note may also occasionally serve as the secondary tonal center here."

This is according to the words of the Sage <note>referring to Bharata Muni, the author of the Natyashastra</note>. In the pure note arrangement of the Middle Scale <term>Madhyama Grama</term>, the first rhythmic section <term>Kala</term> consists of: one middle-register P <note>Panchama, the fifth note</note>, one combined D-N <note>Dhaivata and Nishada, the sixth and seventh notes</note>, one P, one D-N, and four Gs <note>Gandhara, the third note</note>; thus making eight short beats <term>Laghu</term>. In the third section: two D-Ns, one high-register S <note>Shadja, the first note</note>, one middle-register S, and four Rs; thus eight short beats. The syllables are *Vi-bhra-ma-vi-la-sa*, with the second and seventh notes being the remaining ones (3). In the fourth section: three middle-register Ss, one R-G, and three Ms; thus eight short beats. The syllables are *Ti-la-ka-yu-ta*, with the remaining notes being Ms (4). In the fifth section: M-D-N-D-M-D-M-P in the lower register <term>Mandra</term>; eight short beats. The syllables are *Mur-dhor-dhva-ba-la*, with the second, fourth, and seventh being the remaining notes (5). The syllables are *So-ma-ni-bha*—*So-ma-ni* are G-S-D, *bha* is the first R, and the rest are others (6). In the seventh section: two middle-register G-Rs, two Ss, two Ds, and two Ms; thus eight short beats. The syllables are *Mu-kha-ka-ma-la*, with the sixth note onwards being the remaining ones (7). In the tenth section: two high-register Gs, two Ns, one N-D, and three Ps...

<header>The Jewel Mine of Music [Jatis]</header>

### Now, the Madhyamodicyava

> The Madhyamodicyava is considered to always have the fifth note <note>Panchama</note> as its primary note <note>Amsha</note> and is always complete <note>Purna, meaning it uses all seven notes of the scale</note>. The remaining characteristics should be understood as being the same as those of the Gandharodicyava. || 99 ||
> The melodic scale <term>Murchana: the structured ascent and descent of notes</term> should be the one beginning with the middle note <note>Madhyamadi</note>, and the rhythmic cycle <term>Tala</term> is considered to be the Chanchatputa. Its application is in the Dhruva song of the fourth dramatic performance. || 100 ||

In this way, there are eight short beats <note>Laghus</note>. The five syllables "Hridi sukhadam" <note>Pleasant to the heart</note> follow in order, with the rest following (10). On the eleventh beat, take the middle and highest notes <note>Ma and Pa</note> in the high register; these are to be maintained; there are two middle notes <note>Ma</note>, thus making eight short beats. The syllables are "Pranamami loche," with the fourth and eighth beats being the remainder (11). On the twelfth beat, take the tonic, middle, and third notes <note>Sa, Ma, and Ga</note> in the high register; one for the end, two of the seventh note <note>Ni</note>, and two of the middle and third notes <note>Ma and Ga</note>. Thus there are eight short beats. The syllables are "Navishesham"—the syllables "Navishe" fall on the tonic, middle, and third notes; "bhi" is the seventh note; the others are the remainder (12).

> I bow to that unique eye, which possesses the playful grace of the body of the God of Love struck by sport, adorned with a forehead mark, resembling the moon on the crest of the head, and whose lotus-face surpasses the golden lotus, bringing joy to the heart.
-> Thus ends the Kaishiki variation. || 13 || <-

**Kallinatha's Commentary:** Regarding "Panchamansha": this means it has the fifth note <note>Panchama</note> as its sole primary note <note>Amsha</note>. "Always complete" means that it never becomes a six-note <note>Shadava</note> or five-note <note>Auduva</note> scale. The "remaining characteristics"—such as the weakness of the second and sixth notes <note>Ri and Dha</note>, their mutual association, and the sixteen-beat structure—should be understood as coming from the Gandharodicyava; this means they should be applied here as well. The scale beginning with the middle note <note>Madhyamadi Murchana</note> is known as Sauviri. The rest is easy to understand. || 99, 100 ||

**Simhabhupala's Commentary:** He defines the Madhyamodicyava: "Panchamansha" etc. In Madhyamodicyava, the fifth note <note>Panchama</note> is the primary note. "Completeness" refers to having all seven notes. The six-note and five-note states do not exist here. The remaining characteristics are to be known as being like the Gandharodicyava. The scale is Madhyamadi. The rhythm is Chanchatputa. The application is in the fourth performance of the Dhruva song. || 99, 100 ||

<note>The notation above uses abbreviated Sanskrit notes: Sa (Shadja), Ri (Rishabha), Ga (Gandhara), Ma (Madhyama), Pa (Panchama), Dha (Dhaivata), and Ni (Nishada). The lyrics are a hymn to Shiva.</note>

-> **Commentary by Kallinatha** <-

<note>Kallinatha was a 15th-century commentator who explained the technical complexities of the Sangita Ratnakara.</note>

In the arrangement of pure notes <term>Shuddha-svara-melana; the standard tuning of the notes</term> belonging to the <term>Madhyama Grama; the scale starting on the fourth note, Madhyama</term>, the first <term>Kala; a unit of musical time</term> contains: one Pa, one Dha-Ni, two Ni notes, and four notes consisting of Ma-Pa-Ni-Pa. This totals eight <term>Laghus; short time-units</term>. The syllables of the phrase "Having a form that is half the body" <note>original: "Dehardharupa"</note> are distributed as follows: *De* is on Pa, the remaining are on Dha-Ni; *Ha* is on Ni, the remainder on Ni; *Rdha-ru* are on Ma-Pa, the remainder on Ni; and *Pa* is on Pa (1).

In the second unit, there are three Rishabhas, two Ga-Sas, one Ri-Ga, and two Ga notes, totaling eight short units. These correspond to the syllables "With the purity of intellect and beauty" <note>original: "Matikantimamala"</note>; the fourth and seventh units are remainders (3).

In the third unit, there are eight short units of Nishada notes. These correspond to the syllables "Pure like the moon and the jasmine flower" <note>original: "Mamalendukunda"</note>; the fourth and seventh units are remainders (3).

In the fourth unit, there are two Ni notes, one Dha-Pa, one Ma, one Ni-Dha, one Ni-Dha, and two Pa notes, totaling eight short units. The syllables are "Resembling a white water-lily" <note>original: "Kumudanibham"</note>. ### Now, the Karmaravi Mode

In the *Karmaravi* mode, the <term>Amshas</term> <note>the dominant or "soul" notes of a melody</note> are Nishada, Rishabha, Panchama, and Dhaivata. These are declared to be numerous because of their role in the <term>Antaramarga</term> <note>the "inner path" or transitional movement between notes</note>. || 101 ||

The note Gandhara is extremely frequent and is used in conjunction with all the dominant notes. The rhythmic cycle used is *Chanchatputa* <note>a specific eight-beat time cycle</note> consisting of sixteen <term>Kalas</term> <note>units of time</note>, and the scale starts from the note Shadja. || 102 ||

This mode is to be employed in the *Dhruva* <note>the fixed introductory song of a drama</note> during the *Panchama Prekshana* <note>the fifth stage of a theatrical performance</note>.

> I bow to Shiva, whose form is half-bodied <note>referring to Ardhanarishvara, the half-male, half-female form</note>, of supreme and pure luster, resembling the pure moon, the jasmine, and the white lily;
> Who possesses the divine brilliance of a golden lotus, who is worshiped by the foremost of the divine hosts, and who is invincible;
> Who is praised by the gods, who is as swift as the mind, whose voice is like the thunder of clouds and the ocean, and who is full of laughter;
> Who is auspicious, peaceful, the destroyer of the demon armies, and whose feet are bowed to by the three worlds.

->Thus ends the Madhyamodichyava mode. || 14 ||<-

---

<margin>(Commentary) Regarding *Karmaravi*:</margin> The <term>Anamshas</term> <note>non-dominant notes</note> here are Shadja, Gandhara, and Madhyama. Being non-dominant, they are also weak. Because of the "inner path" (*Antaramarga*), which involves the frequent transition and association of all notes with the dominant ones, many notes appear frequently. Now, if frequency is common to both, one might ask: what is the difference between a dominant note (*Amsha*) and a non-dominant note (*Anamsha*)? It is explained thus: the note that is used frequently as a stable, resting point is the *Amsha*. However, the note that is used frequently as a transitory or passing note is the *Anamsha*, relying on the *Antaramarga*. This is the distinction to be made. Even in the definition where "pervasiveness in frequent usage is the characteristic of the dominant note," it must be understood that the frequency refers to the stability mentioned in the definition "that which provides color/beauty." By this, it is said that the *Antaramarga* must be performed in this *Jati* <note>musical mode</note>. And so says Bharata <note>the legendary sage and author of the Natyashastra</note>:
> "The non-dominant notes are strong only through constant usage in performance."
The note Gandhara is extremely frequent because of its association with all the dominant notes, even in alternating sequences. This association with all dominant notes is also...

<insert>
(Sudhakara commentary) He defines *Kamarkhi*: In *Kamarkhi*, the notes *Nishada* (7th), *Rishabha* (2nd), *Panchama* (5th), and *Dhaivata* (6th) are the primary notes (*Amshas*). Other than these primary notes, *Shadja* (1st), *Gandhara* (3rd), and *Madhyama* (4th) are frequent according to the rules of internal melodic transition (*Antaramarga*). There is an extreme abundance of the note *Gandhara*. It has a relationship with all the primary notes. The rhythm is *Chachchatputa*. It consists of sixteen beats (*Kalas*). The scale starts from *Shadja* (*Shadjadi Murchana*). It is used in the *Dhruva* song-type during the *Panchama-prekshana* <note>a specific stage or viewing in a theatrical performance</note>. || 101—102 ||

### Now, the Gandharapanchami Mode

In the Gandharapanchami mode, the <term>Amsha</term> <note>the dominant or melodic center</note> is the note Panchama (G). Furthermore, the <term>Sangati</term> <note>the melodic combination or pairing of notes</note> should be performed here by many notes, just as in the Gandhari and Panchami modes. || 103 ||

The <term>Chanchatputa</term> <note>a specific rhythmic cycle of 8 or 16 beats</note> rhythm is used with sixteen <term>Kalas</term> <note>rhythmic units</note>, and the <term>Murchana</term> <note>the scale or melodic progression</note> begins with the note Gandhara (E). || 104 ||

Its application is in the singing of the <term>Dhruva</term> <note>a specific type of stage song</note> associated with the fourth theatrical performance.

There are four Nishadas (B), making eight <term>Laghu</term> <note>short rhythmic beats</note> units. The syllables are "Yaj-ño-pa-vī-te"; the second, fourth, and seventh are the remaining ones (15). In the sixteenth unit, there are two high-register Nishadas (B), two Dhaivatas (A), and four Panchamas (G), making eight short beats. The first Nishada (B) takes the syllable "Kam," and the others follow (16).

-> I bow to the divine sacred thread, which is attached to the beautiful left side of Lord Shiva, <-
-> possessing the brilliance of a flood of intense light like the moon, <-
-> whose chest is a vast ocean-abode for the king of serpents, exceedingly lovely with the white lord of snakes, <-
-> and which provides amusement through the playful movements of the fingers of the sprout-like hands of the six-faced god (Kartikeya). <-
-> Thus ends the Karmaravi mode. || 15 || <-

<term>(Kallinatha's Commentary)</term> Regarding "The Amsha in Gandharapanchami": The melodic combinations (<term>Sangati</term>) should be performed by many notes here as well, just as in Gandhari and Panchami. In Gandhari, it was said that combinations occur "with the <term>Nyasa</term> <note>the final note or cadence</note> and the <term>Amsha</term> and others"; similarly here, combinations of the other notes—Shadja, Rishabha, Madhyama, Dhaivata, and Nishada—occur with the cadence and dominant notes (Gandhara and Panchama). In the Panchami mode, it was said "of Rishabha and Madhyama"; therefore, here too, the mutual combination of Rishabha (D) and Madhyama (F) is intended by the reference to "many notes." The rest is easy to understand. || 103—104 ||

<term>(Simhabhupala's Commentary)</term> He defines Gandharapanchami: "The Amsha..." In Gandharapanchami, the dominant note is Panchama (G). The combination of notes is like that of Gandhari and Panchami. The rhythm is <term>Chanchatputa</term>. There are sixteen units (<term>Kalas</term>). The scale progression begins with Gandhara. Its application is in the <term>Dhruva</term> song of the fourth theatrical scene. || 103—104 ||

->### Now, the Andhra Jati<-

In the Andhra jati, the <term>Amshas</term> <note>the dominant or "soul" notes of the melody</note> are Ni, Ri, Ga, and Pa <note>Nishada, Rishabha, Gandhara, and Panchama</note>. Between Ri and Ga, as well as between Ni and Dha, || 105 ||
there should be a <term>Sangati</term> <note>a melodic pairing or close association</note>. One should proceed from the Amsha in sequence until reaching the <term>Nyasa</term> <note>the final note or cadence</note>.
It is <term>Shadava</term> <note>a six-note scale</note> through the omission of Sa <note>Shadja</note>. The <term>Murchana</term> <note>the foundational scale or mode</note> begins on Ma <note>Madhyama</note>. || 106 ||
The application of <term>Kala</term> <note>units of time</note> and <term>Tala</term> <note>rhythm</note> is said to be the same as in the previous jati <note>referring to Gandharapanchami</note>.

<term>(Kallinatha's Commentary)</term> Regarding the phrase "In the Andhra, the Amshas...": Ni, Ri, Ga, and Pa serve alternately as the Amshas and the <term>Grahas</term> <note>the starting notes</note>. "Between Ri and Ga, as well as between Ni and Dha": here, the word "as well as" <note>original: "tatha"</note> is a particle used for conjunction, meaning "and also between Ni and Dha." "Sangati" refers to mutual proximity or a relationship of blending. The word "should be performed" is implied. Since the instruction for "mutual association" might be interpreted too loosely, the author provides a rule: "One should proceed from the Amsha in sequence until reaching the Nyasa." "In sequence from the Amsha" means that among Ni, Ri, Ga, and Pa, whichever note is currently accepted as the dominant, one should follow its sequence—pronouncing that dominant note first and then the non-dominant or alternate dominant notes—until reaching the Nyasa, which is the note that ends the song. The rule is to play in this manner until the completion of the song. Thus, Bharata <note>the legendary sage and author of the Natyashastra</note> says:

> "In this jati, there is a mutual interplay between Gandhara and Rishabha,
> and between the seventh <note>Ni</note> and the sixth <note>Dha</note>,
> following the sequence toward the final cadence."

And in another text:

> "Performing the pervasiveness of its own Amsha in sequence, one should proceed to the limit of the Nyasa."

The remaining details are the same as before. || 105—106 ||

<term>(Simhabhupala's Commentary)</term> He defines the Andhra jati: In the Andhra, the Amshas are Nishada, Rishabha, Gandhara, and Panchama. There is a melodic pairing between Rishabha and Gandhara, and between Nishada and Dhaivata. There is an ascent from the Amsha to the Nyasa. It is a six-note scale due to the omission of Shadja. The scale begins on Madhyama. The application of rhythmic units and time-measures is like that of the Gandharapanchami jati. || 105—106 ||

### Now, the Nandayanti Mode

In the *Nandayanti* mode, the fifth note <term>Panchama: the fifth note of the scale, equivalent to 'So'</term> is the primary note <term>Amsha: the predominant or melodic center</term>, while the third note <term>Gandhara: the third note, equivalent to 'Mi'</term> is traditionally considered the starting note <term>Graha: the note upon which a melody begins</term>. || 107 ||

However, some experts in the science of song state that the fifth note is the starting note in this mode. There is an abundance of the low-register second note <term>Mandra-Rishabha: the note 'Re' played in the lower octave</term>. It is a six-note scale <term>Shadava: a hexatonic scale</term> formed by the omission of the first note <term>Shadja: the tonic or 'Do'</term>. || 108 ||

The melodic scale <term>Murchhana: a specific sequence of notes</term> is *Hrishyaka*. The rhythmic cycle <term>Tala</term> is the same as previously mentioned, but with the time-units <term>Kala</term> doubled in duration. Its application <term>Viniyoga</term> is for the *Dhruva* songs performed during the first act of a play. || 109 ||

In this *Nandayanti*, the third note is the final note <term>Nyasa: the note that concludes a phrase or composition</term>. The fourth and fifth notes <term>Madhyama and Panchama</term> are the intermediate stopping notes <term>Apanyasa</term>.
The following is its musical notation <term>Prastara: a formal representation of the melodic structure</term>:

#### 18. Nandayanti

| Line | Musical Notation | Lyrics/Syllables |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1. | Ga Ga Ga Ga Pa Pa Dha-Pa Ma | Sau |
| 2. | Dha Dha Dha Dha Dha Ni Sa-Ni-Ni Dha | [Rest] |
| 3. | Pa Pa Pa Pa Pa Pa Pa Pa | Myam |
| 4. | Dha Ni Ma Pa Ga Ga Ga Ga | Ve-da-ga-ve-da |
| 5. | Ma Ri Ga Ga Ga Ga Ga Ga | Ka-ra-ka-ma-la-yo-ni |
| 6. | Ma Ma Pa Pa Dha Ni-Dha Pa Pa | Ta-mo-ra-jo-vi-va |

(Ka.) <note>This refers to the commentary by Kallinatha.</note> Regarding the *Nandayanti* mode: It is stated that the note *Gandhara* (Ga) is the starting note <term>Graha: the initial note of a composition</term>. Here, one must understand that while the Sage <note>Bharata Muni</note> generally stated that "the dominant note should also be the starting note" for all modes, the specific rule stating "Gandhara should be the starting note in this particular mode" overrides the general rule, following the logic of "the exception proves the rule" <note>original: "Takra-Kaundinya-nyaya," a grammatical principle where a specific rule supersedes a general one</note>. However, some teachers who are experts in musical theory and performance have mentioned an alternative view where *Panchama* (Pa) is the starting note.

Regarding the "abundance of the low-register *Rishabha* (Ri)": Since *Nandayanti* belongs to the *Madhyama-grama* <term>the scale based on the middle note</term>, even if there is a lack of low-register movement down to the note *Rishabha*, an abundance of low *Rishabha* should be maintained. This is because it relies on the *Hrishyaka* scale-progression <term>Murchana</term> which begins on the low *Panchama*. Because the dominant low *Panchama* is in consonance with *Rishabha*, the low *Rishabha* is emphasized more than in other positions. As Bharata says:

> "In this mode, there is an abundance of *Rishabha*, and that is remembered as being in the low register."

The rhythm <term>Tala</term> is "as before": just as in the *Andhri* mode, the rhythm is *Chatchatputa* <note>a specific rhythmic cycle of four beats</note>. The "units of time are doubled": this means they are double compared to the previous mode. Where the previous mode had sixteen units, this one has thirty-two units. By this, it is meant that there are four repetitions of the *Chatchatputa* rhythm in the "Southern Style" <term>Dakshina-marga: a sophisticated, slow tempo style</term>. The rest is easy to understand. In the first unit of the pure note arrangement of the *Madhyama-grama*—

# Chapter 7] The First Chapter on Notes

->Where not explicitly stated, the rhythm should be of three types, starting with one unit of time.<-
->The paths are, in order: the Pictorial, the Professional, and the Southern; the song-styles are likewise:<-
->The Magadhi, the Sambhavita, and the Prithula, as they have been described in sequence. || 110 ||<-

---

->The Gandharodichyava, the Karmaravi, and the Gandharapanchami;<-
->The Madhyamodichyava, the Andhra, and the Shadjakaishiki.<-
->Three of these—the Panchami, Arshabhi, and Madhyama—consist of eight units of time.<-
->One, known as the Nandayanti, is celebrated as having thirty-two units of time. || 107-109 ||<-

---

(Simhabhupala) <note>Simhabhupala is a 14th-century commentator on this text.</note> He defines the Nandayanti: In the Nandayanti, the fifth note <term>Panchama: the note 'Pa', equivalent to the dominant</term> is the primary note <term>Ansha: the predominant note that governs the melody</term>. The third note <term>Gandhara: the note 'Ga'</term> is the starting note <term>Graha: the note upon which a composition begins</term>. Now, it was previously stated that the primary note itself should be the starting note. Do not think so; that was merely a general rule which is here set aside. In an alternative school of thought, however, the fifth note is said to be the starting note. There is an abundance of the second note <term>Rishabha: the note 'Ri'</term> in the lower register. Because the first note <term>Shadja: the tonic 'Sa'</term> is omitted, it is a six-note scale <term>Shadava: a hexatonic scale</term>. The melodic scale <term>Murchana: a structured ascent and descent</term> is Hrishyaka. The rhythmic pattern is Chanchatputa. It consists of thirty-two units of time <term>Kala: a unit of rhythmic measurement</term>. Its application is for the first viewing of the Dhruva song. || 107-109 ||

(Kallinatha) <note>Kallinatha is a 15th-century commentator known for his technical depth.</note> Previously, in the definition of the Shadjya mode alone, it was stated that "the rhythm is of three types, the Panchapani," etc., and that in these rhythmic variations, the three "paths" <term>Marga: the style of rhythmic spacing</term> such as the Pictorial <note>Chitra</note>, and the three "song-styles" <term>Vritti: styles of lyrical/rhythmic integration</term> such as the Magadhi, should be applied in sequence. Likewise, in the definitions of modes like Dhaivati, it was shown through extended application that "the rhythm, path, and song-styles are like those of the Shadjya," and "the song-style and rhythm are like the Shadjya." However, in the definitions of others like the Arshabhi, it was only stated that "the rhythm is considered to be Chanchatputa; there are eight units of time," or "sixteen units are celebrated." In those cases, there is a total silence regarding the specific time-divisions (one-unit, etc.), the paths, and the song-styles. In response to the question of how they should be performed there, he says: "Where not explicitly stated." Here, in the definitions of the Jatis <term>Jati: the melodic prototypes preceding the Raga system</term>, if the specific time-divisions, paths, and song-styles are not mentioned, the rhythm mentioned in the rhythmic definitions—either Chanchatputa or Panchapani—should be of three types: one-unit, and so on.

->**The number of rhythmic units (Kalas) we have mentioned belongs to the Southern Path (Dakshina Marga). || 111 ||**<-
->**In the Professional style (Varttika), that number should be known as double; in the Elegant style (Chitra), it is fourfold.**<-
->**In all melodic modes (Jatis), one should recognize the emotional essence (Rasa) as residing in the dominant note (Amsha). || 112 ||**<-

This serves as a qualifying attribute for what is to be performed. The phrase "in three ways" and so on has already been explained in the section on the *Shadji* <note>The first of the seven primary Jatis</note> mode; it should be understood from that context. || 110, 110- ||

**Sudhakara Commentary (by Simhabhupala):** Where no specific distinction is mentioned, he states the general rule: "In the absence of specific instruction..." Where no specific rhythmic cycle (Tala) is mentioned, the *Chanchatputa* <note>A specific rhythmic pattern of four units</note> should be understood in its one-unit, two-unit, and four-unit forms. The paths (Margas) for these, in the order of one-unit etc., are the Elegant (Chitra), the Professional (Varttika), and the Southern (Dakshina). The song-forms (Gitis) are respectively *Magadhi*, *Sambhavita*, and *Prithula*. || 110, 110- ||

**Kalanidhi Commentary (by Kallinatha):** If one asks, "Among the various types of rhythmic cycles, paths, and song-forms, to which specific category does the number of rhythmic units (Kalas) mentioned in the definitions of *Shadji* and other modes belong?"—he replies: "The number of rhythmic units we have mentioned..." By "we," he means himself and others following the school of Bharata <note>The legendary sage and author of the Natyashastra</note>. The number of units mentioned—such as twelve in the *Panchapani* rhythm, or eight in some versions of *Chanchatputa*, sixteen in others, and thirty-two in one specific case—within the definitions of *Shadji* and the rest, should be understood as belonging to the **Southern Path** (Dakshina Marga). By identifying this specific path, the specific rhythm (the four-unit Tala) and the song-form (*Prithula*) are also implied. Having stated that the mentioned rhythmic count belongs to the Southern Path (based on the systematic grouping of the three elements of rhythm, path, and song-form), he now shows how a singer, by their own choice, may apply other paths: "In the Professional style..." and so on. That same number of units mentioned for the Southern path should be known as doubled in the **Professional Path** (Varttika). For example, the twelve units mentioned for *Shadji* in the Southern style become twenty-four in the Professional style. The intention is that one should move from a unit consisting of eight short syllables to a unit consisting of four short syllables. The word "that same" is repeated for emphasis. That—

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of Jatis (melodic frameworks) and their relationship to Ragas and rhythmic structures (Tala) from the previous section.</meta>

# Chapter 7] First Chapter on Notes
<page-num>273</page-num>

->Those who know the science see the components of derived melodies <term>Janya Ragas; melodies born from a parent scale</term> within the parent classes <term>Janaka Jatis; the primary melodic frameworks</term>.<-
->These were properly described previously <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "prayukta" (employed/used)</note> in the praise of Lord Shiva using the words spoken by Brahma. || 113 ||<-
->These Jatis purify even those guilty of the most heinous sins, such as the killing of a priest.<-
->Just as the Rig, Yajur, and Sama Vedas can never be altered, || 114 ||<-
->so too are the Jatis, which originated from the Sama Veda, considered equal to the Vedas themselves.<-

The number of <term>Kalas; units of time-measurement</term> mentioned for the "Southern" style <note>Dakshina Marga</note> should be understood as four times that amount in the "Pictorial" style <note>Chitra Marga</note>. This means that for the *Shadji* Jati, there are forty-eight *Kalas*. The intention is that these should be divided into units consisting of two short syllables <note>Laghu</note>. By this same logic, it is stated that in the "Varttika" style, the song is performed with a two-unit beat, while in the "Pictorial" style, it is a one-unit beat with the *Magadhi* style of singing. This should be inferred for the other Jatis as well. Thinking it too tedious to state the emotional flavors <term>Rasas; aesthetic sentiments</term> for each individual Jati in their definitions, the author shows the application of *Rasa* for all of them briefly by saying: "In all Jatis..." One should understand the specific *Rasa* associated with whichever note is the dominant <term>Amsha; the primary or 'soul' note of a scale</term> at that time in that Jati, according to the rule previously stated: "Sa and Ri are for the Heroic flavor," and so on. Having understood this, one should sing with words that manifest those specific sentiments. || 111, 112 ||

**(Sudhakara Commentary)** He explains the specific time-units according to the different musical paths: "That which was stated by us..." The count of *Kalas* stated as "eight long syllables <note>Guru</note> per unit" refers to the Southern path. In the Varttika path, a *Kala* consists of sixteen long syllables. In the Pictorial path, a *Kala* consists of thirty-two long syllables. The emotional flavors of the notes were stated previously: "Sa and Ri are for the Heroic, the Wondrous, and the Furious," etc. Whichever note is the dominant in a Jati, its corresponding flavor should be understood as the flavor of that Jati. || 111, 112 ||

**(Kallinatha Commentary)** Previously, in some Jatis like *Shadji*, the components of derived melodies were shown only as a mere indication—for example, "the *Varati* melody is seen here"—while in others they were not shown. Now, in order to show the components of the melodies everywhere in a summary, he says: "They are seen..." The derived—

# Sangita Ratnakara [Chapter 7: On Jatis]

**Raga-components** <note>original: "Rāgāṃśā"</note>, such as the ten kinds of Grama-ragas and others, are indeed melodies born from the *Jatis* <note>The primary melodic frameworks of ancient Indian music</note> either directly or through a lineage. These are parts or components of them; as will be stated later: "A Raga-component is a portion of another Raga." This means they are fragments of a Raga. In the parent *Jatis*—those that produced them either directly or through a tradition—these components are "seen" or identified by experts who understand the distinctions between Ragas.

Now, the author demonstrates the extraordinary spiritual merit <note>original: "adṛṣṭa-phala," referring to unseen or transcendental rewards</note> of singing the *Jatis* according to the rules: **"By the words spoken by Brahma..."** In former times, for the praise of Lord Shiva <note>original: "Śaṅkara"</note>, these were composed using words uttered by the four-faced Brahma, such as "Him, who has the moon on his forehead" <note>original: "taṃ bhava-lalāṭa"</note> and so on. If these *Jatis*, such as *Shadji* and the rest, are performed properly—without omission or excess—they purify even a person who has killed a Brahmin <note>original: "brahma-ghnam," the most serious sin in ancient Indian law</note>, releasing them from that great sin. By this, it is said that the correct singing of *Jatis* serves as an atonement for the greatest of crimes.

Having considered that *Jatis* possess such power when performed with the stated rules—making them equal to sacred mantras like the Rig Veda—the author forbids their irregular performance: **"As the Rig..."** Just as the *Rig*, *Yajur*, and *Sama* Vedas are not altered—meaning they are not performed with any reversal of tone or syllable pronunciation—likewise, the *Jatis*, which are born from the *Sama Veda* and are therefore like the Vedic collections <note>original: "Veda-saṃhitā"</note> themselves, must not be altered. This means they should not be performed with any deviation in tone, word, or rhythm <note>term: Tala (rhythmic cycle)</note>. By this, it is implied that a contrary or incorrect performance results in spiritual demerit. || 113-114 ||

<margin>(Commentary by Simhabhupala)</margin> Regarding the phrase "are seen": in those derived *Jatis* where specific Raga-components are not explicitly mentioned, one should understand them through their parent *Jatis*. The author praises the mentioned *Jatis* with the phrase "By the words spoken by Brahma." The words used in the praise of Shiva were spoken by Brahma and set in the rhythmic expansion <note>term: Prastara</note>. When these *Jatis* are performed properly, without deviating from their characteristics, they sanctify even a slayer of a Brahmin, let alone those who have committed lesser sins. Regarding the danger of incorrect performance, he says "As the Rig." Since *Jatis* are equal to the Vedas, they must be performed perfectly to avoid fault. || 113-114 ||

---

->Thus ends the seventh section, on Jatis, in the first book concerning Notes.<-

## Now, the Eighth Section: On Songs

**I shall now describe the *Kapalas* <note>literally "skulls" or "shards," here referring to specific ancient song structures</note> which arise from the pure parent modes (*Jatis*). The melodic forms (*Ragas*) of these parent modes are contained within these *Kapalas*. (1)**

**Where the note *Shadja* <note>the tonic or 'Sa'</note> is the starting note (*Graha*), the predominant note (*Amsha*), and the secondary pause (*Apanyasa*); where *Gandhara* <note>'Ga'</note> is the final note (*Nyasa*); where *Gandhara* and *Madhyama* <note>'Ma'</note> are very frequent; where *Rishabha* <note>'Ri'</note>, *Panchama* <note>'Pa'</note>, *Nishada* <note>'Ni'</note>, and *Dhaivata* <note>'Dha'</note> are infrequent; where *Rishabha* is skipped; and which consists of twelve rhythmic units (*Kalas*)— (2)**

**—that is declared by the experts of song <gloss>1. experts of the sacred path</gloss> to be the *Shadji-Kapala*. Where *Rishabha* is the predominant note and secondary pause, *Madhyama* is the final note, and *Gandhara*, *Nishada*, *Panchama*, and *Dhaivata* are infrequent— (3)**

(Kallinatha's Commentary) Now, following the established order, the author defines the *Kapalas*, first stating his intent by showing their origin: **"Arising from the pure modes..."** Now, after defining the nature of the *Jatis* <term>melodic parent modes</term>, he describes the *Kapalas* produced from the pure *Jatis*. These are produced from the seven pure modes, such as *Shadji*. By this, it is implied that *Kapalas* do not arise from the "mixed" (*Samsargaja*) modes. If one asks why they do not arise from mixed modes since they are all equally *Jatis*, it is answered: the mixed modes themselves are born from the pure ones. The *Kapalas* also come from those same pure ones. Since both share a single cause and arise without mediation, the mixed modes cannot be the cause of the *Kapalas*. 

He then demonstrates the practical purpose of knowing the *Kapalas*: **"The Ragas..."** Regarding the "parent modes," here the pure *Jatis* are intended as the parents. Their "offspring Ragas"—such as the *Sri-Raga*, which will be described later with the phrase "In the note *Shadja* is the *Sri-Raga* born from *Shadji*"—are "contained" within those *Kapalas*. This means they are perceived as having a similar form to the *Kapalas* of *Shadji* and the others. The purpose here is the thorough understanding of the nature of the *Raga*. Just as "shards" (*Kapalas*), being parts of a jar, produce the recognition of the jar itself, these songs, being parts of a *Raga*, produce the recognition of the *Raga*. Thus, they are called *Kapalas* <note>metaphorically "shards" of the full melodic form</note>; this is not an arbitrary name...

---
<note>1. original: "margavedibhih" — those who know the 'Marga' or ancient sacred musical path.</note>

# The Ocean of Music [On Song-Forms]

That [Shadjika Kapala] is very brief, consisting of eight beats <term>kala: a unit of time in ancient music</term>. Next is the Kapala derived from the Arshabhi scale. In this, the note *Ma* (the fourth) <gloss>some manuscripts suggest *Ga* (the third)</gloss> serves as the predominant note <term>ansha: the melodic center</term>, the starting note <term>graha</term>, and the concluding note <term>nyasa</term>. The secondary conclusion <term>apanyasa</term> is also *Ma*, while the note *Dha* (the sixth) is used frequently. || 4 ||

Where the notes *Sa, Ri,* and *Ga* are used sparingly, and by omitting *Ri* and *Pa*, it becomes a five-note <term>auduva: pentatonic</term> scale—that is the Gandhari Kapala, constructed of eight beats. || 5 ||

Where *Ma* is the predominant note, and *Ni, Ri, Ga,* and *Pa* are used minimally, and which consists of nine beats—that is the Madhyama Kapala, according to the opinion of the Fearless One <note>original: "Nishshanka," a title for the author Sharngadeva</note>. || 6 ||

The Kapala born from the Panchami scale is known to have *Ri* as its predominant and starting note, with *Ni, Dha, Sa,* and *Ga* appearing in a series, consisting of eight beats. || 7 ||

With *Ri* and *Ga* being very sparse, *Pa* as the secondary conclusion, and *Ma* and *Dha* appearing in abundance—similar to the Shadjika Kapala—is the Dhaivati Kapala, consisting of eight beats. || 8 ||

With *Sa* as the starting, predominant, and concluding note, with *Ri* and *Ga* used sparingly, and with *Ni, Dha,* and *Ma* used in great abundance, the eight-beat song is the Naishadi Kapala. || 9 ||

By singing these seven Kapalas using the verses spoken by Brahma <note>The Creator deity</note> and the proper musical notes in praise of the Beloved of Parvati <note>The god Shiva</note>, one becomes a recipient of auspiciousness. || 10 ||

---

-> Commentary <-

It should be understood thus. Alternatively, there is a tradition <term>aitihya</term> regarding the name: long ago, during the time Lord Shambhu <note>Shiva</note> wandered for alms, he sang the Shadjika and other scales. Because of the expression of unsurpassed aesthetic delight <term>rasa</term>, the crescent moon on his crest—which is the essence of nectar—began to flow. The Brahma-skulls <note>Kapalas</note> that served as his ornaments were sprinkled with that nectar and became animated. They then began to sing, imitating his music. Because they were sung by the skulls, they are named "Kapalas." The characteristics of the Shadjika-Kapala and others are clear. Their difference in form from the parent scales <term>jatis</term> should be seen in the specific differences of their concluding notes and other technical factors. The author also mentions the spiritual merit <term>adrushta-phala: "unseen fruit" or karmic reward</term> for the singer who follows these rules in the verse beginning "Thus the seven Kapalas..." || 1-10 ||

->**Where the starting note, the dominant note, and the secondary ending are the fifth; where the second note is frequent;**<-
->**where the final note is the same, and the fourth and third notes are sparse—that is considered the Kambala.** <note>Verse 11 describes the 'Kambala', a specific melodic structure or 'vessel' melody.</note> **॥ 11 ॥**

(Su.) <note>Sudhakara commentary by Simhabhupala</note> Following the order of topics established in the summary of contents—"the Kapalas and the Kambala; and various types of songs"—and without skipping the intended sequence due to their utility, he first begins to describe the Kapalas, saying: "Pure Jatis..." <note>Jatis are the ancient melodic frameworks, the ancestors of modern Ragas.</note> Whichever Kapala is produced from a specific Jati, the Ragas of that Jati are to be understood as being present in that Kapala. ॥ 1 ॥

He defines the **Shadji-kapala**: In which the note <term>Shadja</term> <note>The first note, 'Sa'</note> is the <term>Graha</term> <note>starting note</note>, the <term>Amsha</term> <note>dominant/soul note</note>, and the <term>Apanyasa</term> <note>secondary ending</note>; where the <term>Gandhara</term> <note>third note, 'Ga'</note> is the <term>Nyasa</term> <note>final note</note>; where there is a great abundance of the fourth and third notes; where the second, fifth, seventh, and sixth notes are sparse; where the second note is skipped or only slightly touched; consisting of twelve <term>Kalas</term> <note>rhythmic units</note>—that is called the Shadji-kapala by Bharata and others. ॥ 2, 2- ॥

He defines the **Arshabhi-kapala**: Where the second note is the dominant and secondary ending; the fourth note is the final; but the third, seventh, fifth, and sixth notes are sparse; the first note is sparse; consisting of eight rhythmic units—that is the Arshabhi-kapala. ॥ -3, 3- ॥

He defines the **Gandhari-kapala**: Where the fourth note is the dominant, the starting note, the final, and the secondary ending; there is an abundance of the sixth note; the first, second, third, and fifth notes are sparse; it is <term>Auduva</term> <note>pentatonic/five-toned</note> due to the omission of the second and fifth notes; consisting of eight rhythmic units—that is the Gandhari-kapala. ॥ -4, 5 ॥

He defines the **Madhyama-kapala**: Where the fourth note is the dominant; the seventh, second, third, and fifth notes are very sparse; consisting of nine rhythmic units—that is the Madhyama-kapala. ॥ 6 ॥

He defines the **Panchami-kapala**: Where the second note is the dominant; the first note is the starting note; the seventh, sixth, first, third, and fourth notes are sparse; consisting of eight rhythmic units—that is the Panchami-kapala. ॥ 7 ॥

He defines the **Dhaivati-kapala**: Where the second and third notes are very sparse; the fifth note is the final; there is an abundance of the fourth and sixth notes; consisting of eight rhythmic units; the rest is like the Shadji-kapala—that is the Dhaivati-kapala. ॥ 8 ॥

He defines the **Naishadi-kapala**: Where the first note is the starting note, the dominant, and the final; the second and third notes are sparse; the seventh, sixth, and fourth notes are very abundant; consisting of eight rhythmic units—that is the Naishadi-kapala. ॥ 9 ॥

He states the fruit (benefit) of singing the Kapalas: Thus, by singing these seven Kapalas with the words spoken by Brahma and the notes mentioned in the arrangement of Jatis, one attains auspiciousness. ॥ 10 ॥ **This concludes the definition of the Kapalas.**

(Ka.) <note>Kalanidhi commentary by Kallinatha</note> Now, having defined the Kambala according to the intended order, and having shown its origin and its many varieties, he states the benefit of singing it, starting with: "Where the starting note, the dominant, and the secondary ending..."

# The Ocean of Music [Song Section]

Through the variations of scarcity and abundance of notes arising from the *Panchami* melodic parent-scale <note>original: "jati"</note>, many varieties of this song were described by the ancients. ## 12 ##

In ancient times, the Enemy of Tripura <note>Shiva</note> was pleased by the singing of the serpent Kambala and granted him a boon; therefore, Shiva is still pleased by those songs today. ## 13 ##

We shall now state, in order, the sequence of words for the *Kapala* songs as spoken by Brahma:

-> Jhandum Jhandum (1) Bearer of the skull-topped staff (2) Having formidable fangs (3) With a tongue like lightning (4) Hau Hau Hau Hau Hau Hau Hau Hau (5) Many-faced with a roar like a thick thundercloud (6) Hau Hau Hau Hau Hau Hau Hau Hau (7) Om Om Ham Rau Haum Haum Haum Haum (8) Adorned with a garland of human skulls (9) Hum Hum Kaha Kaha Hum Hum (10) Having a fierce, distorted face (11) I bow to the Divine Bhairava <note>The terrifying form of Shiva</note> (12). These are the lyrics for the Shadji-Kapala. ## 1 ## <-

This has been explained through the literal text. Because it was sung by the serpent king Kambala, who serves as an earring for the wielder of the axe <note>Shiva</note>, this song is known as *Kambala*. ## 11–13 ##

<insert>(Sudhakara Commentary)</insert> He defines the *Kambala*: "Wherein..." Where the fifth note <note>Panchama</note> is the starting, predominant, and secondary-ending note; where the second note <note>Rishabha</note> is abundant; the first note <note>Shadja</note> is the final note; and the fourth, sixth, and third notes <note>Madhyama, Dhaivata, Gandhara</note> are scarce—that song, arising from the *Panchami* scale, is called *Kambala*. Many variations of this *Kambala* based on the scarcity or abundance of notes were described by ancient teachers like Bharata; these should be looked for in their respective books. They are not mentioned here for fear of making this book too long. He explains the reason for the name *Kambala* and the fruit of singing it: "Pleased..." Because the serpent Kambala sang it, it is called the *Kambala* song. The Lord is pleased by it. Through His pleasure, the attainment of all human goals <note>Purushartha: Dharma, Artha, Kama, and Moksha</note> is the result. ## 11–13 ## This concludes the definition of *Kambala*.

<insert>(Kallinatha Commentary)</insert> Regarding the rule for *Kapala* singing—"Singing with words spoken by Brahma"—he presents the nature of those words spoken by Brahma, including the rhythmic syllable-sounds <note>stobha</note> like "Hum," according to the number of beats specified for each *Kapala*...

->The act of singing, adorned with melodic movements and ornaments, and endowed with words and tempo, || 14 ||<-

These are the sixty-three ornaments like *Prasanna* <note>clarity</note> and others. For example:

-> Ma  Ga  Ma  Dha <-
-> De  -   -   vam <-

-> Dha-Ni  Dha-Ni  Sa-Ni  Dha <-
-> De      va      ru      dram <-

-> Ri-Ga  Ri-Ga  Ma-Ga  Ri-Sa <-
-> De-vam  Ru-dram  vam  de <-

And so on. To define these in order, the author says: **Of these...** He defines the *Magadhi* style starting with: **Having sung...** For the sake of illustration, one should imagine <term>Kalas</term> <note>units of musical time</note> consisting of four <term>Matras</term> <note>beats</note> each. In the first of these, there is a word in <term>Vilambita Laya</term> <note>slow tempo</note>, where the resting time is four times the duration of the intended unit. Here, having sung the word *Devam* <note>meaning "the God"</note>—which consists of two syllables—one sings two beats for each syllable. In the second <term>Kala</term>, which is in <term>Madhya Laya</term> <note>medium tempo</note> with a resting time twice as fast, it is joined with another word, *Rudram* <note>a name for Shiva</note>. It should be understood that one sings the word *Devam* (sung in the first unit) followed by the word *Rudram*. The meaning is that one should sing each syllable of the two words *Devam Rudram* measured by either two notes or a single note. In the third <term>Kala</term>, in <term>Druta Laya</term> <note>fast tempo</note>—which is the quickest rest of action compared to the slow and medium tempos—it is joined with a third word, *Vande* <note>meaning "I bow/praise"</note>, alongside those two words *Devam* and *Rudram* sung in the second unit. Because of the word "and" in the text, the instruction to "sing" carries over here as well. In this <term>Kala</term>, the meaning is that one should sing by joining *Devam* to the first beat, *Rudram* to the second, *Vam* to the third, and *De* to the fourth. In the manner described, because the word *Devam* is repeated three times across the three units, the wise—the experts in <term>Sangita Shastra</term> <note>the science of music</note>—call this song-style <term>Magadhi</term>. This same logic should be applied to other examples beyond the one written here. The sage Matanga states the etymology is <term>Magadhi</term> because it originated in the Magadha region. —14-17—

<summary>This page defines the Magadhi Giti, a melodic style characterized by repeating a phrase across three different tempos (slow, medium, and fast) while adding new words in each stage. It provides a specific notation example using a hymn to Lord Rudra to illustrate how syllables are mapped to musical beats.</summary>

<header>The Ocean of Music [Song-</header>

### When the final halves of the first two words are repeated twice¹ || 18 ||
### ...then they call it Ardhamagadhi.

For example:

| Ma | Ri | Ga | Sa |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| De | | va | |

(Sudhakara Commentary) The <term>utility of Jati songs</term> <note>sacred melodic structures</note> has been stated. In response to the question "What are the characteristics of these songs?", he says: <term>adorned with Varnas and others</term>. <term>Varnas</term> refer to the <term>steady melodic movements (Sthayi) and others</term>; "and others" refers to <term>ornaments (Alankaras)</term> such as <term>clarity (Prasanna) and others</term>, by which the song is beautified. It is endowed with words (Pada) and tempo (Laya). "Words" are well-known; <term>Tempo</term> is defined as <term>fast (Druta), medium (Madhya), and slow (Vilambita)</term>, which is the interval of time within a beat (Tala) to be discussed in the chapter on Tala. The <term>act of singing</term> endowed with these two is called <term>Giti</term> <note>Song-style</note>. It is of four types: <term>Magadhi, Ardhamagadhi, Sambhavita, and Prithula</term>. Among these, he describes the characteristics of <term>Magadhi</term> by saying "Having sung...". One should sing the word in the first unit of time (Kala) in a <term>slow tempo</term>. In the second unit, one should sing that same word joined with another word in a <term>medium tempo</term>. In the third unit, one should sing those two words along with a third word in a <term>fast tempo</term>. Thus, the wise experts in song have declared the Magadhi to consist of three units with words repeated three times. For example, having sung "Devam" <note>God</note> in a slow tempo, in the second unit that same word "Devam" is sung with the word "Rudram" <note>The Roarer/Shiva</note> as "Devam Rudram" in a medium tempo. In the third unit, the two words "Devam Rudram" are joined with another word "Vande" <note>I praise</note> and sung as "Devam Rudram Vande" in a fast tempo. || 14—17 ||

(Kalanidhi Commentary) He defines <term>Ardhamagadhi</term> <note>Half-Magadhi</note> by saying "Of the first two...". Of the three words mentioned, "Devam" and "Rudram," the final half of the first two—the final half of the word "Devam" being "vam," and the final half of the word "Rudram" being "dram"—when those two halves, "vam" and "dram," are uttered twice, then they call it <term>Ardhamagadhi</term>. The meaning is this: having uttered the word "Devam" in the first unit as prescribed for Magadhi, one should then utter "Rudram" in the second.

## Others describe it as having words repeated twice¹ <note>original: "dvirāvṛttapadāṃ pare"</note>.

For example:

| Ma | Ma | Ma | Ma |
|---|---|---|---|
| De | | va | |

| Dha | Sa | Dha | Ni |
|---|---|---|---|
| de | vam | ru | dram |

| Pa | Ni-Dha | Ma | Ma |
|---|---|---|---|
| ru | dram | vam | de |

Then, in the third section, one should chant "dram vande" <note>The phrase "Vande Devam Rudram" translates to "I bow to the Lord Rudra (Shiva)"</note>. In this manner, the final parts of the previous two phrases are repeated. Regarding the phrase **"Others describe it as having words repeated twice"**: other teachers state that in the "Half-Magadhi" <term>Ardhamagadhi: a melodic style where words are repeated in a specific structural pattern</term> style, the word "Devam" spoken in the first rhythmic unit <term>Kala: a unit of musical time</term> is repeated in the second unit as "Devam Rudram," and the word "Rudram" is repeated in the third unit as "Rudram vande." Thus, they call this style Ardhamagadhi because of the double repetition of words. 

However, the sage Matanga <note>An ancient musicologist, author of the Brhaddeshi</note> describes this as a variation of the Magadhi style itself. As he says: "Others read this as the 'Twice-Returned' Magadhi." Furthermore, since Ardhamagadhi is essentially included within the category of Magadhi, the use of Ardhamagadhi in place of Magadhi is considered acceptable in certain contexts. 

Here, Matanga addresses the potential criticism that repeating words might cause the fault of tautology <note>Punarukti: the literary flaw of needless repetition</note> or render the meaning of the parts nonsensical. He resolves this by stating: "In the Sama Veda <note>The Veda of Melodies and Chants</note>, where song is primary, the literal meanings are not strictly disregarded during repetitions." This is even illustrated by the Veda itself—for instance, in the hymn "Udu tyam jatavedasam" <note>A famous Vedic hymn to the Sun God</note>, the chant proceeds through a series of repetitions up to the word "Veda"...

¹ <margin>In another version: "Within the twice-repeated words."</margin>

# Page 284
### [The Gitis]

### The *Sambhavita* style is considered to have condensed words and many long syllables. || 19 ||

For example:

-> Dha  Ma  Ma  Ri  Ga <-
-> With de-vo-tion <-
-> Ri  Ga  Sa  Sa <-
-> to God <-
-> Ni  Dha  Sa  Ni <-
-> Ru-dra <-
-> Dha  Ni  Ma  Ma <-
-> I bow <-

<note>The example uses Solfège-like syllables (Sargam) mapped to a short prayer: "Bhaktya devam rudram vande" (With devotion, I bow to God Rudra).</note>

It is sung as "Jatavedasam" <note>A Vedic title for Agni, the Fire God</note>; here too, there is no breaking of the sense even when the words are fragmented. Therefore, in music derived from the *Sama Veda* <note>The Veda of Melodies</note>, it should be understood that the repetition or partial utterance of words due to the requirements of the singing is not a fault. || 18, 18 ||

<gloss>(Sudhakara commentary)</gloss> He defines <term>Ardhamagadhi</term> <note>A specific ancient melodic style</note> by saying "of the previous two." When the final half of the previous two words is repeated—for example, after singing the word "Devam" (God) in the first rhythmic unit (*Kala*), one sings the word "Rudram" in the second unit along with the syllable "vam" (the final half of the first word). Thus, it is sung as "vam-Rudram." In the third unit, the word "Vande" (I bow) is sung along with the syllable "dram" (the final half of the second word). Here too, the slow, medium, and fast tempos (*Laya*) should be understood across the three units. || 18, 18 ||

<gloss>(Kalanidhi commentary)</gloss> He defines <term>Sambhavita</term> <note>The "Possibility" style</note> as having "condensed words." This means its words are shortened. In this context, the "extension" of words refers to applying a syllable to every single musical note within a rhythmic unit; "condensing" is the reduction of that. From the word "Sankshepa" (condensation), the form "Sankshepita" (condensed) is derived. By this, it is meant that syllables should be applied to only a few of the notes present in a rhythmic unit. "Many long syllables" means there is an abundance of heavy or long-voweled characters.

<summary>This page defines the Sambhavita and Ardhamagadhi musical styles, explaining how lyrics are condensed or partially repeated across rhythmic units without losing their sacred meaning. It emphasizes that such linguistic fragmentation is acceptable in music derived from the Sama Veda.</summary>
<keywords>Sambhavita, Ardhamagadhi, Sangitaratnakara, rhythmic units (Kala), musical tempo (Laya), Sama Veda, Rudra, Sanskrit musicology</keywords>

# The *Prithula* style is considered by the wise to consist of words with many short syllables.

**For example:**

| Ma | Ga | Ri | Ga |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Su | ra | na | ta |

<note>The table shows a musical notation where each syllable of the word "Suranata" (bowed to by gods) corresponds to a specific musical note.</note>

This is the nature of that style. By this definition, the use of occasional long syllables is also accepted. In the case of <term>Kalas</term> <note>units of musical time</note> consisting of four measures, one should sing the five notes of the first unit by joining the first note with the heavy syllable *Bhak*, the third note with the heavy syllable *tya*, and the remaining two notes as extensions of those. For the four notes of the second unit, the first and third should be joined with the heavy syllables of the word *Devam*. Similarly, for the four notes of the third unit, the first and third are joined with the syllables of *Rudram*, and for the fourth unit, the first and third are joined with the syllables of *Vande*. The remaining notes are sung as extensions of those respective syllables. The shortened phrase is: "I worship Lord Rudra with devotion" <note>original: "Bhaktya Devam Rudram Vande"</note>. One should infer other examples from this written one. Regarding the specific notes of the units, they should be applied according to whatever <term>Jati</term> <note>melodic classification or parent scale</note> is being used. A song performed in this manner is known as **Sambhavita**. The etymology given by the sage Matanga is: "That in which the words are considered to be condensed is called *Sambhavita*."

> (Su.) <note>Commentary by Simhabhupala</note> He defines **Sambhavita**: It is the *Sambhavita* song-style which has condensed words and many heavy syllables. Having sung the four words of the first unit as "I worship Lord Rudra with devotion," the two middle words are sung twice in the second unit as "Lord, Lord, Rudra, Rudra," and the third unit is sung like the first.

> (Ka.) <note>Commentary by Kallinatha</note> He defines **Prithula**: It consists of words with many short syllables. The meaning is clear. Regarding the phrase "Suranata-Hara" <note>The Destroyer (Shiva) bowed to by gods</note>, the syllables are applied to every note across the four units of time. Matanga’s etymology states: "It is called *Prithula* (the 'Broad' or 'Extensive') because of the abundance of words."

<summary>This page defines two classical song-styles (Gitis): Sambhavita, characterized by heavy syllables and condensed phrasing, and Prithula, characterized by many short syllables mapped to individual notes.</summary>
<keywords>Sambhavita, Prithula, Giti, Matanga, musical meter, syllables, Rudra, devotional song, Indian classical music theory</keywords>

Alternatively, in the "Even" rhythm <note>original: "Yugma," referring to the Chachchatputa rhythm</note>, when the first two long syllables <note>original: "Guru"</note> are used, || 20 ||
Each one is performed in the "Pictorial" tempo <note>original: "Chitra-marga"</note> and so on, consisting of a four-beat metrical unit <gloss>1</gloss>,
And is joined with eight beats in the "Southern" tempo <note>original: "Dakshina-marga"</note> using hand-gestures like the "Fixed-Beat" <note>original: "Dhruvaka"</note> and others; || 21 ||
When it is performed in this way, the song-style is called Magadhi.

**(Sudhakara Commentary)** He defines the Prithula style: **"Having many short-syllable words."** That in which there are many short <note>light</note> syllables is Prithula; other characteristics are the same as the Sambhavita style. For example, after singing the four words "Bow down to the pair of Shiva's feet worshipped by the gods" in the first rhythmic section <note>original: "Kala"</note>, one repeats the middle two words twice in the second section, and the third section is like the first. This is the Prithula style according to a different school of thought. || 19- ||

**(Kallinatha Commentary)** Having thus defined the song-styles based on the words, he now defines them based on the rhythm <note>original: "Tala"</note>: **"Alternatively," etc.** In the "Even" rhythm consisting of two long, one short, and one extra-long syllable, within the first two long syllables (each being two beats), one employs each long syllable in the "Pictorial" tempo—which is naturally suited for two beats—and joins it with the "Fixed-Beat" gesture. Then, it is made into a four-beat unit <note>original: "Chagana"</note>. A *Chagana* is a specific four-beat metrical unit; as he will say later: "The *Cha* group consists of four beats." This unit is then doubled <note>original: "Dvikali-krita"</note> to become four beats by adopting the "Business" tempo <note>original: "Varttika-marga"</note>, using the hand-gestures named *Dhruvaka*, *Sarpini*, *Pataka*, and *Patita*...

# Chapter 8] First Chapter on Notes
Page 287

->**When the third element, the short syllable (Laghu) of the pair, is joined with half of a Cha-gana,**<-
->**And is combined with the first two and the last two time-measures (Matras),**<-
->**And then the prolonged syllable (Pluta) is performed joined with one and a half ganas.**<-

This means each should be performed individually. Then, in the "Southern Path" <note>Dakshina-marga: a sophisticated, slow-tempo style of ancient music</note>, using the <term>Dhruvaka and others</term> <note>Dhruvaka, etc.: specific hand gestures or rhythmic units used to keep time</note>—namely Dhruvaka, Sarpini, Krishna, Padmini, Visarjita, Vikshipta, Pataka, and Patita—which are the eight time-measures (Matras) whose characteristics will be described later. Here, due to the metaphorical treatment of the attribute and the attributed as identical, these gestures like Dhruvaka should be understood as the time-measures themselves. The connection is: when each single long syllable (Guru) is performed by making it four-fold (four units of time) using those measures. When performed in this way, it is called the **Magadhi Giti** <note>Magadhi Giti: one of the four ancient styles of song, characterized by repeating phrases at different speeds</note>. The intention is that the pair of long syllables is repeated three times. || 20 — 21 ||

<note>(Su.) refers to the Sudhakara commentary by Simhabhupala.</note>
(Su.) He states the definition of these songs in another way: "Or rather..." In the "pair" (Yugma) known as the <term>Chaccatputa</term> <note>Chaccatputa: a fundamental rhythmic cycle (tala) consisting of 8 units: Long-Long-Short-Prolonged</note> in its basic form, one performs each of the first two long syllables (Gurus) suitable for the "Pictorial Path" (Chitra-marga) joined with a Cha-gana. He will describe these groups (Ganas) like Cha, Pa, and Ca in the Chapter on Compositions. When those same first two long syllables of the Chaccatputa are performed in the Southern Path, joined with the eight time-measures—Dhruvaka, Sarpini, Krishna, Padmini, Visarjita, Vikshipta, Pataka, and Patita—as will be described in the Chapter on Rhythm (Tala), then it is the Magadhi Giti. || 20 — 21 ||

<note>(Ka.) refers to the Kalanidhi commentary by Kallinatha.</note>
(Ka.) Now he defines the <term>Ardhamagadhi</term> <note>Ardhamagadhi: literally "Half-Magadhi," a style where the repetition and rhythmic structure are halved or modified</note>: "The third..." Of the pair (Yugma), meaning the Chaccatputa in its basic form, the third component of the rhythm following the two long syllables is the short syllable (Laghu). This is "joined with half of a Cha-gana." A Cha-gana is a specific rhythmic group of six units (Matras); half of that is three units. Joined with that, it means it is made into the equivalent of four short syllables. It is then combined with the "first two measures," meaning Dhruvaka and Sarpini, and the "last two," meaning Pataka and Patita. After that, the prolonged syllable (Pluta), which is the final component of the Chaccatputa, is "joined with one and a half ganas." Here, the general word "gana" refers to the nearby Cha-gana, and "half" refers to half of that. Thus, it means a group (six units) plus half (three units), totaling nine units of time.

<page-num>288</page-num>
<header>Ocean of Music [Song-</header>

With the eight elements starting with *Dhruvaka* <note>A specific rhythmic pattern or beat</note>, and by repeating the final two elements twice, the *Ardhamagadhi* <note>Half-Magadhi style</note> is formed. These two styles should be applied similarly in other rhythmic cycles (*Talas*) as well. || 24 ||

The *Sambhavita* style is considered to have many long syllables (*Gurus*) and is used in the *Varttika* <note>The "professional" or medium-tempo</note> path with two-beat units. The *Prithula* style is considered to have many short syllables (*Laghus*) and is used in the *Dakshina* <note>The "southern" or elaborate/slow</note> path with four-beat units. || 25 ||

->Thus ends the 8th section on Songs in the first chapter on Notes. || 8 ||<-

->Thus ends the first chapter on Notes in the *Sangita Ratnakara* <note>Ocean of Music</note>, composed by Sri Sarngadeva, the son of Sri Sodhala, the Lord of Srikarana and a delight to the flawless arts and sciences.<-

It is joined with that half-group. A *Cha-gana* <note>A metrical unit</note> consists of six measures (*Matras*), and a half consists of three measures; thus, when joined with nine measures, the triple-length *Pluta* <note>An extra-long vowel or beat</note> becomes twelve measures in total. By making the *Pluta* take this form and using it sequentially with the eight elements starting with *Dhruvaka*, the remaining four measures are used by repeating the final two twice—specifically the final two measures known as *Pataka* and *Patita* <note>Hand gestures used to mark time</note>. This means that if the remaining four measures are used sequentially as *Pataka-Patita-Pataka-Patita*, it is called *Ardhamagadhi*. These two, *Magadhi* and *Ardhamagadhi*, should be applied in other rhythmic cycles like *Panchapani* just as they are in *Chanchatputa*. The definitions of *Sambhavita* and *Prithula* are clear in their meaning. It should be understood that these song-styles (*Gitis*) are to be used in the *Shadji* <note>The first primary scale or Jati</note> and others according to their respective rules and the chosen musical path (*Chitra*, etc.). || 22–25 ||

->On this earth, the wise Kallinatha, who knows both the theory and practice of musical definitions, has himself explained this chapter on Notes.<-

->Thus ends the first chapter on Notes in the *Kalanidhi* <note>The Treasure-House of Art</note>, the commentary on the *Sangita Ratnakara* composed by the clever Kallinatha, son of Lakshmanacharya, the modern Master Bharata and the Royal Treasurer (*Todarmal*). || 1 ||<-

(Su. <note>Abbreviation for Sudhakara, the name of the commentary by Simhabhupala</note>) He defines the *Ardhamagadhi* <note>literally "Half-Magadhi," a specific style of melodic-rhythmic composition</note> style: "The third..." etc. The third short syllable (*laghu*) of the *Cancatputa* <note>a standard eight-beat rhythmic cycle</note> rhythm, joined with half of a *chagana* <note>a specific rhythmic foot</note>, is employed using the first two beats—the *dhruvaka* <note>unaccented snap</note> and *asarpini* <note>hand movement to the left</note>—and the final two beats—the *pataka* <note>hand lifted</note> and *patita* <note>hand falling</note>. Then, when the fourth beat of the *Cancatputa*, known as the *pluta* <note>a triple-duration beat</note>, is combined with one and a half rhythmic units and half a *chagana*, and is performed with the eight beats starting from *dhruvaka* along with the *pataka* and *patita* beats doubled, it is called *Ardhamagadhi*. Just as these two—*Magadhi* and *Ardhamagadhi*—are applied to the *Cancatputa* rhythm, they should also be understood to apply to other rhythms such as *Cacaputa*.

He defines the *Sambhavita* style: "*Sambhavita*..." etc. In the two-unit *Cancatputa* rhythm, following the *Varttika* path <note>the "professional" or medium tempo style of performance</note>, a song style consisting of many long syllables (*guru*) according to the previously mentioned rule is known as *Sambhavita*. In the four-unit *Dakshina* <note>the "southern" or slow, elaborate tempo</note> path, a song style consisting of many short syllables (*laghu*) according to the previously mentioned method is to be known as *Prithula* ॥ 22—25 ॥ Thus ends the definition of song styles (*Gitis*). ॥ 8 ॥

## Appendix

The Kaisiki Nishada, the Displaced Shadja, and the Modified Rishabha—these are to be employed in the Shadja-grama <note>the primary scale starting on the tonic</note>, though they are considered "enemies" or incompatible with the Madhyama-grama <note>the scale starting on the fourth</note>. || 1 ||

In the Madhyama-grama alone, one should employ the Displaced Madhyama, the Sadharana Gandhara, and the two types of Modified Panchama. || 2 ||

The Modified Dhaivata is also used there; the remaining notes are "dual-movers" <note>original: "ubhayacharinah"; notes that can function in both scales</note>. These notes of the Madhyama-grama depend upon their mutual existence and relationship. || 3 ||

The Sadharana Gandhara and the Kaisiki Panchama, as well as the Displaced Madhyama, are considered companion notes that move together. || 4 ||

The Kakali Nishada and the Displaced Shadja are mutually dependent; in the same way, the Antara Gandhara and the Displaced Madhyama are paired notes. || 5 ||

The Panchama of three microtones <note>Trishruti Panchama</note> is considered the "enemy" or incompatible with the Displaced Madhyama. The Modified Dhaivata is held to be dependent upon the Madhyama-grama system. || 6 ||

<note>The text describes the complex microtonal shifts (shruti) required to move between the two primary ancient Indian scales, the Shadja-grama and Madhyama-grama. Certain notes are "enemies" because their specific pitch heights cannot coexist within the same melodic structure without destroying the scale's integrity.</note>

<summary>This page details the specific modified notes (Vikrita Swaras) used in the two primary ancient Indian musical scales, explaining their microtonal values and their functional compatibility or "enmity" with one another.</summary>

# The Permutation of Musical Notes

<note>original: "Svaraprastāraḥ". This refers to the systematic arrangement or mathematical permutation of musical notes (Svaras).</note>

**The Archika Permutation (One-Note Patterns):**—(1) Sa (2) Ri (3) Ga (4) Ma (5) Pa (6) Dha (7) Ni
<note>The Archika style refers to the oldest layer of Vedic chanting, traditionally associated with the Rigveda, which primarily utilizes a limited melodic range.</note>

# The Ocean of Music
## Chapter on Notes (3) 12—

<page-num>330</page-num>

<note>This page consists of a table of "Kuta-tanas" or "crooked" melodic permutations. In Indian classical music theory, these tables systematically list every possible mathematical arrangement of notes. The abbreviations used here refer to the seven notes: Sa (Shadja), Ri (Rishabha), Ga (Gandhara), Ma (Madhyama), Pa (Panchama), Dha (Dhaivata), and Ni (Nishada). Note that 'Pa' is omitted in these specific hexatonic sequences.</note>

<term>Sangitaratnakara</term>: "The Ocean of Music," a definitive 13th-century Sanskrit treatise on Indian music and dance.
<term>Kuta-tana</term>: Non-sequential or "crooked" permutations of notes within a scale.
<term>Svara</term>: A musical note or pitch.
<term>Shadava</term>: A hexatonic scale, consisting of six notes.
<term>Shat-svara</term>: Six-note combinations.
<term>Svarakrama</term>: The specific order or succession of notes.
